Learned Special Public Prosecutor for the CBI opposed the petition, submitting that whether the agricultural income and spouse's earnings were genuine is a matter of defense evidence to be evaluated during trial.

title: Test #20: The Doctrine of Piercing the Corporate Veil
text: The doctrine of piercing (or lifting) the corporate veil represents one of the most fundamental exceptions to the bedrock principle of corporate jurisprudence: the separate legal personality of a company. Under classical company law, crystallized in the seminal English decision of Salomon v. A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22, an incorporated company is recognized as an independent juristic entity distinct from its shareholders, directors, and officers. Incorporation creates a metaphorical "veil" between the company and its human constituents. This separation confers limited liability, shielding investors from personal responsibility for the corporation’s debts and liabilities. However, because this legal fiction is granted by the legal order to facilitate legitimate enterprise and commercial risk-taking, the law cannot permit it to be perverted into an instrument of deception. Where the corporate form is deliberately abused to perpetrate fraud, evade legal obligations, or defeat statutory mandates, courts possess an equitable jurisdiction to "pierce the corporate veil," disregarding the entity's distinct personality to attribute liability directly to the individuals orchestrating the enterprise. Historically, judicial intervention in this sphere suffered from conceptual ambiguity, with courts invoking colorful metaphors such as "sham," "facade," "cloak," or "mere puppet" without establishing a unified test. In modern common law, the doctrine was rigorously rationalized by the UK Supreme Court in Prest v. Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013] UKSC 34. Delivering the leading judgment, Lord Sumption drew a crucial distinction between the "concealment principle" and the "evasion principle": The evasion principle is illustrated by foundational authorities such as Gilford Motor Co Ltd v. Horne [1933] Ch 935, where a former managing director bound by a non-compete covenant incorporated a company to conduct a rival business in breach of his restraint. The court enjoined both the director and the newly formed company, treating the entity as a mere channel for evading an extant personal covenant. Similarly, in Jones v. Lipman [1962] 1 WLR 832, a vendor who had contracted to sell real property transferred the land to a wholly owned company to defeat the purchaser’s decree for specific performance. The court ordered specific performance directly against the company, holding that it was a creature devised specifically to avoid equitable obligations. In United States jurisprudence, the doctrine is commonly framed around the "alter ego" theory or "instrumentality rule". American courts typically mandate a two-pronged threshold: first, that there exists such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist; and second, that adhering to the fiction of separate corporate existence would promote fraud, sanction an injustice, or lead to an inequitable result. Beyond common law fraud, legislative frameworks frequently mandate statutory lifting of the veil. Examples include wrongful and fraudulent trading provisions under insolvency codes, anti-tax evasion statutes, environmental remediation liability, and anti-money laundering regulations where beneficial ownership must be established. In modern commerce characterized by complex multinational group structures, holding-subsidiary networks, and special purpose vehicles (SPVs) the doctrine functions as an indispensable safety valve. However, courts exercise it with extreme circumspection. As reaffirmed in Adams v. Cape Industries plc [1990] Ch 433, courts will not pierce the veil merely because justice might seem to require it or because a group of companies operates as a single economic unit. Piercing the corporate veil remains a remedy of last resort, invoked only when conventional legal doctrines, such as the law of torts, agency, contract interpretation, or trusts, prove inadequate to defeat unconscionable abuse.

title: Test #21: A 2000 Year Revolt In India
text: More than 2,000 years ago the king of the Magadha dispatched one of his less favoured sons to quell a people’s revolt in an extremely important city. The revolt was dealt with not through repression but dialogue. This is regarded as India’s first recorded rebellion anywhere in the subcontinent. The prince would later become India’s most celebrated emperor, one who claimed to embrace ahimsa, and emphasised religious tolerance in his rock-edicts throughout his empire. Emperor Ashoka Maurya remains an enigmatic figure in ancient India. Buddhist texts like the hagiographical Ashokavadana have portrayed the revolt and its pacification in terms that show Ashok as the noble and wise prince who overcomes both the maliciousness of his father as well as the uprising through sagacity and dialogue. His name was lost to history until 1837, when James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script of his inscriptions, and it was only in 1915, with the Maski inscription, that the king of the edicts was explicitly named “Asoka”. The accounts lack historical basis and have been characterised by scholars as more legend than verifiable history. What followed was a nearly millennium long dominance of Buddhism in the sub-continent, the remnants of which are abundant in the forms of stupas, statues, monasteries, and other monuments; Buddhist tradition, as recorded in the Ashokavadana, credits Ashok with building 84,000 stupas. He founded the first recorded Indian empire which stretched from Cuttack to Taxila and from Kashmir to deep Karnataka. He is remembered the most for the war and massacre in Kalinga in which tens of thousands of people were killed, and after which, filled with remorse, Ashok embraced Buddhism and non-violence. But, the journey to becoming India’s most celebrated emperor began with a test in Taxila, now part of Pakistan. According to the Ashokavadana, the trouble began when local ministers turned into oppressors trampling upon commoners and elites alike. Bindusara dispatched Ashok who was then a prince and was despised by his brother and heir-to-the throne, Sushima. Till the taking over of the city by the Mauryas of Pataliputra, the city had maintained an independent status. It is believed to have been a ploy to get rid of Ashok because the local ministers in Taxila were known to be brutal and fierce. Furthermore, in the process of centralisation the Mauryas may well have been harsh in their treatment of outlying cities”. Thapar writes, “King Bindusara desired to besiege Taxila, which was in rebellion. The king ordered his despised son Asoka to undertake the siege, and yet would not supply him with chariots or the needful munitions of war. Ill-supplied as he was, the prince obediently started to carry out the king’s orders, whereupon the earth opened, and from her bosom supplied all his wants. When Asoka with his army approached Taxila, the citizens came forth to meet him, protesting that their quarrel was only with oppressive ministers, not with the king or the king’s son. Taxila and the kingdom of the Svasas made their submission to the prince, who in due course returned to the capital.” Taxila was a major trade hub on the Uttarapatha that connected the regions east of the Indus to those in the west. It was a rich and powerful city, and was a pre-eminent centre of education till Huns destroyed the city completely in the 5th century. Its ruins, first excavated by Sir John Marshall from 1913, were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980. According to Taranath’s account, after successfully defusing the rebellion and winning people’s support by presumably sacking the local minister who had abused power, Ashok captured the kingdom of Khwasa in modern-day south Kashmir. For Ashok, this was an extremely crucial life lesson, one that he would use in Ujjain, where too he was sent to quell another revolt. He also became adept at negotiations within the Pataliputra court and won over his father Bindusara’s erstwhile confidants who joined his camp and anointed him.

title: Test #21: Starlink and the Digital Sovereignty Question
text: APJ Abdul Kalam once recalled that after the 1998 nuclear tests, American sanctions led a US partner to withdraw from the Light Combat Aircraft’s flight-control programme. The partner retained Indian equipment, software, and technical information held at its premises. Digital sovereignty is not freedom from the world. It is the ability to keep essential services running when foreign-laws, suppliers, or sanctions restrict access to technology. The Institutions exercising that power must also answer to citizens, with remedies when digital systems deny them services or violate their rights. Territorial sovereignty has never insulated countries from economic pressure. Digital systems spread practical control across several countries. An Indian service may use American software and Taiwanese chips, with maintenance performed remotely and access controlled through licences issued abroad. Indian law may govern the service without ensuring continued access to the licences, updates, and support it needs. On September 21, 2026, the Delhi High Court ordered SAP India to restore software support to Nayara Energy. The Indian arm of the German software group had cited European Union sanctions against the refiner. Nayara had encountered a similar problem with Microsoft. In July 2025, the American company suspended digital services following EU sanctions against the refiner, whose shareholders include Russia’s Rosneft. The prospect of Starlink’s entry into India raises a similar question about connectivity. Satellite broadband could connect remote communities and provide backup when terrestrial networks fail. Ukraine offers a warning: Officials there said unannounced restrictions on Starlink connectivity disrupted military drone missions during Russian attacks. Data localisation establishes where information sits, without necessarily settling who can operate the system, repair move it elsewhere. Domestic production can improve our options, although reproducing every component would consume resources India needs for other priorities. Dependence becomes a sovereignty problem when an outside actor can interrupt an essential service, and India cannot restore it before serious harm follows. Geopolitics is changing the terms of India’s technology choices. American export controls affect access to advanced chips. Chinese mineral restrictions can unsettle manufacturing. EU regulations shape access to an important market. These instruments have different purposes and consequences, but their effect can be similar. An Indian firm may discover that access is conditional on decisions made elsewhere. Friendly relations cannot guarantee that a foreign supplier will remain free to serve Indian customers. A technology partnership needs attention to licensing conditions and plans for what happens if access is cut. Elon Musk said the US government controlled operating limits for Starshield, the military service. India’s civilian needs differ, but local ground stations would not ensure control over the network. Before essential services depend on it, India needs workable alternatives. India has faced such tests before. Indian teams completed the system through sustained development and testing, drawing on expertise and institutions built over many years. UPI demonstrates an ability to build digital public infrastructure at scale. Our software firms serve global markets; Indian engineers help develop technologies used worldwide. Such connections bring knowledge, income and influence. Restricting legitimate data flows or making useful foreign technology needlessly expensive could weaken the very institutions and businesses from which greater Indian capability must grow. Participation in global technology markets does not by itself give Indian firms control over the technology they use. More Indian research must move from papers and prototypes into products we can maintain and improve here. Subsidies should support demonstrable capacity, including the skills to keep systems running after the foreign supplier has left.

title: Test #22: Rajput Dynasties: Confederacies and Resistance
text: The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 was a turning point in Indian history. The new state introduced administrative practices that led to greater centralisation of authority. In the early 1500s, the weakening and subsequent decline of the Delhi Sultanate under its last ruler, Ibrahim Lodi, opened the door to two parallel developments. First, Zahiruddin Muhammad, also known as Babur, from Central Asia launched an invasion on India. Second, Indian rulers began to assert their own authority. In 1526, Babur defeated the Lodi forces in the First Battle of Panipat, bringing the Sultanate to an end. Mewar’s Resistance against Mughals Akbar attacked the kingdom of Mewar and laid siege to the fort at Chittor in 1567-1568. For example, the Iqta system, under which territories were assigned to military commanders in lieu of salaries, became a mechanism for land-revenue collection and a system that increased the burden on the peasantry. Furthermore, during their military campaigns for territorial expansion, the forces of the Sultanate demolished sites sacred to the local communities. This led to stiff resistance from several kingdoms and chieftains. Therefore, resistance throughout the Delhi Sultanate was fuelled by both political factors and the determination to preserve socio-cultural continuity. For instance, the Yadava dynasty of western Deccan (Devagiri), several Rajput dynasties of present-day Rajasthan, the Kakatiya rulers of eastern Deccan (Warangal), and the Hoysalas of present-day Karnataka repeatedly resisted the Sultans of Delhi. These states played an important role in checking the expansion of the Sultanate. Over the years and under different Sultans, the Delhi Sultanate faced opposition and defiance from several states and regions including Mewar, Gwalior, Malwa, Awadh, Etawah, Ajmer, Jalore, Kalinjar, and Kannauj. In 1527, Rana Sangram Singh-I, popularly known as Rana Sanga, of Mewar led a Rajput confederacy against Babur in the Battle of Khanua. The battle ended in favour of Babur and is seen as an important turning point in Indian history. The Mughal army paid a heavy price in the campaign. Under Rana Udai Singh, the Rajputs put up a stiff resistance for more than five months before the fort was captured by the Mughals. By this time, Akbar had already concluded several successful campaigns and the empire was at the peak of its power. In a strategic move, Rana Udai Singh retreated to the Aravalli Hills along with a large number of his subjects. In 1576, Akbar launched another attack on Mewar. This time, Maharana Pratap, the son and successor of Rana Udai Singh, fought against Mughal forces in the Battle of Haldighati. Continuing his fierce resistance, Maharana Pratap modified his military strategy and adopted guerrilla warfare. He used the rugged Aravalli terrain to his advantage and conducted surprise attacks, raids, and ambushes on the Mughal forces and their networks. He continued to resist and eventually reclaimed most of his ancestral territories in the 1580s. The Battle of Dewair fought near Udaipur in 1582 was significant as it resulted in the collapse of key Mughal military outposts in Mewar and helped Maharana Pratap reclaim control over Mewar. Maharana Pratap’s son and successor, Maharana Amar Singh, continued Mewar’s tradition of military resistance against the Mughals. Jahangir made military advances towards Mewar in 1605, 1608, and 1609. But each attempt was countered by a strong and organised resistance from the Rajputs. Eventually, the Mughals were compelled to acknowledge Mewar’s distinct political position. As Mughal rule consolidated its power, relations between the Rajputs and the Mughals evolved over time, shaped by strategic considerations. Some Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar, maintained stiff resistance to Mughal authority, while others like the Kachhwaha Rajputs of Amber, negotiated cooperative relationships. The Mughals, for their part, had a strong incentive to collaborate with the Rajputs they needed the Rajputs’ military might, their loyalty as well as their administrative strength to consolidate and stabilise the Mughal Empire.

title: Test #22: Kalam's Unfinished Dream - A Developed India
text: Every October-15, classrooms across India fill with quizzes, speeches and posters. It is the birthday of the “People’s President”, celebrated as World Students’ Day. Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam, born on 15-October 1931, was indeed a president unlike any other-a remarkable, humble and inspirational scientist. He rose through the ranks, sold newspapers in his childhood and, through sheer grit and determination, went on to become the ‘Missile Man of India’ and then the country’s President. The day is often described wrongly, so a correction belongs here. The day has not been declared by the United Nations, but it is celebrated in India as Students’ Day. No resolution created it. A grateful country did, because Kalam had earned it. Tamil Nadu goes further and observes the date as Youth Renaissance Day-an official recognition of his influence. Why students? Because Kalam never stopped being one, and never stopped being a teacher. As President from 2002 to 2007, he met students constantly, and he kept doing so after leaving office. He returned to the classroom as a visiting professor at the IIMs in Ahmedabad, Indore and Shillong. On July 27, 2015, he collapsed while lecturing IIM Shillong students on creating a livable planet and died soon after, aged 83. He was teaching until his last hour. The nation’s debt to him is larger than the classroom. As Project Director of SLV-III, India’s first satellite launch vehicle designed and produced at home, he helped put the Rohini satellite into orbit in July 1980 and bring India into the select circle of space-faring nations. At the DRDO, he led the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme, which delivered Agni and Prithvi and earned him the name “Missile Man”. He then played a central scientific and technical role in the Pokhran-II tests of May 1998, which made India a declared nuclear-weapon state. Every Indian who sleeps behind a credible deterrent owes him a quiet thank-you. The honours followed: the Padma Bhushan in 1981, the Padma Vibhushan in 1990 and the Bharat Ratna in 1997. Yet his most lasting work may be the one that carried no title. Wings of Fire, published in 1999, gave millions of young Indians a story in which a modest background was no barrier to ambition. India 2020 gave them a target to build towards. His vision aimed at a developed India by 2020. That year has passed, and the work is unfinished. Kalam would have been the last person to call this an embarrassment. He would have called it homework. Behind the scientist stood a modest beginning. Kalam was born in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu, to a boat-owning father who also led prayers at the local mosque - a family of limited means but unlimited values. He studied physics at St. Joseph’s College in Tiruchirappalli and then aeronautical engineering at the Madras Institute of Technology. His dream of becoming a fighter pilot ended when he missed selection by a single rank, yet he turned that disappointment into a lifelong career in science. He joined the DRDO in 1958, moved to ISRO in 1969 and worked closely with Vikram Sarabhai, whose guidance shaped his thinking about space research for national development. Later, from 1999 to 2001, he served as the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India. In 2002 he became the eleventh President of India, elected with wide support across party lines - a rare consensus in Indian politics. Rashtrapati Bhavan under him opened its gardens and its doors to children, farmers and scientists alike. He wrote more than a dozen books, including Ignited Minds and Turning Points, and he spoke often about PURA, a plan to provide urban facilities in rural areas. He also championed the idea that science should serve the poorest citizen - not only the powerful institution. For students preparing for competitive examinations, his life offers a practical lesson: talent matters, but disciplined, daily practice matters far more. Persistence, he believed, turns ordinary effort into extraordinary results.

title: Test #23: Navratri - Journet from Form to Formless
text: The universe, and everything within it, exists in three fundamental states: gross, subtle, and causal. Just as the five elements manifest in these three forms, so does the supreme cosmic energy we revere as Goddess Durga. While some traditions envision the Divine strictly in a masculine form, our profound spiritual heritage has worshipped the supreme as feminine – Bhagavati. In her causal, cosmic form, she is the golden womb from which the entire universe is born. The very name Durga signifies the one who resides within the fortress of this physical world. Because the human mind cannot easily comprehend this boundless energy, sages gave her a beautiful, visible form so we could connect with her through devotion. Yet, the divine extends far beyond this physical representation. Consider the mechanism of your own vision: you can look in a mirror and see your physical eyes, which is the gross form. However, you cannot physically capture or see the actual power of sight the subtle energy that communicates with your brain and allows you to perceive the world. Similarly, while we worship murtis of goddess, the subtle cosmic energy she represents remains invisible, functioning silently and continuously throughout the universe. Most of us remain focused on the gross, visible form of goddess, approaching her merely out of fear or greed. True devotion is never born from a transactional desire for protection or material gain. The wise seeker does not pray out of fear, but instead seeks the ultimate, causal truth: Satchidanand. This divine presence is not a distant deity residing in heavens; she is the life force blooming in leaves, flowing in oceans, and acting as the very power of sight and speech within you. In yogic tradition, she is recognised as dormant kundalini at the base of the Sushumna Nadi, waiting to be awakened through sincere practice. She resides within the fortress of your own body and mind. To awaken this inner power, Navratri provides a framework of profound physical and mental discipline. Ancient sages recognised the delicate relationship between human health and nature’s rhythms, placing Navratri at junctions of seasonal change when the body’s internal fire naturally weakens. This is the time for fasting. Today, fasting has often been distorted into an alternative feast of heavy, substitute grains. A genuine fast is a conscious withdrawal. When the body rests, it triggers autophagy, clearing out dead cells, balancing glucose, and healing from within. We draw inspiration from the Goddess herself, who, in her ultimate state of penance, gave up even leaves to sustain herself, earning the name Aparna. Alongside purifying the body is anchoring of mind. During these nine days, rituals we perform are deeply symbolic. We do not light a pure ghee lamp merely to illuminate an idol; we light it to perform tratak gazing steadily at the flame to centre our scattered awareness and improve our physical and inner vision. Ultimately, these nine days are a journey from ordinary human to spiritual aspirant who has mastered the senses and the mind. When the mind is purified and the body is cleansed, you realise that Devi is not outside. Fasting and ritual are supported by the discipline of speech and thought. During Navratri, devotees are encouraged to practise silence, mantra repetition, and sattvic living, for the mind takes the colour of whatever it consumes. Japa of the Devi mantra is not a mechanical counting of beads; it is the gentle gathering of a restless mind into a single stream of attention. Just as a river, when channelled, can illuminate a city, the scattered thoughts, when directed inward, become a source of clarity and strength. Reading the Durga Saptashati, offering gratitude, and serving the needy are equally significant, because the Goddess is present in every being we encounter. The nine forms of Devi, from Shailaputri to Siddhidatri, mirror the stages of inner ascent: stability, discipline, courage, creativity, compassion, and finally liberation.

title: Test #23: Jodhpur - Rajasthan Famous Blue City
text: Jodhpur is the second largest city in Rajasthan. It was founded in 1459 AD by Rao Jodha of the Rathore clan as the capital of the historic Kingdom of Marwar. Located at the edge of the Thar Desert, serving as a gateway to the desert region. Mehrangarh Fort, Umaid Bhawan Palace, Jaswant Thada, Toorji Ka Jhalra, and Ghata Ghar are some of the top attractions across the city that invite people around the world. Imagine walking through narrow lanes lined with blue houses, with the imposing Mehrangarh Fort rising above the city. This is Jodhpur, Rajasthan's much-loved Blue City, where the colour blue has become an unmistakable part of the old city's identity. Nestled on the edge of the Thar Desert, Jodhpur in Rajasthan is famous for its striking blue-painted houses, winding lanes and grand forts. Blue colour is considered a sacred colour in Hinduism and is often associated with Lord Krishna and Lord Shiva. The usage of blue colour in the city’s architecture is a reflection of the city’s deep-rooted cultural traditions. The colour is not just aesthetically pleasing but also symbolises the city’s connection to rich heritage and traditions. The blue colour of Jodhpur houses and architectural structures creates a sense of uniformity and harmony. The widespread use of blue paint gives a unique look to the city, setting it apart from any other cities in India. Jodhpur’s blue colour is also a reflection of its rich history and heritage. The architectural uniformity is a testament to its strategic location and the city’s ability to adapt and evolve, incorporating influences from different cultures. The blue colour of Jodhpur originated with the Brahmin community, who used to paint their houses in blue colour to signify their social status and utmost devotion to Lord Shiva. Over time, the blue hue spread throughout the city, becoming an integral part of its architecture. Nestled in Rajasthan, Jodhpur’s hot desert climate inspired people to find creative ways to keep their houses cool. The blue signifies a cooling effect as it reflects the sun’s rays and keeps the interiors comfortable. This practical idea of blue paint added to its popularity, and people started painting their houses in blue. Another popular belief links the blue colour to protection from insects. Traditionally, houses were whitewashed with lime mixed with copper sulphate, which gave the walls their bluish tint and was believed to repel termites and mosquitoes. Today, the blue lanes of Brahmapuri, below the ramparts of Mehrangarh, attract photographers, travellers and artists who wander through its narrow alleys, admiring colourful doorways, carved balconies and friendly local residents. Visitors often climb to the fort and look down upon a sea of blue rooftops stretching towards the desert horizon, a sight that remains unforgettable. Nearby, the bustling markets around the famous clock tower offer spices, textiles, handicrafts and traditional Rajasthani sweets, adding vibrancy to the experience. Preserving this living heritage is important, because the blue city is not merely a tourist attraction but also a home, a community and a cultural legacy passed down through generations and worth safeguarding for future travellers. odhpur’s charm extends beyond its colour. The city is also known as the Sun City because of its bright, sunny weather throughout the year. Its cuisine is equally memorable, with local favourites such as mirchi bada, pyaaz kachori and the creamy makhaniya lassi delighting visitors after a long day of sightseeing. The city has even given the world the Jodhpuri bandhgala coat and jodhpur trousers, which became popular among riders and royalty alike. Every year, festivals such as the Marwar Festival and the Rajasthan International Folk Festival fill the streets with music, dance and colourful turbans, celebrating the spirit of the desert. Skilled artisans continue to craft furniture, leather goods and block-printed fabrics using methods inherited from earlier generations.

title: Test #24: Navi Pillay - Voice for Justice in a World at War
text: Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a South African jurist of Indian origin, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Her recognition brings global attention to a woman who has spent decades fighting racial discrimination, defending political prisoners and helping strengthen international justice. Her life shows that the fight for peace begins with the protection of human rights. Born in Durban, South Africa, on September 23, 1941, Pillay grew up in a modest family. The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize recognises not only Pillay’s achievements but also the importance of defending human rights in an increasingly troubled world. Her life carries a message that is relevant to every nation: peace cannot be built on fear, discrimination or silence. Her father was a bus driver, while her mother looked after their eight children. Her grandfather had migrated from Tamil Nadu to South Africa as an indentured labourer. The family faced financial difficulties, and the racial discrimination of the apartheid era made life harder for people of Indian origin and Black South Africans. Pillay refused to let these barriers determine her future. She studied law at the University of Natal and, in 1967, opened her own legal practice. At a time when racial discrimination shaped almost every aspect of life in South Africa, she stood beside those who challenged the system. She defended anti-apartheid activists and political prisoners and spoke out against the ill-treatment of people in custody. For Pillay, the law was not simply a profession. It was a way to protect people who had little power to defend themselves. Her work taught her an important lesson: justice must be available to everyone, not just the rich and powerful. She later pursued higher studies at Harvard Law School, earning a master’s degree in law and a doctorate in 1988. In 1995, she became a judge of the South African High Court, marking another milestone in her remarkable career. Her contribution to international justice became especially important during her service at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. She served as its president from 1999 to 2003. The tribunal was established to prosecute those responsible for the 1994 Rwandan genocide, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. One of the most important legal developments associated with the tribunal was the recognition that rape and sexual violence could form part of genocide. The landmark Akayesu judgment helped establish this principle. It was a major step towards recognising the suffering of women during wars and ensuring that sexual violence could not be ignored in the pursuit of justice. Pillay went on to serve as a judge at the International Criminal Court from 2003 to 2008. She then became the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, holding the position from 2008 to 2014. In this role, she raised concerns about human rights violations in conflict zones and called for greater protection for vulnerable communities. Her message was clear: governments must respect human rights, and those responsible for serious crimes must be held accountable. Peace cannot last when victims are forgotten and perpetrators escape justice. Pillay also supported women’s rights through her association with Equality Now, an international organisation working to end discrimination against women and girls. She contributed to efforts against the death penalty and took part in international initiatives promoting freedom of information and democracy. Her career reminds us that peace is much more than the absence of war. A ceasefire may stop the guns for a while, but lasting peace requires justice, dignity and trust. When innocent people suffer and serious crimes go unpunished, the wounds of conflict remain open. Independent courts and international institutions can help victims seek justice and make it harder for powerful individuals to act without fear of accountability. Pillay’s Indian roots make her story particularly meaningful to readers in India.

title: Test #24: Food is the Great Medicine - Ahro Mahabhaishajyam
text: World Food Day is observed every year on 16-October, the date on which the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) was founded in 1945. Between 1979-1981, the FAO Conference proclaimed the observance and the first World Food Day was marked. Between 1979-1981, the FAO Conference proclaimed the observance, and the first World Food Day was marked; over 150 countries now observe it. In 2026, the day is a good occasion to examine how Ancient Bharat developed a sophisticated, systematic dietetics, in which food was not merely fuel, pleasure or ritual but a primary instrument for maintaining health, preventing disease and supporting the treatment of ailments. This idea is captured in the celebrated maxim Aharo Mahabhaishajyam, which means “food is the great medicine”. In Ayurveda, ahara encompasses not only what we eat but also how, when, how much, in what season and in what physical and mental state. Ayurveda places ahara among the trayo’pastambha, the three “sub-pillars” of life, along with nidra (sleep) and brahmacharya (regulated conduct). In this worldview, good health is not accidental; it is sustained daily through disciplined living. Food is, therefore, both nourishment and a health intervention. The Charaka Samhita states that the body, disease and well-being depend fundamentally on nutrition. Improper food can generate disorder, while appropriate food can restore balance. Aharo Mahabhaishajyam should be perceived correctly. It does not mean that every meal cures every illness, nor that diet can replace surgery, antibiotics, insulin or emergency care. Rather, it means that food is a constant medicine. Taken three or four times a day, it continuously shapes digestion, metabolism, immunity, energy, health and long-term disease risk. What makes ancient Indian food wisdom distinctive is that it treats eating as a complete system rather than a list of nutrients. Ayurveda takes cognisance of the fact that the same food does not affect everyone the same way. Diet should be adjusted to one’s constitution (prakriti), digestive capacity (agni), age and pathological state. Diet should be adjusted to a person’s constitution (prakriti), digestive capacity (agni), age and medical condition. This anticipates a cardinal concern of modern personalised nutrition: individual variability in metabolism and dietary response. The traditional Indian platter, the thali, often combines grains and legumes: rice with dal, roti with rajma or chana, and millet porridge with buttermilk. This blend gives amino acids, fibre, minerals and slow-release carbohydrates. India’s food heritage also includes idli, dosa, dhokla, kanji, pickles and fermented gruels. Fermentation can aid digestion, preserve food, add flavour and, in some cases, raise nutrient availability. Modern research recognises the gut microbiome as a major regulator of metabolism and immunity. Indian spices are not merely flavouring agents. Turmeric, ginger, black pepper, cumin, coriander, fenugreek, cardamom, cinnamon, clove and asafoetida have long been used in cooking and healing. Ghee is valued in Ayurveda for its digestibility, its lubricating quality and its role as a carrier for herbs. Traditional fats were used in measured, context-specific ways alongside fibre-rich foods, spices and active lifestyles. The problem in many modern diets is not fat alone but refined carbohydrates, ultra-processed foods and excess calories. The Charaka Samhita underlines the ashta ahara vidhi visheshayatana, the eight determinants of the effect of food: the nature of the food, processing, combination, quantity, place, time, rules of intake and the person consuming it. Food recommendations change with ritu (season) and desha (region). The categories of pathya and apathya, meaning wholesome and unwholesome, are salient. Pathya is not simply “healthy food” in a generic sense; it is food suitable for a particular person, condition, season and therapeutic goal. This is why Ayurvedic treatment often begins with dietary correction before or alongside medicinal treatment.

title: Test #25: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 248 of 1974
text: The prosecution case stemmed from a vigilance trap conducted by the Anti-Corruption Branch on 14th October, 1969. The complainant (PW-2), an applicant seeking a municipal commercial trade licence, alleged that the appellant, functioning as a municipal health inspector, demanded an illegal gratification of Rs. 150/- to clear sanitation verification reports. A trap party was assembled, phenolphthalein-treated marked currency notes were handed to the complainant, and a shadow decoy witness (PW-3) was instructed to accompany the complainant and observe the transaction. At the trial, the complainant (PW-2) resiled from his statement, deposing that he placed the money on the office desk without any demand from the appellant. However, the High Court reversed the trial court's acquittal, relying exclusively upon the uncorroborated testimony of the shadow trap witness (PW-3) to infer demand and acceptance. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court committed serious legal error in basing conviction solely upon the testimony of a trap witness. It was argued that a decoy or trap witness is in the nature of an accomplice under Section 133 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, whose uncorroborated testimony cannot be acted upon without independent corroboration under illustration (b) to Section 114 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Prakash Chand v. State (Delhi Administration), reported in (1979) 3 SCC 90, and Somabhai Gopalbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2014) 14 SCC 682, authoritatively re-examined the evidentiary status of trap and decoy witnesses in corruption prosecutions. The Court held that an accomplice is a person who participates in the commission of the crime with criminal mens rea. A trap witness or decoy who acts under official instructions to detect public corruption is not an accomplice in the strict sense of Section 133 of the Evidence Act, as he lacks criminal intent. However, a trap witness is an interested and partisan witness who is keenly interested in the success of the trap operation he participated in. Therefore, as a rule of prudence and caution, the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness cannot form the sole basis for convicting a public servant unless it is corroborated in material particulars by independent, disinterested testimony. In the present case, the complainant turned hostile and denied any verbal demand, no independent civilian witnesses from the municipal office were joined, and hand-wash evidence was inconclusive. In the absence of corroboration establishing demand, the statutory presumption under Section 4 of the 1947 Act cannot be triggered. The conviction is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant public servant under Section 379 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 read with Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, challenges the judgment and order dated 14th August, 1973 passed by the High Court of Delhi in Criminal Appeal No. 112 of 1971, setting aside the judgment of acquittal rendered by the learned Special Judge, Delhi and convicting the appellant under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, based upon decoy trap evidence. Furthermore, in Sabitri Samantaray v. State of Odisha, reported in (2023) 11 SCC 813, this Court reaffirmed that Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not shift the primary burden of proof, which always remains on the prosecution under Article 21. Section 106 cannot be used to bridge missing links in a defective investigation. In the complete absence of motive, weapon recovery, or forensic links, the conviction cannot stand on mere suspicion. The judgment of the High Court is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted of all charges.

title: Test #25: The Altruist in Politics - By Cardozo
text: There comes not seldom a crisis in the life of men, of nations, and of worlds, when the old forms seem ready to decay, and the old rules of action have lost their binding force. The evils of existing systems obscure the blessings that attend them; and, where reform is needed, the cry is raised for subversion. The cause of such phenomena is not far to seek. "It used to appear to me," writes Count Tolstoi, in a significant passage, "it used to appear to me that the small number of cultivated, rich and idle men, of whom I was one, composed the whole of humanity, and that the millions and millions of other men who had lived and are still living were not in reality men at all." It is this spirit the spirit that sees the whole of humanity in the few, and throws into the background the millions and millions of other men it is this spirit that has aroused the antagonism of reformers, and made the decay of the old forms, the rupture of the old restrictions, the ideal of them and of their followers. When wealth and poverty meet each other face to face, the one the master and the other the dependent, the one exalted and the other debased, it is perhaps hardly matter for surprise that the dependent and debased and powerless faction, in envy of their opponents' supremacy, should demand, not simple reform, but absolute community and equality of wealth. That cry for communism [socialism or collectivism] is no new one in the history of mankind. Thousands of years ago it was heard and acted on; and, in the lapse of centuries, its reverberations have but swelled in volume. Again and again, the altruist has arisen in politics, has bidden us share with others the product of our toil, and has proclaimed the communistic dogma as the panacea for our social ills. So today, amid the buried hopes and buried projects of the past, the doctrine of communism still lives in the minds of men. Under stress of misfortune, or in dread of tyranny, it is still preached in modern times as Plato preached it in the world of the Greeks. Yet it is indeed doubtful whether, in the history of mankind, a doctrine was ever taught more impracticable or more false to the principles it professes than this very doctrine of communism.2 In a world where self-interest is avowedly the ruling motive, it seeks to establish at once an all-reaching and all-controlling altruism.3 In a world where every man is pushing and fighting to outstrip his fellows, it would make him toil with like vigor for their common welfare. In a world where a man's activity is measured by the nearness of reward, it would hold up a prospective recompense as an equal stimulant to labor. "The more bitterly we feel," writes George Eliot, "the more bitterly we feel the folly, ignorance, neglect, or self-seeking of those who at different times have wielded power, the stronger is the obligation we lay on ourselves to beware lest we also, by a too hasty wresting of measures which seem to promise immediate relief, make a worse time of it for our own generation, and leave a bad inheritance for our children." In the future, when the remoteness of his reward shall have weakened the laborer's zeal, we shall be able to judge more fairly of the blessings that the communist offers. Instead of the present world, where some at least are well-to-do and happy, the communist holds before us a world where all alike are poor. For the activity, the push, the vigor of our modern life, his substitute is a life aimless and unbroken. And so we have to say to communists what George Eliot might have said: Be not blinded by the passions of the moment, but when you prate about your own wrongs and the sufferings of your offspring, take heed lest in the long run you make a worse time of it for your own generation, and leave a bad inheritance for your children. Little thought has been taken by these altruistic reformers for the application of the doctrines they uphold.

title: Test #26: Legal - AHC Writ C. No. 15115 of 2025
text: The historical facts disclose that statutory proceedings were initiated against the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 (Act No. 33 of 1976), culminating in a final statement under Section 9 and a notification declaring surplus land under Section 10(1) published on 14th June, 1988. A notification declaring vesting under Section 10(3) was published on 12th January, 1989, followed by an administrative notice to surrender possession under Section 10(5) issued on 22nd March, 1991. However, the tenure holders refused voluntary surrender, and the state authorities omitted to take forceful physical possession by issuing a notice under Section 10(6) or drawing a contemporaneous possession panchnama. The petitioners and their ancestors remained in uninterrupted physical and cultivatory possession, harvesting seasonal crops and paying agricultural land revenue. Following the enactment of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, adopted by the State of Uttar Pradesh on 18th March, 1999, the petitioners applied for deletion of state ceiling endorsements, which was summarily rejected by the authorities relying on constructive paper vesting. This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and jurisdiction of the administrative communication dated 18th November, 2024 issued by Respondent No. 2, the Competent Authority under the Urban Land Ceiling / Additional District Magistrate (Administration), Bareilly, refusing to delete ceiling encumbrances from revenue records and rejecting building plan clearances in respect of agricultural land comprised in Gata No. 342, admeasuring 4,820 square meters situated at Village Tilyar, Tehsil Sadar, District Bareilly, under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners contended that mere paper vesting under Section 10(3) does not extinguish ownership. Placing heavy reliance upon the landmark ruling of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. Hari Ram, reported in (2013) 4 SCC 280, it was argued that where de facto physical possession was not taken under Section 10(6) prior to 18th March, 1999, all pending ceiling proceedings stood abated by operation of Section 3 and Section 4 of the Repeal Act. Learned Additional Chief Standing Counsel for the State submitted that once a notification under Section 10(3) is published, the land vests in the State free from all encumbrances, and peaceful possession was deemed to have been acquired. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that symbolic possession on official files cannot defeat the beneficial provisions of the Repeal Act. In Hari Ram (supra), affirmed in Gajanan Kamlya Patil v. Additional Collector, reported in (2014) 12 SCC 523, the Supreme Court authoritatively established that requirement of taking physical possession under Section 10(5) and Section 10(6) of the 1976 Act is mandatory. Mere paper transfer or mutation in revenue records does not constitute actual physical dispossession. The State failed to place any panchnama or independent witness testimony establishing that physical custody was wrested from the tenure holders prior to 18th March, 1999. Since the petitioners retained physical cultivating possession, the ceiling proceedings abated in toto under Section 4 of the Repeal Act, 1999. The impugned order dated 18th November, 2024 is quashed, and Respondent No. 2 is commanded to correct the revenue khatauni records and mutate the petitioners' names within six weeks. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that settled revenue entries spanning two decades cannot be obliterated through summary administrative overreach. In Saroj Devi v. State of U.P., reported in 2019 SCC OnLine All 1842, and Hari Ram v. Collector, Saharanpur, reported in (2004) 2 RD 360, this Court held that where the statute specifically vests the power of cancellation in the Collector, an order passed by a subordinate revenue official is void.

title: Test #26: The Effects of El NIno Could Creep Into
text: In August, the Reserve Bank of India flagged El Nino and uneven rainfall as risks to agriculture and inflation. It projected consumer inflation at 5% for 2026-27 and pointed to grain stocks and timely supply management as buffers. In the El Nino drought of 2009, the monsoon was 22% below normal. Foodgrain production fell by 17 million tonnes and wholesale food inflation reached 20% in December 2009. The drought was not the only cause, as bottlenecks in the supply of essential commodities also mattered. Human-caused global warming has heated up our oceans, which absorb over 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. El Nino releases some of that extra ocean heat into the atmosphere, and the effect often lasts for months after the event peaks. Meteorological agencies predict that 2027 will be the warmest year on record, as a result of unabated global warming and an exceptionally strong El Nino. This means that the coming seasons may unfold in a world unlike any in the past several thousand years. The Pacific Ocean usually goes through a cycle of warm and cool phases every few years. An El Nino is its warm phase and a La Nina is its cool phase. When a large part of the ocean warms, it changes where clouds form and rain falls. The changes reach far beyond the Pacific, altering the chances of drought or heavy rain in different parts of the world. In India, El Nino often weakens the summer monsoon. Many earlier El Ninos peaked with central Pacific waters about 1-DegreeC warmer than usual. Several in recent decades have exceeded 2-DegreeC. The current El Nino, however, has already exceeded earlier observed peaks. Forecasts indicate that the central Pacific could be nearly 4-DegreeC warmer than usual by November or December, when El Nino usually peaks. The southwest monsoon closed with a 13% rainfall deficit. Punjab, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and the northeastern states recorded stark rainfall deficits. Meanwhile, Odisha received 30% more than usual. Bihar and Assam experienced severe floods in a monsoon that remains markedly deficient overall. The effects could creep into coming seasons through crops, water, heat, food prices, forests, and seas. In parts of Maharashtra, soybean farmers have already had to contend with long dry spells. A late shower cannot save a crop that lost moisture at a critical stage, and rain at harvest can cause fresh damage. The winter (rabi) crops that follow, including wheat, chickpea, and mustard, will depend on the moisture left in the ground and the water available for irrigation. The economic costs begin before a harvest is counted. Less fodder raises the cost of keeping livestock. More pumping for water means more spending on electricity or diesel. A smaller harvest reduces farm income and spending in local shops, while shortages of particular foods can raise prices in towns and cities. A household may face dearer pulses or vegetables even when the national foodgrain total looks reassuring. India in 2026 has more ways to respond than it did in 2009. Irrigation covers about 56% of the gross cropped area. Grain stocks, food security law, crop insurance, farm credit and better forecasts give governments more options. Decisions about water, crops and food supply can address shortages before they appear in an inflation reading. These tools need to reach farmers and districts whose losses do not show up in national totals. October-December brings the northeast monsoon, the main rainy season for Tamil Nadu and parts of the southeast coast. El Nino can bring more rain there, sometimes in intense spells. A state dealing with water shortage after the summer monsoon may also need to prepare for floods. In the north, the coming winter brings a different risk. A CEEW analysis found slightly weaker winds over Delhi during El Nino than La Nina winters, which can make pollution harder to disperse. If kharif harvesting is delayed, the time before rabi sowing becomes even tighter, adding pressure to burn crop residue.

title: Test #27: Jantar Mantar When It was Not a Protest Site
text: Jantar Mantar is synonymous with protests against the government. That perception could perhaps change with the government denotifying it as a protest site. This may end an era, since the term ‘Jantar Mantar’ has been closely connected to the expression of dissent in India since the 1990s. Jantar Mantar and its environs have always occupied a very distinctive place in Delhi’s landscape. Its history begins sometime in the 16th century, when Akbar occupied the Mughal throne. The young emperor married the princess of Amer in early 1562, an event that marked the beginning of close ties between the Mughal royal family and the Kachhwaha Rajputs of Amer. Though Akbar moved his capital to Agra in 1558, Delhi remained an important city of the Mughal Empire, and many saw it as the true capital of Hindustan. Akbar himself had ruled from the city for a few years, living in the fortress built by his father Humayun, which we now call Purana Qila. Two distinct settlements, Jaisinghpura, founded by Maharaja Jai Singh (reigned 1621-67), and Madhoganj, named after Madho Singh (reigned 1750-68), were founded. The construction of the Jantar Mantar was the work of a later ruler, Sawai Jai Singh, who also founded the new capital of Amer Jaipur in 1727. In the 1720s, Sawai Jai Singh, who had a deep interest in astronomy, also embarked on a related project. Astronomical observations were a matter of interest for the Mughal rulers, too, as the determination of auspicious timings depended on accurate astronomical readings. Emperor Muhammad Shah was concerned that many errors had crept into the astronomical tables, and Jai Singh pressed for the need to take fresh and accurate readings to update the charts. This paved the way for the construction of several large observatories across various cities within the imperial territories Ujjain, Varanasi, Mathura, the new city of Jaipur, and within the raja’s own land in the imperial capital, Delhi. The set of giant astronomical instruments, or yantra, built in Delhi is what we today call Jantar Mantar. Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and the surrounding settlements remained the property of the rajas of Jaipur for more than two centuries thereafter, though Delhi experienced many political upheavals. In the second half of the 18th century, the city was battered by civil wars and invasions; during this period, the buildings that made up the Jantar Mantar complex sustained significant damage. General disorder within the Mughal Empire also led to neglect of the buildings. Despite this, the complex remained a prominent, imposing landmark. The British artists, Thomas and William Daniell, who visited Delhi in 1789, chose to include two sketches of the Jantar Mantar among the total of 10 views of Delhi that made it into their published aquatints of Indian scenery. Despite Delhi coming under the rule of the British East India Company in 1803 and direct Crown rule in 1858, Jantar Mantar and the lands around it continued to be the property of the Jaipur rajas. In 1852, the Delhi Archaeological Society carried out repairs on some of the instruments, with 600 given for the purpose by the then maharaja. In 1910, repairs were again carried out in anticipation of prominent visitors who would come to Delhi for the Coronation Durbar of George V. The year 1913 marked a major reorganisation of the lands in Delhi. Most of the Jaipur lands were acquired for the construction of the new British capital New Delhi. The old settlements of Jaisinghpura and Madhoganj were cleared away, though Jai Singh Road acknowledged the nomenclature for posterity. Jantar Mantar, of course, was too important a monument to be demolished. It, in fact, remained the property of the maharajas of Jaipur, who gave 30,000 for the creation of a garden around it and handed over the maintenance to the government of India. The flag of the Jaipur State continued to flutter over Jantar Mantar for many years. The observatory was transferred to the state of Rajasthan only in 1949 and eventually came under the government of India.

title: Test #27: Legal - AHC Writ C. No. 10667 of 2019
text: The petitioners, belonging to underprivileged agricultural labour communities, were granted residential and agricultural leases by the Land Management Committee on 14th June, 1984 pursuant to a lawful resolution approved by the Sub-Divisional Officer. The names of the allottees were mutated in revenue records, and continuous cultivatory possession was reflected in Khatauni records spanning 1388 to 1396 Fasli for over twenty-two years. This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and jurisdiction of the cancellation order dated 17th July, 2006 passed by the learned Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Khurja, District Bulandshahr, along with the revisional order dated 27th August, 2008 passed by the Additional Commissioner (Administration), Meerut Division, Meerut in Revision No. 42 of 2006, whereby agricultural lease allotments (patta) granted in favour of the petitioners over Gaon Sabha land comprised in Gata No. 214 were cancelled under Section 198(4) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. In March 2006, upon a complaint filed by private respondents alleging irregular allotment procedures, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate initiated suo motu proceedings and cancelled the allotment, recording a summary finding that the original allotment files were missing from the tehsil record room and inferring that the lease was tainted with fraud. The revisional authority affirmed the cancellation without examining the statutory bar of limitation. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioners contended that the impugned orders are wholly without jurisdiction. It was argued that under the plain statutory text of Section 198(4) of the UPZA&LR Act, 1950 (now corresponding to Section 66 of the U.P. Revenue Code, 2006), the Collector alone is clothed with exclusive statutory jurisdiction to cancel agricultural allotments. An order passed by a Sub-Divisional Officer is coram non judice. Furthermore, under Section 198(6), proceedings for cancellation of allotment on grounds of procedural irregularity must be initiated within five years from the date of allotment. Learned Standing Counsel for the State submitted that where an allotment is void ab initio or obtained through collusion with the Gram Pradhan, statutory limitation periods do not curtail executive powers under Section 122-B. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that settled revenue entries spanning two decades cannot be obliterated through summary administrative overreach. In Saroj Devi v. State of U.P., reported in 2019 SCC OnLine All 1842, and Hari Ram v. Collector, Saharanpur, reported in (2004) 2 RD 360, this Court held that where the statute specifically vests the power of cancellation in the Collector, an order passed by a subordinate revenue official is void. The mere loss of official allotment files from tehsil archives cannot justify a finding of fraud against illiterate rural allottees when verified khatauni records establish long, continuous possession. Furthermore, allegations of irregularity cannot be entertained after the expiry of the mandatory five-year limitation prescribed under Section 198(6) without proving foundational fraud through regular inquiry. The impugned orders dated 17th July, 2006 and 27th August, 2008 are quashed, and the respondents are commanded to restore the petitioners' names in the revenue records within six weeks. The Court held that the grant of sanction under Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 is not an idle administrative formality, but a solemn statutory safeguard intended to protect honest public servants from malicious and frivolous harassment. A court of competent jurisdiction is statutorily prohibited from taking cognizance of an offence punishable under Sections 7, 10, 11, 13, and 15 without the previous sanction of the authority competent to remove the public servant from office. This Court ruled that a sanction granted by an authority not empowered in law is without jurisdiction and an absolute nullity.

title: Test #28: India’s Traditional Entrepreneurial Community
text: Entrepreneurship in India has deep roots among traditional communities, where skills, occupations, and occupational knowledge have been passed down through generations. Long before modern startups, these communities practised self-employment, innovation, and trade, forming the backbone of India’s local economy. The Chettiar (Nattukottai Chettiar) community from Tamil Nadu, whose banking thrived well before the Reserve Bank of India was set up in 1935, is a well-known traditional entrepreneurial community. Annamalai University (1929) and Indian Overseas Bank (1937) were founded by Chettiar leaders. Burma gained independence in 1948. Historically, Chettiars were traders, bankers, and moneylenders, operating not only across India but also in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia, and other parts of Southeast Asia. They were known for: Strong business ethics and trust-based lending; Excellent accounting and record-keeping skills; Reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education, and community welfare. The Chettiar community built wealth through trade in salt, rice, textiles, and finance, often without formal banks. Even today, Chettiar entrepreneurship inspires modern India by showing how risk-taking, discipline, and long-term vision can build sustainable businesses rooted in tradition. Management and operations are essential for running a business smoothly. Management involves planning, organising, and guiding the use of resources to achieve business goals, such as increasing market share through customer satisfaction. Operations focuses on producing and delivering goods or services efficiently and on time. For example, in a bakery, you must choose the right equipment, arrange ingredients, monitor quality, and plan daily production to ensure fresh and high-quality products are made regularly without delay or wastage. Accounting is the process of recording, organising, and reporting a business’s financial transactions. Every entrepreneur needs to understand basic accounting concepts to know how their business is doing. It means keeping track of the money coming in (revenue) and the money going out (expenses), and making sure all records or documents are correct. One important record is the profit and loss account (or income statement). It shows whether the business has made a profit or a loss over a period of time, such as a month or a year. This helps to make informed decisions about spending and investment. We can track what the business owns and how much has been borrowed. It also enables compliance with tax laws and regulations of the country. Revenue is the total money earned by a business from its main operations or sale of goods and services. The Chettiar example shows that management, operations, and accounting work together rather than separately. A trader who plans purchases carefully, stores goods safely, and delivers them on time improves customer trust. When every sale, loan, and repayment is recorded correctly, the entrepreneur can see which activities earn profit and which cause losses. Chettiar merchants relied on trust, and written records helped them maintain that trust over long distances and many years. Expenses are the costs a business incurs to earn its revenue, such as rent, wages, raw materials, transport, and electricity. If expenses exceed revenue, the business suffers a loss and must either reduce its costs or increase its sales. Regular review of accounts helps an entrepreneur identify wasteful spending early and correct it before it harms the business. Another useful record is the cash book, which notes the actual cash received and paid on each day. Together with the profit and loss account, it gives a clear picture of the financial health of the enterprise. Lenders, investors, and tax authorities also depend on such accurate records to judge whether a business is reliable and well managed. Records also help an entrepreneur plan ahead. By comparing the accounts of one year with those of the next, a business owner can decide whether to expand.

title: Test #28: DHC PA Typing - 10/03/2019
text: There is no law prescribing reservation for general category candidates in public employment and therefore there is no question of reserved category candidates being selected against their seats as no general category candidate can be appointed against a slot in the roster which is kept for reserved category candidates. Some newspapers have misreported a recent judgment of the Supreme Court, claiming that the judgment states that candidates from the reserved category cannot claim seats in the general category in any case. Such claims state that 50% of all seats are completely reserved for the general category, and no scheduled castes scheduled tribe/originally backward class person can have a claim on such seats, even on the basis of merit. However, the actual judgment does not imply anything of this sort. Moreover, the law on this point "whether reserved category candidates can claim seats in the general category on the basis of merit" is very clear. In the said case, the appellant belonged to the OBC category and had availed age relaxation (as was granted to other similarly situated candidates of the same category). Since no candidate from the general category had secured the minimum cut-off score, the appellant filed a writ petition before the high court to be accommodated in the general category. The High Court dismissed the petition. The Supreme Court affirmed this decision and held that the appellant, who has applied under reserved category by availing age relaxation and also attending the interview under the reserved category cannot claim right to be appointed under the general category. The reason, as per the court, was that there is an express bar for the candidates belonging to SC/ST/OBC who have availed relaxation for A being considered for general category candidates. The court was reading the existing rules and proceedings of Department of Personnel and Training, which stated that when a relaxed standard is applied in selecting the reserved category candidates, for example in the age-limit, experience, qualification, permitted number of chances in written examination, extended zone of consideration larger than what is provided for general category candidates, etc., the reserved candidates are to be counted against reserved vacancies only. Such candidates would be deemed as unavailable for consideration against unreserved vacancies. On similar lines, in 2015, in another case, the Gujarat High Court had held that considering the reservation policy applicable in the State of Gujarat contained in the relevant circular and relevant statutory provisions, i.e., the Recruitment Rules, it was held that all those candidates belonging to the reserved category if they avail the benefit of age relaxation, it is held to be relaxation in the standard, and therefore, are not entitled to their cases being considered for general category vacancies and that their cases are required to be considered for the reserved category vacancies only. The proposition developed by the courts in these two judgments is that when there is an existing policy regarding the express bar for reserved category candidates who have availed relaxation, such as age-relaxation, in a selection process, such reserved category candidates would not be entitled to seats in the general category, even on the basis of merit. However, in the earlier case, the court had also observed that the appellant had not challenged the constitutional validity of the proceedings read with Rule 9 of the Recruitment Rules. The appellant had only sought for a declaration that the proceedings were not binding on the appellant. No argument was canvassed challenging the constitutional validity of the proceedings before the learned Single Judge or before the Division Bench of the High Court. This observation by the Supreme Court is quite important in context of the correct position of the law on this issue. title: Test #29: Resistance & Resilience During Indian HIstory
text: The period between 1000-1700 CE, witnessed profound political, social, and cultural changes. The Indian subcontinent experienced repeated invasions and wars accompanied by religious discrimination and social distress. Regional powers frequently resisted invaders who were making inroads into their territories. Let us begin by understanding the meaning of resistance and resilience in the context of the period under study and how they are interconnected. Resilience refers to the capacity to, survive and adapt in challenging situations, including times of political unrest and instability. Resistance may take the form of warfare, alliances, diplomacy, negotiation, or other political actions. Resistance and resilience are, in fact, closely linked. Resilience is the backbone of resistance. From the mid-7th century, Arab forces launched invasions by sea and land. These early invaders were confronted and repulsed by Indian rulers across the Deccan, Malwa, Kashmir, and Rajasthan. Mahmud, the Sultan of Ghazni (in present-day Afghanistan and northeastern Iran), launched his first invasion in 1001 against Jayapala of the Hindu Shahi dynasty. During the 11th and 12th centuries, rulers of the Hindu Shahi kingdom, and the Chandellas, Solankis, and Chauhans opposed and fought against the Turkish invaders. In 1178, Queen Naiki Devi of the Chaulukya kingdom defeated Muhammad Ghuri at Kasahrada, near Mount Abu. It is also about how communities and groups across diverse regions respond to challenges and opportunities. This capacity to absorb and adapt to hardship while preserving inherited socio-cultural and spiritual traditions can also be understood as resilience. The idea of India’s resilient spirit extends beyond political and military spheres. For instance, rulers and communities restored places of worship, modified customs to suit changing circumstances and, in many regions, established lasting patterns of coexistence across religious and cultural lines. Resistance means actively opposing or challenging a force, authority, or threat in order to protect political power, territory, interests, or cultural and spiritual identity. This resistance took both military and cultural forms. Nonetheless, this period manifested the resilience of the Indian civilisation, which safeguarded its core ideas and values. Indian society not only defended itself from external threats but also preserved its traditions. While a political cause or leadership provides the condition for resistance, the ability to endure comes from resilience. Together, resistance and resilience help explain how Indian society sustained itself through different ages, particularly the period under study. This period is characterised by both conflict and cooperation, rather than being merely a story of invasion and resistance. From the 7th century onwards, the Indian subcontinent witnessed successive phases of invasions driven by territorial expansion and religious motives. It may also be noted that the surplus agrarian produce of the fertile plains fed by perennial river systems contributed to the people’s economic well-being and also became a major reason for the invasions. Against this backdrop, let us examine instances of resistance, as well as the strategic alliances and confederacies that emerged in these centuries at both the regional and pan-Indian level. In northern India, some powers, such as the Chauhans, Gahadavalas, and Senas, however came under Turkic control towards the end of the 12th century, even as Gujarat, Malwa, and Bundelkhand under the Chandellas put up stiff resistance for about a hundred years thereafter. The Turks failed to conquer present-day Odisha, and parts of present-day Assam. Several states of Rajputana, in particular, remained centres of sustained resistance throughout the period under study. Thus, during the 11th and 12th centuries, northern and western India bore the brunt of Turkish invasions, while peninsular India remained free from Turkic control.

title: Test #29: Columbus - Divisive Figure in American History
text: The second Monday of October is observed as Columbus Day, a federal holiday commemorating voyager Christopher Columbus’ arrival in the Americas on October 12, 1492. This occasion has a contentious history: While Columbus’ arrival has long been celebrated as bringing civilisation to the continent, greater attention has since been paid to the violence, conquest and colonisation that followed. The celebration of Columbus Day varies across states. In 1492, Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator seeking a route to Asia, ventured westward across the Atlantic rather than sailing around Africa. European powers were searching for alternative trade routes to Asia. Columbus set sail from Spain on August 3, 1492, on a journey funded by the Spanish Crown. After a brief stop in the Canary Islands, his three ships sailed across the Atlantic to the Bahamas on October 12. Over the next few months, Columbus sailed to Cuba, Hispaniola, and other Caribbean islands, imprisoning Indigenous people and collecting goods to take back to Spain. His voyages helped lay the foundations of Spanish colonisation of the Americas. However, he had not realised he had reached what Europeans would come to call the “New World” and continued to refer to the Americas as being located “at the end of the Orient”. Despite this, Columbus remained a relatively marginal figure in American history until the late 18th century, when the newly independent United States sought to construct a national history distinct from its colonial British past. Two books played a crucial role in elevating his stature in the US. William Robertson’s 1777 biography of Columbus portrayed him as a bold explorer constrained by the Old World, with a supposed mission to bring civilisation to Indigenous peoples. Washington Irving’s The Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (1828) dubbed “stunningly inaccurate” became the basis of the popular history of Columbus taught to generations of American children in schools. From the late 18th century, Columbus’ name became embedded in American identity. Towns and streets, including state capitals in South Carolina (1786) and Ohio (1812), were named for him. The renaming of King’s College in New York City as Columbia University in 1784, and the establishment of the national capital in the Territory of Columbia, later the District of Columbia, were further nods to his legacy, were all nods to his legacy, according to an article in The Nation magazine. For the 400th anniversary of Columbus’ voyage in 1892, then US President Benjamin Harrison declared October 12 a one-time national celebration. This came as a wider effort to placate Italian Americans following a mob lynching that ended up killing 11 Italian immigrants in New Orleans. For Italian migrants who set sail across the Atlantic to make a better life in the US, Columbus was an icon. For many Italian Americans, Columbus Day remains a celebration of their heritage, rather than of Columbus himself. In 1971, Columbus Day became an officially recognised federal holiday in the US, to be observed each year on the second Monday of October. During the 20th and 21st centuries, there was a growing recognition of the violence and exploitation associated with Columbus’ arrival in the Americas and the consequences of European colonisation for the millions of Indigenous people already living there. There are three main controversial aspects concerning his interactions with the Americas’ indigenous people: the use of violence and slavery, the forced conversion of native peoples to Christianity, and the introduction of diseases that would kill millions of native Americans. On his very first day in the Americas, Columbus imprisoned six natives. His journal entry from October 12, 1492 stated: “They should be good and intelligent servants, for I see that they say very quickly everything that is said to them. Our Lord pleasing, at the time of my departure I will take six of them from here to Your Highnesses in order that they may learn to speak.”

title: Test #30: Magnesium - Crucial But Don't as Supplements
text: Magnesium is vital to 300 chemical processes in the body, from energy production, muscle and nerve function to blood pressure regulation, heart and bone health. Magnesium glycinate works like a dream. Sore muscles? Rub on magnesium chloride. Tired? Magnesium malate is the perfect pick-me-up. In 1926, scientists established magnesium as a vital nutrient for life. A hundred years on, it appears to have grown larger than life. But despite what social media algorithms insist, how many mg of Mg does the human body actually needed as a supplement? “Zero,” says biochemist former professor at School of Bio-sciences. One argument, though, is that food may not contain as many minerals as it once did. A 2022 study published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition which compared the mineral content of fruits and vegetables available in the UK in 1940, 1991 and 2019-found magnesium concentrations had declined by 10% over the 80 years. One must first establish whether there is a deficiency, and a routine blood test does not do that. “Only 1% of the magnesium is found in the blood. Everything else is stored in the body, in bones and soft tissues.” “Magnesium is an intracellular ion. A deficiency cannot happen in a biological system unless one has certain disorders, diseases or medications that prevent absorption or result in excessive losses. Otherwise, a normal diet is enough. Every food, from legumes and seeds to vegetables, fruit and meat, has magnesium in it.” For example, for improved sleep, magnesium glycinate is recommended. "Magnesium is not doing the magic here, the amino acid glycine is. It lowers body temperature, which is calming. When you take a magnesium glycinate supplement, it gets hydrolysed in the gastrointestinal tract as magnesium and glycine. Kidneys filter out surplus magnesium through urine."
