Clinicians look at symptoms before recommending magnesium. "Cramping muscles, ‘I did not get enough sleep’, ‘my bones ache a little’, ‘my eye twitches’, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and diarrhoea. Now, these are statements that make me check for magnesium deficiency." The problem with self-supplementation, is that what works for one person may not work for another. "You go to a party, and every Tom, Dick and Harry who has run a marathon is spouting nutritional advice. And while it’s okay as long as they are talking about food, when people start handing out advice on supplements, you’re setting yourself up for issues in the long run." He says a runner came to his clinic with what appeared to be IBS symptoms, underwent a colonoscopy and endoscopy but the results were normal. "Among the products he was taking daily were a protein powder and a magnesium supplement. We stopped both. The gut improved. Then we brought the protein powder back, and he was fine. But the moment we brought back the magnesium supplement, his diarrhoea started. For another client with constipation, the same supplement worked brilliantly, which is why I say magnesium is not a one-size-fits-all." But certain demographics may benefit from supplementation. The elderly may need it, as their digestive systems absorb less from food. Recreational and professional athletes lose magnesium through sweat and urine. So, while a balanced diet is sufficient for the general population, research shows that 50% of athletes may have a magnesium deficiency. He says it shows up as reduced endurance, muscle soreness or lack of sleep. Diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal cramping are among the recognised effects of too much supplementation. Very high doses can have more serious consequences such as low blood pressure, muscle weakness and abnormal heart rhythms. People with impaired renal function must be careful because the kidneys play an important role in getting rid of excess magnesium, including antibiotics and bisphosphonates used for osteoporosis, can interact negatively with magnesium. The bottom line: Do we need magnesium? Absolutely. From a bottle? Not always.

title: Test #30: Sir Sayed - Visionary Make Education Agent of Change
text: More than a-century ago, when large sections of Indian Muslims were struggling to reconcile traditional learning with the demands of a rapidly changing world, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan saw education as the bridge between the two. A reformer, educationist and champion of scientific thought, he believed that a community unwilling to embrace modern knowledge risked being left behind. As his 209th birth anniversary is observed on Oct-17, his call for education, rational inquiry and social reform remains remarkably relevant. The most enduring institutional legacy of that vision is Aligarh Muslim University (AMU). In 1864, he founded the Scientific Society, with the objective of making modern knowledge more accessible through translations into Urdu. Decades later, the Constitution of India would include the development of scientific temper among the fundamental duties of citizens under Article-51A. Sir Syed firmly believed that a Muslim equipped with modern education and knowledge could become an asset to the country and contribute meaningfully to nation-building. Without education, he feared, the community would struggle to participate fully in economic and national progress. His emphasis on scientific thinking was strikingly forward-looking. Over the decades, the university has produced scientists, litterateurs, sportspersons and professionals who have distinguished themselves in their respective fields and contributed to the country. Sir Syed pioneered the Aligarh Movement, aimed at modernising education among Muslims in the 19th century. During his eventful career, he also served in the judicial and administrative system, including as a sub-judge. In the aftermath of the Industrial Revolution, the world was evolving rapidly in education, science and industry. The Muslim community, however, remained inadequately equipped to keep pace with these developments. This educational backwardness was among Sir Syed’s biggest concerns. In the 19th century, apart from religious instruction, Muslim education relied heavily on classical works such as Bostan and Gulistan, two celebrated works of Persian literature by Sheikh Saadi Shirazi. These were, undoubtedly, great works of literature, wisdom and moral philosophy, but contemporary education also needed greater engagement with science and economics to prepare the community for the approaching 20th century. Sir Syed’s vision was that Muslims should break the shackles of orthodoxy and provide their children with modern scientific education. A famous couplet aptly captures the dilemma confronting society: To be afraid of new ways and stubbornly cling to old customs is indeed a difficult stage in the life of nations. Sir Syed not only advocated modern education but also championed scientific rationalism and supported women’s education. The foundation of Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1877 marked a significant milestone in the history of modern education in India. Its origins can be traced to an educational institution established at Aligarh in 1875. Inspired by the universities of Oxford and Cambridge, Sir Syed sought to create an environment where traditional values could coexist with scientific knowledge and intellectual freedom. His efforts extended beyond classrooms, encouraging debate, independent thinking and social responsibility. In 1870, he launched the journal Tehzibul Akhlaq to promote social awareness and encourage reform within the community. Recognising the importance of collective participation, he established the Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886 to advance educational opportunities and promote cooperation. His vision gradually attracted scholars, teachers and reformers who shared his commitment to intellectual development. Following his death in 1898, the movement continued to inspire educational initiatives across the country. In 1920, Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College became Aligarh Muslim University, fulfilling an important institutional objective of the movement. Today, his educational philosophy offers a valuable reminder.

title: Test #31: India's Ancient Trees - Are we Protecting?
text: Trees are a symbol and a reminder of this and the interconnectedness of all things and need to be revered as such. Nature’s designs are full of such rhythmic, repetitive patterns called fractals complicated mathematical models built from simple repeated shapes diminishing in size every time they are repeated. India is full of old-growth trees, and the longest-lived ones often are spiritually significant. Many are Banyans (Ficus benghalensis), bustling and brooding mini-worlds of their own, spreading over acres in different parts of the country and living up to 500 years. Including the great Banyan of the Theosophical society in Chennai that once covered nearly 40,000 sq. ft. Then there are its cousins, the Peepals (Ficus religiosa). Like the Bodhi at Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment. The present tree is only around 145 years old, but traces its direct lineage back to over 2,500 years, with descendants spreading across the world. In the high Himalayas, the magnificent Himalayan Cedars (Cedrus deodara) live up to their name as the trees of the gods. For long, it was thought that there were no trees in India that were more than a thousand years old, but that may be changing now. How long a tree lives is decided by a combination of inherent and external factors, including genetic makeup, which dictates its potential growth rate and resistance to stressors that enable them to withstand harsh conditions and resist disease, contributing to long lives. Conversely, fast-growing species are shorter-lived. This is also likely to impact how climate change and related impacts drive tree population and ages across the world. As a direct result of their long-livedness, many trees alive today have been a silent witness to significant historical, social and ecological events. In the U.S., such trees are identified and listed as ‘Witness Trees’ and receive special protection and preservation under a ‘Witness Tree Protection Program’. This is something India could potentially mimic, considering its extraordinary cultural riches and the speed at which some of them are being lost. The complexity of the world cannot be understood fully by the limited shapes and lines of our invented geometry. Nature is wrinkled and rumpled, full of rough edges; irregular, yet perfect. A particular specimen in the arid zone of Lahaul in Himachal Pradesh has been reported to be more than 1,500 years old. Two particularly large specimens growing near a cluster of Shiva temples in Jageshwar in Uttarakhand are believed to be older than 900 years each. The related Shurs or Himalayan Pencil Cedars (Juniperus polycarpos) are also very long-lived, with many individuals growing in remote high-altitude regions believed to be more than 1,000 years old as well. Some of the oldest trees in India are not even Indian. The extraordinary Baobab (Adansonia digitata) has come to India from Africa over the millennia through trade relations, through Ethiopian warlords and later the Europeans. This “tree of life” is present across the country, most notably in Mandu, but nowhere in large numbers. And, perhaps, fractals are not just spatial but temporal as well. What if time were not the relentlessly ticking, linear movement we think it to be, but a 4D block where the past, present, and future co-exist? That is pretty much what long-lived trees do. They stand as silent witnesses to the passage of time, but on their own terms. Operating on principles beyond our frazzled timescales through mathematical patterns like the golden ratio. Measuring time as a physical record through seasons and growth rings, and slow conversations through root and fungal networks. Slowness, a virtue and strategy. Trees are living sentinels of history, witnesses to dramatic transformations of the earth’s landscape. Trees are also the way many of us instinctively connect to nature first as I do, for instance. My childhood memories of climbing trees, playing games with flowers and seeds, and writing fantasy stories inspired by my favourite tree giants drew me to urban ecology as an adult.

title: Test #31: Only People can Win India's Battery Race
text: India’s battery industry is at an inflection point, moving from ambition and investment to large-scale execution. We have announced more than 30 gigafactory projects, with ambitions of over 290 GWh by 2030. But factories and technology alone do not create a competitive industry. The question is not only how much we can build, but whether we have the people and the skills to build, run and continuously improve it. The challenge is evident. The India will need one to two lakh EV skilled professionals by 2030, but we are adding roughly 15,000 a year against a requirement closer to 30,000. Specialised talent lags demand by 20 to 25% across battery sciences, electrochemistry, power electronics and recycling. This is not only a skilling problem. Certifications get people to the factory gate. The hardest capabilities are built after that. Yield improvement, process discipline and troubleshooting come from repetition, and more often from failure. That knowledge is tacit and somewhere territorial that is nontransferable. It sits with the person who has seen a process fail and knows what to look for next time. Global experience shows where this learning happens. Scrap rates of 15 to 30% are common in the first years of cell manufacturing and stay near 10% after five years. Yield outputs, material optimisations, applications and flexibility are least understood in the initial phases till the process matures. Every point of scrap is money lost, and a lesson someone must capture and pass on. The shop floor will be India’s largest training cell. Workforce architecture and a pipeline around future skills: Industry, academia and government should define a common battery skills framework covering cell process engineering, electrochemistry, materials, automation, quality, BMS, safety and recycling. Map every role required and for every role: Skills required, proficiency level, scarce skills, India talent availability, salary benchmarks, transferable talent pools. It should shape curricula, apprenticeships and certification, and success must be measured by capability, not by MoUs. That is also why the talent we already have matters. Around 35% of the ICE-trained shop floor workforce needs structured reskilling for battery, software and grid roles. But these are people who already know quality systems and what a process drifting out of control feels like. They learn a new chemistry faster than a new hire learns a factory. The opportunity is to redeploy experience India has already paid for. This gets harder because lithium ion, sodium ion and solid-state technologies are advancing faster than curricula can follow. Anyone trained only on today’s chemistry will be behind in a few years. Professionals need grounding in the fundamentals of electrochemistry, materials science and manufacturing, because fundamentals travel across chemistries in a way product training does not. The same logic applies to AI and automation. A predictive system can flag an anomaly, but someone still has to interpret it, question the output and respond when the process changes. The faster the technology moves, the more it needs people who understand why it behaves as it does. AI raises the premium on human judgement. The additional challenge is national policy sponsorship or institutions that standardise skills the way NASSCOM has done for IT skills. India needs a system that builds capability, converts it into expertise, and multiplies that expertise. Nurture expertise through apprenticeship: Structured 12-to-24-month pathways across manufacturing, quality, maintenance, process engineering and R&D can turn qualifications into expertise. Take people from adjacent industries and convert them. Then create an industry-backed battery academy where companies can actually hire the graduates. A destination for battery talent: We compete with China, Korea, Germany and the US, and with semiconductors and aerospace, for ambitious engineers. Battery careers must offer meaningful technology, a steep learning curve and mobility across R&D, manufacturing and leadership.

title: Test #32: Digital India Needs Wi-Fi for Everyone
text: India has around 4-lakh public hotspots. France, with a population a fraction of ours, has more than 13-million; the world has over 600-million. For a nation that prides itself on its digital public infrastructure, this is a gap worth explaining and closing. The idea was born in April 2016, Any consumer, should be able to walk up to any Wi-Fi hotspot and connect with a single click “like an Uber for hotspots” and anyone with a spare connection could sell a little of it to a passer-by. At TRAI, we built exactly that: An open, interoperable architecture with no central gatekeeper, in which anyone could set up or aggregate a hotspot, and a single app would discover the nearest one, verify the user, take his few rupees through any wallet, and connect him seamlessly across every provider. We called the retail outlet a Public Data Office, or PDO, and the analogy we kept returning to was the humble PCO the public call office that put a telephone within walking distance of nearly every Indian by turning a shopkeeper into its keeper. The PDO was the PCO reborn for the internet: The corner shop or tea stall selling connectivity by the sachet, a rupee’s worth at a time. India has done what no other country has: Made digital payments free, instant, and universal, and leads the world in mobile-data use. Yet, in one adjacent field we remain a laggard. Public Wi-Fi the cheap, shared, last-mile connectivity that lets a citizen buy a little internet wherever she is has barely taken root. TRAI issued a consultation paper in July 2016, submitted formal recommendations in March 2017, and piloted the idea with eight entities running some six hundred hotspots. The pilot worked: One-time registration, interoperability, easy payment all proven. The Prime Minister himself was shown the system in June 2018 and was greatly taken with it; he wanted it launched within weeks. Yet it was not until December 2020 that the framework was finally approved by the Union cabinet, as PM-WANI the Prime Minister’s Wi-Fi Access Network Interface. Five years on, the promise remains largely unfulfilled. Why? The single biggest reason is the cost of backhaul: A small PDO is made to pay more for the very same fibre broadband that a household buys cheaply, which destroys the shopkeeper’s economics before he has sold a single sachet. Add to this a persistent official tenderness towards incumbent telecom operators, never enthusiastic about a million small competitors selling connectivity outside their control. The commonest objection now is that mobile data is so cheap that nobody needs Wi-Fi by the sachet. It is plausible, and wrong. Data now comes bundled in fixed monthly plans priced from a couple of hundred rupees, which the poorest cannot always afford, and which are of little help to a student joining an online class when the family’s one data plan is on someone else’s phone. The sachet has not become unnecessary; it has merely been abolished by the operators’ tariff design, even as demand has exploded online education, telemedicine, government services precisely where mobile signal serves worst. There is a strategic case too. Public Wi-Fi runs on unlicensed spectrum, sparing congested mobile networks the costly spectrum they buy at auction. Leaving a billion-plus people’s connectivity entirely to two or three mobile companies, besides, is a dangerous dependence on a duopoly. A dense, open, independent Wi-Fi layer is a strategic de-risking of the nation’s digital life an alternative no single commercial interest can switch off. What makes the delay especially galling is that the missing piece is already lying in the ground. BharatNet, begun in 2011 to carry optical fibre to every one of India’s 2.5 lakh gram panchayats, has absorbed more than Rs 48,000 crore more than five times what Aadhaar cost and reached over 2 lakh of them. Yet it returns almost nothing, for a great trunk of bandwidth with no retail distribution is a pipe with no taps. Even a fully monetised BharatNet will leave gaps in hilly, forested terrain fibre may never reach and that is where Starlink and the other satellite-broadband entrants see a market;

title: Test #32: MPHC JJA 2023 - 210/09/2023 - S2
text: Section 18 of the Domestic Violence Act relates to protection order. In terms of Section 18 of the Act, intention of the legislature is to provide more protection to woman. Section 20 of the Act empowers the court to order for monetary relief to the aggrieved party. When acts of domestic violence are alleged, before issuing notice, the court has to be prima facie satisfied that there have been instances of domestic violence. In the present case, the respondent has made allegations of domestic violence against fourteen appellants. Appellant No.14 is the husband and appellants No.1 and 2 are the parents-in-law of the respondent. All other appellants are relatives of parents-in-law of the respondent. Appellants No. 3, 5, 9, 11 and 12 are the brothers of father-in-law of the respondent. Appellants No. 4, 6 and 10 are the wives of appellants No. 3, 5 and 9 respectively. Appellants No. 7 and 8 are the parents of appellant No. 1. Appellants No. 1 to 6 and 14 are residents of Chennai. Appellants No. 7 to 10 are the residents of Rajasthan and appellants No. 11 to 13 are the residents of Gujarat. Admittedly, the matrimonial house of the respondent and appellant No. 1 has been at Chennai. In so far as appellant No.14 husband of the respondent and appellants No. 1 and 2 Parents-in-law, there are averments of domestic violence alleging that they have taken away the jewellery of the respondent gifted to her by her father during marriage and the alleged acts of harassment to the respondent. There are no specific allegations as to how other relatives of appellant No.14 have caused the acts of domestic violence. It is also not known as to how other relatives who are residents of Gujarat and Rajasthan can be held responsible for award of monetary relief to the respondent. The High Court was not right in saying that there was prima facie case against the other appellants No. 3 to 13. Since there are no specific allegations against appellants No. 3 to 13, the criminal case of domestic violence against them cannot be continued. The Domestic Violence Act is a piece of remedial and beneficial legislation, and it must be construed so as to advance the protection of women from abuse within the shared household. At the same time, the beneficial nature of the enactment does not dispense with the need for a foundation in fact. A court exercising jurisdiction under the Act is required to examine whether the application discloses, at least prima facie, acts of domestic violence attributable to the persons against whom relief is sought. The Act cannot be used as an instrument to rope in every relative of the husband, irrespective of the role played by each of them. The definition of the expression respondent under the Act extends to relatives of the husband, and this widens the class of persons against whom proceedings may be initiated. However, the width of the definition is not a licence for indiscriminate implication. Where the pleadings are vague and omnibus, and where the complaint is silent about the time, place and manner in which a particular relative committed an act of violence, the court cannot presume complicity merely on the basis of kinship. A general allegation that all the relatives joined in harassing the aggrieved woman, without particulars, does not satisfy the requirement of prima facie satisfaction before notice is issued. It is equally relevant that the relatives in question did not reside in the matrimonial home and lived in different States, far away from the place where the couple cohabited. Domestic violence presupposes a domestic relationship and some measure of shared living or proximity, in which the alleged acts could actually have taken place. In the absence of any averment showing that such relatives visited the household, interfered in the marital life of the couple, or participated in the alleged harassment, it is difficult to see how they could be made answerable for protection orders or monetary relief under Sections 18 and 20.

title: Test #33: Patan's Burried Water Palace
text: Quixotic as it sounds, an exquisite, seven-storey palace once vanished beneath ordinary mud for nearly 900 years, hidden just beneath a dusty riverbank in Gujarat: Rani ki Vav, the Queen’s Stepwell at Patan. Commissioned by Queen Udayamati, wife of the Chaulukya king Bhima-I (reign roughly 1022-1064), the structure honours his memory; one historian dates its construction to 1032, while a later chronicle claims work began in 1063 and lasted nearly two decades. Either way, what emerged was not a simple water source but an inverted temple: seven descending levels, zealously carved with over 500 major sculptures and well beyond 1,000 smaller figures, arranged around 212 pillars. Archaeologists working through the 1980s carefully removed centuries of packed silt, revealing stair after stair of sculpture in near-pristine condition, protected rather than damaged by its long burial underground. Among the finds was a weathered image believed to depict Udayamati herself, a rare instance of an Indian queen commemorated within her own commissioned monument. The Archaeological Survey of India now maintains the site, which measures roughly 65 metres long, 20 metres wide, and 28 metres deep, with its central well reaching about 30 metres down a narrow 10-metre shaft. Modern recognition came gradually. UNESCO inscribed the stepwell on its World Heritage List on 22 June 2014, citing both its artistic merit and its rare architectural form among the many stepwells scattered across western India. Four years later, in July 2018, the Reserve Bank of India placed an image of Rani ki Vav on the reverse of the new hundred-rupee note, giving the monument sudden, nationwide visibility far beyond heritage circles. Why build a temple pointing downward? Because for Udayamati’s Maru-Gurjara architects, water itself was sacred, and journeying toward it meant journeying toward the divine a quixotic, almost paradoxical idea executed with astonishing precision. Jagged panels depict Vishnu’s ten avatars, elephants, warriors, and courtly dancers, carved from local sandstone with an exactitude that still puzzles engineers studying the site’s drainage and symmetry today. Standing on the banks of the long-vanished Saraswati River, the stepwell eventually fell victim to its own setting. Repeated flooding buried the entire structure under silt, and by the nineteenth century only a well shaft and a few scattered pillars still rose above the surrounding fields. Local memory of its purpose faded almost entirely; villagers reportedly knew only that something old and carved lay beneath the soil. When British surveyors Henry Cousens and James Burgess examined the site in the 1890s, they found barely enough exposed stonework to guess at the scale of what lay hidden below, and serious excavation did not begin until the 1940s, under the former Baroda State administration. Full restoration took decades more. Tourists who once needed detailed directions now arrive with the banknote itself as an informal map, comparing the printed image against the real stonework in front of them. Historians still debate several points. Was Udayamati a widow when she commissioned the project, or did King Karna, her son, complete major portions after her death? Records remain thin, and later chronicles sometimes contradict each other on both dates and sequence. What nobody disputes is the scale of ambition: a queen choosing to build not a palace for living but a monument meant to outlast her, carved entirely by hand across a generation of skilled labour. Officials in Gujarat describe the stepwell as a prominent part of the state’s wider heritage push, often placing it beside other major sites when courting a global tourism audience. Public records held by the state archaeology department now have documented roughly 7 lakh visits each year, a figure officials call both remarkable and, by past standards, almost unimaginable. Various heritage experts argue the site offers a rich case worth close study: an enduring example of how patient.

title: Test #33: Indina Rhino Vision - A True Conservation
text: As the Indian Forest Service marks the 60th year of its inception, the spectacular revival of the rhinoceros in Indian jungles is one of the greatest conservation success stories in modern history. Centuries ago, the animal roamed freely across the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Relentless hunting and rapid agricultural expansion left just 20-animals surviving in Assam’s Kaziranga by the early 20th century. By the mid-2000s, India’s herd stabilised at 2,500. The Indian Rhino Vision-2020 (IRV2020) was launched in 2005 to push up the population to 3,000 across seven protected areas in Assam. Today, the count exceeds 3,200, with Kaziranga alone housing 2,600. This resurgence has occurred alongside a broader environmental milestone: India significantly expanded its green cover despite a growing human population. To anchor these habitat gains, the Wildlife Institute of India is currently mapping a National Grassland Atlas. This initiative supports India’s 2070 net-zero carbon target, a goal that the rhino naturally champions. Using its prehensile upper lip to pluck grass cleanly without uprooting it, the rhino mirrors sustainable land management. Protecting them also safeguards dense grasslands, which act as vital carbon sinks. Unlike elephants, rhinos rely on a solitary, reactive, and localised instincts, depending entirely on intense, site-specific territorial attachment. Consequently, saving the species requires strict, localised “fortress protection” rather than expansive landscape corridors. While Africa holds larger populations across its vast savannas, India’s rhinos are packed into tiny, high-density sanctuaries in Assam, West Bengal’s floodplains, and Uttar Pradesh’s Dudhwa National Park. Operating under immense demographic strain, the available area per animal in Pobitora has shrunk drastically, resulting in the highest rhino density in the world. Surrounded by human settlements, these sanctuaries have become ecological islands. Under IRV2020, translocating rhinos to restored habitats like Assam’s Manas National Park has successfully mitigated epidemic risks. When organised poaching syndicates targeted the park, the threat forced a swift enforcement evolution. The forest department deployed armed police commandos, drone surveillance, and advanced real-time satellite tracking. Today, the annual poaching rate in Kaziranga has dropped to zero. Crucially, this model was built alongside local communities. The government publicly burned thousands of confiscated horns to shatter medicinal myths, while forest departments transformed local youth into active anti-poaching stakeholders. Tourism revenue now funds village schools and health care, ensuring that when rhinos stray into fields, communities herd them back safely. Karbi elders tell a beautiful folktale: “The Goddess Kajir used the rhinos to till her heavenly fields. When a rhino wanders into our paddies and eats our grain, it is not a loss; it is the footprint of the Goddess bringing good fortune.” Yet, challenges loom. Trapped on disconnected ecological islands, rhinos are forced by annual monsoon floods to migrate toward higher ground, crossing heavily trafficked roads where their predictable tracks make them easy targets. Expanding secure wildlife corridors remains imperative to ensure that the rhino’s resonant, primitive bellow never falls silent in our wild landscapes. Several new initiatives are now underway to address these vulnerabilities. Forest authorities have constructed elevated artificial highlands and designated safe passages, allowing rhinos to retreat swiftly from rising floodwaters. Speed restrictions, night-time traffic bans, and prominent warning signs are being enforced along vulnerable highways to prevent fatal collisions. Meanwhile, scientists use radio collars and GPS technology to monitor animal movements, making it easier to anticipate emerging threats. Ultimately, the combined strength of community participation, tourism revenue, and continuous surveillance offers the most reliable guarantee for the species’ secure future, demonstrating that coexistence between people and wildlife is not merely desirable but entirely achievable.

title: Test #34: Legal - SCI Civil Appeal No. 7650 of 2021
text: This civil appeal, preferred jointly by the appellant husband and respondent wife under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, challenges the judgment and order dated 17th November, 2021 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Application No. 1420 of 2021, affirming the order of the learned Principal Judge, Family Court, Hisar, rejecting the joint application filed by the spouses seeking waiver of the statutory six-month cooling-off period under Section 13-B(2). The matrimonial union between the parties, both highly qualified senior government professionals, was solemnized on 10th September, 2020 at Chandigarh according to Hindu rites. Due to acute incompatibility and divergent lifestyle philosophies, the marriage proved a complete non-starter, and the spouses separated permanently after cohabiting for only three days. After living apart for more than fourteen months, during which multiple counseling sessions conducted by senior family elders and institutional mediators failed completely, the parties executed a comprehensive settlement agreement dated 28th September, 2021. Under the settlement, the parties resolved all claims regarding return of streedhan, permanent alimony, and mutual maintenance, and filed a joint petition for dissolution of marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 before the Family Court, Hisar on 30th September, 2021. Contemporaneously, the parties moved a joint application praying for waiver of the statutory six-month waiting period prescribed under Section 13-B(2). The Family Court rejected the waiver, holding that it possessed no statutory discretion to reduce the six-month period, which order was affirmed by the High Court. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for both parties submitted that forcing parties whose marriage has irretrievably broken down to wait for six months serves no public purpose, prolonging mental agony. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Amit Kumar v. Suman Beniwal, reported in 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1270, and Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur, reported in (2017) 8 SCC 746, authoritatively settled the interpretation of Section 13-B(2) of the Act. The Court held that the six-month cooling-off period prescribed in Section 13-B(2) is directory and not mandatory. The legislative object of the waiting period was to safeguard against hasty divorces and provide an opportunity for reconciliation. However, where the court is satisfied that the marriage has irretrievably broken down, all genuine efforts at mediation and conciliation have proved futile, and the parties have settled all ancillary issues regarding permanent alimony, streedhan, and custody, the court must exercise sound judicial discretion to waive the statutory waiting period. In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan, reported in 2023 SCC OnLine SC 544, the Constitution Bench reaffirmed that forcing spouses to cohabit in an empty legal shell causes deep emotional cruelty. The parties lived together for only three days, have lived apart for fifteen months, and are adamant on parting peacefully. Requiring them to wait for six months is an exercise in futility. The orders of the Family Court and the High Court are set aside, the statutory cooling-off period is waived, and a decree of divorce by mutual consent is granted, dissolving the marriage between the parties. Where there is a chance of reconciliation, however slight, the cooling period of six months from the date of filing of the divorce petition should be enforced. However, if there is no possibility of reconciliation, it would be meaningless to prolong the agony of the parties to the marriage. Thus, if the marriage has broken down irretrievably, the spouses have been living apart for a long time, but not been able to reconcile their differences and have mutually decided to part, it is better to end the marriage, to enable both the spouses to move on with the life.

title: Test #34: What are Chirality and Handedness?
text: Many chemical molecules that make up substances, including the organic molecules that make up things like DNA, also possess this property of chirality. The mirror-images of a molecule, the left and right-glove so to say, are called ‘enantiomers.’ Paradoxically the organic molecules that make up living organisms are overwhelmingly either left-handed or right-handed and in nature do not present themselves in 50:50 proportions. This property, of ‘homochirality,’ is as if a fashion house decided to base its entire business on making only left-handed gloves and accessories customised to it. In 1953 Charles Frank, a theoretical physicist at the University of Bristol, used mathematics to analyse why the molecules of life presented themselves so biased. His model needs three things: a substance those catalyses its own production (autocatalysis), one that does so for a single hand (enantioselective catalysis), and one that suppresses its mirror twin, what he called an “anti-catalyst” for its antimer. Asymmetric, or enantioselective catalysis, had already earned Nobels in 2001 and 2021. What nobody had shown was mutual antagonism, or the marriage of autocatalysis and asymmetry and this was where Kagan, in 1986, and Soai, in 1995, made their contribution. Every amino acid, the building blocks of protein, comes in the “left” (L) form, every sugar in your DNA the “right” (D) form. The puzzle is that an ordinary laboratory reaction cannot manage this in sufficient numbers. When amino acids are synthesised in labs they yield a 50:50 mix, or a ‘racemate,’ as the term goes. The French chemist Louis Pasteur observed this as far back as 1848, when bacteria devoured one mirror form of tartaric acid and left the other untouched. A drug works by attaching to the surface of enzymes or receptors; like a password fits to lock. In the world of enantiomers, the same letters of the password in the wrong order can at best be harmless and at worst be positively harmful. Like repeated wrong passwords can completely lock you out of a system. The drug thalidomide offers a cautionary tale. First marketed as a sedative, it left thousands of children with birth defects in the early 1960s. For a long time it was attributed to the presence of both enantiomers when the drug was made available, however subsequent analysis says that’s only part of the explanation. However the broader principle is that enantiomers matter. Another example is ethambutol, a first-line tuberculosis drug. Its (S,S) form is about 500 times more potent against the bacillus than its (R,R) mirror image. Yet the optic-nerve damage that is its chief side effect is, according to the pharmacology literature, equal across the isomers and rises with dose and duration. Therefore ensuring that labs must try making and administering as much of the (S,S) form and minimise the other matters because it means that a patient might need less of the curative drug and be less exposed to nerve damage. But the problem remains, how to ensure that labs make extremely pure versions of the desired form. Combine them and even a tiny initial difference, where one form is present slightly more than the other, snowballs exponentially. It took decades. Autocatalysis was known. Kagan, then at Paris-Sud, challenged a dogma. Chemists believed that for more product purity, more of a catalyst’s chiral ingredient had to be proportionally pure. Therefore the race was for ever purer ingredients. Kagan asked what the metal in a catalyst actually does, and reasoned that it grips not one but two chiral molecules (the “ligands” that give the catalyst its handedness). Suppose you build the catalyst from a mix of the two enantiomers, say 75% right-handed and 25% left-handed. The metal picks its two partners at random, so three kinds of catalyst form: right-right (about 56%), left-left (about 6%) and a mixed right-left pair (about 38%). The two matched pairs work well. The mixed pair barely works at all, so it sits idle and takes its share of both hands out of play.

title: Test #35: Legal - PHHC Cr. No. 9266 of 2025 (O&M)
text: The respondent-landlord instituted the civil suit in February 2021 seeking possession of commercial shop premises and recovery of arrears of rent. In his original written statement filed on 14th October, 2021, the petitioner admitted the existence of a registered commercial lease agreement dated 15th March, 2018, contending merely that rent was regularized up to date through cash receipts. The trial proceeded, issues were settled under Order XIV Rule 1 CPC, and the respondent plaintiff concluded his entire oral and documentary evidence. At the stage when the suit was posted for defendant evidence, the petitioner filed an application under Order VI Rule 17 CPC seeking to amend paragraph 3 of the written statement, proposing to substitute his earlier admission with a plea asserting that no lease deed was ever executed and that the registered instrument produced by the plaintiff was forged and fabricated. This civil revision petition, preferred under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, challenges the order dated 18th November, 2025 passed by the learned Civil Judge (Junior Division), Gurugram in Civil Suit No. 412 of 2021, whereby the application filed by the petitioner-defendant under Order VI Rule 17 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 seeking leave to amend his written statement post-commencement of trial was dismissed on the ground of complete absence of due diligence under the statutory proviso. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that procedural rules are handmaids of justice, and liberal amendment should be permitted to resolve the real controversy between the parties under Order VI Rule 17 CPC without causing prejudice to the opposing party. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that the statutory proviso to Order VI Rule 17 enacts an inflexible bar against entertaining amendments after commencement of trial unless due diligence is established. Dismissing the revision petition, this Court holds that the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 acts as a jurisdictional embargo. In the seminal ruling in Vidyabai v. Padmalatha, reported in (2009) 2 SCC 409, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that once the trial has commenced with the filing of affidavits of evidence under Order XVIII Rule 4 CPC, the court has no jurisdiction to permit amendments unless it records a definite finding that in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the plea before the commencement of trial. In Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons, reported in (2009) 10 SCC 84, it was authoritatively settled that an amendment that withdraws an unequivocal judicial admission or introduces an entirely contradictory stand to displace the plaintiff's case cannot be permitted. The petitioner had admitted the execution of the lease deed in 2021 and offered no plausible explanation as to why the plea of forgery was not raised initially. Permitting such belated amendments after the closure of the plaintiff's evidence defeats the legislative objective of expeditious trials and prejudices substantive justice. Finding no jurisdictional error or patent perversity in the impugned order, the revision petition is dismissed with costs of Rs. 20,000/-. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Ramesh Chand @ Baag v. State of Himachal Pradesh, rendered on 8th September, 2025, and Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of M.P., reported in (2012) 9 SCC 750, authoritatively restated the statutory hierarchy governing age determination. Furthermore, medical ossification is not an exact science and carries a recognized margin of error of one to two years, which must invariably enure to the benefit of the accused. The school records being authentic, the appellant is declared a juvenile on the date of the offence. The sentence of life imprisonment is set aside, remitting the matter to the Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate reformative orders.

title: Test #35: Patriarchy - Bird with Unequal Wings Can't Fly
text: Systemic barriers must be dismantled to achieve true gender justice. The Right to Equality is enshrined as a Fundamental Right under Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India. Yet, legal text alone cannot change lived realities without shifting cultural consciousness. There are legislative reforms removing discriminatory laws, increased female representation in governance, and decline in child marriage and female genital mutilation. However, women hold only 30% of managerial positions globally; India has a dismal record of pervasive sexual violence and dowry deaths. As the current international order fractures under the combined weight of rising inequality, geopolitical fragmentation, democratic erosion, climate instability, and a fraying respect for international law, we must confront a foundational crisis: pervasive malaise of patriarchy. Baha’i teachings assert that patriarchy fosters a regressive mindset. By sustaining structural inequality between women and men, it paralyses collective human progress. Patriarchy fosters a regressive mindset by sustaining structural inequality between women and men; it paralyses collective human progress. Baha’is view humanity as a bird with two wings: male and female. If these two wings are unequal in strength, the bird cannot fly. Adding insult to injury is the uneven distribution of resources and opportunities. If we are on top of the food chain and are conscious beings, then why does discrimination persist against half the global population? Why don’t we strengthen the weakened wing? Extensive empirical research supports the Baha’i premise: societies that deprive women and girls of their rights invariably lag. When nations oppress or exclude women from the mainstream, they self-inflict a massive brain drain, starving themselves of diverse ideas and untapped potential. Furthermore, because patriarchal societies operate strictly through rigid power dynamics, they default to aggression rather than paternal, nurturing care. This is devastatingly obvious in conflict zones and failed nation-states. Baha’i teachings recognise that patriarchy severely restricts men, too: “As long as women are prevented from attaining their highest possibilities, so long will men be unable to achieve greatness which might be theirs.” Religion has historically been weaponised to reinforce patriarchy in three intersecting ways: Using religious ideology to legitimise male authority; employing faith-based personal laws to restrict women’s rights regarding inheritance and autonomy; allowing patriarchal norms to subtly govern across major religious traditions. The Baha’i writings declare: “Women and men have always been and shall be equal before God.” The denial of this equality breeds harmful attitudes in men that bleed from the family unit into the workplace, political arenas, and ultimately onto the stage of international relations. Only when women are welcomed into full partnership will the moral and psychological climate change sufficiently for international peace to emerge. The elimination of prejudice requires a global system of justice built upon equity and fairness for the entire human family. Justice finds its ultimate fulfilment in unconditional love. It clears the path for unity, secures human well-being, and possesses the power to transform society. It is important to ensure that the bird must have equally strong wings to carry the civilisation forward with elan. Education offers the most reliable pathway towards this transformation. When a girl is educated, she uplifts her family, her community, and eventually her nation, for knowledge multiplies when shared. Baha’i teachings therefore urge that, where resources are scarce, the daughter’s education be prioritised, since she is the mother and first teacher of the next generation. Equally vital is the role of men and boys, who must become active allies rather than passive observers, nurturing empathy and shared responsibility within the household.

title: Test #36: Jantar Mantar - Host Varying Degrees of Discontent
text: Until the early 1990s, Jantar Mantar was more likely to feature in a school excursion itinerary than on a protest banner. The 18th-century astronomical observatory, built by Jaipur’s Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh-II, was a Delhi sightseeing stop, its Misra Yantra even inspiring the logo of the 1982 Asian Games in the Capital. Today, the neem-lined stretch outside the observatory is better known not only in Delhi, but across India as a place where people come to make themselves heard. Farmers, workers, veterans, students, activists and ordinary citizens have gathered here over three decades to challenge decisions they believe have ignored their grievances. On Monday, however, Delhi Police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest venue, redirecting demonstrators to three other sites across the city. The decision marks another turn in the history of a space that became central to Delhi’s protest culture after demonstrations were banned at the Boat Club lawns near India Gate in the early 1990s. In 1988, farmer leader Mahendra Singh Tikait had led a week-long agitation at the Boat Club. But the scale of the gathering and the unease it caused eventually led to restrictions on protests there. Jantar Mantar Road was then notified as a designated protest site. Historian Ramachandra Guha, in India After Gandhi, describes how Rajpath in the early 1990s became a village of tents, each representing a different cause. Hill peasants gave way to industrial workers, Maharashtra farmers to Tibetan refugees, and Konkani speakers to Hindu monks demanding a ban on cow slaughter. Worried about the impression such demonstrations made on foreign visitors, the government dismantled the tents and cleared the lawns. The protesters regrouped near Jantar Mantar, Guha writes, moving away from the immediate gaze of the state but into view of citizens passing through the busy Connaught Place shopping district. For the next 33 years, the half-kilometer stretch became a public ledger of discontent from across India. According to Delhi Police estimates, the Parliament Street police station receives more than 24,000 requests annually for permission to hold protests. In 2017, Tamil Nadu farmers held mice in their hands and mouths to draw attention to the agrarian crisis. A man from Madhya Pradesh spent years protesting after government records declared him dead. Ex-servicemen staged a relay hunger strike lasting more than 700 days over the implementation of One Rank One Pension (OROP), while followers of jailed self-styled godmen camped at the site seeking the release of their leaders. Jantar Mantar was also among the early epicentres of the Anna Hazare-led anti-corruption movement in April 2011. Parents and relatives of murdered Noida teenager Aarushi Talwar gathered there in 2011 and 2013 demanding justice. Retired military and paramilitary personnel returned over several years to press their OROP demands. The annual Delhi Queer Pride movement, too, has found space in the area. Its history also includes campaigns that are not as conventional: protests by animal lovers against the use of cow’s milk, demonstrations by those opposed to street dogs, the Akhil Bharatiya Joota Maaro Andolan, and a lone protester from Chandauli who believed satellites were hacking into people’s brains in his hometown. More recently, the site hosted the January 2023 protest by women wrestlers seeking an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment by then Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) president Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh. Later, in 2026, demonstrations and a hunger strike involving Sonam Wangchuk and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), between June 6 and July 25, spilled on to Tolstoy Marg and Sansad Marg. The agitation culminated in the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. But the protest site has been contested territory. Residents of nearby houses have complained of noise, blocked entrances, garbage and sanitation problems.

title: Test #36: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 793-94 of 2022
text: These criminal appeals, preferred by the convict appellants under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, challenge the judgment and order dated 12th February, 2021 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh in Criminal Appeal No. 214 of 2018, affirming the conviction recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the search and seizure panchnama violated the mandatory provisions of Section 100(4) Cr.P.C. The prosecution case involved a blind double homicide committed on 14th September, 2014 in an urban commercial warehouse in Gwalior. The police case rested entirely upon circumstantial evidence, with the principal incriminating circumstance being the alleged recovery of a country-made firearm and bloodstained clothing pursuant to disclosure memos (Exhibits P-12 and P-13) recorded under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. During the trial, it emerged that the investigating officer conducted the search and recovery in a crowded commercial marketplace at broad daylight on 18th September, 2014, but failed to associate independent local residents as panch witnesses. Instead, the seizure memo was witnessed solely by two subordinate police constables attached to the same police station. In cross-examination, the investigating officer admitted that civilian shopkeepers and passersby were present at the scene, but no written notices were issued to them under Section 100(8) Cr.P.C. to join the search. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the complete failure to join independent panch witnesses rendered the alleged discovery untrustworthy and fabricated. It was submitted that under Section 100(4) of the Cr.P.C., the association of independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality is a mandatory statutory requirement. Allowing the appeals, this Court in Rajesh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, reported in (2023) 9 SCC 691, authoritatively restated the statutory duties governing searches and seizures under Section 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (now Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). The Court held that Section 100(4) is a vital statutory safeguard enacted to ensure the fairness, credibility, and transparency of police recoveries, guarding citizens against planted evidence and fabricated recoveries. While the testimony of police officers is not inherently untrustworthy, when recoveries of lethal weapons are allegedly made in populated localities, the total omission to associate independent local witnesses without plausible explanation casts a heavy shadow of doubt over the genuineness of the panchnama. In Gorakh Nath Prasad v. State of Bihar, reported in (2018) 2 SCC 745, and Sanjeev v. State of H.P., reported in (2022) 6 SCC 294, this Court established that where independent civilian witnesses are readily available but intentionally bypassed in favour of subordinate police constables, the recovery cannot be relied upon to sustain a conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC. The circumstantial chain being deprived of its foundational link, the prosecution failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence of life imprisonment are set aside, and the appellants are acquitted. Quashing the process qua the petitioner, this Court holds that vicarious liability in penal law is an exception created by statute and must be strictly construed. In the landmark rulings in National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal, reported in (2010) 3 SCC 330, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry, reported in (2022) 10 SCC 152, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that mere reproduction of the statutory wording of Section 141 is insufficient. The complainant must plead specific overt roles demonstrating that the director was responsible for the transaction leading to the issuance of the dishonoured cheque. A non-executive or independent director who does not participate in executive administration cannot be subjected to criminal trial merely because of holding a board directorship.

title: Test #37: A Photon That is Conscious
text: Light, one of the most mysterious entities, it has baffled scientists, philosophers, poets, and thinkers for centuries. It remains an enigma, almost a metaphysical conundrum for Physics. Max Planck, widely regarded as the father of quantum theory, was investigating black-body radiation to understand how the spectrum of radiation emitted by a heated body varies with temperature. When existing theories failed to explain experimental observations, Planck introduced a revolutionary idea: energy could be emitted or absorbed in discrete packets, or quanta, rather than continuously. This breakthrough, announced in 1900, laid the foundation for quantum physics. This unravelled an entirely new understanding of the subatomic realm. Exploring the properties and mysteries of light has provided rich dividends for the entire scientific community. Sunlight, the benefactor of life, powers photosynthesis through chlorophyll. It is a natural, eternal source of energy that sustains life on this planet. The photon surely must be more than just a Bosonic subatomic particle. The special theory of relativity was a moment of epiphany for Albert Einstein. He imagined what would happen if he could run fast enough to catch up to a beam of light. This revealed a deep contradiction in the physics of his era and changed how humanity understands time and space. Just imagining being alongside a beam of light led to one of the greatest discoveries. A ray of light that enlightened entire mankind. This year’s Nobel Prize in Medicine was given to a group of scientists for their work in optogenetics, a biological technique used to manipulate the activity of neurons or other cells with light. Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel discovered a unique protein, channel rhodopsin, in a single-celled alga. Karl Deisseroth transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells. This discovery has opened new frontiers and laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience. Receptors that are activated by light triggering genetic activity in neuronal cells and networks. The photon is the fundamental particle of light, named after the Greek word phos, meaning ‘light’. The photon is the quantum, or smallest possible unit, of light. This quaint particle is known to alter its behaviour depending on whether it is being observed. The modified double-slit experiment has unambiguously proven this fact and stunned physicists. A photon that is conscious. This is perhaps what Saint Dnaneshwar alluded to when he proclaimed that every particle of this universe is a manifestation of intelligent consciousness. Observation is untenable without the medium of light. And quantum physics mandates an observer for collapse of the wave function. Could interaction between photons and a cognitive apparatus trigger this collapse of the wave function? This collapse remains an enigma in quantum physics. Advait Vedanta postulates experiencing the underlying undifferentiated singularity that unites the triputi, trinity, of observer, observed and observation as a state of realisation. Tukaram, in a famous composition, equates the merging of this trilogy with enlightenment: Sandili triputi, deep ujala ghati – triad fell away; the lamp within vessel was illuminated. The trinity of observer, observed and observation sublimates, instantly illuminating the light of realisation. Could the photon create an illusion of observation? Is that what our scriptures mean by maya? A massless particle that sustains life, eliminates darkness, triggers genes, and is simultaneously a wave and a particle. A particle that collapses the wave function. A particle that might even cast a spell of an illusory universe. A particle that will forever intrigue, stimulate, perhaps never reveal its true nature. Perhaps that is why light continues to humble the finest minds. Every answer it yields seems to open a deeper question, whether about the nature of reality or the role of the observer within it. Physics may measure its speed and describe its behaviour with elegant equations, yet its essence remains elusive.

title: Test #37: Legal - BHC Writ P. No. 2788 of 2019
text: The Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation Limited (MMRCL) submitted an application to the Tree Authority seeking permission to clear vegetation for the Colaba-Bandra-SEEPZ Metro Line-3 project. The Tree Officer published public notices in local newspapers inviting objections. In response, over eighty-two thousand public objections were submitted by environmentalists, residents, and civil society organizations, highlighting that Aarey Colony serves as the unfragmented green lung of Mumbai, contiguous with Sanjay Gandhi National Park, sheltering rich biodiversity, wildlife corridors, and natural water catchments. The Tree Authority, constituted under Section 3 of the Trees Act with nineteen members including municipal corporators and nominated botanical experts, convened a site inspection on 4th July, 2019. However, during the final meeting on 29th August, 2019, amidst dissent from nominated botanical experts regarding unverified geo-tagging and poor historical survival rates of transplanted trees, the municipal authority approved the resolution authorizing mass tree felling. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the Tree Authority abdicated its statutory duty under Section 7 and Section 8 of the Trees Act, 1975. It was argued that the authority failed to consider public objections meaningfully, omitted to conduct a scientific tree census, and failed to explore alternative industrial brownfield sites, thereby violating the public trust doctrine and intergenerational equity under Article 21. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the project proponents submitted that mass urban public transit is essential to decongest roads and reduce carbon vehicular emissions, arguing that MMRCL had undertaken compensatory afforestation of over twenty thousand saplings. Dismissing the challenge, this Court holds that balancing infrastructural public utility with environmental preservation is the prerogative of planning experts. In M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, reported in (1997) 1 SCC 388, and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights v. State of West Bengal, reported in (2021) 5 SCC 466, the Supreme Court held that while environmental protection is paramount, large-scale public transport projects that mitigate atmospheric carbon pollution cannot be stalled if statutory procedures are substantially complied with. The Tree Authority considered public representations, imposed binding compensatory plantation conditions under Section 8(5), and secured corporate undertakings for five years of post-plantation maintenance. The scope of judicial review under Article 226 is confined to the decision-making process, not the merits of planning policy. Finding no procedural perversity, the writ petition is dismissed, subject to strict monitoring of compensatory afforestation. This public interest writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and decision-making process of Resolution No. 42 dated 29th August, 2019 passed by the Tree Authority of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai under Section 8 of the Maharashtra (Urban Areas) Protection and Preservation of Trees Act, 1975, sanctioning the felling of 2,185 trees and transplantation of 461 trees across thirty-three hectares of green cover in Aarey Milk Colony, Goregaon East, for the construction of a metro rail car depot. Quashing the process qua the petitioner, this Court holds that vicarious liability in penal law is an exception created by statute and must be strictly construed. In the landmark rulings in National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal, reported in (2010) 3 SCC 330, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry, reported in (2022) 10 SCC 152, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that mere reproduction of the statutory wording of Section 141 is insufficient. The complainant must plead specific overt roles demonstrating that the director was responsible for the transaction leading to the issuance of the dishonoured cheque.

title: Test #38: The Future of Himalayan Pheasants
text: The Himalayas, stretching nearly 2,400 km across the northern edge of the Indian subcontinent, are home to some of the most spectacular birds on Earth. With peaks such as Mount Everest rising to 8,849 metres, the range shelters more than 10,000 plant species and feeds around 15,000 glaciers, creating habitats of remarkable variety. Among its birds, pheasants stand out for their brilliant colours, distinctive plumage and fascinating behaviour. The dazzling Himalayan Monal, for instance, is usually found between 2,100 and 4,500 metres, where oak, rhododendron and alpine meadows meet. From the Monal to other rare pheasant species, these birds are an important part of the mountain ecosystem and a symbol of the natural beauty of the Himalayas. Yet behind their colourful appearance lies a growing struggle for survival. Human activities are changing mountain habitats at a rapid pace, creating increasing pressure on pheasant populations. Himalayan pheasants depend on forests, grasslands, shrubs and undisturbed mountain habitats for food, shelter and breeding. But expanding roads, tourism, settlements, agriculture, construction and other development activities are fragmenting these natural habitats. When forests are divided into smaller patches, birds may find it more difficult to move, feed and reproduce safely. Climate change is adding another challenge. Rising temperatures and changing rainfall and snowfall patterns can alter the vegetation on which pheasants depend. As climate conditions change, suitable habitats may shift to higher elevations. Birds that are unable to adapt or move to new areas may face increasing difficulties. Human disturbance is also a concern. Growing tourism in Himalayan regions brings economic opportunities and connects people with nature, but uncontrolled tourism can disturb breeding birds and damage sensitive habitats. Noise, traffic, litter and careless behaviour can have consequences for wildlife that are not always immediately visible. Hunting and illegal wildlife trade have historically posed serious threats to many pheasant species. Although conservation laws and protected areas provide important protection, effective enforcement and community participation remain essential. Pheasants are not merely beautiful birds to be admired. They play ecological roles in mountain forests, including participating in food webs and helping maintain the balance of their habitats. Their presence can also serve as an indicator of the health of mountain ecosystems. Protecting them requires more than protecting individual birds. Their habitats must be conserved. Forest corridors should be maintained, development should be carefully planned, and sensitive breeding areas should receive greater protection. Tourism must become more responsible, with visitors encouraged to respect wildlife and leave natural habitats undisturbed. Local communities are equally important partners in conservation. People living in the Himalayas possess valuable knowledge about forests, wildlife and seasonal changes. Conservation programmes that provide education, sustainable livelihood opportunities and incentives for protecting wildlife are more likely to succeed in the long term. Scientific monitoring is equally important. Regular surveys, camera traps and citizen-science records help researchers understand how pheasant populations are changing across seasons and altitudes. Reliable field data allows forest departments and conservation organisations to identify threatened habitats early and respond with well-informed, timely decisions rather than belated, reactive emergency measures. Schools can also play an important role. Children who learn about Himalayan wildlife today can become tomorrow’s conservationists, researchers, forest officers and responsible citizens. Birdwatching, nature clubs and local biodiversity projects can help create a deeper connection between young people and their natural surroundings. The future of Himalayan pheasants ultimately depends on the choices humans make.

title: Test #38: To Make India's Demography a Dividend
text: Nations, like individuals, occasionally encounter transformational opportunities that demand decisive action. Demographic dividend a period when a country’s working-age population expands while the proportion of young and elderly dependents shrinks to historic lows is one such. Properly leveraged, it can dramatically boost a nation’s economic trajectory, raising productivity, increasing savings and investment capacity, strengthening tax revenues, and easing pension burdens. However, this window opens only rarely in a nation’s history, making its utilisation critical. India’s demographic dividend began in 2005, and is projected to last till 2055, with the peak expected around 2036. We’re near the midpoint of this favourable period, and roughly a decade remains before the dependency ratio starts climbing again. This raises two urgent questions: does favourable demographics automatically translate into economic gains; if not, is India capitalising on this opportunity? A growing working-age population creates only the potential for accelerated growth it does not guarantee it. In Africa, countries like Nigeria, Chad, Niger, Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Mali, and Angola, experienced favourable demographic shifts, but failed to convert them into economic prosperity. Nigeria is a cautionary tale. While East Asian nations and China successfully harnessed their demographic dividends starting in the 1980s, Nigeria couldn’t because its fertility rate declined too slowly, the economy remained overly dependent on oil without diversifying into job-creating sectors, the education system produced graduates lacking employable skills, and governance failures, combined with infra deficits and regional security problems, created additional obstacles. Closer home, Sri Lanka’s demographic advantage peaked around 2010, but benefits were largely negated by civil war, Covid, and the severe economic crisis of 2022. Among major South Asian economies, both India and Bangladesh currently have expanding working-age populations. However, there’s a growing consensus that India has not fully capitalised on this demographic opportunity yet. GDP growth since 2005 has been robust. Falling dependency ratios account for nearly 20% of per capita GDP growth since the 1980s, and the expanding workforce has supported growth in IT services and manufacturing. But job creation is the core problem. India needs to generate employment to keep pace with its expanding working-age population (15-64 years). But, in sharp contrast to China and East Asia, where export-oriented manufacturing booms readily absorbed surging worker populations, India’s manufacturing sector continues to underperform despite govt incentives and policies. There are several reasons for this: difficulties in conducting business, inadequate infra (particularly unreliable power supply), and an education system – especially govt schools that struggles to produce employable graduates. Additionally, India’s female labour force participation ranks among the lowest globally, representing a significant underutilised resource. The large informal employment sector further limits productivity and economic value addition. With the demographic window narrowing, India must pursue simultaneous reforms across multiple fronts, treating this as an urgent national priority: As India transitions from youth-heavy to working-age-heavy demographics, dramatically improving education quality particularly in govt schools becomes essential. This must be paired with expanded vocational training and apprenticeship programmes, requiring close collaboration between govt, NGOs, and industry. India should rapidly adopt successful strategies from East Asian economies. Complexity of starting and operating businesses in India calls for business environment reform. Common complaints centre on excessive approval requirements and sluggish bureaucratic processes, compared with other nations. Multiple regulatory bodies and complicated tax, labour and other laws should be streamlined and aligned with global best practices.

title: Test #39: Principles of Inheritance & Variation
text: Genetics is a branch of biology which deals with principles of inheritance and its practices. Progeny resembling the parents in morphological and physiological features has attracted the attention of many biologists. Mendel was the first to study this phenomenon systematically. The chromosomes which were different in two sexes were named as sex chromosomes. The remaining set was named as autosomes. In humans, a normal female has 22 pairs of autosomes and a pair of sex chromosomes (XX). A male has 22 pairs of autosomes and a pair of sex chromosome as XY. In chicken, sex chromosomes in male are ZZ, and in females are ZW. Mutation is defined as change in the genetic material. A point mutation is a change of a single base pair in DNA. Sickle-cell anemia is caused due to change of one base in the gene coding for beta-chain of hemoglobin. Inheritable mutations can be studied by generating a pedigree of a family. Some mutations involve changes in whole set of chromosomes (polyploidy) or change in a subset of chromosome number (aneuploidy). This helped in understanding the mutational basis of genetic disorders. When Mendel studied the inheritance of two characters together, it was found that the factors independently assort and combine in all permutations and combinations (Law of Independent Assortment). Different combinations of gametes are theoretically represented in a square tabular form known as ‘Punnett Square’. The factors (now known as gene) on chromosomes regulating the characters are called the genotype and the physical expression of the characters is called phenotype. After knowing that the genes are located on the chromosomes, a good correlation was drawn between Mendel’s laws : segregation and assortment of chromosomes during meiosis. The Mendel’s laws were extended in the form of ‘Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance’. While studying the pattern of inheritance in pea plants of contrasting characters, Mendel proposed the principles of inheritance, which are today referred to as ‘Mendel’s Laws of Inheritance’. He proposed that the ‘factors’ (later named as genes) regulating the characters are found in pairs known as alleles. He observed that the expression of the characters in the offspring follow a definite pattern in different-first generations (F1 ), second (F2 ) and so on. Some characters are dominant over others. The dominant characters are expressed when factors are in heterozygous condition (Law of Dominance). The recessive characters are only expressed in homozygous conditions. The characters never blend in heterozygous condition. A recessive character that was not expressed in heterozygous condition may be expressed again when it becomes homozygous. Hence, characters segregate while formation of gametes (Law of Segregation). Not all characters show true dominance. Some characters show incomplete, and some show co-dominance. Later, it was found that Mendel’s law of independent assortment does not hold true for the genes that were located on the same chromosomes. These genes were called as ‘linked genes’. Closely located genes assorted together, and distantly located genes, due to recombination, assorted independently. Linkage maps, therefore, corresponded to arrangement of genes on a chromosome. Many genes were linked to sexes also, and called as sex-linked genes. The two sexes (male and female) were found to have a set of chromosomes which were common, and another set which was different. Down’s syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome 21, where there is an extra copy of chromosome 21 and consequently the total number of chromosome becomes 47. In Turner’s syndrome, one X chromosome is missing and the sex chromosome is as XO, and in Klinefelter’s syndrome, the condition is XXY. These can be easily studied by analysis of Karyotypes.

title: Test #39: Legal - DHC Writ P. No. 1376 of 2020
text: Quashing the FIR qua the petitioner, this Court holds that internet intermediaries cannot be transformed into private arbitral censors. In the landmark authority in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, reported in (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Hon’ble Supreme Court authoritatively read down Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, establishing that the expression ‘actual knowledge’ requires an intermediary to receive an order of a court of competent jurisdiction or an authorized government notification directing takedown. A commercial platform cannot be expected to judge complex intellectual property infringement claims upon unilateral private notices from brand owners. In Google India Private Limited v. Visakha Industries, reported in (2020) 4 SCC 162, this Court reaffirmed that where an e-commerce platform merely provides access, does not initiate the transmission, and enforces seller terms prohibiting illicit products, it satisfies Section 79(2). Prosecuting the intermediary for independent copyright violations committed by third-party sellers without establishing criminal conspiracy constitutes an abuse of process. The FIR qua the petitioner is accordingly quashed. This criminal writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeks the quashing of First Information Report No. 182 of 2020 registered at Police Station Crime Branch, Cyber Cell, New Delhi under Sections 420, 468, 471, and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957, insofar as it relates to the petitioner e-commerce marketplace entity, claiming statutory safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The prosecution case stemmed from a private complaint lodged by an international cosmetics brand, alleging that counterfeit luxury perfumes bearing forged registered trademarks were being sold on the petitioner’s online platform. The brand owner issued a private cease-and-desist email on 12th February, 2020, requesting immediate removal of ten third-party seller URLs. The petitioner promptly deactivated four listings where specific infringing merchant codes were identified, but advised the complainant to secure a court order regarding the remaining disputed storefronts to avoid breach of merchant vendor contracts. Thereupon, the complainant lodged an FIR, arraigning the marketplace as a co-conspirator. The petitioner challenged the FIR, demonstrating that it is an intermediary under Section 2(1)(w) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, operating as an automated marketplace where independent registered sellers upload product listings, and that it observed strict statutory due diligence under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediaries Guidelines) Rules, 2011. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that under Section 79 of the IT Act, an intermediary is completely immune from criminal and civil liability for third-party information hosted on its network. Learned Additional Public Prosecutor and counsel for the complainant resisted the petition, arguing that safe harbour under Section 79 does not apply when the intermediary fails to remove infringing listings despite receiving private notices. The student is the creator and owner of the knowledge articulated in the script, and the relationship between the examinee and the university is one of candidate and testing authority, not fiduciary trustee and beneficiary under Section 8(1)(e).
