While a fiduciary relationship exists between the university and the examiners regarding the identity of the evaluators, the university can easily protect examiners' privacy by masking their names, signatures, and code numbers through the severability procedure prescribed under Section 10 of the Act. Transparent access to evaluated scripts enables students to verify totaling errors, check omitted evaluations, and pursue legitimate academic careers.

title: Test #40: Legal - APHC Writ P. No. 18080 of 2016
text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeks a writ of mandamus declaring the action of Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the State of Andhra Pradesh represented by its Principal Secretary to Government, Revenue Department, and the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, in adopting the Sealed Cover Procedure and deferring the promotion of the petitioner to the post of Assistant Commissioner of State Tax in the Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) panel meeting held on 18th March, 2016, as illegal, arbitrary, and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The petitioner, a Commercial Tax Officer appointed through the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission in 2004, maintained an unblemished service record and fell within the direct zone of consideration for promotion to the post of Assistant Commissioner for the panel year 2015-2016. When the DPC convened on 18th March, 2016, juniors ranking below the petitioner in the integrated seniority list were promoted, while the petitioner's assessment was placed in a sealed cover. The respondents defended the sealed cover procedure citing a preliminary surprise check conducted by the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) on 14th February, 2015, which resulted in the registration of an exploratory Regular Inquiry. However, the record conclusively established that on the date the DPC met, the petitioner was neither placed under suspension, nor had any disciplinary charge memo been served under Rule 20 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991, nor had any criminal charge sheet been filed in a court of competent jurisdiction under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the right to be considered for promotion is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 16 of the Constitution of India. It was argued that placing recommendations in a sealed cover on the basis of a preliminary vigilance inquiry without a formal charge sheet violates binding constitutional precedents. Learned Government Pleader for Services opposed the petition, submitting that public interest demands that officers facing serious vigilance scrutiny should not be entrusted with higher administrative responsibilities. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that the adoption of the sealed cover procedure is impermissible in the absence of formal disciplinary or criminal proceedings. In the landmark Three-Judge Bench decision in Union of India v. K.V. Jankiraman, reported in (1991) 4 SCC 109, and Union of India v. Anil Kumar Sarkar, reported in (2013) 4 SCC 161, the Hon'ble Supreme Court authoritatively established that the sealed cover procedure can be resorted to only when three explicit conditions exist at the time of DPC consideration: (i) the government servant is under suspension, (ii) a formal charge memo has been framed and served in departmental proceedings, or (iii) a charge sheet has been filed in a criminal court. Mere pendency of a preliminary investigation, confidential vigilance inquiry, or registration of an FIR without filing a charge sheet does not justify withholding promotion. To deny promotion at the stage of preliminary inquiry impairs career progression and violates Article 14 and Article 16. The respondents are commanded to open the sealed cover within four weeks and, if found fit, grant notional promotion to the petitioner from the date his immediate junior was promoted, with all consequential seniority and pay fixation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that registered ownership is the sole criterion for fastening third-party statutory liability. In the landmark Three-Judge Bench decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Naveen Kumar v. Vijay Kumar, reported in (2018) 3 SCC 1, and Prakash Chand Daga v. Saveta Sharma, reported in (2019) 2 SCC 747, the law was conclusively settled. The Supreme Court held that Parliament consciously enacted the definition of 'owner' in Section 2(30) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to mean the person in whose name the motor vehicle stands registered.

title: Test #40: Khadi - Weaving a Global Story
text: A charkha spinning in a village once spoke of nationalism. Today, that spirit is taking new shape through a growing ecosystem of rural enterprises. Honey, herbal products, banana fibre, textiles and other village industries are creating new possibilities for traditional skills. This growing connection between local enterprise and consumers is also reflected in the Khadi Mahotsav. The Khadi Mahotsav takes place annually from 2 October to 31 October. With a particular focus on youth, the campaign sensitises them towards Khadi and “Vocal for Local” and encourages the public to buy Khadi and local products. The spirit of self-reliance continues to resonate with the vision of “Vocal for Local” and Atmanirbhar Bharat. Traditional skills and local resources are finding new markets through access to finance, technology and training. At the centre of this transformation is the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC). It is a statutory body established under the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956. The Act mandates KVIC to plan, promote, facilitate, organise and assist village industries. It covers measures related to training, raw materials, marketing, research, and quality improvement. It also supports skill development and research, while providing technical information and facilities related to Khadi and village industries. Across village industries, traditional skills and local resources are being developed into new businesses and products, supported by technology, training and market linkages. Research and development efforts are strengthening productivity, quality and competitiveness. After receiving support in 2010, the enterprise gradually expanded its export presence through participation in international exhibitions. KVIC facilitated participation in exhibitions across Dubai, the United States and the Middle East, helping the enterprise connect with overseas buyers. Today, the business exports to 36 countries and is developing a second unit in Rajpura, Punjab, to expand honey exports to European markets. KVIC has expanded both digital and physical channels for reaching consumers. It has an online Khadi India store offering a range of products, including clothing and fabrics, grocery, beauty products, essential oils, perfumes and incense sticks. One hank is equivalent to 840 yards of yarn in length and one pound by weight. From acquiring skills to accessing markets, a range of interventions is supporting artisans and village industries. Training is complemented by interventions including toolkit and equipment distribution, marketing support and other measures. The Khadi India brand is supported through dedicated publicity and marketing initiatives. These efforts connect traditional products with contemporary consumers. The marketing network extends across the country. It includes 8 departmental Khadi India sales outlets and 15 KVIC branches. Khadi Institutions operate another 8,035 sales outlets nationwide. National, zonal, state and district exhibitions provide additional market opportunities. KVIC also promotes participation in domestic and international trade fairs. The growth of Khadi and Village Industries is reflected in higher production and sales, expanding employment, increased artisan remuneration and new rural businesses. As traditional skills connect with technology, finance and markets, the sector continues to open new avenues for enterprise across rural India. Khadi is finding new expressions in fashion, with its distinctive craftsmanship showcased at platforms such as New Zealand Fashion Week 2026 and Lakme Fashion Week 2025. In these events, the heritage techniques were brought together with contemporary designs to create a distinctly modern identity. Shri S.P. Singh built his enterprise around honey and cookies, with support under the PMEGP scheme through KVIC. Based in Punjab, his business now provides employment to around 200 workers and exports its products to international markets. Honey and cookies are among its key products, with the United States accounting for a major share of exports.

title: Test #41: India's Ocean and Coastal Areas Economy
text: Our fish catch has plateaued at about 3.5 million tonnes, despite serious efforts to raise it. The government is ably supported by the country’s premier ocean science institute, the National Institute of Oceanography (NIO), headquartered in Goa. Established in 1966 under the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), it documents marine biodiversity and pollution and conducts multidisciplinary research, including deep-sea mineral research, notably polymetallic nodule exploration, a long-running programme to extract value from the ocean floor. Part of the State’s new ambition is a Rs 81,000-crore project to develop Great Nicobar Island (GNI). The plan includes a mega port, new city, international airport, military base, and industrial park. This is explicitly framed as a way to strengthen India’s strategic position in the region. This project is a centrepiece in the country’s shift from a defensive to a power-projecting maritime posture, harking back perhaps to the Chola empire. The tropical Indian Ocean has warmed faster than other oceans and marine heatwave days are expected to rise tenfold by 2050. We already know that this year’s El Nino might be a once-in-a thousand-year event. The government has spoken of the development projects in both the Andaman and Nicobar Islands as a blue economy hub. This idea covers fisheries and aquaculture, and coastal and marine tourism. It acknowledges the unique marine biodiversity there yet desires deep-sea mineral exploration and oil and gas extraction in the North Andaman Basin. There are in-built contradictions here that will require meaningful trade-offs between development and the environment. It may also need a fresh economic assessment of potential stranded assets in a seismically and climatically vulnerable region. These are among the more contested infrastructure projects in India today. GNI has one of the last remaining pristine rainforests in the country, and hosts the Shompen, one of the last tribes living in voluntary isolation. Both indigenous communities and environmentalists oppose the project for its estimated ecological and human costs. Mainland Indians, partly because of our lack of knowledge about our strategic maritime assets and about the way of life of offshore islanders, may not understand what the fuss is all about. We may well believe that the trade-offs are worth the strategic advantage to be had. Does India not need strategic self-reliance in turbulent global waters? If some low-lying islands may be submerged in a few decades from global warming and sea rise anyway, is it not a good idea to exploit their potential now? These questions may be valid, yet the developing context broadens the issues way beyond the GNI project. India’s coast faces a polycrisis. We cannot speak separately about climate change, biodiversity loss, rising sea levels and food insecurity. The oceans force us to bring it all together. If the projections are close to reality, this Super El Nino will destroy many coral reefs and coastal fisheries. In the low-lying atolls of Lakshadweep, coral reef cover has already fallen by about half. Many “sensitive taxa” are already gone and only slow-growing and structurally simple corals remain. After this El Nino, marine ecosystems may take far longer to recover, as the ability to self-repair and grow is further compromised. The provisioning services and protection that marine ecosystems give and that we take for granted are weakening before our eyes. If business continues as usual, Lakshadweep may be among the first internally displaced territories of India before the end of the century. And while it might be difficult for people far away on the mainland, with worries of their own, to care about a small island and its few-thousand residents, Lakshadweep might be our canary in the coal mine. Our coastline is more densely populated and more vulnerable than it has ever been. Meanwhile, fish remains one of the cheapest sources of animal protein available for millions.

title: Test #41: Indian Air Force Operating with Margin
text: With fighter strength at roughly 29 squadrons against an authorised 42, the Indian Air Force is operating with a margin that is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. This is why the delays involving GE F404 engines, radar and missile integration, and software certification surrounding the Tejas Mk-1A are strategically important. The root problem is that engine supply, certification and HAL’s production capacity have each been managed as separate problems. Until one authority owns delivery timelines, the aircraft will keep arriving late. The IAF has several streams through which it can begin rebuilding squadron strength. The first is the Tejas Mk-1A. The immediate objective should be to enable HAL to reach production rates of 20 or more Tejas annually. The second is the proposed Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft (MRFA) programme, involving roughly 114 aircraft and potentially centred on the Rafale, with substantial production in India. Once established, this could provide another stream of around 12 aircraft annually. The additional Su-30 aircraft already envisaged would provide further reinforcement. If these programmes proceed on schedule, India could approach the 35-40 aircraft-a-year induction rate. But that requires procurement, industrial production, engines, certification, and logistics to be treated as an integrated national-security problem. India continues to face the possibility of a two-front contingency involving China and Pakistan, and both are modernising their air forces. China’s rapid progress in stealth technology and reports of a potential Chinese fifth-generation aircraft being supplied to Pakistan point to a changing regional balance. India cannot afford to allow its numerical disadvantage to widen further. The debate over air power often becomes a choice between quantity and quality. But India needs both. Advanced aircraft, precision weapons, sensors and networks provide qualitative advantages, but they cannot compensate indefinitely for insufficient numbers. Aircraft need maintenance, training and rotation. A force that is too small has limited surge capacity and reduced flexibility across multiple theatres. Also, the existing fleet must be kept combat-ready. Su-30s, Rafales, Mirage-2000s, Jaguars and Tejas Mk-1s need reliable spares, high serviceability, and rapid integration of indigenous weapons such as the Astra family. Numbers matter only when aircraft are available for operations. India’s long-term answer must remain the indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA). If AMCA timelines slip substantially, India will eventually have to consider interim options, including the Russian Su-57 offer. This would involve difficult questions concerning cost, technology access, interoperability and industrial benefits. Nevertheless, the choice should be made on the basis of strategic necessity rather than institutional inertia. Modern air warfare is increasingly about systems rather than individual platforms. Sensors, electronic warfare, missiles, communications, command-and-control networks, training and doctrine can be as important as the aircraft itself. India, therefore, needs an integrated combat system rather than a fixation on individual platforms. Unmanned systems and loitering munitions will increasingly shape the battlefield, but must not become an excuse for accepting inadequate fighter numbers. The future battlefield will involve manned aircraft, unmanned systems, missiles, electronic warfare and air-defence networks operating together. The objective should be integration, not creating parallel structures that fragment command. Humans are likely to remain in the decision loop for the foreseeable future. Indigenous weapons such as Astra, Akash and BrahMos need to be produced and integrated rapidly. AI should augment human decision-making. Integrated air and missile defence must keep pace with increasingly complex threats involving aircraft, cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and unmanned systems.

title: Test #42: Forgotten Queen - Malika Kishwar's Grave
text: Queen Malika Kishwar, mother of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, the last ruler of Awadh, and one of the most remarkable yet forgotten figures of India’s colonial history. Known as Janab-i-Aliya, Malika Kishwar occupied a revered position in the royal household of Awadh. Her life changed dramatically in 1856 when the East India Company annexed the kingdom on the pretext of maladministration. Wajid Ali Shah believed that the British sense of justice would ultimately prevail. He travelled to Calcutta to appeal to Governor-General Lord Canning for restoration of his kingdom, but his efforts failed. The Nawab then considered travelling to England to place his case directly before Queen Victoria. Ill health, however, prevented him from undertaking the voyage. At that crucial moment, his mother stepped forward. On June 15, 1856, she sailed from Calcutta aboard the SS Bengal. Accompanying her were her son Prince Mirza Sikandar Hashmat, her grandson Prince Hamid Ali Bahadur and a retinue of around seventy attendants. Their objective was clear: to seek justice through Queen Victoria and the British Parliament and secure the restoration of Awadh. The journey was long and arduous. More than two months later, the royal party reached Southampton. Crowds gathered to catch a glimpse of the Indian queen and her entourage. But her observance of strict purdah presented an unusual challenge. To protect her privacy, she was transported in a covered sedan chair. During the journey from Southampton to London, attendants held up large sheets of calico to form a moving screen so that she could pass unseen through public spaces. Malika Kishwar arrived in England believing that a personal appeal to Queen Victoria might succeed where previous efforts had failed. She soon discovered the limitations of royal authority within Britain’s constitutional system. The annexation had been carried out by the East India Company, and there was little interest in either political or commercial circles for reversing that decision. Still, her delegation did not give up. Lawyers were engaged, petitions drafted and parliamentarians approached. The campaign became a sustained exercise in diplomacy, lobbying, legal advocacy and public persuasion. After months of waiting, Malika Kishwar was finally received by Queen Victoria at Buckingham Palace on July 4, 1857. She was accorded full honours. Yet the timing could hardly have been worse. The uprising of 1857 had spread across much of northern and central India, altering the political atmosphere. British authorities were preoccupied with suppressing the rebellion, while Wajid Ali Shah had been arrested on June 15, 1857, and placed under house arrest at Fort William in Calcutta. The audience with Queen Victoria proved deeply disappointing. Malika Kishwar realised that the Queen lacked the power to undo the annexation. Nevertheless, one final effort was made. On August 6, 1857, Lord Campbell, Chief Justice of the Queen’s Bench, presented a petition before the House of Lords. It was rejected on technical grounds. A subsequent attempt in the House of Commons also failed. The mission that had inspired such courage and sacrifice had effectively come to an end. Yet another chapter remained. Determined to return home via Mecca and perform the pilgrimage, Malika Kishwar sought permission to leave Britain. The British authorities initially refused to provide the necessary documents. Only after intervention by the French Embassy was she allowed to depart. On January 22, 1858, she reached Paris with around 40 members of her delegation. By then, prolonged illness, disappointment and the strain of two difficult years had severely weakened her. Just two days after arriving in the French capital, she died. She was buried at Pere-Lachaise Cemetery in accordance with Islamic rites. Representatives of the Ottoman Empire and Persia attended the funeral, paying tribute to a queen whose determination had earned widespread respect. The tragedies did not end there. Her young granddaughter, Rifat Ara Begum, also died and was buried beside her grandmother.

title: Test #42: India Centre of Maritime World
text: For more than 2,000 years, with its coastal and oceanic habitats spanning the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Andaman Sea and Indian Ocean, India has been at the centre of the maritime world. Lothal in Gujarat has one of the world’s earliest known dockyards, dating to the Harappan Civilisation (c.2400 BCE), providing physical evidence of maritime trade between the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia. There was trade in sea turtles with the Roman Empire too, going back more than 2,000 years. The Chola dynasty famously had a maritime legacy that flourished between the 9th and 13th centuries CE. Originating in Tamil Nadu, these rulers strategically pivoted from an agrarian culture to a maritime power, expanding their hegemony across South India, Sri Lanka and South-East Asia. They saw the seas as channels through which to exert influence and power. Long before European colonial forces came to militarise the routes, maritime trade flourished between the peoples of regions such as Gujarat, Malabar and Bengal, and those of West Asia and beyond. Historically, Indian civilisations understood the ocean as central to identity and political strategy. One could argue that India now suffers from a deep amnesia about its seafaring past. A mental model sets us up as a land-based civilisation. We are more likely to celebrate the Guptas and Mauryas than the Cholas, who represent our own blue-water imperial ambitions. Despite having a coastline of about 11,000 km (a revision from the older figure using higher spatial data, including islands), the modern State has treated our waters as an afterthought, especially when it comes to livelihoods, conservation and sustainability. Even though about 16 million people depend directly on marine fisheries for their primary livelihood, fisheries until recently came under the Ministry of Agriculture, and marine conservation remains but a footnote in a conservation agenda designed around tigers and forests. India’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), which gives the country rights extending up to 200 nautical miles from the coasts, covers about 2 million sq km. India accounts for about 6.4% of global marine biodiversity across its coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass meadows, estuaries and mudflats. More than 20,000 animal species and 1,100 plant species have been recorded across the country’s marine ecosystems. We have five of the world’s seven sea turtle species in our waters. They are a keystone species, controlling jellyfish populations, maintaining coral-reef health, and transporting nutrients between marine and terrestrial ecosystems. India is among the world’s top three shark- and ray-fishing nations. Our EEZ holds roughly 170 species of sharks, rays and chimaeras, including about 30 that are endemic to the Arabian Sea and adjacent waters. As predators, they help keep marine food webs in balance. They also support the livelihoods and food security of numerous communities. Nevertheless, sharks and rays are among the most threatened groups in Indian waters, and catches have declined steadily across decades. Meanwhile, despite these treasures, only about 5% of the country’s coastal and marine areas are designated as protected according to the Sixth National Report under the Convention on Biological Diversity. India is rushing to meet its commitment to get 30% of its waters declared as protected areas under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, but so far we are nowhere close. On the research front, marine science remains neglected and siloed across different institutions and we have barely any long-term monitoring of ocean life. This is concerning, given that commercial fishing now operates at a very different scale from the artisanal fishing it competes with, and needs a more rigorous application of fish biology and scientific evidence. Recent research suggests that even the annual fishing ban overlaps with the breeding periods of only 40% of commercially fished species, leaving the other 60% unprotected. The current government is more ambitious when it comes to our oceans.

title: Test #43: Japanese Guide to Keeping it Together
text: Since 1981, Tokyo has had a series of bosai or disaster-ready residential zones, focused on fire safety. Here, firebreaks or non-combustible spaces such as roads, rivers and rail corridors are woven into the city’s grid system, to separate neighbourhoods in ways that would keep a large fire from spreading. A major firebreak belt appears every 2-km. The grid curves with natural breaks such as rivers. In addition, along narrower streets, where it would be easier for flying embers to spread, building codes specify that non-combustible material must make up at least 40% of all street-facing walls. In 1923, amid the Great Kanto earthquake and the massive fire that followed, an estimated one million Tokyo residents survived because they escaped to open tracts of land. This unique culture is full of such workarounds, some of which Mazereeuw details in her book, Design Before Disaster. Simple examples include architecture that ensures schools can double as evacuation sites during earthquakes and floods. This means sturdier-than-normal construction, as well as more toilets, and reservoirs in the form of rooftop swimming pools “that also keep the school buildings cool in summer,” Mazereeuw says. Homes within were built on stone platforms about 1.5 ft high. Storehouses for grain were built much higher, 8 metres or more above the ground, and served as emergency evacuation spaces too. One of the largest, Takasu Waju, built in 1653, still encircles homes, granaries and rice fields, all technically at sea level, across a sprawl of 4,260 hectares. In the post-earthquake reconstruction of Tokyo, statesman Shinpei Goto even introduced a plan for refuge parks that would be equipped to house thousands at a time. Tokyo is still building more. Today, such spaces are fitted with solar-powered charging stations for electric bicycles and phones, public benches that can turn into cooking stoves, and manholes that double as emergency toilets. Perhaps the best-known of these is the Tokyo Rinkai disaster prevention park, a 33-acre space where lampposts serve as LAN connections too. There’s a lot more to Japan’s famous sakura tradition than gathering to admire cherry blossoms. This delicate annual rite is in fact a form of disaster-preparedness. Every winter, moisture in the soil near riverbanks would freeze and expand. In centuries gone by, the spring thaw would loosen the mud, and rain could trigger landslides. So, way back in the 8th century, Nara rulers began to encourage spring picnics in April, a practice that then spread from the nobility to the general populace over time. The weight of hundreds of people walking about and sitting on blankets helped compact the soil, “creating a man-made solidity,” says Miho Mazereeuw, an associate professor of architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she also set up and heads the Urban Risk Lab. Stairs are situated on the outsides of these buildings, so they can serve as an instant escape route during floods. Japan, of course, has a long history of negotiating earthquakes and volcanoes, situated as it is above four tectonic plates. It has responded, Mazereeuw notes, by creating a collective culture of preparedness that the world at large could now benefit from. Hearing stories from her Japanese parents of how this culture saves lives, and is woven into daily life, inspired her interest in this field. In the Nobi Plain where three rivers intersect, severe flooding is common. So, centuries ago, local communities devised a system of massive waju or circular embankments that protected homes, farms and granaries, while allowing the waters to flow around them. Through a complex network of sluice gates, they also managed to direct water through these flat, low-flying but rich and fertile lands, to irrigate fields. Public parks then provided camping space for thousands who had lost their homes. This forever changed how Japan viewed its parks. They became a key feature in emergency-response plans. Tokyo alone has 58 such park-refuges.

title: Test #43: Next Fundamental Right - Freedom of Mind
text: On Sept 28, a Supreme Court Bench asked the Centre to consider binding rules that would make 18 the minimum age for opening a social media account, because a minor cannot sign a contract under Indian law. The Solicitor General’s reply was unusually direct: “Something can be done; something should be done and will be done.” The case is about children, but the question beneath it concerns every Indian who owns a phone: ‘Who gets to shape what happens inside our heads?’ In Nov 2025, with little fanfare, UNESCO’s 194 member states adopted the first global standard on the ethics of neurotechnology, the devices that can read, and increasingly influence, brain activity. In a 2014 study, Facebook’s own researchers reported that they had altered the news feeds of 689,003 users for a week to see if they could shift their moods. They could, if only slightly. At Facebook’s scale, slightly is a lot. The third argument is about children, because here the danger is no longer abstract. UNESCO reports that 58% of countries now ban phones in schools, up from about a quarter in 2023. A 2017 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showed how well this works. Advertisements matched to people’s personalities, guessed from little more than their Facebook likes, reached 3.5 million people and drew up to 40% more clicks and 50% more purchases. The effects show up in daily life. Psychologist Gloria Mark found that the average time people stay on one screen before switching fell from about two and a half minutes in 2004 to 47 seconds in recent years. Indians spent about five hours a day on their phones in 2024, according to an EY report, and nearly 70% of that time went to social media, games and video. In Puttaswamy (2017), a nine-judge Bench read the right to privacy into Article 21 and protected the citizen’s data. It was one of the Republic’s finest modern judgments. But the technology of the last decade raises a harder question. It is no longer only about who may see our information. It warns, among other things, against using brain data in recommender systems to manipulate people. The human mind has become a subject of rights. For all of history, the space behind the forehead was the one place no ruler could search. That certainty is now fading, and not mainly because of brain implants. The bigger reason is already installed on nearly every Indian smartphone. It is the recommendation engine. The system is given one goal, to maximise engagement, and it chases that number with endless patience, learning what makes each user stop, scroll and come back. The engine is not evil. It simply obeys, and its goal is not the user’s well-being. It is about who may shape our wants. Scholars such as Daniel Susser, Beate Roessler and Helen Nissenbaum offer a workable test. Persuasion speaks to my reasons. Manipulation goes around them, quietly using one’s biases, habits and tiredness to produce choices one might not have made. In 2017, neuroethicists Marcello Ienca and Roberto Andorno argued that cognitive liberty and mental privacy should be recognised as new human rights. The tradition that carried Article 21 from Maneka Gandhi (1978) to Puttaswamy can carry it one step further, to a freedom of the mind from hidden, engineered influence. The second argument is that the world has already moved, and India has taken the first step at home. In 2023, India’s Central Consumer Protection Authority named and restricted 13 “dark patterns”, deceptive designs that trick users into buying. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, goes further for children. It bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising aimed at them, with full effect from May 2027. The principle is already on our books, for the wallet and for the child. Extending it to the mind is one logical step, and India would be the first democracy of a billion people to take it. An engagement engine runs an experiment on a nation every hour. Closer home, the Economic Survey 2025-26 called for age-based limits on social media.

title: Test #44: Era of Budget Flying in India
text: Fourteen years after Air Deccan started the era of budget flying in India, low-cost carriers (LCC) here are finally coming of age and preparing to straddle the entire space from short regional flights on turboprops to. long hauls using wide body planes. This tectonic shift comes with India's largest airline by domestic market share, IndiGo, declaring it will have turboprops in its fleet for regional flying. And, SpiceJet which already has turboprops saying it is looking at medium to long haul budget flights on wide-body planes. "The LCCS.. are open to changing their old business models. IndiGo, which till recently maintained it would have a single, aircraft fleet of Airbus A-320s, is inducting ATRs. And Spice-Jet, which had both turboprops and Boeing 73.7, is working out the math for having wide body Dreamliners in its flect," said a top aviation ministry source with whom airlines have held these discussions. The top ministry source said that apart from SpiceJet, some other LCCs are also examining medium to long haul flights. "We are now looking at LCCs having a hub and spoke model where their turboprops and single aisle planes get traffic into their metro hubs from where their wide body planes offer connectivity to destinations that are eight to nine hours away," the source said. Led by IndiGo, budget airlines account for almost two-third of all domestic flyers today. Airbus has for years been trying to convince IndiGo to look at its Airbus A-330 for longer flights but the profitable LCC remained firm. to its one-type-of-aircraft business model. While announcing its decision to have ATRs in its fleet, the IndiGo president said the airline is "embarking on a journey to build a nation-wide regional network and connect cities, that have not benefitted from the growth in Indian aviation." "SpiceJet continues to study the viability of low-cost long-haul travel and a decision will be taken in due course," said the Chairman of SpiceJet, when asked if and by when the LCC will start flights to Western Europe. The airline said it is looking at London, Birmingham, Paris, Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Zurich as possible destinations. The reason for the shift by" India's biggest LCCs is not surprising. The big growth in air travel is coming from small towns and the present" government's subsidized regional flying model to ensure reasonably priced tickets, will provide a further push to that. Secondly, Indian travellers to rest of the world are increasingly opting for foreign LCCs which offer connections to as far as Australia and Eastern Europe through their hubs in Dubai and Singapore. Indian: budget airlines want a share of this growing pic. The biggest foreign LCCs currently operating to India are. Singapore-based Scoot and Tiger (both part of Singapore Airlines' Group); Kuala Lumpur based AirAsia; Dubai-based flydubai and Sharjah's Air Arabia. While the budget carriers from Singapore offer connections to China, Southeast Asia and Australia from their hub, the Gulf LCCs do so to Eastern Europe, West Asia and Africa. In fact, flydubai gets significant transfer traffic for its flights to Europe from India. A recent study by Cox & Kings showed that overseas travel for leisure has doubled in the last one year from Tier-2 cities like Lucknow, Ahmedabad, Amritsar and Kochi as foreign airlines now offer direct connections from these places to their hubs in the Gulf and Southeast Asia. Industry observers say the strategic pivot also reflects mounting pressure on profitability. Domestic fares remain highly sensitive to fuel prices and airport charges, and carriers see diversification across routes and aircraft types as a hedge against slowing growth on trunk routes. Longer sectors typically yield better revenue per aircraft, while regional flights open up untapped demand and, with government support, offer relatively assured loads. The model is not without risk, however. Wide-body operations require heavier capital investment, specialised crew training and complex maintenance arrangements, and low-cost carriers will have to prove that they can keep unit costs low while managing multiple fleet types.

title: Test #44: MPHC JJA 2023 - 21/09/2023 - S1
text: The new proviso to Section-19 mandating that the competent authority shall endeavour to convey the decision on the proposal for sanction within a period of three months can only be read and understood as a compelling statutory obligation. In the first place, the consistent effort made by all branches of the State, the Judiciary, the Legislative, and the Executive, to ensure early decision-making by the competent authority cannot be watered down by lexical interpretation of the expression endeavour in the proviso. Public confidence in the maintenance of the Rule of Law, which is fundamental in the administration of justice, is at stake here. By causing delay in considering the request for sanction, the sanctioning authority stultifies judicial scrutiny, thereby vitiating the process of determination of the allegations against the corrupt official. Delays in prosecuting the corrupt breeds a culture of impunity and leads to systemic resignation to the existence of corruption in public life. Such inaction is fraught with the risk of making future generations getting accustomed to corruption as a way of life. Viewed in this context, the duty to take an early decision inheres in the power vested in the appointing authority to grant or not to grant sanction. The intention of the Parliament is evident from a combined reading of the first proviso to Section-19, which uses the expression endeavour with the subsequent provisions. The third proviso mandates that the extended period can be granted only for one month after reasons are recorded in writing. There is no further extension. The fourth proviso, which empowers the Central Government to prescribe necessary guidelines for ensuring the mandate, may also be noted in this regard. It can thus be concluded that the Parliament intended that the process of grant of sanction must be completed within four months, which includes the extended period of one month also. If it is mandatory for the sanctioning authority to decide in a time-bound manner, the consequence of non-compliance with the mandatory period must be examined. The criminal proceedings must be quashed if the decision is not taken within the prescribed period. The new proviso to Section 19 also has to be read against the backdrop of the larger purpose of the Prevention of Corruption Act, which is to ensure that those who hold public office are held answerable for the abuse of that office. The requirement of prior sanction was introduced as a protective filter, so that honest public servants are shielded from frivolous and vexatious prosecution. It was never meant to operate as a shield for the dishonest. When the sanctioning authority sits over a request for months or years without any explanation, the safeguard is turned into an instrument of obstruction, and the very object of the statute stands defeated. A protection designed for the innocent cannot be allowed to become a refuge for the guilty. The statutory timeline must therefore be treated as an integral part of the sanctioning power itself. Delay is not a neutral act. Witnesses grow old or pass away, documents are misplaced or destroyed, memories fade, and the evidentiary foundation of the prosecution steadily erodes. The accused, on the other hand, continues to hold office or to enjoy the benefits of the position, sometimes even influencing the very evidence on which the case depends. A prolonged silence on the part of the competent authority thus prejudices both the prosecution and the fairness of the trial, and it is the public interest that ultimately suffers. It is true that the legislature has employed the word endeavour, and ordinarily that expression would indicate an effort rather than an absolute command. But the meaning of a word cannot be divorced from its setting. Where the first proviso is followed by a limit on extension, a bar on further extension, and an enabling power to frame guidelines, the scheme as a whole point unmistakably towards a firm outer limit.

title: Test #45: DHC PA Typing - 09/03/2019
text: The learned Senior Civil Judge has dismissed the application reasoning that there are no admissions of the respondent/defendant and the respondent/defendant has disputed the landlord-tenant relationship and has rather claimed having been cheated. It is further reasoned that according to the respondent/defendant, he remains the owner of the property and though the respondent/defendant admits receipt of legal notice but a decree on admissions cannot be sought on the basis thereof. On 9th August, 2017 when this petition came up first before this court, it was enquired from the counsel for the petitioner plaintiff, whether there are any other proceedings filed by the respondent defendant or by any of his siblings for setting aside of the sale deed and the lease deed and whether the respondent defendant has filed any counter-claim in the suit. On the counsel for the petitioner plaintiff answering in the negative, it was further observed that the respondent defendant, without having initiated any proceedings for setting aside of the sale deed and the lease deed, the same being registered documents have to prevail and the petitioner plaintiff appeared to be entitled to a decree for possession on admissions. Hence, notice of this petition was issued. The counsel for the respondent/defendant though has not disputed that the respondent/defendant or any of his siblings have not taken any proceedings for setting aside of the sale deed or lease deed or for rescission of the same and have also not filed any counter-claim in the suit from which this petition arises but contends that filing of such a suit by the respondent defendant is still within limitation, inasmuch as the respondent/defendant learnt of the misrepresentation only in December 2014. Neither counsel is able to state the date on which the respondent defendant was served with the summons of the suit. However, the counsel for the petitioner plaintiff states that the suit was preceded by a legal notice and to which a reply was given and the respondent/defendant on receipt of legal notice also had knowledge of the claim of the petitioner plaintiff. It is further the contention of the counsel for the petitioner/plaintiff that the case of the petitioner plaintiff is squarely covered by Karan Madaan V. Nageshwar Pandey, 209 (2014) DLT 241 and that even if the counter-claim were to be filed, the same would have been rejected in terms of the said judgment. The passing of a decree for possession cannot be deferred, if the petitioner plaintiff were to be found entitled thereto, for the reason of the respondent/defendant intending to file a suit for setting aside of the sale deed and the lease deed, even if such suit is still within limitation. The fact remains that notwithstanding the written statement in the suit having been filed in February 2015, the respondent defendant till now has not filed any such suit. Thus, as of now there is no step taken by the respondent defendant for rescission of the registered documents aforesaid which establish the title of the petitioner plaintiff to the property (though in a suit between landlord and tenant, such title is not necessary) and the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties. The said registered documents have to prevail, particularly when the execution and registration thereof is admitted. The plea of the documents having been got executed by misrepresentation, cannot be a defence to a suit on the basis of the said documents unless the said documents are so declared by a competent court of law. Supreme Court in Gorakh Nath Dube v. Hari Narain Singh, 1973 (SLT Soft) 620, though in the context of jurisdiction of the Consolidation Officer under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, held that a distinction has to be made between cases where a document is wholly or partially invalid so that it can be disregarded by any court or authority and a document which has to be actually set aside before it can cease to have legal effect.

title: Test #45: Lucknow's Culural Biographer and Literary Feud
text: Apart from the short-lived ‘Lakhnau Akhbar’, first published in 1847, the growth of print journalism in Awadh gained momentum following the British annexation of the region in 1856. One of the earliest notable publications of this period was ‘Tilism-e-Lakhnau’, popularly known as ‘Tilism’, which began publication in 1856 under the editorship of Maulvi Yakub Ansari. This was followed by ‘Oudh (Awadh) Akhbar’, launched by Munshi Nawal Kishore in 1859, and ‘Oudh Punch’, founded by Mohammad Sajjad Hussain in 1877. In 1886, Abdul Halim Sharar brought out ‘Dil Gudaz’, further enriching the region’s literary and journalistic landscape. We now turn to the life and struggles of Pandit Brij Narayan Chakbast, who was born in Faizabad in 1882 into a Kashmiri family. He emerged as a distinguished nazm poet associated with the Lucknow school of Urdu poetry, drawing inspiration from literary giants such as Mirza Ghalib and Mir Anis. Brij Narayan also participated in the freedom movement and was actively involved in socio-political movements of his time. In 1905, Chakbast published an edition of a ‘masnavi’ (a kind of poem written in rhyming couplets on the Sufi tradition) called ‘Gulzar-e-Nasim’ by Pandit Daya Shankar Kaul ‘Nasim.’ Sharar responded vehemently against this in ‘Dil Gudaz’ with other writers and editors taking sides. Sharar apparently wanted to exclude the ‘Kashmiri’ element from chaste Urdu literature, which he felt should be confined to Lucknow and nearby areas. In an era where ethnic, linguistic and religious identities were assuming importance during colonial rule, this rivalry soon spread wide, with writers and printing presses from Kanpur and even Hyderabad joining the fray. The ‘Awadh Akhbar’ chose to stay away from the controversy, but ‘Awadh Punch’ remained at the forefront of this debate. Young Chakbast gained a certain amount of notoriety in this whole episode, due to his confrontation with Sharar, a much senior and distinguished writer and journalist during that period. One of the fallouts of this controversy between the Sharar and the Chakbast was that as the debate got more acrimonious, many personal skeletons started emerging from cupboards. Sharar was at the receiving end of all this. Sajjad Hussain of ‘Awadh Punch’ wrote deprecatingly of Sharar, labelling him as a writer who was ‘easily able to create historical events about which it is impossible to find historical witness, but his ‘Khāyāl’ (imagination) was so strong that it was not difficult to create strange and wondrous events in this head of his.’ Sharar had tried to advance the premise that the ‘masnavi’ in question was the work of Atish, and simultaneously, it also fell short of the language of Lucknow. Thus, Sharar’s faulty logic not only downplayed Chakbast and Nasim - according to him, Atish had also failed to express himself in the ‘Lakhnavi andaz’ in the debated masnavi. In those days, Sheikh Imam Baksh ‘Nasikh’ and Khwaja Haider Ali ‘Atish’ were considered to be the founders of the Lucknow school of poetry. Thus, Sharar’s allegations were unacceptable to the public. Sharar had been known for his respectable lineage in the erstwhile Nawabi court, both at Lucknow and Metia Burz, Calcutta, as well as his connections in the state of Hyderabad. ‘Awadh Punch’ being a journal devoted to satire, took this opportunity to lampoon Sharar, drawing upon his roots in Kursi (an area then on the outskirts of Lucknow, with the dubious reputation of having slow-witted inhabitants). Today, Sharar is best known for his series of articles on Lucknow, published in ‘Dil Gudaz’ in which he had described the history of Lucknow and the lifestyle of its people. The articles were later compiled into a single volume called ‘Guzishta Lucknow’, its English translation being titled as ‘Lucknow: The Last Phase of an Oriental Culture’. Although Sharar’s writings had earned him fame and respectability, disclosures about his rustic origins and propensity to write in hyperbole, rendered his accounts of Lucknow’s former Nawabi court as debatable.

title: Test #46: Reefs, Lagoons, Light & Coastal Islands
text: Gulf of Mannar’s bizarre, jewel-toned reefs puzzled nineteenth-century naturalists; between 1880-1920, surveyors catalogued roughly 3,600 marine species across just twenty-one tiny islands scattered off Tamil Nadu’s southeastern coast. Quartz-white sand, jagged limestone, and exquisitely fragile coral polyps combine there to form what zoologists now call India’s most biodiverse marine ecosystem a ‘living laboratory’, as one exasperated researcher put it after losing count of the species. Was such extraordinary density even plausible in shallow, often turbulent water? Declared a National Park in 1986 and a Biosphere Reserve by 1989 (India’s first marine biosphere reserve), the zone now spans roughly 10,500 square kilometres, protecting seagrass meadows, mangrove fringes, and four major coral families: Acropora, Favia, Porites, and the slower-growing Montipora. Zealous conservationists, exhausted fishermen, and curious tourists all converge each winter along this narrow, jagged coastline, each group pursuing wildly different objectives. Roughly eight hundred kilometres west, across open sea, the twenty-two inhabited islands and atolls of Lakshadweep form a strikingly different reef system. Unlike the fringing reefs of Mannar, these are true atolls rings of coral growing atop ancient, submerged volcanic cones that sank slowly over several million years. Lagoons here average barely two metres deep, yet they shelter parrotfish, moray eels, and reef sharks in astonishing abundance. The entire landmass totals just 32 square kilometres, among the smallest Union Territories in the country, though the surrounding lagoon area is roughly four thousand square kilometres. Severe bleaching events struck both regions in 1998, 2010, and again in 2016, when unusually warm currents lingered for weeks rather than days, killing large sections of shallow reef almost overnight. Scientists studying these events discovered that corals expel the symbiotic algae living within their tissue once water temperatures climb even slightly above normal thresholds, a process now widely known as bleaching. Without that algae, coral tissue turns ghostly white and, if warm conditions persist for more than a few weeks, the coral itself eventually starves and dies. Restoration teams near Mandapam and Kavaratti now grow fragments on underwater nurseries built from cement frames, metal racks, and even old fishing nets, transplanting healthy coral onto damaged reef sections once the fragments mature. Early results suggest survival rates above sixty percent for several hardy species, though scientists caution that nursery-grown coral remains vulnerable to the same warming trends that caused the original damage. Local fishing communities have mixed feelings about these marine protected areas. Many families depend entirely on reef fisheries for both food and income, and strict conservation rules sometimes restrict traditional fishing grounds that households have used for generations. Government programmes now try to balance these competing needs by training former fishermen as reef guides, dive instructors, or restoration workers, creating alternative income streams that reduce pressure on fragile reef zones. Several cooperative societies around Rameswaram report encouraging results, though officials admit that enforcement across scattered, hard-to-reach islands remains genuinely difficult. Climate change now poses the gravest long-term threat to both reef systems. Rising sea surface temperatures, increasing ocean acidity, and more frequent cyclones all threaten to outpace whatever local conservation efforts can achieve. Researchers from several national institutes continue mapping reef health using satellite imagery combined with underwater surveys, hoping to predict future bleaching events before they strike rather than merely documenting damage afterward. Some scientists argue that only substantial global reductions in carbon emissions can ultimately secure these reefs beyond this century, while others insist that strong local protection still buys valuable time for coral populations to adapt naturally.

title: Test #46: Darwin Review - The Evolution of a Life
text: “That everlasting Origin,” Charles Darwin complained in 1868 as he was readying yet another version of “On the Origin of Species,” first published in 1859. “I am sick of correcting.” Yet he went on correcting, as he had done for several previous editions, cutting and replacing words, rearranging sentences, even adding a new chapter to the sixth edition. It was as if the message Darwin hoped to convey that life was a constant process of loss, change and renewal was also true of the book that has come to define him. If Darwin (1809-82) was a committed reviser, it appears that his biographer Janet Browne, an emeritus professor of scientific history at Harvard, has taken some inspiration from her subject. Take the consequential months after Darwin’s return to England in October 1836 after his nearly five-year voyage around the world on HMS Beagle, when his theory of evolution was a flicker in his mind. Ms. Browne’s original account of that period proceeded accordingly, as if in slow motion. We learned that Darwin celebrated New Year’s Eve 1836 with a snowball fight in Cambridge. We found out that the daughters of the geologist Leonard Horner invited Darwin to come over for a visit in Maori, which they thought would impress the world traveler. And we looked over Darwin’s shoulder as he filled his notebooks, sized “just right for slipping into a pocket,” and sorted through the maze in his mind as he met with people who helped him make sense of the specimens he had brought back. In the new version, stripped of detours and detail, the same period occupies only a few pages. Ms. Browne’s prose takes on a balletic quality as she captures the excitement Darwin felt on the cusp of discovery: “Daringly, Darwin began to dance with the notion of transmutation as he had never danced before.” Ms. Browne recounts how Darwin experimented with “cascades of ideas” and “oscillated between recording things he had read or heard and tackling on his own the deepest themes of metaphysics.” Buffered by wealth and social position, Darwin was able to reconcile, like few of his peers, the secluded life of a country squire with the exacting demands of scientific work. Down House, his home in Kent became his refuge as well as his lab. “Where does your father do his barnacles?” one of Darwin’s boys innocently asked when visiting a friend’s house. The eight years Darwin spent dismembering these tiny invertebrates at home took up more than 20 pages in Ms. Browne’s old version; they now receive barely four. What we gain is a concise reminder of why barnacles and the many forms they take were so important to Darwin. He loved the rudimentary males he found embedded in the females of one particular species precisely the kind of weird transitional form his theory of evolution would depend upon. In Ms. Browne’s compression, the reader immediately understands how Darwin’s diverse interests came to fit together like the pieces of a puzzle. There are other benefits to Ms. Browne’s winnowing. “After this, Darwin turned back to barnacles with a heavy heart,” she had written previously about his attempt to come to terms with the death of his 10-year-old daughter, Annie, in 1851. The sentence is now pared down to a simpler but rhythmically effective line mimicking the weight that was on Darwin: “With a heavy heart he buried himself in barnacles.” Late in life, Darwin became infatuated with earthworms, a fitting preoccupation for an aging naturalist. In the original biography, Ms. Browne gave us a memorable image of him following the progress of the worms in his backyard: “Darwin became at the end what he had always been in his heart, almost part of nature himself, a man with time to lean on a spade and think, a gardener.” Yet the notion of a working gardener suggests continuous activity, watering down the image of a man slowing down. Ms. Browne now cuts the word, leaving the reader with a pithier portrait of Darwin (almost) at rest, a man finally permitted to be a leaner and loafer, the Walt Whitman of natural science.

title: Test #47: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1730 of 2012
text: The prosecution case rested exclusively on circumstantial evidence, alleging that the appellant, an unmarried rural woman, delivered an infant out of wedlock on 14th November, 2004, murdered the newborn to conceal her pregnancy, and threw the corpse into a village pond. The trial court and the High Court convicted the appellant, relying primarily upon the post-mortem report and the testimony of lady medical officer (PW-11), who deposed that clinical examination revealed physical symptoms consistent with recent parturition. However, scrutiny of the trial record disclosed that during the recording of the appellant's statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the trial judge framed only four vague, composite questions regarding village rumours, completely omitting to confront her with the medical opinion of PW-11 or the findings of the post-mortem examination. Furthermore, the trial court treated her denial of pregnancy as a false defense, utilizing it as a missing link to complete the circumstantial chain. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the omission to put material incriminating circumstances to the accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. vitiates the conviction. The Court held that Section 313 is not an empty judicial ritual, but an essential manifestation of natural justice rooted in the maxim audi alteram partem. Its primary object is to establish a direct dialogue between the court and the accused, ensuring that every incriminating circumstance appearing in prosecution evidence is specifically, clearly, and separately put to the accused to afford him a fair opportunity of explanation. In Premchand v. State of Maharashtra, reported in (2023) 5 SCC 522, and Kalicharan v. State of U.P., reported in (2023) 2 SCC 583, this Court reaffirmed that an incriminating circumstance not put to the accused in Section 313 examination must be completely excluded from judicial consideration. Furthermore, the answers given under Section 313 or a false denial cannot be utilized by the prosecution to fill up gaps or supply missing links in a defective circumstantial chain. The accused has a constitutional right to silence under Article 20(3) and a fundamental right to dignity and privacy under Article 21. Since the foundational medical circumstances were never put to the appellant, they could not be used to convict her. The circumstantial evidence being incomplete, the conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC are set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is directed against the judgment and order dated 20th April, 2010 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Baikunthpur in Criminal Appeal No. 605 of 2005, affirming the judgment of conviction and sentence of life imprisonment recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Baikunthpur under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the trial court failed to put essential incriminating circumstances to the appellant during her examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Indrakunwar v. State of Chhattisgarh, reported in (2024) 14 SCC 595, authoritatively restated the constitutional and statutory significance of Section 313 Cr.P.C. (now Section 351 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). The Court held that an accomplice is a person who participates in the commission of the crime with criminal mens rea. A trap witness or decoy who acts under official instructions to detect public corruption is not an accomplice in the strict sense of Section 133 of the Evidence Act, as he lacks criminal intent. However, a trap witness is an interested and partisan witness who is keenly interested in the success of the trap operation he participated in. Therefore, as a rule of prudence and caution, the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness cannot form the sole basis for convicting a public servant.

title: Test #47: Trouble at the Bottom of the Pyramid
text:
For some time, the Indian economy has presented a puzzle. GDP growth has been fabulous 7.1% and 8.2% in the last two years, followed by 7.2% in the first quarter of the new fiscal year 2024-25. Given sluggish conditions in many countries, this looks excellent. Yet consumer goods sales have been rising only modestly, almost sluggishly. Bank credit is growing well below earlier rates. How can a country have a fantastic GDP boom but slack sales and modest credit growth? The bottom of the income pyramid should benefit most in a sustained GDP boom. Economists have differed on whether or not rural India is in economic trouble. But we are now witnessing something close to a crash in microfinance institutions (MFIs) that lend to the poor and small businesses. Small Finance Banks (SFBs), which are MFIs that have graduated to become full banks, also face a sharp rise in loan defaults. Spandana Sphoorty, a microfinance pioneer, had record profits of Rs 468 crore in 2023-24. But in the July-Sept quarter alone, it suffered a huge loss of Rs 204 crore, mainly because of loans gone sour. Credit Access Grameen is a well managed MFI, but its profit halved in the July-Sept quarter. Equitas, one of the top SFBs, saw profits fall almost 90% in July-Sept compared with the earlier quarter. Big banks have finally got rid of bad loans accumulated in the 2010s, and have been preparing for a lending boom. They are not dependent on the bottom of the pyramid, and their big business clients are doing well. Even so Bajaj Finance, the biggest and best non-bank lender, doubled its provisions for defaults in the latest quarter, mostly from smaller borrowers. Why are borrowers defaulting at the bottom of the pyramid? The problem is not just rural distress, as some aver, but a mini-lending boom gone badly. In 2022, RBI substantially de-regulated the MFI sector, abolishing caps on interest rates while stipulating that monthly repayments should not exceed 50% of borrower income. Delighted with de-regulation, small lenders went on a lending spree with insufficient scrutiny, and with higher interest rates to make up for the increased risk. Earlier, lenders were supposed to avoid borrowers who already had three loans, but in the deregulated euphoria, there were cases of even six or six loans from different, competing MFIs. Disturbed, RBI told the sector to pull back on lending without collateral. This was too late to stop defaults from surging. MFIs had, unsurprisingly, raised lending rates after deregulation. But RBI has suddenly decided to penalize four MFIs for usurious interest rates.

title: Test #48: Economic Nobel - Post Keynes Smarts
text: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford have helped develop what’s called “New Keynesian economics”. They’re dealing with the same economic problems that exercised Keynes’ mind, but with a fundamentally different approach. So, Hall and Woodford are credited with giving “microeconomic foundations” to “macroeconomic stabilisation”. Macroeconomic stabilisation refers to policies that governments and central banks use to “stabilise” an economy. Nobody wants a recession or, for emerging economies, a slowdown. For decades, Keynes’ fix slash interest rates and increase govt spending worked. Until it didn’t in the oil crisis of 1970s, and even 2008’s financial crisis when, despite rock-bottom interest rates, spending and employment didn’t pick up. That’s why thousands of economists around the world have been trying to find better “cures” for all kinds of economic instability booms and busts, high inflation and deflation. This year’s economics Nobel recognises the efforts of two such economists, both American, whose work has helped govts and central banks tackle recessions and high inflation faster. Instead of basing policy only on macroeconomic indicators like inflation, production, and consumption, they recommend zooming into the behaviours of households and individual businesses that make up the economy. That’s because they believe every individual in an economy acts on the basis of information available to them. If you’re in the market for a refrigerator, and know that consumer loans will be cheaper next week, you’ll put off the purchase. They’ve shown that how millions of households spend, gives an idea of what the entire economy expects. Hall, who’s the older of the two, first presented his ideas in a 1978 paper. He argued that since household spending depends on expectations of future income, consumption decisions can indicate economic expectations. Will hiring increase, will incomes grow, etc. The way to influence individual behaviour, then, is to provide more information. What’s now called “forward guidance”. For example, RBI’s monetary policy committee recently hinted at no rate cuts in the months ahead. Woodford’s additionally known for his work on restoring balance in an economy, after a disruptive shock. The Iran war is a good example. It’s pushed up energy prices and inflation globally, and impacted growth, and central banks everywhere are trying to minimise these effects, with some help from Hall and Woodford’s theories. Over the past few years, the global economy has faced an exceptional number of risks and challenges: from a global pandemic that brought all economic activity to a sudden halt, crushing incomes and businesses, to a growing number of wars that have spiked prices of essential commodities, to policy missteps like tariffs. And yet, far from a recession, the economic growth continues to surprise on the upside. A big reason why policymakers worldwide have been able to avoid worse outcomes is because their policies are informed by the work of academics such as Hall and Woodford. For instance, the Reserve Bank of India last week raised interest rates with a view to contain inflation. Inflation in India has been going up owing to a rise in crude oil prices and prices of other commodities in the wake of the US-Iran war, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, etc. There are also worries that inflation will rise further because deficient rainfall and higher temperatures due to El Nino may hurt food production and push up food prices. If the government and the central bank followed the dictum that the government should not intervene and that the markets will price things correctly on their own, inflation can potentially soar quite high. That would hurt most Indians, since they are not rich enough to handle such a situation. It could lead to people cutting down all other expenses to focus on the essentials, which would cause many businesses to fail and lots of job losses. The economy, as a whole, may take a much longer time to recover possibly years.

title: Test #48: Gaining Knowledge via Quantum Entaglement
text: What is thought? It is a hologram produced via photons emitted in the synaptic cleft, an extremely small, 20-nanometre region between neurons where one neuron talks with another by exchanging neurotransmitters. These NTs are chemicals that are exchanged between neurons and once exchanged; they are converted into electrical signals inside the neuron for the onward journey. A large number of such neuron interactions produce neural pathways, and each set of such neural pathways is responsible for the thought production of a particular object. During this exchange of neurotransmitters, weak photons, also called biophotons, are produced at each synaptic cleft. The synchronization of millions and millions of such synaptic cleft photons produces a hologram, which we can call thought. Most of these holograms are continuously produced in the brain. When the focus is not there, they also fade immediately. This is called brain chatter and is the genesis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD. However, a concentrated thought hologram, which, according to Sage Patanjali, results in Sanyam, concentration, focus, and Samadhi, has enough energy to be transmitted out of the brain; it is what we call a leaky thought. This thought hologram interacts with the object or subject of our interest and gets its knowledge. How does this interaction take place, and more importantly, how do our brains receive this knowledge? For objects that we can see and feel, it is quite easy because our senses guide through hologram in doing so. But for concepts and subjects that we do not see and are beyond our reach, what is the mechanism? The science of quantum entanglement may provide a possible answer. Quantum entanglement spooky action at a distance, as Einstein described it states that photons or even particles created or generated are entangled with each other in such a manner that knowledge of one can describe the other, no matter how far apart they are. We can conjecture that our concentrated thought hologram, which leaks out of the brain and interacts with the object or subject of our interest, somehow changes the property of hologram in the brain via the entanglement process. This continuous exchange of information through quantum entanglement allows ideas and reality to match in an induced-fit arrangement; thus, knowledge is perceived. The induced-fit model is used in drug design and is based on the hypothesis that the drug binds to the active site; in the process of binding, changes the shape of the active site to achieve a precise fit. This enhances drug action. The same action of induced fit may occur in hologram interaction with the object of interest, affecting the hologram in the brain. Sage Patanjali has also alluded to this mechanism in his Yoga Sutras. All great discoveries such as Einstein’s theory of gravitation; Newton’s theory of light, gravity, motion; music of Beethoven, Mozart among others, and knowledge of the universe by sages and scientists have been obtained by this process. However, when our senses do not feel and guide thoughts, yet knowledge is perceived, it can happen only through quantum entanglement of thought.

title: Test #49: Can AI Ever be Conscious?
text: Extraordinary progress of artificial intelligence (AI) has brought us face to face with a profound question: can a machine ever become conscious. But there is another possibility. Before asking whether a machine can become conscious, perhaps we should first ask whether we understand what consciousness itself is. This question takes us beyond conventional science into philosophy, and perhaps into experiences of those rare individuals who claimed to have gone beyond the ordinary human mind. Neuro-science can identify correlations between brain activity and conscious experience, but correlation alone does not explain why there is something it feels like to see a colour, experience pain, or hear music. Ramana goes further. In his view, consciousness is not mind. The brain may be an instrument through which consciousness is expressed without being its ultimate source. If this is correct, reproducing every observable function of the human mind would not necessarily reproduce consciousness. This is why experiences of contemplative sages may have philosophical relevance to the AI debate, because they claim to have discovered the Self that is beyond mind. Ramana Maharshi, for instance, taught that the true Self is distinct from the body, mind and stream of thoughts that normally constitute our sense of personal identity. For Ramana, the Self was something that could be directly realised by turning attention inward and stilling the mind. His argument has remarkable implications for artificial consciousness. Al is essentially an extraordinary development of capabilities of what we call ‘mind’. It may eventually perform virtually every intellectual task that we can perform. It could become so convincing that, from its outward behaviour, it would be impossible to distinguish it from a conscious hu-man being. But would that establish that it is actually conscious? Ramana would have challenged the assumption underlying the question. For him, mind is not the Self. Thoughts appear and disappear. Emotions and memories do likewise. Even our ordinary sense of ‘i am this person’ can be observed. If something can be observed, Ramana argued, it cannot be the ultimate observer. His argument be-comes particularly intriguing when we consider deep sleep. When awake, we experience our body, senses, thoughts and the external world. In dreams, the waking world disappears and another mental world appears. In deep sleep, however, even the ordinary mind and its thoughts disappear. For Ramana, this points to some-thing fundamental: mind can disappear without the Self disappearing. Mind comes and goes; the Self remains. There is an interesting, though limited, parallel with Thomas Aquinas, who belonged to an entirely different philosophical and theological tradition. Aquinas argued that human intellectual activity cannot simply be described by biology alone. An artificial system can be constructed to perform mental functions calculating, remembering, reasoning, communicating and perhaps even simulating introspection. But these functions do not necessarily demonstrate the existence of an experiencing subject behind them. An AI could say, ‘i am conscious. It could describe its feelings and insist that it possesses an inner life. It might even pass every behavioural test de-vised to distinguish a conscious being from an unconscious machine. Yet we would still face the fundamental question: is there actually someone experiencing these processes? This is related to what philosopher David Chalmers called the ‘hard problem of consciousness.’ If Ramana Maharshi was right, the answer may not be found by examining increasingly sophisticated minds, whether biological or artificial. We may first have to understand consciousness, and whether it is something that a mind can create.

title: Test #49: SSC Typing Passage - The Families of Labourers
text:
You will find that a very few industrialists really look into the different welfare aspects of the labourers. Take the example of families and children of the labourers. Do their employers make proper arrangement for their health care and education; leave aside their cultural upliftment or their cultural life? The families of the labourers are not looked after properly and a great deal needs to be done and in this regard voluntary organisations can play some role. A small amount has been provided for the welfare of children and women in the unorganised sector. I would urge upon the hon. Minister that the allocations to the voluntary organisations for the betterment of women and children in the organised as well as unorganised sectors should be increased. Sir, as regards the lockouts, wherever there is a lockout of the industry, the labourers have a great deal of suffering. They do not know what to do. They are just left to their lot. But the employer does not suffer as such. Just look at the employers of different big industries. Their standard of living does not change after locking the industry but the people in the factories are left on the street. I suggest that whenever the question of lock-out in a particular industry comes up, the question should be considered whether the labourers will be able to run a particular industry and a lot of consideration should be given to this particular aspect and, if possible, that particular industry should be kept alive. Sir, migration is a very important problem of labourers and it has got multi-dimensions, that is, labourers within the country and those who are going outside the country. Lot of labourers is exported outside the country and they are facing lot of problems because of the agencies. I would like to mention here one thing that we have entrusted this work to many of the private agencies. But there is need to consider whether we can have a manpower corporation and assign this work to the corporation. Also, there are problems of inter-State migration of the labourers. There is an Act but it is causing difficulties to the labourers who migrate to other States. Assessing whether existing rates are sufficient to meet the needs of workers and their families can be challenging. First, needs of workers and their families cannot be considered in a vacuum; they must be understood in relation to a country level of economic and social development, taking into account the views of social partners.
