सीएफ एंड्रूज और कांग्रेस के संस्थापकों में से एक एओ ह्यूम, जॉर्ज यूल का नाम शामिल है। इन विदेशी लोगों में एक विदेशी महिला का नाम सबसे प्रमुखता से लिया जाता है। आजादी के लिए ब्रिटिश हुकूमत के खिलाफ आवाज उठाने वाली इस विदेशी महिला का नाम एनी बेसेंट था, जो कि आयरलैंड की समाज सेविका थीं। लंदन में एक उच्च मध्यम वर्ग परिवार में जन्मीं एनी बेसेंट 1917 में कोलकाता में कांग्रेस की पहली महिला अध्यक्ष चुनी गईं। वह मूल रूप से आयरलैंड की रहने वाली थीं, लेकिन उन विदेशियों में शामिल थीं, जिन्होंने भारतीय स्वतंत्रता संग्राम में अहम भूमिका निभाई। महिला अधिकार कार्यकर्ता एनी बेसेंट का जन्म 01 अक्तूबर सन 1847 में हुआ था। उनके पिता डाक्टर थे। बेसेंट 16 नवंबर 1893 को मद्रास के अडयार में थियोसोफिकल सोसायटी के वार्षिक सम्मेलन में हिस्सा लेने पहली बार भारत आईं और फिर यहीं कि हो कर रह गई। उन्होंने साल 1898 में वाराणसी में सेंट्रल हिंदू कॉलेज की स्थापना की। पहले विश्व युद्ध के दौरान वर्ष 1914 में एनी बेसेंट ने साप्ताहिक समाचार पत्र कॉमनविल की स्थापना की। इसी वर्ष उन्होंने मद्रास स्टैंडर्ड को खरीद कर उसे न्यू इंडिया नाम दिया। बेसेंट साल 1917 में भारतीय राष्ट्रीय कांग्रेस की अध्यक्ष बनीं। भारत में फैली सामाजिक बुराइयों जैसे बाल विवाह, जाति व्यवस्था, विधवा विवाह आदि को दूर करने के लिए बेसेंट ने ब्रदर्स ऑफ सर्विस संस्था बनाई।

आधुनिक समाज के सर्वांगीण विकास के लिए बुनियादी ढांचे, जनस्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा और पर्यावरण संरक्षण का समन्वित विकास अपरिहार्य है। ग्रामीण एवं शहरी क्षेत्रों में संचालित विकास योजनाओं के वित्तीय आंकड़ों, प्रगति आख्याओं और लाभार्थी सूचियों का सटीक डिजिटल अभिलेखीकरण सरकारी नीतियों की सफलता तय करता है। जब विभागीय कर्मचारी आधुनिक कंप्यूटर उपकरणों और त्वरित टंकण कौशल से संपन्न होते हैं तो शासकीय कार्यों में अनावश्यक विलंब समाप्त हो जाता है।

प्रतियोगी टंकण परीक्षा में सम्मिलित होने वाले अभ्यर्थियों को चाहिए कि वे विविध सामाजिक, आर्थिक एवं विधिक विषयों से संबंधित अनुच्छेदों पर टंकण का गहन अभ्यास करें। अभ्यास के दौरान शुद्धता को सर्वोच्च प्राथमिकता देनी चाहिए क्योंकि शुद्ध टंकण ही नेट गति को बढ़ाता है और परीक्षा में सफलता का मार्ग प्रशस्त करता है। उत्तर प्रदेश पुलिस भर्ती एवं प्रोन्नति बोर्ड द्वारा आयोजित कंप्यूटर ऑपरेटर परीक्षा में निर्धारित गति एवं उच्च शुद्धता प्राप्त करना ही अंतिम चयन का आधार बनता है।

title: Test #72: Parivahan Kshetra Ko Carbon Mukta Hona Hoga
text:
भारत का सड़क परिवहन क्षेत्र मुख्य रूप से पेट्रोल और डीजल पर निर्भर है और यह देश का सबसे बड़ा तेल उपयोगकर्ता क्षेत्र भी है। देश में पेट्रोलियम पदार्थों के कुल उपभोग में ऑटोमोबाइल सेक्टर की हिस्सेदारी 44 प्रतिशत है। जहां तक वैकल्पिक ईंधन का सवाल है, तो उसकी भूमिका बहुत सीमित है। जाहिर है, उत्सर्जन में परिवहन क्षेत्र के भारी योगदान को देखते हुए इस क्षेत्र को डीकार्बनाइज करने के प्रयास नेट-जीरो लक्ष्यों को हासिल करने के लिहाज से अहम हैं। परिवहन क्षेत्र को डीकार्बनाइज किए बिना नेट-जीरो लक्ष्यों को हासिल करना मुश्किल साबित होगा। जाहिर है, इसके लिए भारत को ज्यादातर इलेक्ट्रिक वाहनों पर निर्भर रहना होगा। नतीजतन इलेक्ट्रिक वाहनों के निर्माण, नई टेक्नोलॉजी और अनुसंधान एवं विकास पर बहुत बड़े पैमाने पर निवेश करना जरूरी हो गया है। क्लाइमेट एंड सस्टेनेबिलिटी इनीशिएटिव की एक रिपोर्ट के मुताबिक, परिवहन क्षेत्र को डीकार्बनाइज किए जाने से परिवहन उद्योग, खासकर इलेक्ट्रिक वाहन क्षेत्र में विकास के अवसर पैदा हो सकते हैं। इंडिया ऑटो इंडस्ट्री मैपिंग कोर्स टू नेट जीरो 2070 शीर्षक वाली रिपोर्ट में कहा गया है कि वर्ष 2070 तक देश में ऑटो सेक्टर का रूपांतरण होने से 197 खरब डॉलर का बाजार तैयार हो सकता है। इसमें 63 प्रतिशत हिस्सेदारी कारों की होगी और इनका योगदान 155 खरब डॉलर का होगा। रिपोर्ट के अनुसार, वर्ष 2070 तक करीब 263 अरब डॉलर का सबसे बड़ा निवेश चार पहिया इलेक्ट्रिक वाहनों के लिए जरूरी हो सकता है। ट्रक निर्माताओं द्वारा वर्ष 2070 तक घरेलू मांग को पूरा करने के लिए 45 अरब डॉलर से अधिक के निवेश का अनुमान है। इसके अलावा, वर्ष 2020 से 2070 के बीच ऑटोमोबाइल क्षेत्र के रूपांतरण से माल एवं सेवा कर के रूप में 41 खरब डॉलर का राजस्व भी हासिल होने का अनुमान है। बड़े-बड़े महानगरों की हवा मानव स्वास्थ्य हानिकारक हो चुकी है, इसके पीछे उद्योगों से निकलने वाला धुआं और विनिर्माण क्षेत्र के अलावा डीजल-पेट्रोल से चलने वाले वाहन भी हैं। इसलिए हम और हमारी आने वाली पीढ़ियां स्वच्छ हवा में सांस ले सकें, इसके लिए मौजूदा परिदृश्य में इलेक्ट्रिक वाहन सबसे अच्छा विकल्प हैं। भारत का सड़क परिवहन क्षेत्र मुख्य रूप से पेट्रोल और डीजल पर निर्भर है और यह देश का सबसे बड़ा तेल उपयोगकर्ता क्षेत्र भी है। देश में पेट्रोलियम पदार्थों के कुल उपभोग में ऑटोमोबाइल सेक्टर की हिस्सेदारी 44 प्रतिशत है। जहां तक वैकल्पिक ईंधन का सवाल है, तो उसकी भूमिका बहुत सीमित है।

आधुनिक समाज के सर्वांगीण विकास के लिए बुनियादी ढांचे, जनस्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा और पर्यावरण संरक्षण का समन्वित विकास अपरिहार्य है। ग्रामीण एवं शहरी क्षेत्रों में संचालित विकास योजनाओं के वित्तीय आंकड़ों, प्रगति आख्याओं और लाभार्थी सूचियों का सटीक डिजिटल अभिलेखीकरण सरकारी नीतियों की सफलता तय करता है। जब विभागीय कर्मचारी आधुनिक कंप्यूटर उपकरणों और त्वरित टंकण कौशल से संपन्न होते हैं तो शासकीय कार्यों में अनावश्यक विलंब समाप्त हो जाता है।

प्रतियोगी टंकण परीक्षा में सम्मिलित होने वाले अभ्यर्थियों को चाहिए कि वे विविध सामाजिक, आर्थिक एवं विधिक विषयों से संबंधित अनुच्छेदों पर टंकण का गहन अभ्यास करें। अभ्यास के दौरान शुद्धता को सर्वोच्च प्राथमिकता देनी चाहिए क्योंकि शुद्ध टंकण ही नेट गति को बढ़ाता है और परीक्षा में सफलता का मार्ग प्रशस्त करता है। उत्तर प्रदेश पुलिस भर्ती एवं प्रोन्नति बोर्ड द्वारा आयोजित कंप्यूटर ऑपरेटर परीक्षा में निर्धारित गति एवं उच्च शुद्धता प्राप्त करना ही अंतिम चयन का आधार बनता है।

title: Test #73: Ek Desh Ek Chunav Se Kitna Fayda
text: देश में लंबे समय से एक देश एक चुनाव की चर्चा हो रही है। प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी के सत्ता में आने के बाद इसमें तेजी आई। सरकार ने इसे लेकर कमेटी बनाई। जिस तरह से कमेटी ने काम किया, उससे पता चलता है कि सरकार इसे लेकर कितनी गंभीर है। एक देश एक चुनाव को लागू करने के लिए एक जटिल प्रक्रिया होगी। सरकार को इससे जुड़ी जटिलताओं पर काम करना होगा। अगर कहीं सरकार बीच में गिर जाती है तो क्या होगा? छोटे दलों की चिंताओं को कैसे दूर किया जाएगा? इन सवालों के जवाब सरकार को तलाशने होंगे। सरकार की कोशिश होगी कि इसे लेकर आम सहमति बनाई जाए। मेरा मानना है कि यह एक बहुत बड़ा सुधारवादी कदम है। यह भाजपा सरकार का एजेंडा है। यह जनसंघ के जमाने से उनके एजेंडे में रहा है। उसी से यह एक देश एक चुनाव निकला है। आजादी के बाद यह होता भी था, लेकिन बाद में इसमें बदलाव आया। संविधान में इसे लेकर कोई व्यवस्था नहीं थी। मेरा मानना है कि मूल रूप से यह लोकतंत्र की मूल धारणा को नुकसान पहुंचाएगा। कहने में भले ही यह बहुत अच्छा दिखता हो। यह तर्क कि चुनाव के दबाव में काम नहीं हो पाता, मैं इससे सहमत नहीं हूं। यह एकाधिकारवाद की ओर ले जाने वाली व्यवस्था होगी। जो अस्थिरता का दौर हमारे देश ने देखा उस समय इसकी चर्चा ज्यादा थी। 1999 के बाद से देश में स्थिर सरकारें रही हैं, इसलिए इस दौर में यह उतना क्रांतिकारी कदम नहीं दिखाई दे रहा होगा। कोविंद समिति की रिपोर्ट जो भी ध्यान से पढ़ेगा उसमें उन सारे प्रश्नों के उत्तर हैं जो हमारे मन में उठ रहे हैं। यहां तक कि दुनिया के अलग-अलग देशों के उदाहरण भी इसमें दिए गए हैं। मूल सवाल यह है कि क्या एक देश एक चुनाव फलीभूत होगा या नहीं? मेरा मानना है कि यह फलीभूत होगा। चुनाव की प्रक्रिया में लगातार सुधार हो रहा है। अब एक नए सुधार की बात हो रही है। तमाम तरह की जो चिंताएं जाहिर की जा रही हैं, उन्हें कुछ तो कोविंद समिति की रिपोर्ट में कुछ आगे जो मसौदा तैयार किया जएगा उसमें उन्हें दूर करने का प्रयास किया जाएगा। जिस दिन ईवीएम आई थी उस दिन भी सवाल उठे थे। सवाल अनंत काल तक जारी रहेंगे। चुनाव कराने की जिम्मेदारी चुनाव आयोग की है और व्यवस्था। इस विचार की आलोचना के वैध कारण हैं। चुनाव आयोग चार राज्यों का तो एक साथ चुनाव नहीं करा पा रहा है फिर कैसे 28 राज्यों के चुनाव एक साथ कराएंगे।

The Doctrine of Pith and Substance represents one of the most vital principles of constitutional interpretation employed in federal and quasi-federal jurisdictions to preserve the delicate equilibrium of legislative competence between central and regional governing bodies. Originating in the nineteenth-century jurisprudence of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council while interpreting the distribution of legislative powers under the British North America Act of 1867 most notably articulated in decisions such as Cushing v. Dupuy and Russell v. The Queen the doctrine addresses the inescapable reality that complex modern legislation cannot always be compartmentalized into neat, water-tight constitutional compartments. This doctrine gained widespread prominence and rigorous institutional development in the constitutional jurisprudence of India, where it was extensively applied to resolve federal disputes under the Government of India Act of 1935 and subsequently embedded into the post-independence constitutional framework under Article 246. In the landmark case of Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce, Khulna (1947), the Privy Council upheld the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, which capped loan interest rates a topic of provincial competence regarding money-lending even though it incidentally affected negotiable instruments such as promissory notes, a field reserved exclusively for the federal legislature, because the dominant pith and substance of the law was agrarian debt relief rather than commercial banking. This judicial approach was reaffirmed and cemented by the Supreme Court of India in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where the Bombay Prohibition Act was sustained as a valid exercise of state legislative power over intoxicating liquors, despite incidentally affecting the importation and exportation of goods across borders, which constituted a central union subject. The doctrine functions not as an instrument to permit subversion of constitutional boundaries, but as a pragmatic rule of constitutional accommodation that recognizes the organic interconnectedness of contemporary socioeconomic life and prevents the paralysis of governmental functioning. It operates in close dialogue with related constitutional doctrines, contrasting sharply with the Doctrine of Colourable Legislation which invalidates laws where a legislature covertly accomplishes that which it cannot do directly and providing a crucial threshold inquiry before questions of repugnancy or direct statutory inconsistency arise. In the contemporary regulatory state, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance remains profoundly relevant in resolving jurisdictional friction over emerging digital economies, data privacy, environmental protection, and unified taxation regimes, ensuring that federalism remains dynamic, functional, and anchored in substantive legal reality. In federal constitutional systems featuring distinct legislative lists or enumerated fields of authority, such as those found in Canada, Australia, and India, a statute enacted by one tier of government under its legitimate constitutional mandate may inevitably touch upon, overlap with, or incidentally encroach upon a subject matter allocated exclusively to another tier. Rather than mechanically invalidating an enactment the moment an incidental overlap occurs, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance commands constitutional courts to scrutinize the enactment holistically to ascertain its true nature, character, and foundational essence—its "pith," meaning the true center or core, and its "substance," signifying its essential material reality. Under this interpretive methodology, if the substantive core, primary objective, and dominant effect of the challenged statute fall squarely within the legislative competence of the body that enacted it, the statute is upheld as constitutionally valid, notwithstanding the fact that it incidentally or tangentially trenches upon an unauthorized legislative head of power reserved for another legislature.
title: Test #01: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance

text: The respondent owned a commercial goods vehicle, a multi-axle freight truck bearing registration No. MH-09-CV-4120, insured comprehensively with the appellant insurer for an Insured Declared Value (IDV) of Rs. 18,50,000/-. On the night of 12th October, 2015, while parked securely at a transport logistics yard in Ichalkaranji, the vehicle was stolen by unidentified culprits. The respondent’s driver discovered the theft the following morning and immediately lodged an oral report at the local police station, culminating in the registration of First Information Report No. 184 of 2015 on 13th October, 2015 under Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 within twenty-four hours. After an exhaustive investigation, the police submitted a final untraced report under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., accepted by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class on 18th March, 2016. However, when the insured submitted the claim on 27th October, 2015, fourteen days after the incident, the insurance company repudiated the entire claim, asserting a fundamental breach of Condition No. 1 of the policy, which mandated immediate notice in writing to the insurer upon occurrence of any accidental loss or theft. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant insurance company contended that prompt intimation is a vital condition precedent. It was argued that delay deprives the insurer of its statutory opportunity to appoint private investigators and assist law enforcement in tracing the stolen vehicle. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent insured submitted that when an FIR is promptly registered, delay in reporting to the insurer cannot vitiate a genuine insurance claim. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that insurance companies cannot repudiate legitimate claims on hyper-technical procedural pretexts. In the authoritative Three-Judge Bench decision in Gurshinder Singh v. Shriram General Insurance Company Limited, reported in (2020) 11 SCC 612, affirmed in Jaina Construction Company v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd., reported in (2022) 4 SCC 527, the Hon’ble Supreme Court authoritatively settled the law. The Supreme Court established that the primary purpose of Condition No. 1 is to ensure that the theft is reported to the police without delay so that law enforcement can investigate the crime. When the insured immediately lodges an FIR, the police machinery is set in motion. The insurer’s investigator cannot do anything more than what the police do. Mere delay in communicating the theft to the insurance company after an immediate police FIR cannot be made a ground to repudiate a genuine total loss claim. In Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance, reported in (2017) 9 SCC 724, it was affirmed that a consumer cannot be deprived of statutory indemnity where the delay is explained by trauma and search efforts. The decree passed by the trial court directing payment of the full IDV with nine percent interest per annum is accordingly affirmed. Modifying the award, this Court holds that fixing a pittance as notional income of a homemaker offends constitutional equality and gender justice under Article 14 and Article 21. In the seminal ruling in Kirti v. Oriental Insurance Company Limited, reported in (2021) 2 SCC 166, the Hon’ble Supreme Court established that fixing the notional income of a homemaker is a recognition of the unpaid labor, time, and emotional sacrifices rendered to the family unit. The Court held that it is not necessary to produce documentary proof of income, and the notional income must be assessed on the basis of minimum wages applicable to skilled workers, taking into account the educational background and responsibilities of the homemaker. Furthermore, as reaffirmed in Arun Kumar Agrawal v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., reported in (2010) 9 SCC 218, and National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi, reported in (2017) 16 SCC 680, an addition of forty percent must be granted towards future prospects where the deceased was below forty years of age.

text: The doctrine of piercing (or lifting) the corporate veil represents one of the most fundamental exceptions to the bedrock principle of corporate jurisprudence: the separate legal personality of a company. Under classical company law, crystallized in the seminal English decision of Salomon v. A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22, an incorporated company is recognized as an independent juristic entity distinct from its shareholders, directors, and officers. Incorporation creates a metaphorical "veil" between the company and its human constituents. This separation confers limited liability, shielding investors from personal responsibility for the corporation’s debts and liabilities. However, because this legal fiction is granted by the legal order to facilitate legitimate enterprise and commercial risk-taking, the law cannot permit it to be perverted into an instrument of deception. Where the corporate form is deliberately abused to perpetrate fraud, evade legal obligations, or defeat statutory mandates, courts possess an equitable jurisdiction to "pierce the corporate veil," disregarding the entity's distinct personality to attribute liability directly to the individuals orchestrating the enterprise. Historically, judicial intervention in this sphere suffered from conceptual ambiguity, with courts invoking colorful metaphors such as "sham," "facade," "cloak," or "mere puppet" without establishing a unified test. In modern common law, the doctrine was rigorously rationalized by the UK Supreme Court in Prest v. Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013] UKSC 34. Delivering the leading judgment, Lord Sumption drew a crucial distinction between the "concealment principle" and the "evasion principle": The evasion principle is illustrated by foundational authorities such as Gilford Motor Co Ltd v. Horne [1933] Ch 935, where a former managing director bound by a non-compete covenant incorporated a company to conduct a rival business in breach of his restraint. The court enjoined both the director and the newly formed company, treating the entity as a mere channel for evading an extant personal covenant. Similarly, in Jones v. Lipman [1962] 1 WLR 832, a vendor who had contracted to sell real property transferred the land to a wholly owned company to defeat the purchaser’s decree for specific performance. The court ordered specific performance directly against the company, holding that it was a creature devised specifically to avoid equitable obligations. In United States jurisprudence, the doctrine is commonly framed around the "alter ego" theory or "instrumentality rule". American courts typically mandate a two-pronged threshold: first, that there exists such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist; and second, that adhering to the fiction of separate corporate existence would promote fraud, sanction an injustice, or lead to an inequitable result. Beyond common law fraud, legislative frameworks frequently mandate statutory lifting of the veil. Examples include wrongful and fraudulent trading provisions under insolvency codes, anti-tax evasion statutes, environmental remediation liability, and anti-money laundering regulations where beneficial ownership must be established. In modern commerce characterized by complex multinational group structures, holding-subsidiary networks, and special purpose vehicles (SPVs) the doctrine functions as an indispensable safety valve. However, courts exercise it with extreme circumspection. As reaffirmed in Adams v. Cape Industries plc [1990] Ch 433, courts will not pierce the veil merely because justice might seem to require it or because a group of companies operates as a single economic unit. Piercing the corporate veil remains a remedy of last resort, invoked only when conventional legal doctrines, such as the law of torts, agency, contract interpretation, or trusts, prove inadequate to defeat unconscionable abuse.
title: Test #02: The Doctrine of Piercing the Corporate Veil

text: Under Section-15 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), state govts can appoint executive magistrates or police officers of at least superintendent of police rank as SEMs for specific areas, periods or duties. Depending on state-specific notifications, these officers can also be Deputy Collectors or tehsildars or senior police officers of ACP rank. Their primary role is to take preventive measures to maintain public order and stop anticipated breaches of peace. Under BNSS Section-9, the state govt establishes courts of judicial magistrates in consultation with HC, which appoints their presiding officers. Judicial magistrates deal with criminal cases and trials while SEMs exercise executive powers, including initiating preventive proceedings. SEMs cannot conduct criminal trials or convict people through these proceedings, but are authorised to release or grant police or judicial remand. Under the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the corresponding provision for SEMs was Section-21. Though a common feature in cases involving summary or preventive detention by police, the powers of special executive magistrates (SEMs) have come into focus due to their prominent role in deciding if those involved in recent protests rocking Delhi are released or remain behind bars. A person not familiar with the rare, overlapping functions and powers of the executive and judiciary may conclude SEMs are a rung of the judiciary where a person picked up by police is produced within 24 hours. Under Section-126, an SEM can initiate proceedings if there is sufficient ground to believe a person is likely to breach the peace or disturb public tranquillity. Under Section-130, the magistrate must issue a written order explaining the basis for the proceedings, the proposed bond amount, its duration and the number of sureties required. A peace bond can be required for up to one year, and the amount must not be excessive. The person must be given an opportunity to explain why they should not be required to furnish the bond. The magistrate then conducts an inquiry under Section-135. Separately, Section-163 allows an executive magistrate to issue urgent orders to prevent specified dangers or disturbances, including restricting public gatherings when legal conditions are met. Detention is not automatic once proceedings begin. Under Section-135(3), an SEM may require immediate security if necessary to prevent a breach of peace or danger to public safety. If the person fails to furnish it, they may be detained until the inquiry concludes. Under Section-136, the magistrate can order security if the inquiry establishes it is necessary. Under Section-137, the person must be discharged if the need for security isn’t established. Failure to furnish security: Section-141 provides for imprisonment in specified circumstances, including failure to furnish security after a final order or breach of a qualifying bond. A surety undertakes responsibility under a bond to help ensure the person concerned meets its conditions. Under Section-140, an SEM can reject a surety found unfit, but must conduct an inquiry, give the parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard and record reasons in writing. The first surety’s photograph on the bond allegedly didn’t match his Aadhaar. He reportedly failed to produce another valid ID and gave unsatisfactory answers during questioning. The SEM concluded the sureties didn’t have sufficient control over the activists to ensure their presence when required. The inquiry under Section-135 is conducted like the trial of a summons case, and it must be completed within six months, failing which the proceedings end unless the magistrate records special reasons. A bond for keeping the peace, if ordered, may be forfeited if its conditions are breached. A person aggrieved by an order requiring security, or by the rejection of a surety, can appeal to the Court of Session. Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section-58 of the BNSS require that anyone arrested be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
title: Test #02: How SEMs Different from Judicial Magistrate?

text: The prosecution case stemmed from a vigilance trap conducted by the Anti-Corruption Branch on 14th October, 1969. The complainant (PW-2), an applicant seeking a municipal commercial trade licence, alleged that the appellant, functioning as a municipal health inspector, demanded an illegal gratification of Rs. 150/- to clear sanitation verification reports. A trap party was assembled, phenolphthalein-treated marked currency notes were handed to the complainant, and a shadow decoy witness (PW-3) was instructed to accompany the complainant and observe the transaction. At the trial, the complainant (PW-2) resiled from his statement, deposing that he placed the money on the office desk without any demand from the appellant. However, the High Court reversed the trial court's acquittal, relying exclusively upon the uncorroborated testimony of the shadow trap witness (PW-3) to infer demand and acceptance. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court committed serious legal error in basing conviction solely upon the testimony of a trap witness. It was argued that a decoy or trap witness is in the nature of an accomplice under Section 133 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, whose uncorroborated testimony cannot be acted upon without independent corroboration under illustration (b) to Section 114 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Prakash Chand v. State (Delhi Administration), reported in (1979) 3 SCC 90, and Somabhai Gopalbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2014) 14 SCC 682, authoritatively re-examined the evidentiary status of trap and decoy witnesses in corruption prosecutions. The Court held that an accomplice is a person who participates in the commission of the crime with criminal mens rea. A trap witness or decoy who acts under official instructions to detect public corruption is not an accomplice in the strict sense of Section 133 of the Evidence Act, as he lacks criminal intent. However, a trap witness is an interested and partisan witness who is keenly interested in the success of the trap operation he participated in. Therefore, as a rule of prudence and caution, the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness cannot form the sole basis for convicting a public servant unless it is corroborated in material particulars by independent, disinterested testimony. In the present case, the complainant turned hostile and denied any verbal demand, no independent civilian witnesses from the municipal office were joined, and hand-wash evidence was inconclusive. In the absence of corroboration establishing demand, the statutory presumption under Section 4 of the 1947 Act cannot be triggered. The conviction is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant public servant under Section 379 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 read with Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, challenges the judgment and order dated 14th August, 1973 passed by the High Court of Delhi in Criminal Appeal No. 112 of 1971, setting aside the judgment of acquittal rendered by the learned Special Judge, Delhi and convicting the appellant under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, based upon decoy trap evidence. Furthermore, in Sabitri Samantaray v. State of Odisha, reported in (2023) 11 SCC 813, this Court reaffirmed that Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not shift the primary burden of proof, which always remains on the prosecution under Article 21. Section 106 cannot be used to bridge missing links in a defective investigation. In the complete absence of motive, weapon recovery, or forensic links, the conviction cannot stand on mere suspicion. The judgment of the High Court is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted of all charges.
title: Test #03: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 248 of 1974

text: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance represents one of the most vital principles of constitutional interpretation employed in federal and quasi-federal jurisdictions to preserve the delicate equilibrium of legislative competence between central and regional governing bodies. Originating in the nineteenth-century jurisprudence of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council while interpreting the distribution of legislative powers under the British North America Act of 1867 most notably articulated in decisions such as Cushing v. Dupuy and Russell v. The Queen the doctrine addresses the inescapable reality that complex modern legislation cannot always be compartmentalized into neat, water-tight constitutional compartments. This doctrine gained widespread prominence and rigorous institutional development in the constitutional jurisprudence of India, where it was extensively applied to resolve federal disputes under the Government of India Act of 1935 and subsequently embedded into the post-independence constitutional framework under Article 246. In the landmark case of Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce, Khulna (1947), the Privy Council upheld the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, which capped loan interest rates a topic of provincial competence regarding money-lending even though it incidentally affected negotiable instruments such as promissory notes, a field reserved exclusively for the federal legislature, because the dominant pith and substance of the law was agrarian debt relief rather than commercial banking. This judicial approach was reaffirmed and cemented by the Supreme Court of India in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where the Bombay Prohibition Act was sustained as a valid exercise of state legislative power over intoxicating liquors, despite incidentally affecting the importation and exportation of goods across borders, which constituted a central union subject. The doctrine functions not as an instrument to permit subversion of constitutional boundaries, but as a pragmatic rule of constitutional accommodation that recognizes the organic interconnectedness of contemporary socioeconomic life and prevents the paralysis of governmental functioning. It operates in close dialogue with related constitutional doctrines, contrasting sharply with the Doctrine of Colourable Legislation which invalidates laws where a legislature covertly accomplishes that which it cannot do directly and providing a crucial threshold inquiry before questions of repugnancy or direct statutory inconsistency arise. In the contemporary regulatory state, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance remains profoundly relevant in resolving jurisdictional friction over emerging digital economies, data privacy, environmental protection, and unified taxation regimes, ensuring that federalism remains dynamic, functional, and anchored in substantive legal reality. In federal constitutional systems featuring distinct legislative lists or enumerated fields of authority, such as those found in Canada, Australia, and India, a statute enacted by one tier of government under its legitimate constitutional mandate may inevitably touch upon, overlap with, or incidentally encroach upon a subject matter allocated exclusively to another tier. Rather than mechanically invalidating an enactment the moment an incidental overlap occurs, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance commands constitutional courts to scrutinize the enactment holistically to ascertain its true nature, character, and foundational essence—its "pith," meaning the true center or core, and its "substance," signifying its essential material reality. Under this interpretive methodology, if the substantive core, primary objective, and dominant effect of the challenged statute fall squarely within the legislative competence of the body that enacted it, the statute is upheld as constitutionally valid, notwithstanding the fact that it incidentally or tangentially trenches upon an unauthorized legislative head of power reserved for another legislature.
title: Test #03: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance

text: This civil appeal, preferred jointly by the appellant husband and respondent wife under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, challenges the judgment and order dated 17th November, 2021 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Application No. 1420 of 2021, affirming the order of the learned Principal Judge, Family Court, Hisar, rejecting the joint application filed by the spouses seeking waiver of the statutory six-month cooling-off period under Section 13-B(2). The matrimonial union between the parties, both highly qualified senior government professionals, was solemnized on 10th September, 2020 at Chandigarh according to Hindu rites. Due to acute incompatibility and divergent lifestyle philosophies, the marriage proved a complete non-starter, and the spouses separated permanently after cohabiting for only three days. After living apart for more than fourteen months, during which multiple counseling sessions conducted by senior family elders and institutional mediators failed completely, the parties executed a comprehensive settlement agreement dated 28th September, 2021. Under the settlement, the parties resolved all claims regarding return of streedhan, permanent alimony, and mutual maintenance, and filed a joint petition for dissolution of marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 before the Family Court, Hisar on 30th September, 2021. Contemporaneously, the parties moved a joint application praying for waiver of the statutory six-month waiting period prescribed under Section 13-B(2). The Family Court rejected the waiver, holding that it possessed no statutory discretion to reduce the six-month period, which order was affirmed by the High Court. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for both parties submitted that forcing parties whose marriage has irretrievably broken down to wait for six months serves no public purpose, prolonging mental agony. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Amit Kumar v. Suman Beniwal, reported in 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1270, and Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur, reported in (2017) 8 SCC 746, authoritatively settled the interpretation of Section 13-B(2) of the Act. The Court held that the six-month cooling-off period prescribed in Section 13-B(2) is directory and not mandatory. The legislative object of the waiting period was to safeguard against hasty divorces and provide an opportunity for reconciliation. However, where the court is satisfied that the marriage has irretrievably broken down, all genuine efforts at mediation and conciliation have proved futile, and the parties have settled all ancillary issues regarding permanent alimony, streedhan, and custody, the court must exercise sound judicial discretion to waive the statutory waiting period. In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan, reported in 2023 SCC OnLine SC 544, the Constitution Bench reaffirmed that forcing spouses to cohabit in an empty legal shell causes deep emotional cruelty. The parties lived together for only three days, have lived apart for fifteen months, and are adamant on parting peacefully. Requiring them to wait for six months is an exercise in futility. The orders of the Family Court and the High Court are set aside, the statutory cooling-off period is waived, and a decree of divorce by mutual consent is granted, dissolving the marriage between the parties. Where there is a chance of reconciliation, however slight, the cooling period of six months from the date of filing of the divorce petition should be enforced. However, if there is no possibility of reconciliation, it would be meaningless to prolong the agony of the parties to the marriage. Thus, if the marriage has broken down irretrievably, the spouses have been living apart for a long time, but not been able to reconcile their differences and have mutually decided to part, it is better to end the marriage, to enable both the spouses to move on with the life.
title: Test #04: Legal - SCI Civil Appeal No. 7650 of 2021

text: The petitioner enrolled in the Punjab Police in 1994, completing over twenty-two years of disciplined service with fourteen commendation certificates and clean annual confidential reports. On 12th July, 2016, while deployed on security duty at a sensitive border post, the petitioner suffered severe acute lumbar radiculopathy and spinal disc herniation, rendering him completely bedridden and incapacitated. The petitioner was admitted to Guru Gobind Singh Medical College Hospital, Faridkot, where he underwent intensive traction and spinal rehabilitation until 4th October, 2016. The petitioner's family dispatched medical certificates and leave applications by registered post, but the department treated him as absent without leave, initiating a summary departmental inquiry under Rule 16.24. The inquiry officer conducted ex-parte proceedings without verifying the government hospital records, concluding that the absence was established. On that basis, the Senior Superintendent of Police passed an order of dismissal, holding that unauthorized absence in a disciplined uniform police force constitutes the gravest act of misconduct proving incorrigibility under Rule 16.2(1). Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the extreme penalty of dismissal is shockingly disproportionate and violative of Article 14 and Article 21 of the Constitution. It was submitted that absence occasioned by sudden medical incapacitation without willful defiance does not constitute the gravest misconduct. Learned State counsel defended the dismissal, submitting that in a disciplined police force, unapproved absence compromises border security, demonstrating unfitness for public service. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that Rule 16.2(1) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 requires a high threshold of culpability before stripping a police officer of livelihood and pension. In the landmark authority in State of Punjab v. Ram Singh, Ex-Constable, reported in (1992) 4 SCC 54, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that dismissal under Rule 16.2 is reserved solely for the 'gravest acts of misconduct' or continued persistent misconduct proving incorrigibility and complete unfitness for police service. The word 'misconduct' implies a conscious, intentional transgression of duty. In Krushnakant B. Parmar v. Union of India, reported in (2012) 3 SCC 178, it was authoritatively settled that unauthorized absence cannot be treated as misconduct if it was due to compelling circumstances beyond the employee's control, such as certified illness. The petitioner was medically incapacitated in a tertiary government hospital, and the department produced no evidence to suggest that his medical records were fabricated. Dismissing an officer on the verge of pensionary retirement for involuntary medical absence is punitive and arbitrary. The impugned dismissal order dated 14th March, 2017 is quashed, directing reinstatement of the petitioner with continuity of service and fifty percent back wages. This civil writ petition, preferred under Article 226 and Article 227 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and proportionality of the departmental punishment order dated 14th March, 2017 passed by Respondent No. 3, the Senior Superintendent of Police, Ferozepur, dismissing the petitioner from service as a Head Constable under Rule 16.2(1) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 on the ground of unauthorized absence from duty for eighty-four days, as affirmed by the appellate and revisional orders. Quashing the FIR and consequential proceedings, this Court holds that the search of a private vehicle is governed strictly by Section 42 and not Section 43 of the NDPS Act. In the authoritative Three-Judge Bench decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Boota Singh v. State of Haryana, reported in (2021) 19 SCC 606, the law was conclusively settled. The Supreme Court held that the Explanation to Section 43 defines a public place to include any public conveyance such as public buses, trains, or taxis;
title: Test #04: Legal - PHHC Civil Writ P. No. 24812 Of 2018

text: The respondent-landlord instituted the civil suit in February 2021 seeking possession of commercial shop premises and recovery of arrears of rent. In his original written statement filed on 14th October, 2021, the petitioner admitted the existence of a registered commercial lease agreement dated 15th March, 2018, contending merely that rent was regularized up to date through cash receipts. The trial proceeded, issues were settled under Order XIV Rule 1 CPC, and the respondent plaintiff concluded his entire oral and documentary evidence. At the stage when the suit was posted for defendant evidence, the petitioner filed an application under Order VI Rule 17 CPC seeking to amend paragraph 3 of the written statement, proposing to substitute his earlier admission with a plea asserting that no lease deed was ever executed and that the registered instrument produced by the plaintiff was forged and fabricated. This civil revision petition, preferred under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, challenges the order dated 18th November, 2025 passed by the learned Civil Judge (Junior Division), Gurugram in Civil Suit No. 412 of 2021, whereby the application filed by the petitioner-defendant under Order VI Rule 17 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 seeking leave to amend his written statement post-commencement of trial was dismissed on the ground of complete absence of due diligence under the statutory proviso. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that procedural rules are handmaids of justice, and liberal amendment should be permitted to resolve the real controversy between the parties under Order VI Rule 17 CPC without causing prejudice to the opposing party. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that the statutory proviso to Order VI Rule 17 enacts an inflexible bar against entertaining amendments after commencement of trial unless due diligence is established. Dismissing the revision petition, this Court holds that the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 acts as a jurisdictional embargo. In the seminal ruling in Vidyabai v. Padmalatha, reported in (2009) 2 SCC 409, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that once the trial has commenced with the filing of affidavits of evidence under Order XVIII Rule 4 CPC, the court has no jurisdiction to permit amendments unless it records a definite finding that in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the plea before the commencement of trial. In Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons, reported in (2009) 10 SCC 84, it was authoritatively settled that an amendment that withdraws an unequivocal judicial admission or introduces an entirely contradictory stand to displace the plaintiff's case cannot be permitted. The petitioner had admitted the execution of the lease deed in 2021 and offered no plausible explanation as to why the plea of forgery was not raised initially. Permitting such belated amendments after the closure of the plaintiff's evidence defeats the legislative objective of expeditious trials and prejudices substantive justice. Finding no jurisdictional error or patent perversity in the impugned order, the revision petition is dismissed with costs of Rs. 20,000/-. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Ramesh Chand @ Baag v. State of Himachal Pradesh, rendered on 8th September, 2025, and Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of M.P., reported in (2012) 9 SCC 750, authoritatively restated the statutory hierarchy governing age determination. Furthermore, medical ossification is not an exact science and carries a recognized margin of error of one to two years, which must invariably enure to the benefit of the accused. The school records being authentic, the appellant is declared a juvenile on the date of the offence. The sentence of life imprisonment is set aside, remitting the matter to the Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate reformative orders.
title: Test #05: Legal - PHHC Cr. No. 9266 of 2025 (O&M)

text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and jurisdiction of the revisional order dated 14th August, 2024 passed by Respondent No. 1, the Deputy Director of Consolidation, Azamgarh under Section 48(1) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, whereby the appellate order dated 22nd October, 2021 passed by the Settlement Officer of Consolidation in Appeal No. 142/SO/2020 confirming the rectangular chak allotment made in favour of the petitioner on his original holding was set aside, creating an isolated flying chak. During consolidation operations in Village Bhadwan, the Assistant Consolidation Officer prepared a provisional consolidation scheme under Section 19 of the Act. The petitioner was allotted his primary chak on Gata No. 312, which was his largest original mool holding containing a private masonry tubewell and boundary plantation established in 2005. Private Respondent No. 4 filed objections under Section 20, claiming allocation over the same plot. The Consolidation Officer and the Settlement Officer of Consolidation concurrently held that under the statutory principles enacted in Section 19(1)(e) of the Act, every tenure holder must, as far as possible, be allotted a compact chak on his original holding and around his private source of irrigation. However, in revision filed under Section 48, the Deputy Director of Consolidation disturbed the concurrent findings, truncating the petitioner's rectangular holding and carving out an unviable flying chak three kilometers away in an uncultivated waterlogged depression on Gata No. 514. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the revisional authority acted in flagrant violation of the mandatory principles of Section 19. It was submitted that under Section 48(1) of the UPCH Act, the Deputy Director of Consolidation exercises supervisory jurisdiction and cannot sit as a court of fact to reappreciate oral evidence or re-carve chaks without recording manifest illegality. Learned Standing Counsel for the state supported the revisional order, contending that adjustments were necessitated to provide equitable roadside frontage to the private respondent. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that the primary objective of consolidation is agricultural efficiency through compact holdings. In Preetam Singh v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, reported in (2014) 124 RD 312, and Ram Niwas v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, reported in (2021) SCC OnLine All 1142, this Court authoritatively established that under Section 19(1) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, preserving a tenure holder's original holding containing his private tubewell is a mandatory statutory rule. Flying chaks are an administrative evil that frustrates agricultural mechanization and defeats the statutory purpose of the Act. The revisional power under Section 48 is not an appellate power to arbitrarily rearrange established chaks to accommodate influential local tenure holders. The Deputy Director omitted to demonstrate any procedural perversity in the orders of the Consolidation Officer and Settlement Officer of Consolidation. Carving out an unviable plot in an uncultivated depression violates the principles of equity. The impugned revisional order dated 14th August, 2024 is quashed, restoring the appellate order confirming the petitioner's compact chak allotment. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the trial court failed to exercise jurisdiction under Section 227 Cr.P.C. It was argued that the expression 'known sources of income' in Section 13(1)(e) means sources known to the prosecution and lawfully derived by the public servant. Learned Special Public Prosecutor for the CBI opposed the petition, submitting that whether the agricultural income and spouse's earnings were genuine is a matter of defense evidence to be evaluated during trial.
title: Test #06: Legal - AHC Writ-B No. 35694 of 2024

text: The respondent owned a commercial goods vehicle, a multi-axle freight truck bearing registration No. MH-09-CV-4120, insured comprehensively with the appellant insurer for an Insured Declared Value (IDV) of Rs. 18,50,000/-. On the night of 12th October, 2015, while parked securely at a transport logistics yard in Ichalkaranji, the vehicle was stolen by unidentified culprits. The respondent’s driver discovered the theft the following morning and immediately lodged an oral report at the local police station, culminating in the registration of First Information Report No. 184 of 2015 on 13th October, 2015 under Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 within twenty-four hours. After an exhaustive investigation, the police submitted a final untraced report under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., accepted by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class on 18th March, 2016. However, when the insured submitted the claim on 27th October, 2015, fourteen days after the incident, the insurance company repudiated the entire claim, asserting a fundamental breach of Condition No. 1 of the policy, which mandated immediate notice in writing to the insurer upon occurrence of any accidental loss or theft. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant insurance company contended that prompt intimation is a vital condition precedent. It was argued that delay deprives the insurer of its statutory opportunity to appoint private investigators and assist law enforcement in tracing the stolen vehicle. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent insured submitted that when an FIR is promptly registered, delay in reporting to the insurer cannot vitiate a genuine insurance claim. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that insurance companies cannot repudiate legitimate claims on hyper-technical procedural pretexts. In the authoritative Three-Judge Bench decision in Gurshinder Singh v. Shriram General Insurance Company Limited, reported in (2020) 11 SCC 612, affirmed in Jaina Construction Company v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd., reported in (2022) 4 SCC 527, the Hon’ble Supreme Court authoritatively settled the law. The Supreme Court established that the primary purpose of Condition No. 1 is to ensure that the theft is reported to the police without delay so that law enforcement can investigate the crime. When the insured immediately lodges an FIR, the police machinery is set in motion. The insurer’s investigator cannot do anything more than what the police do. Mere delay in communicating the theft to the insurance company after an immediate police FIR cannot be made a ground to repudiate a genuine total loss claim. In Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance, reported in (2017) 9 SCC 724, it was affirmed that a consumer cannot be deprived of statutory indemnity where the delay is explained by trauma and search efforts. The decree passed by the trial court directing payment of the full IDV with nine percent interest per annum is accordingly affirmed. Modifying the award, this Court holds that fixing a pittance as notional income of a homemaker offends constitutional equality and gender justice under Article 14 and Article 21. In the seminal ruling in Kirti v. Oriental Insurance Company Limited, reported in (2021) 2 SCC 166, the Hon’ble Supreme Court established that fixing the notional income of a homemaker is a recognition of the unpaid labor, time, and emotional sacrifices rendered to the family unit. The Court held that it is not necessary to produce documentary proof of income, and the notional income must be assessed on the basis of minimum wages applicable to skilled workers, taking into account the educational background and responsibilities of the homemaker. Furthermore, as reaffirmed in Arun Kumar Agrawal v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., reported in (2010) 9 SCC 218, and National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi, reported in (2017) 16 SCC 680, an addition of forty percent must be granted towards future prospects where the deceased was below forty years of age.
title: Test #07: Legal - BHC First Appeal No. 892 of 2019

text: The prosecution case stemmed from a vigilance trap conducted by the Anti-Corruption Branch on 14th October, 1969. The complainant (PW-2), an applicant seeking a municipal commercial trade licence, alleged that the appellant, functioning as a municipal health inspector, demanded an illegal gratification of Rs. 150/- to clear sanitation verification reports. A trap party was assembled, phenolphthalein-treated marked currency notes were handed to the complainant, and a shadow decoy witness (PW-3) was instructed to accompany the complainant and observe the transaction. At the trial, the complainant (PW-2) resiled from his statement, deposing that he placed the money on the office desk without any demand from the appellant. However, the High Court reversed the trial court's acquittal, relying exclusively upon the uncorroborated testimony of the shadow trap witness (PW-3) to infer demand and acceptance. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the High Court committed serious legal error in basing conviction solely upon the testimony of a trap witness. It was argued that a decoy or trap witness is in the nature of an accomplice under Section 133 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, whose uncorroborated testimony cannot be acted upon without independent corroboration under illustration (b) to Section 114 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Prakash Chand v. State (Delhi Administration), reported in (1979) 3 SCC 90, and Somabhai Gopalbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2014) 14 SCC 682, authoritatively re-examined the evidentiary status of trap and decoy witnesses in corruption prosecutions. The Court held that an accomplice is a person who participates in the commission of the crime with criminal mens rea. A trap witness or decoy who acts under official instructions to detect public corruption is not an accomplice in the strict sense of Section 133 of the Evidence Act, as he lacks criminal intent. However, a trap witness is an interested and partisan witness who is keenly interested in the success of the trap operation he participated in. Therefore, as a rule of prudence and caution, the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness cannot form the sole basis for convicting a public servant unless it is corroborated in material particulars by independent, disinterested testimony. In the present case, the complainant turned hostile and denied any verbal demand, no independent civilian witnesses from the municipal office were joined, and hand-wash evidence was inconclusive. In the absence of corroboration establishing demand, the statutory presumption under Section 4 of the 1947 Act cannot be triggered. The conviction is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant public servant under Section 379 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 read with Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, challenges the judgment and order dated 14th August, 1973 passed by the High Court of Delhi in Criminal Appeal No. 112 of 1971, setting aside the judgment of acquittal rendered by the learned Special Judge, Delhi and convicting the appellant under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, based upon decoy trap evidence. Furthermore, in Sabitri Samantaray v. State of Odisha, reported in (2023) 11 SCC 813, this Court reaffirmed that Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not shift the primary burden of proof, which always remains on the prosecution under Article 21. Section 106 cannot be used to bridge missing links in a defective investigation. In the complete absence of motive, weapon recovery, or forensic links, the conviction cannot stand on mere suspicion. The judgment of the High Court is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted of all charges.
title: Test #07: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 248 of 1974

text: These criminal appeals, preferred by the convict appellants under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, challenge the judgment and order dated 12th February, 2021 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh in Criminal Appeal No. 214 of 2018, affirming the conviction recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the search and seizure panchnama violated the mandatory provisions of Section 100(4) Cr.P.C. The prosecution case involved a blind double homicide committed on 14th September, 2014 in an urban commercial warehouse in Gwalior. The police case rested entirely upon circumstantial evidence, with the principal incriminating circumstance being the alleged recovery of a country-made firearm and bloodstained clothing pursuant to disclosure memos (Exhibits P-12 and P-13) recorded under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. During the trial, it emerged that the investigating officer conducted the search and recovery in a crowded commercial marketplace at broad daylight on 18th September, 2014, but failed to associate independent local residents as panch witnesses. Instead, the seizure memo was witnessed solely by two subordinate police constables attached to the same police station. In cross-examination, the investigating officer admitted that civilian shopkeepers and passersby were present at the scene, but no written notices were issued to them under Section 100(8) Cr.P.C. to join the search. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the complete failure to join independent panch witnesses rendered the alleged discovery untrustworthy and fabricated. It was submitted that under Section 100(4) of the Cr.P.C., the association of independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality is a mandatory statutory requirement. Allowing the appeals, this Court in Rajesh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, reported in (2023) 9 SCC 691, authoritatively restated the statutory duties governing searches and seizures under Section 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (now Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). The Court held that Section 100(4) is a vital statutory safeguard enacted to ensure the fairness, credibility, and transparency of police recoveries, guarding citizens against planted evidence and fabricated recoveries. While the testimony of police officers is not inherently untrustworthy, when recoveries of lethal weapons are allegedly made in populated localities, the total omission to associate independent local witnesses without plausible explanation casts a heavy shadow of doubt over the genuineness of the panchnama. In Gorakh Nath Prasad v. State of Bihar, reported in (2018) 2 SCC 745, and Sanjeev v. State of H.P., reported in (2022) 6 SCC 294, this Court established that where independent civilian witnesses are readily available but intentionally bypassed in favour of subordinate police constables, the recovery cannot be relied upon to sustain a conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC. The circumstantial chain being deprived of its foundational link, the prosecution failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence of life imprisonment are set aside, and the appellants are acquitted. Quashing the process qua the petitioner, this Court holds that vicarious liability in penal law is an exception created by statute and must be strictly construed. In the landmark rulings in National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal, reported in (2010) 3 SCC 330, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry, reported in (2022) 10 SCC 152, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that mere reproduction of the statutory wording of Section 141 is insufficient. The complainant must plead specific overt roles demonstrating that the director was responsible for the transaction leading to the issuance of the dishonoured cheque. A non-executive or independent director who does not participate in executive administration cannot be subjected to criminal trial merely because of holding a board directorship.
title: Test #08: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 793-94 of 2022

text: The historical facts disclose that statutory proceedings were initiated against the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 (Act No. 33 of 1976), culminating in a final statement under Section 9 and a notification declaring surplus land under Section 10(1) published on 14th June, 1988. A notification declaring vesting under Section 10(3) was published on 12th January, 1989, followed by an administrative notice to surrender possession under Section 10(5) issued on 22nd March, 1991. However, the tenure holders refused voluntary surrender, and the state authorities omitted to take forceful physical possession by issuing a notice under Section 10(6) or drawing a contemporaneous possession panchnama. The petitioners and their ancestors remained in uninterrupted physical and cultivatory possession, harvesting seasonal crops and paying agricultural land revenue. Following the enactment of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, adopted by the State of Uttar Pradesh on 18th March, 1999, the petitioners applied for deletion of state ceiling endorsements, which was summarily rejected by the authorities relying on constructive paper vesting. This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and jurisdiction of the administrative communication dated 18th November, 2024 issued by Respondent No. 2, the Competent Authority under the Urban Land Ceiling / Additional District Magistrate (Administration), Bareilly, refusing to delete ceiling encumbrances from revenue records and rejecting building plan clearances in respect of agricultural land comprised in Gata No. 342, admeasuring 4,820 square meters situated at Village Tilyar, Tehsil Sadar, District Bareilly, under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners contended that mere paper vesting under Section 10(3) does not extinguish ownership. Placing heavy reliance upon the landmark ruling of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. Hari Ram, reported in (2013) 4 SCC 280, it was argued that where de facto physical possession was not taken under Section 10(6) prior to 18th March, 1999, all pending ceiling proceedings stood abated by operation of Section 3 and Section 4 of the Repeal Act. Learned Additional Chief Standing Counsel for the State submitted that once a notification under Section 10(3) is published, the land vests in the State free from all encumbrances, and peaceful possession was deemed to have been acquired. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that symbolic possession on official files cannot defeat the beneficial provisions of the Repeal Act. In Hari Ram (supra), affirmed in Gajanan Kamlya Patil v. Additional Collector, reported in (2014) 12 SCC 523, the Supreme Court authoritatively established that requirement of taking physical possession under Section 10(5) and Section 10(6) of the 1976 Act is mandatory. Mere paper transfer or mutation in revenue records does not constitute actual physical dispossession. The State failed to place any panchnama or independent witness testimony establishing that physical custody was wrested from the tenure holders prior to 18th March, 1999. Since the petitioners retained physical cultivating possession, the ceiling proceedings abated in toto under Section 4 of the Repeal Act, 1999. The impugned order dated 18th November, 2024 is quashed, and Respondent No. 2 is commanded to correct the revenue khatauni records and mutate the petitioners' names within six weeks. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that settled revenue entries spanning two decades cannot be obliterated through summary administrative overreach. In Saroj Devi v. State of U.P., reported in 2019 SCC OnLine All 1842, and Hari Ram v. Collector, Saharanpur, reported in (2004) 2 RD 360, this Court held that where the statute specifically vests the power of cancellation in the Collector, an order passed by a subordinate revenue official is void.
title: Test #08: Legal - AHC Writ C. No. 15115 of 2025

text: The Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation Limited (MMRCL) submitted an application to the Tree Authority seeking permission to clear vegetation for the Colaba-Bandra-SEEPZ Metro Line-3 project. The Tree Officer published public notices in local newspapers inviting objections. In response, over eighty-two thousand public objections were submitted by environmentalists, residents, and civil society organizations, highlighting that Aarey Colony serves as the unfragmented green lung of Mumbai, contiguous with Sanjay Gandhi National Park, sheltering rich biodiversity, wildlife corridors, and natural water catchments. The Tree Authority, constituted under Section 3 of the Trees Act with nineteen members including municipal corporators and nominated botanical experts, convened a site inspection on 4th July, 2019. However, during the final meeting on 29th August, 2019, amidst dissent from nominated botanical experts regarding unverified geo-tagging and poor historical survival rates of transplanted trees, the municipal authority approved the resolution authorizing mass tree felling. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the Tree Authority abdicated its statutory duty under Section 7 and Section 8 of the Trees Act, 1975. It was argued that the authority failed to consider public objections meaningfully, omitted to conduct a scientific tree census, and failed to explore alternative industrial brownfield sites, thereby violating the public trust doctrine and intergenerational equity under Article 21. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the project proponents submitted that mass urban public transit is essential to decongest roads and reduce carbon vehicular emissions, arguing that MMRCL had undertaken compensatory afforestation of over twenty thousand saplings. Dismissing the challenge, this Court holds that balancing infrastructural public utility with environmental preservation is the prerogative of planning experts. In M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, reported in (1997) 1 SCC 388, and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights v. State of West Bengal, reported in (2021) 5 SCC 466, the Supreme Court held that while environmental protection is paramount, large-scale public transport projects that mitigate atmospheric carbon pollution cannot be stalled if statutory procedures are substantially complied with. The Tree Authority considered public representations, imposed binding compensatory plantation conditions under Section 8(5), and secured corporate undertakings for five years of post-plantation maintenance. The scope of judicial review under Article 226 is confined to the decision-making process, not the merits of planning policy. Finding no procedural perversity, the writ petition is dismissed, subject to strict monitoring of compensatory afforestation. This public interest writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and decision-making process of Resolution No. 42 dated 29th August, 2019 passed by the Tree Authority of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai under Section 8 of the Maharashtra (Urban Areas) Protection and Preservation of Trees Act, 1975, sanctioning the felling of 2,185 trees and transplantation of 461 trees across thirty-three hectares of green cover in Aarey Milk Colony, Goregaon East, for the construction of a metro rail car depot. Quashing the process qua the petitioner, this Court holds that vicarious liability in penal law is an exception created by statute and must be strictly construed. In the landmark rulings in National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal, reported in (2010) 3 SCC 330, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry, reported in (2022) 10 SCC 152, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that mere reproduction of the statutory wording of Section 141 is insufficient. The complainant must plead specific overt roles demonstrating that the director was responsible for the transaction leading to the issuance of the dishonoured cheque.
title: Test #09: Legal - BHC Writ P. No. 2788 of 2019

text: The petitioners, belonging to underprivileged agricultural labour communities, were granted residential and agricultural leases by the Land Management Committee on 14th June, 1984 pursuant to a lawful resolution approved by the Sub-Divisional Officer. The names of the allottees were mutated in revenue records, and continuous cultivatory possession was reflected in Khatauni records spanning 1388 to 1396 Fasli for over twenty-two years. This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and jurisdiction of the cancellation order dated 17th July, 2006 passed by the learned Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Khurja, District Bulandshahr, along with the revisional order dated 27th August, 2008 passed by the Additional Commissioner (Administration), Meerut Division, Meerut in Revision No. 42 of 2006, whereby agricultural lease allotments (patta) granted in favour of the petitioners over Gaon Sabha land comprised in Gata No. 214 were cancelled under Section 198(4) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. In March 2006, upon a complaint filed by private respondents alleging irregular allotment procedures, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate initiated suo motu proceedings and cancelled the allotment, recording a summary finding that the original allotment files were missing from the tehsil record room and inferring that the lease was tainted with fraud. The revisional authority affirmed the cancellation without examining the statutory bar of limitation. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioners contended that the impugned orders are wholly without jurisdiction. It was argued that under the plain statutory text of Section 198(4) of the UPZA&LR Act, 1950 (now corresponding to Section 66 of the U.P. Revenue Code, 2006), the Collector alone is clothed with exclusive statutory jurisdiction to cancel agricultural allotments. An order passed by a Sub-Divisional Officer is coram non judice. Furthermore, under Section 198(6), proceedings for cancellation of allotment on grounds of procedural irregularity must be initiated within five years from the date of allotment. Learned Standing Counsel for the State submitted that where an allotment is void ab initio or obtained through collusion with the Gram Pradhan, statutory limitation periods do not curtail executive powers under Section 122-B. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that settled revenue entries spanning two decades cannot be obliterated through summary administrative overreach. In Saroj Devi v. State of U.P., reported in 2019 SCC OnLine All 1842, and Hari Ram v. Collector, Saharanpur, reported in (2004) 2 RD 360, this Court held that where the statute specifically vests the power of cancellation in the Collector, an order passed by a subordinate revenue official is void. The mere loss of official allotment files from tehsil archives cannot justify a finding of fraud against illiterate rural allottees when verified khatauni records establish long, continuous possession. Furthermore, allegations of irregularity cannot be entertained after the expiry of the mandatory five-year limitation prescribed under Section 198(6) without proving foundational fraud through regular inquiry. The impugned orders dated 17th July, 2006 and 27th August, 2008 are quashed, and the respondents are commanded to restore the petitioners' names in the revenue records within six weeks. The Court held that the grant of sanction under Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 is not an idle administrative formality, but a solemn statutory safeguard intended to protect honest public servants from malicious and frivolous harassment. A court of competent jurisdiction is statutorily prohibited from taking cognizance of an offence punishable under Sections 7, 10, 11, 13, and 15 without the previous sanction of the authority competent to remove the public servant from office. This Court ruled that a sanction granted by an authority not empowered in law is without jurisdiction and an absolute nullity.
title: Test #09: Legal - AHC Writ C. No. 10667 of 2019

text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeks a writ of mandamus declaring the action of Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the State of Andhra Pradesh represented by its Principal Secretary to Government, Revenue Department, and the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, in adopting the Sealed Cover Procedure and deferring the promotion of the petitioner to the post of Assistant Commissioner of State Tax in the Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) panel meeting held on 18th March, 2016, as illegal, arbitrary, and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The petitioner, a Commercial Tax Officer appointed through the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission in 2004, maintained an unblemished service record and fell within the direct zone of consideration for promotion to the post of Assistant Commissioner for the panel year 2015-2016. When the DPC convened on 18th March, 2016, juniors ranking below the petitioner in the integrated seniority list were promoted, while the petitioner's assessment was placed in a sealed cover. The respondents defended the sealed cover procedure citing a preliminary surprise check conducted by the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) on 14th February, 2015, which resulted in the registration of an exploratory Regular Inquiry. However, the record conclusively established that on the date the DPC met, the petitioner was neither placed under suspension, nor had any disciplinary charge memo been served under Rule 20 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991, nor had any criminal charge sheet been filed in a court of competent jurisdiction under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the right to be considered for promotion is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 16 of the Constitution of India. It was argued that placing recommendations in a sealed cover on the basis of a preliminary vigilance inquiry without a formal charge sheet violates binding constitutional precedents. Learned Government Pleader for Services opposed the petition, submitting that public interest demands that officers facing serious vigilance scrutiny should not be entrusted with higher administrative responsibilities. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that the adoption of the sealed cover procedure is impermissible in the absence of formal disciplinary or criminal proceedings. In the landmark Three-Judge Bench decision in Union of India v. K.V. Jankiraman, reported in (1991) 4 SCC 109, and Union of India v. Anil Kumar Sarkar, reported in (2013) 4 SCC 161, the Hon'ble Supreme Court authoritatively established that the sealed cover procedure can be resorted to only when three explicit conditions exist at the time of DPC consideration: (i) the government servant is under suspension, (ii) a formal charge memo has been framed and served in departmental proceedings, or (iii) a charge sheet has been filed in a criminal court. Mere pendency of a preliminary investigation, confidential vigilance inquiry, or registration of an FIR without filing a charge sheet does not justify withholding promotion. To deny promotion at the stage of preliminary inquiry impairs career progression and violates Article 14 and Article 16. The respondents are commanded to open the sealed cover within four weeks and, if found fit, grant notional promotion to the petitioner from the date his immediate junior was promoted, with all consequential seniority and pay fixation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that registered ownership is the sole criterion for fastening third-party statutory liability. In the landmark Three-Judge Bench decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Naveen Kumar v. Vijay Kumar, reported in (2018) 3 SCC 1, and Prakash Chand Daga v. Saveta Sharma, reported in (2019) 2 SCC 747, the law was conclusively settled. The Supreme Court held that Parliament consciously enacted the definition of 'owner' in Section 2(30) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to mean the person in whose name the motor vehicle stands registered.
title: Test #10: Legal - APHC Writ P. No. 18080 of 2016

text: There is no law prescribing reservation for general category candidates in public employment and therefore there is no question of reserved category candidates being selected against their seats as no general category candidate can be appointed against a slot in the roster which is kept for reserved category candidates. Some newspapers have misreported a recent judgment of the Supreme Court, claiming that the judgment states that candidates from the reserved category cannot claim seats in the general category in any case. Such claims state that 50% of all seats are completely reserved for the general category, and no scheduled castes scheduled tribe/originally backward class person can have a claim on such seats, even on the basis of merit. However, the actual judgment does not imply anything of this sort. Moreover, the law on this point "whether reserved category candidates can claim seats in the general category on the basis of merit" is very clear. In the said case, the appellant belonged to the OBC category and had availed age relaxation (as was granted to other similarly situated candidates of the same category). Since no candidate from the general category had secured the minimum cut-off score, the appellant filed a writ petition before the high court to be accommodated in the general category. The High Court dismissed the petition. The Supreme Court affirmed this decision and held that the appellant, who has applied under reserved category by availing age relaxation and also attending the interview under the reserved category cannot claim right to be appointed under the general category. The reason, as per the court, was that there is an express bar for the candidates belonging to SC/ST/OBC who have availed relaxation for A being considered for general category candidates. The court was reading the existing rules and proceedings of Department of Personnel and Training, which stated that when a relaxed standard is applied in selecting the reserved category candidates, for example in the age-limit, experience, qualification, permitted number of chances in written examination, extended zone of consideration larger than what is provided for general category candidates, etc., the reserved candidates are to be counted against reserved vacancies only. Such candidates would be deemed as unavailable for consideration against unreserved vacancies. On similar lines, in 2015, in another case, the Gujarat High Court had held that considering the reservation policy applicable in the State of Gujarat contained in the relevant circular and relevant statutory provisions, i.e., the Recruitment Rules, it was held that all those candidates belonging to the reserved category if they avail the benefit of age relaxation, it is held to be relaxation in the standard, and therefore, are not entitled to their cases being considered for general category vacancies and that their cases are required to be considered for the reserved category vacancies only.
