The proposition developed by the courts in these two judgments is that when there is an existing policy regarding the express bar for reserved category candidates who have availed relaxation, such as age-relaxation, in a selection process, such reserved category candidates would not be entitled to seats in the general category, even on the basis of merit. However, in the earlier case, the court had also observed that the appellant had not challenged the constitutional validity of the proceedings read with Rule 9 of the Recruitment Rules. The appellant had only sought for a declaration that the proceedings were not binding on the appellant. No argument was canvassed challenging the constitutional validity of the proceedings before the learned Single Judge or before the Division Bench of the High Court. This observation by the Supreme Court is quite important in context of the correct position of the law on this issue. This is because if the constitutional validity of these proceedings had been challenged,
title: Test #10: DHC PA Typing - 10/03/2019

text: Quashing the FIR qua the petitioner, this Court holds that internet intermediaries cannot be transformed into private arbitral censors. In the landmark authority in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, reported in (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Hon’ble Supreme Court authoritatively read down Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, establishing that the expression ‘actual knowledge’ requires an intermediary to receive an order of a court of competent jurisdiction or an authorized government notification directing takedown. A commercial platform cannot be expected to judge complex intellectual property infringement claims upon unilateral private notices from brand owners. In Google India Private Limited v. Visakha Industries, reported in (2020) 4 SCC 162, this Court reaffirmed that where an e-commerce platform merely provides access, does not initiate the transmission, and enforces seller terms prohibiting illicit products, it satisfies Section 79(2). Prosecuting the intermediary for independent copyright violations committed by third-party sellers without establishing criminal conspiracy constitutes an abuse of process. The FIR qua the petitioner is accordingly quashed. This criminal writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeks the quashing of First Information Report No. 182 of 2020 registered at Police Station Crime Branch, Cyber Cell, New Delhi under Sections 420, 468, 471, and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957, insofar as it relates to the petitioner e-commerce marketplace entity, claiming statutory safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The prosecution case stemmed from a private complaint lodged by an international cosmetics brand, alleging that counterfeit luxury perfumes bearing forged registered trademarks were being sold on the petitioner’s online platform. The brand owner issued a private cease-and-desist email on 12th February, 2020, requesting immediate removal of ten third-party seller URLs. The petitioner promptly deactivated four listings where specific infringing merchant codes were identified, but advised the complainant to secure a court order regarding the remaining disputed storefronts to avoid breach of merchant vendor contracts. Thereupon, the complainant lodged an FIR, arraigning the marketplace as a co-conspirator. The petitioner challenged the FIR, demonstrating that it is an intermediary under Section 2(1)(w) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, operating as an automated marketplace where independent registered sellers upload product listings, and that it observed strict statutory due diligence under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediaries Guidelines) Rules, 2011. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that under Section 79 of the IT Act, an intermediary is completely immune from criminal and civil liability for third-party information hosted on its network. Learned Additional Public Prosecutor and counsel for the complainant resisted the petition, arguing that safe harbour under Section 79 does not apply when the intermediary fails to remove infringing listings despite receiving private notices. The student is the creator and owner of the knowledge articulated in the script, and the relationship between the examinee and the university is one of candidate and testing authority, not fiduciary trustee and beneficiary under Section 8(1)(e). While a fiduciary relationship exists between the university and the examiners regarding the identity of the evaluators, the university can easily protect examiners' privacy by masking their names, signatures, and code numbers through the severability procedure prescribed under Section 10 of the Act. Transparent access to evaluated scripts enables students to verify totaling errors, check omitted evaluations, and pursue legitimate academic careers.
title: Test #11: Legal - DHC Writ P. No. 1376 of 2020

text: Section 18 of the Domestic Violence Act relates to protection order. In terms of Section 18 of the Act, intention of the legislature is to provide more protection to woman. Section 20 of the Act empowers the court to order for monetary relief to the aggrieved party. When acts of domestic violence are alleged, before issuing notice, the court has to be prima facie satisfied that there have been instances of domestic violence. In the present case, the respondent has made allegations of domestic violence against fourteen appellants. Appellant No.14 is the husband and appellants No.1 and 2 are the parents-in-law of the respondent. All other appellants are relatives of parents-in-law of the respondent. Appellants No. 3, 5, 9, 11 and 12 are the brothers of father-in-law of the respondent. Appellants No. 4, 6 and 10 are the wives of appellants No. 3, 5 and 9 respectively. Appellants No. 7 and 8 are the parents of appellant No. 1. Appellants No. 1 to 6 and 14 are residents of Chennai. Appellants No. 7 to 10 are the residents of Rajasthan and appellants No. 11 to 13 are the residents of Gujarat. Admittedly, the matrimonial house of the respondent and appellant No. 1 has been at Chennai. In so far as appellant No.14 husband of the respondent and appellants No. 1 and 2 Parents-in-law, there are averments of domestic violence alleging that they have taken away the jewellery of the respondent gifted to her by her father during marriage and the alleged acts of harassment to the respondent. There are no specific allegations as to how other relatives of appellant No.14 have caused the acts of domestic violence. It is also not known as to how other relatives who are residents of Gujarat and Rajasthan can be held responsible for award of monetary relief to the respondent. The High Court was not right in saying that there was prima facie case against the other appellants No. 3 to 13. Since there are no specific allegations against appellants No. 3 to 13, the criminal case of domestic violence against them cannot be continued. The Domestic Violence Act is a piece of remedial and beneficial legislation, and it must be construed so as to advance the protection of women from abuse within the shared household. At the same time, the beneficial nature of the enactment does not dispense with the need for a foundation in fact. A court exercising jurisdiction under the Act is required to examine whether the application discloses, at least prima facie, acts of domestic violence attributable to the persons against whom relief is sought. The Act cannot be used as an instrument to rope in every relative of the husband, irrespective of the role played by each of them. The definition of the expression respondent under the Act extends to relatives of the husband, and this widens the class of persons against whom proceedings may be initiated. However, the width of the definition is not a licence for indiscriminate implication. Where the pleadings are vague and omnibus, and where the complaint is silent about the time, place and manner in which a particular relative committed an act of violence, the court cannot presume complicity merely on the basis of kinship. A general allegation that all the relatives joined in harassing the aggrieved woman, without particulars, does not satisfy the requirement of prima facie satisfaction before notice is issued. It is equally relevant that the relatives in question did not reside in the matrimonial home and lived in different States, far away from the place where the couple cohabited. Domestic violence presupposes a domestic relationship and some measure of shared living or proximity, in which the alleged acts could actually have taken place. In the absence of any averment showing that such relatives visited the household, interfered in the marital life of the couple, or participated in the alleged harassment, it is difficult to see how they could be made answerable for protection orders or monetary relief under Sections 18 and 20.
title: Test #11: MPHC JJA 2023 - 210/09/2023 - S2

text: The prosecution case rested exclusively on circumstantial evidence, alleging that the appellant, an unmarried rural woman, delivered an infant out of wedlock on 14th November, 2004, murdered the newborn to conceal her pregnancy, and threw the corpse into a village pond. The trial court and the High Court convicted the appellant, relying primarily upon the post-mortem report and the testimony of lady medical officer (PW-11), who deposed that clinical examination revealed physical symptoms consistent with recent parturition. However, scrutiny of the trial record disclosed that during the recording of the appellant's statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the trial judge framed only four vague, composite questions regarding village rumours, completely omitting to confront her with the medical opinion of PW-11 or the findings of the post-mortem examination. Furthermore, the trial court treated her denial of pregnancy as a false defense, utilizing it as a missing link to complete the circumstantial chain. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the omission to put material incriminating circumstances to the accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. vitiates the conviction. The Court held that Section 313 is not an empty judicial ritual, but an essential manifestation of natural justice rooted in the maxim audi alteram partem. Its primary object is to establish a direct dialogue between the court and the accused, ensuring that every incriminating circumstance appearing in prosecution evidence is specifically, clearly, and separately put to the accused to afford him a fair opportunity of explanation. In Premchand v. State of Maharashtra, reported in (2023) 5 SCC 522, and Kalicharan v. State of U.P., reported in (2023) 2 SCC 583, this Court reaffirmed that an incriminating circumstance not put to the accused in Section 313 examination must be completely excluded from judicial consideration. Furthermore, the answers given under Section 313 or a false denial cannot be utilized by the prosecution to fill up gaps or supply missing links in a defective circumstantial chain. The accused has a constitutional right to silence under Article 20(3) and a fundamental right to dignity and privacy under Article 21. Since the foundational medical circumstances were never put to the appellant, they could not be used to convict her. The circumstantial evidence being incomplete, the conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC are set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is directed against the judgment and order dated 20th April, 2010 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Baikunthpur in Criminal Appeal No. 605 of 2005, affirming the judgment of conviction and sentence of life imprisonment recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Baikunthpur under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the trial court failed to put essential incriminating circumstances to the appellant during her examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Indrakunwar v. State of Chhattisgarh, reported in (2024) 14 SCC 595, authoritatively restated the constitutional and statutory significance of Section 313 Cr.P.C. (now Section 351 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). The Court held that an accomplice is a person who participates in the commission of the crime with criminal mens rea. A trap witness or decoy who acts under official instructions to detect public corruption is not an accomplice in the strict sense of Section 133 of the Evidence Act, as he lacks criminal intent. However, a trap witness is an interested and partisan witness who is keenly interested in the success of the trap operation he participated in. Therefore, as a rule of prudence and caution, the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness cannot form the sole basis for convicting a public servant.
title: Test #12: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1730 of 2012

text: This civil appeal, preferred jointly by the appellant husband and respondent wife under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, challenges the judgment and order dated 17th November, 2021 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Application No. 1420 of 2021, affirming the order of the learned Principal Judge, Family Court, Hisar, rejecting the joint application filed by the spouses seeking waiver of the statutory six-month cooling-off period under Section 13-B(2). The matrimonial union between the parties, both highly qualified senior government professionals, was solemnized on 10th September, 2020 at Chandigarh according to Hindu rites. Due to acute incompatibility and divergent lifestyle philosophies, the marriage proved a complete non-starter, and the spouses separated permanently after cohabiting for only three days. After living apart for more than fourteen months, during which multiple counseling sessions conducted by senior family elders and institutional mediators failed completely, the parties executed a comprehensive settlement agreement dated 28th September, 2021. Under the settlement, the parties resolved all claims regarding return of streedhan, permanent alimony, and mutual maintenance, and filed a joint petition for dissolution of marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 before the Family Court, Hisar on 30th September, 2021. Contemporaneously, the parties moved a joint application praying for waiver of the statutory six-month waiting period prescribed under Section 13-B(2). The Family Court rejected the waiver, holding that it possessed no statutory discretion to reduce the six-month period, which order was affirmed by the High Court. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for both parties submitted that forcing parties whose marriage has irretrievably broken down to wait for six months serves no public purpose, prolonging mental agony. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Amit Kumar v. Suman Beniwal, reported in 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1270, and Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur, reported in (2017) 8 SCC 746, authoritatively settled the interpretation of Section 13-B(2) of the Act. The Court held that the six-month cooling-off period prescribed in Section 13-B(2) is directory and not mandatory. The legislative object of the waiting period was to safeguard against hasty divorces and provide an opportunity for reconciliation. However, where the court is satisfied that the marriage has irretrievably broken down, all genuine efforts at mediation and conciliation have proved futile, and the parties have settled all ancillary issues regarding permanent alimony, streedhan, and custody, the court must exercise sound judicial discretion to waive the statutory waiting period. In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan, reported in 2023 SCC OnLine SC 544, the Constitution Bench reaffirmed that forcing spouses to cohabit in an empty legal shell causes deep emotional cruelty. The parties lived together for only three days, have lived apart for fifteen months, and are adamant on parting peacefully. Requiring them to wait for six months is an exercise in futility. The orders of the Family Court and the High Court are set aside, the statutory cooling-off period is waived, and a decree of divorce by mutual consent is granted, dissolving the marriage between the parties. Where there is a chance of reconciliation, however slight, the cooling period of six months from the date of filing of the divorce petition should be enforced. However, if there is no possibility of reconciliation, it would be meaningless to prolong the agony of the parties to the marriage. Thus, if the marriage has broken down irretrievably, the spouses have been living apart for a long time, but not been able to reconcile their differences and have mutually decided to part, it is better to end the marriage, to enable both the spouses to move on with the life.
title: Test #12: Legal - SCI Civil Appeal No. 7650 of 2021

text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 227 of the Constitution of India read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, calls in question the legality and validity of the order dated 14th June, 2023 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Greater Mumbai in Criminal Revision Application No. 214 of 2022, rejecting the petitioner’s application seeking stay of criminal proceedings in C.C. No. 892/SS/2021 instituted under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 on the ground of statutory interim-moratorium operational under Section 96 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The petitioner executed a personal guarantee in favour of the respondent financial creditor on 14th March, 2018 to secure corporate credit facilities advanced to a textile manufacturing company. Towards discharge of his co-extensive liability, the petitioner issued four post-dated commercial cheques aggregating to Rs. 3,50,00,000/- drawn on Union Bank of India. Upon presentation, the cheques were dishonoured with the endorsement ‘funds insufficient’. Following statutory demand notice, the respondent filed a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Subsequently, on 12th January, 2022, the respondent bank filed an insolvency application against the petitioner personal guarantor before the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench under Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). The petitioner moved the Metropolitan Magistrate, contending that under Section 96(1)(b) of the IBC, an interim-moratorium takes effect immediately upon filing the application, operating to stay all pending legal actions or proceedings in respect of any debt. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that Section 96 is wider in scope than Section 14. Placing heavy reliance upon the seminal three-judge Bench ruling of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in P. Mohanraj v. Shah Brothers Ispat Private Limited, reported in (2021) 6 SCC 258, it was argued that proceedings under Section 138 NI Act are quasi-criminal in nature, aimed at recovery of debt, and therefore fall within the protective umbrella of the moratorium. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that criminal culpability cannot be extinguished through insolvency filings. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court holds that Section 96 of the IBC does not shield individuals from criminal prosecution. In Ajay Kumar Radheyshyam Goenka v. Tourism Finance Corporation of India Limited, reported in (2023) 10 SCC 545, and Saranga Anilkumar Aggarwal v. Bhavesh Dhirajlal Sheth, rendered on 4th March, 2025, the Supreme Court clarified that the ruling in P. Mohanraj was confined strictly to corporate debtors protected under Section 14. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 creates a penal offence enacted to preserve commercial credibility in negotiable transactions. The primary objective of criminal proceedings is penal deterrence, not debt recovery. While Section 96 of the IBC stays civil execution and attachment of assets during individual resolution, it does not immunize a personal guarantor from facing trial for committing a statutory criminal offence. The legislative intent behind Part III of the IBC was never to turn insolvency into a safe haven for cheque-bounce offenders. The learned Magistrate was fully justified in declining to stay the trial. The criminal writ petition is accordingly dismissed. The Tree Authority considered public representations, imposed binding compensatory plantation conditions under Section 8(5), and secured corporate undertakings for five years of post-plantation maintenance. The scope of judicial review under Article 226 is confined to the decision-making process, not the merits of planning policy. Finding no procedural perversity, the writ petition is dismissed, subject to strict monitoring of compensatory afforestation.
title: Test #13: Legal - BHC Cr. Writ P. No. 4182 of 2023

text: The respondent-landlord instituted the civil suit in February 2021 seeking possession of commercial shop premises and recovery of arrears of rent. In his original written statement filed on 14th October, 2021, the petitioner admitted the existence of a registered commercial lease agreement dated 15th March, 2018, contending merely that rent was regularized up to date through cash receipts. The trial proceeded, issues were settled under Order XIV Rule 1 CPC, and the respondent plaintiff concluded his entire oral and documentary evidence. At the stage when the suit was posted for defendant evidence, the petitioner filed an application under Order VI Rule 17 CPC seeking to amend paragraph 3 of the written statement, proposing to substitute his earlier admission with a plea asserting that no lease deed was ever executed and that the registered instrument produced by the plaintiff was forged and fabricated. This civil revision petition, preferred under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, challenges the order dated 18th November, 2025 passed by the learned Civil Judge (Junior Division), Gurugram in Civil Suit No. 412 of 2021, whereby the application filed by the petitioner-defendant under Order VI Rule 17 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 seeking leave to amend his written statement post-commencement of trial was dismissed on the ground of complete absence of due diligence under the statutory proviso. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that procedural rules are handmaids of justice, and liberal amendment should be permitted to resolve the real controversy between the parties under Order VI Rule 17 CPC without causing prejudice to the opposing party. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that the statutory proviso to Order VI Rule 17 enacts an inflexible bar against entertaining amendments after commencement of trial unless due diligence is established. Dismissing the revision petition, this Court holds that the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 acts as a jurisdictional embargo. In the seminal ruling in Vidyabai v. Padmalatha, reported in (2009) 2 SCC 409, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that once the trial has commenced with the filing of affidavits of evidence under Order XVIII Rule 4 CPC, the court has no jurisdiction to permit amendments unless it records a definite finding that in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the plea before the commencement of trial. In Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons, reported in (2009) 10 SCC 84, it was authoritatively settled that an amendment that withdraws an unequivocal judicial admission or introduces an entirely contradictory stand to displace the plaintiff's case cannot be permitted. The petitioner had admitted the execution of the lease deed in 2021 and offered no plausible explanation as to why the plea of forgery was not raised initially. Permitting such belated amendments after the closure of the plaintiff's evidence defeats the legislative objective of expeditious trials and prejudices substantive justice. Finding no jurisdictional error or patent perversity in the impugned order, the revision petition is dismissed with costs of Rs. 20,000/-. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Ramesh Chand @ Baag v. State of Himachal Pradesh, rendered on 8th September, 2025, and Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of M.P., reported in (2012) 9 SCC 750, authoritatively restated the statutory hierarchy governing age determination. Furthermore, medical ossification is not an exact science and carries a recognized margin of error of one to two years, which must invariably enure to the benefit of the accused. The school records being authentic, the appellant is declared a juvenile on the date of the offence. The sentence of life imprisonment is set aside, remitting the matter to the Juvenile Justice Board for appropriate reformative orders.
title: Test #13: Legal - PHHC Cr. No. 9266 of 2025 (O&M)

text: The Petitioners, Ramesh Dattatray Jadhav & Meena Ashok Patil, have approached this Court against the State of Maharashtra & Competent Authority, seeking enforcement of 4% RESERVATION in public employment. The Petitioners challenge the ORDER dated 14.09.2018 alleging failure to implement reservation. The Petitioners relied upon disability certificates, recruitment records, roster statements & Government Resolutions. Ramesh Dattatray Jadhav submitted an application dated 21.03.2018, followed by NOTICE dated 17.07.2018. Meena Ashok Patil produced Exhibit-("P-11") and relied upon Roster Register No. "RR/46/2018". It was contended that 4% reservation must be calculated against sanctioned cadre strength and cannot be denied because the authority claims no suitable vacancy existed. The respondents filed an affidavit-in-reply and raised preliminary objections regarding maintainability, roster position and eligibility. The respondents submitted that recruitment had concluded and the Petitioners lacked requisite merit. Reliance was placed upon Office Memorandum No. "PWD/72/2018" dated 08.08.2018, Selection Statement Exhibit-"R-7" and Document No. "ADM/184/2018". According to the respondents, the roster disclosed no available post during that recruitment year. The Petitioners disputed this and submitted that the authority must identify, maintain, carry forward & fill reserved posts. During the hearing, learned counsel for the Petitioners submitted that non-maintenance of a proper roster would defeat the object of reservation. It was argued that EQUAL OPPORTUNITY under Articles 14 & 16 cannot be a mere FORMALITY. The Court examined certificates, recruitment papers, roster entries, Resolutions & correspondence. Having heard counsel for Ramesh Dattatray Jadhav, Meena Ashok Patil & respondents, and examined the RECORD, this Court finds that compliance with 4% reservation has not been established. The impugned ORDER dated 14.09.2018 gives insufficient reasons for rejecting the claim. Administrative inconvenience cannot override statutory obligation. Accordingly, the Petition is ALLOWED. The impugned ORDER dated 14.09.2018 is QUASHED & SET ASIDE. The Competent Authority shall verify the roster, determine reserved vacancies, consider eligibility and pass a reasoned order within 8 weeks. The Petitioners shall receive an opportunity of HEARING. No order as to costs in law. The decision shall be communicated to all concerned parties, and the entire exercise shall remain subject to applicable statutory provisions, relevant Government Resolutions, roster rules, principles of natural justice & constitutional guarantees governing disability reservation in public service. The mandate of Section 34 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, imposes a positive, affirmative obligation on every appropriate Government establishment to appoint in every government establishment not less than four per cent of the total number of vacancies in the cadre strength in each group of posts. As ruled by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in landmark pronouncements including Union of India v. National Federation of the Blind and Rajeev Kumar Gupta v. Union of India, the computation of reservation for persons with disabilities has to be computed on the total number of vacancies in the strength of a cadre, and not merely on the identified posts. The state cannot escape its constitutional and statutory commitments by pleading that the recruitment process has concluded or that administrative inconveniences preclude retrospective roster realignment. Reservation for disabled citizens is an integral facet of distributive equality guaranteed under Articles 14, 16, and 21 of the Constitution of India. Therefore, the respondents must scrupulously calculate backlog vacancies, maintain reservation registers, and provide equal opportunities without bureaucratic impediments.
title: Test #14: Legal - BHC PIL No. 46 of 2018

text: These criminal appeals, preferred by the convict appellants under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, challenge the judgment and order dated 12th February, 2021 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh in Criminal Appeal No. 214 of 2018, affirming the conviction recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the search and seizure panchnama violated the mandatory provisions of Section 100(4) Cr.P.C. The prosecution case involved a blind double homicide committed on 14th September, 2014 in an urban commercial warehouse in Gwalior. The police case rested entirely upon circumstantial evidence, with the principal incriminating circumstance being the alleged recovery of a country-made firearm and bloodstained clothing pursuant to disclosure memos (Exhibits P-12 and P-13) recorded under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. During the trial, it emerged that the investigating officer conducted the search and recovery in a crowded commercial marketplace at broad daylight on 18th September, 2014, but failed to associate independent local residents as panch witnesses. Instead, the seizure memo was witnessed solely by two subordinate police constables attached to the same police station. In cross-examination, the investigating officer admitted that civilian shopkeepers and passersby were present at the scene, but no written notices were issued to them under Section 100(8) Cr.P.C. to join the search. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the complete failure to join independent panch witnesses rendered the alleged discovery untrustworthy and fabricated. It was submitted that under Section 100(4) of the Cr.P.C., the association of independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality is a mandatory statutory requirement. Allowing the appeals, this Court in Rajesh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, reported in (2023) 9 SCC 691, authoritatively restated the statutory duties governing searches and seizures under Section 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (now Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). The Court held that Section 100(4) is a vital statutory safeguard enacted to ensure the fairness, credibility, and transparency of police recoveries, guarding citizens against planted evidence and fabricated recoveries. While the testimony of police officers is not inherently untrustworthy, when recoveries of lethal weapons are allegedly made in populated localities, the total omission to associate independent local witnesses without plausible explanation casts a heavy shadow of doubt over the genuineness of the panchnama. In Gorakh Nath Prasad v. State of Bihar, reported in (2018) 2 SCC 745, and Sanjeev v. State of H.P., reported in (2022) 6 SCC 294, this Court established that where independent civilian witnesses are readily available but intentionally bypassed in favour of subordinate police constables, the recovery cannot be relied upon to sustain a conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC. The circumstantial chain being deprived of its foundational link, the prosecution failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence of life imprisonment are set aside, and the appellants are acquitted. Quashing the process qua the petitioner, this Court holds that vicarious liability in penal law is an exception created by statute and must be strictly construed. In the landmark rulings in National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal, reported in (2010) 3 SCC 330, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry, reported in (2022) 10 SCC 152, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that mere reproduction of the statutory wording of Section 141 is insufficient. The complainant must plead specific overt roles demonstrating that the director was responsible for the transaction leading to the issuance of the dishonoured cheque. A non-executive or independent director who does not participate in executive administration cannot be subjected to criminal trial merely because of holding a board directorship.
title: Test #14: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 793-94 of 2022

text: The petitioners were absolute owners of agricultural lands comprised in Survey Nos. 114 and 115 situated at Narakodur village, acquired for the public purpose of excavating irrigation canals under the Krishna Western Delta Modernization Project. The Land Acquisition Officer passed an ex-parte award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on 24th October, 2016, evaluating compensation at an arbitrary rate of Rs. 3,50,000/- per acre. Crucially, the Collector omitted to pronounce the award in the presence of the landholders, nor was any mandatory notice of the award served upon the petitioners in terms of Section 12(2) of the Act. The petitioners first acquired knowledge of the award when compensation cheques were deposited into their joint bank accounts on 14th August, 2017. Thereupon, on 20th September, 2017, within five weeks of acquiring knowledge, the petitioners filed an application before the Land Acquisition Officer under Section 18(1), seeking reference to the Civil Court for enhancement of compensation to Rs. 25,00,000/- per acre. The Reference Court dismissed the application as time-barred, calculating the six-month period from the date of the Collector's signature on 24th October, 2016. Learned counsel appearing for the revision petitioners contended that the Reference Court committed a grave jurisdictional error. It was submitted that under Section 18(2)(b), the phrase 'date of the award' means the date on which the award is communicated or the date when the party acquires actual or constructive knowledge of its essential contents. Learned Government Pleader for Land Acquisition supported the dismissal, arguing that Section 18(2) enacts an outer limitation of six months from the date of the award, which admits of no extension under the Limitation Act. Setting aside the order, this Court holds that an uncommunicated administrative decision cannot operate to bar constitutional rights to compensation. This civil revision petition, preferred under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, challenges the order dated 18th March, 2021 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge, Guntur in Land Acquisition Original Petition L.A.O.P. No. 42 of 2018, rejecting the reference application filed under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on the preliminary ground of limitation, holding that the application preferred by the landholder-claimants was barred by time as it was presented beyond six months from the date of the award passed by the Land Acquisition Officer. In the celebrated Constitution Bench authority in Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, reported in AIR 1961 SC 1500, and State of Punjab v. Qaisar Jehan Begum, reported in (1964) 1 SCR 971, the Hon'ble Supreme Court authoritatively settled that the date of the award under Section 18(2)(b) must mean the date when the award is either made known to the party or the date when the party acquired knowledge of the award. The award of the Collector is merely an administrative offer of compensation. If the landholder was not present when the award was made and no notice was issued under Section 12(2), limitation begins to run only from the date when the landowner acquired knowledge of the contents of the award. A citizen cannot be deprived of statutory remedies by keeping an award concealed in government files. Since the application was filed within six weeks of receiving compensation in their bank accounts, the reference was within time. The revision petition is allowed, and the Reference Court is directed to adjudicate the compensation on merits. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the right to be considered for promotion is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 16 of the Constitution of India. It was argued that placing recommendations in a sealed cover on the basis of a preliminary vigilance inquiry without a formal charge sheet violates binding constitutional precedents. Learned Government Pleader for Services opposed the petition.
title: Test #15: Legal - APHC Cr. P. No. 1420 of 2021

text: The Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation Limited (MMRCL) submitted an application to the Tree Authority seeking permission to clear vegetation for the Colaba-Bandra-SEEPZ Metro Line-3 project. The Tree Officer published public notices in local newspapers inviting objections. In response, over eighty-two thousand public objections were submitted by environmentalists, residents, and civil society organizations, highlighting that Aarey Colony serves as the unfragmented green lung of Mumbai, contiguous with Sanjay Gandhi National Park, sheltering rich biodiversity, wildlife corridors, and natural water catchments. The Tree Authority, constituted under Section 3 of the Trees Act with nineteen members including municipal corporators and nominated botanical experts, convened a site inspection on 4th July, 2019. However, during the final meeting on 29th August, 2019, amidst dissent from nominated botanical experts regarding unverified geo-tagging and poor historical survival rates of transplanted trees, the municipal authority approved the resolution authorizing mass tree felling. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the Tree Authority abdicated its statutory duty under Section 7 and Section 8 of the Trees Act, 1975. It was argued that the authority failed to consider public objections meaningfully, omitted to conduct a scientific tree census, and failed to explore alternative industrial brownfield sites, thereby violating the public trust doctrine and intergenerational equity under Article 21. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the project proponents submitted that mass urban public transit is essential to decongest roads and reduce carbon vehicular emissions, arguing that MMRCL had undertaken compensatory afforestation of over twenty thousand saplings. Dismissing the challenge, this Court holds that balancing infrastructural public utility with environmental preservation is the prerogative of planning experts. In M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, reported in (1997) 1 SCC 388, and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights v. State of West Bengal, reported in (2021) 5 SCC 466, the Supreme Court held that while environmental protection is paramount, large-scale public transport projects that mitigate atmospheric carbon pollution cannot be stalled if statutory procedures are substantially complied with. The Tree Authority considered public representations, imposed binding compensatory plantation conditions under Section 8(5), and secured corporate undertakings for five years of post-plantation maintenance. The scope of judicial review under Article 226 is confined to the decision-making process, not the merits of planning policy. Finding no procedural perversity, the writ petition is dismissed, subject to strict monitoring of compensatory afforestation. This public interest writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and decision-making process of Resolution No. 42 dated 29th August, 2019 passed by the Tree Authority of the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai under Section 8 of the Maharashtra (Urban Areas) Protection and Preservation of Trees Act, 1975, sanctioning the felling of 2,185 trees and transplantation of 461 trees across thirty-three hectares of green cover in Aarey Milk Colony, Goregaon East, for the construction of a metro rail car depot. Quashing the process qua the petitioner, this Court holds that vicarious liability in penal law is an exception created by statute and must be strictly construed. In the landmark rulings in National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal, reported in (2010) 3 SCC 330, and Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry, reported in (2022) 10 SCC 152, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that mere reproduction of the statutory wording of Section 141 is insufficient. The complainant must plead specific overt roles demonstrating that the director was responsible for the transaction leading to the issuance of the dishonoured cheque.
title: Test #15: Legal - BHC Writ P. No. 2788 of 2019

text: This criminal appeal, preferred by the accused facing trial for offences punishable under Section 302 and Section 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, challenges the interlocutory order dated 26th July, 2024 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Agra, rejecting the application filed under Section 207 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 seeking supply of the comprehensive list and inspection of un-relied documents seized by the police during investigation in terms of Rule 11 of the Draft Criminal Rules on Practice, 2021. The defense moved an application before the trial court under Section 207 Cr.P.C. read with Rule 11 of the Draft Criminal Rules on Practice, 2021, seeking a verified list and inspection of all seized material objects and un-relied documents. The learned Sessions Judge dismissed the application, holding that under Section 207, the prosecution is obligated to supply only those documents that it proposes to rely upon, and that the accused could seek un-relied documents only at the stage of leading defense evidence under Section 91 Cr.P.C. The High Court declined to interfere under Section 482 Cr.P.C. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that withholding material exculpatory evidence collected during investigation violates the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial under Article 21 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Ashok Kumar Tomar v. State of U.P., rendered on 28th February, 2025, and Manoj v. State of Madhya Pradesh, reported in (2023) 2 SCC 353, authoritatively restated the statutory mandate governing criminal discovery. The Court held that a criminal trial is not an adversarial game of hide-and-seek, but a solemn search for truth. In the landmark suo motu proceedings in In Re: Inadequacies & Deficiencies in Criminal Trials, reported in (2021) 10 SCC 598, this Court mandated the incorporation of Rule 11 in criminal court manuals across all High Courts. Under Rule 11, the investigating agency is under an inflexible legal duty to prepare and furnish along with the police report three distinct lists: (i) a list of statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C., (ii) a list of documents and materials relied upon, and (iii) a comprehensive list of statements, documents, and seized material objects that the prosecution does not propose to rely upon. In Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi), reported in (2010) 6 SCC 1, this Court affirmed that the Public Prosecutor owes an overarching duty of fairness to the court and to the accused. If the police seize exculpatory material that demonstrates innocence, withholding it from the accused violates natural justice and vitiates the trial. Trial courts cannot postpone disclosure of un-relied documents to the defense stage. The impugned orders are set aside, and the prosecution is directed to supply the complete list and permit inspection of all un-relied records before framing charges under Section 228 Cr.P.C. Furthermore, the answers given under Section 313 or a false denial cannot be utilized by the prosecution to fill up gaps or supply missing links in a defective circumstantial chain. The accused has a constitutional right to silence under Article 20(3) and a fundamental right to dignity and privacy under Article 21. Since the foundational medical circumstances were never put to the appellant, they could not be used to convict her. The circumstantial evidence being incomplete, the conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC are set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. During the investigation of a sensational murder case, the police seized twelve mobile telephone handsets, forensic call detail records (CDRs), tower dump analytics, and closed-circuit television (CCTV) hard drives. However, while submitting the charge sheet under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., the investigating officer selected only two call records supporting the prosecution narrative, suppressing eight forensic CDRs and tower location logs that established the plea of alibi set up by the accused.
title: Test #16: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1817 of 2024

text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeks a writ of mandamus declaring the action of Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the State of Andhra Pradesh represented by its Principal Secretary to Government, Revenue Department, and the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, in adopting the Sealed Cover Procedure and deferring the promotion of the petitioner to the post of Assistant Commissioner of State Tax in the Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) panel meeting held on 18th March, 2016, as illegal, arbitrary, and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The petitioner, a Commercial Tax Officer appointed through the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission in 2004, maintained an unblemished service record and fell within the direct zone of consideration for promotion to the post of Assistant Commissioner for the panel year 2015-2016. When the DPC convened on 18th March, 2016, juniors ranking below the petitioner in the integrated seniority list were promoted, while the petitioner's assessment was placed in a sealed cover. The respondents defended the sealed cover procedure citing a preliminary surprise check conducted by the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) on 14th February, 2015, which resulted in the registration of an exploratory Regular Inquiry. However, the record conclusively established that on the date the DPC met, the petitioner was neither placed under suspension, nor had any disciplinary charge memo been served under Rule 20 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991, nor had any criminal charge sheet been filed in a court of competent jurisdiction under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the right to be considered for promotion is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 16 of the Constitution of India. It was argued that placing recommendations in a sealed cover on the basis of a preliminary vigilance inquiry without a formal charge sheet violates binding constitutional precedents. Learned Government Pleader for Services opposed the petition, submitting that public interest demands that officers facing serious vigilance scrutiny should not be entrusted with higher administrative responsibilities. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that the adoption of the sealed cover procedure is impermissible in the absence of formal disciplinary or criminal proceedings. In the landmark Three-Judge Bench decision in Union of India v. K.V. Jankiraman, reported in (1991) 4 SCC 109, and Union of India v. Anil Kumar Sarkar, reported in (2013) 4 SCC 161, the Hon'ble Supreme Court authoritatively established that the sealed cover procedure can be resorted to only when three explicit conditions exist at the time of DPC consideration: (i) the government servant is under suspension, (ii) a formal charge memo has been framed and served in departmental proceedings, or (iii) a charge sheet has been filed in a criminal court. Mere pendency of a preliminary investigation, confidential vigilance inquiry, or registration of an FIR without filing a charge sheet does not justify withholding promotion. To deny promotion at the stage of preliminary inquiry impairs career progression and violates Article 14 and Article 16. The respondents are commanded to open the sealed cover within four weeks and, if found fit, grant notional promotion to the petitioner from the date his immediate junior was promoted, with all consequential seniority and pay fixation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that registered ownership is the sole criterion for fastening third-party statutory liability. In the landmark Three-Judge Bench decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Naveen Kumar v. Vijay Kumar, reported in (2018) 3 SCC 1, and Prakash Chand Daga v. Saveta Sharma, reported in (2019) 2 SCC 747, the law was conclusively settled. The Supreme Court held that Parliament consciously enacted the definition of 'owner' in Section 2(30) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to mean the person in whose name the motor vehicle stands registered.
title: Test #16: Legal - APHC Writ P. No. 18080 of 2016

text: The present Writ Petition, filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, challenges the ORDER dated 18.04.2025 passed by the Competent Authority, whereby the petitioner’s application for restoration of service benefits was rejected. The dispute concerns the legality, validity & procedural fairness of the impugned decision. The following questions arise for consideration: - (i) Whether the authority acted within its statutory jurisdiction? (ii) Whether the petitioner was denied a reasonable opportunity of HEARING? (iii) Whether the impugned order suffers from arbitrariness, non-application of mind & violation of natural justice? The petitioner was appointed as a Clerk on 07.06.2018 and served at the District Treasury Office. On 16.09.2023, a departmental NOTICE was issued alleging unauthorized absence during the period from 03.08.2023 to 21.08.2023. The petitioner submitted an explanation dated 28.09.2023, denying the allegations and producing attendance records, medical documents & correspondence marked Exhibit- "P-11". However, the authority, without considering the documents, passed the disputed order dated 18.04.2025. The petitioner submitted a representation dated 02.05.2025, requesting reconsideration of the findings. The representation was rejected by communication No. "ADM/472/2025" dated 19.06.2025. It was contended that the authority had relied upon an incomplete attendance register and had ignored the written explanation. Reliance was placed upon Document-"P-17", Office Memorandum dated 11.01.2024, and Dispatch Register No. 54/2025. The petitioner submitted that procedural safeguards are not empty formalities and that every affected person is entitled to a fair opportunity before an adverse order is passed. The respondent-authority opposed the Petition and contended that the impugned ORDER was based upon records and that no prejudice had been caused to the petitioner. It was further submitted that the Court, exercising jurisdiction under Article 226, should not ordinarily re-appreciate disputed facts unless the decision is perverse, arbitrary or legally unsustainable. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, examined the RECORD and considered the statutory provisions, this Court finds that the authority failed to consider documents produced by the petitioner. The impugned order does not disclose proper reasons for rejecting the explanation. Such non-consideration amounts to violation of PRINCIPLES OF NATURAL JUSTICE and renders the decision unsustainable. Accordingly, the Writ Petition is ALLOWED. The impugned ORDER dated 18.04.2025 is hereby QUASHED & SET ASIDE. The matter is remitted to the competent authority for consideration after granting opportunity of HEARING to the petitioner. The exercise shall be completed within 8 weeks from receipt of this order. No order as to costs. It is an elemental canon of administrative law that justice must not only be done, but must manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done. When a disciplinary or administrative authority proceeds against an employee on charges of willful absenteeism, the burden lies squarely upon the administration to establish by cogent material that the absence was deliberate and devoid of legitimate justification. The constitutional guarantee enshrined in Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India mandates non-arbitrariness in state action. An administrative order inflicting adverse civil consequences upon an employee without addressing the defense explanations, medical proof, or official dispatch records violates the sacred doctrine of audi alteram partem. Reasons are the indispensable heartbeat of any quasi-judicial adjudication, linking the raw facts to the ultimate administrative conclusion. In the absence of reasoned articulation, the supervisory court exercising extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is duty-bound to intervene and restore procedural equilibrium. Consequently, the competent authority must reconsider the entire defense repository afresh and render a speaking order within the prescribed time limit.
title: Test #17: Legal - BHC Writ Petition No. 3847 of 2025

text: Quashing the FIR qua the petitioner, this Court holds that internet intermediaries cannot be transformed into private arbitral censors. In the landmark authority in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, reported in (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Hon’ble Supreme Court authoritatively read down Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, establishing that the expression ‘actual knowledge’ requires an intermediary to receive an order of a court of competent jurisdiction or an authorized government notification directing takedown. A commercial platform cannot be expected to judge complex intellectual property infringement claims upon unilateral private notices from brand owners. In Google India Private Limited v. Visakha Industries, reported in (2020) 4 SCC 162, this Court reaffirmed that where an e-commerce platform merely provides access, does not initiate the transmission, and enforces seller terms prohibiting illicit products, it satisfies Section 79(2). Prosecuting the intermediary for independent copyright violations committed by third-party sellers without establishing criminal conspiracy constitutes an abuse of process. The FIR qua the petitioner is accordingly quashed. This criminal writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeks the quashing of First Information Report No. 182 of 2020 registered at Police Station Crime Branch, Cyber Cell, New Delhi under Sections 420, 468, 471, and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957, insofar as it relates to the petitioner e-commerce marketplace entity, claiming statutory safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The prosecution case stemmed from a private complaint lodged by an international cosmetics brand, alleging that counterfeit luxury perfumes bearing forged registered trademarks were being sold on the petitioner’s online platform. The brand owner issued a private cease-and-desist email on 12th February, 2020, requesting immediate removal of ten third-party seller URLs. The petitioner promptly deactivated four listings where specific infringing merchant codes were identified, but advised the complainant to secure a court order regarding the remaining disputed storefronts to avoid breach of merchant vendor contracts. Thereupon, the complainant lodged an FIR, arraigning the marketplace as a co-conspirator. The petitioner challenged the FIR, demonstrating that it is an intermediary under Section 2(1)(w) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, operating as an automated marketplace where independent registered sellers upload product listings, and that it observed strict statutory due diligence under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediaries Guidelines) Rules, 2011. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that under Section 79 of the IT Act, an intermediary is completely immune from criminal and civil liability for third-party information hosted on its network. Learned Additional Public Prosecutor and counsel for the complainant resisted the petition, arguing that safe harbour under Section 79 does not apply when the intermediary fails to remove infringing listings despite receiving private notices. The student is the creator and owner of the knowledge articulated in the script, and the relationship between the examinee and the university is one of candidate and testing authority, not fiduciary trustee and beneficiary under Section 8(1)(e). While a fiduciary relationship exists between the university and the examiners regarding the identity of the evaluators, the university can easily protect examiners' privacy by masking their names, signatures, and code numbers through the severability procedure prescribed under Section 10 of the Act. Transparent access to evaluated scripts enables students to verify totaling errors, check omitted evaluations, and pursue legitimate academic careers.
title: Test #17: Legal - DHC Writ P. No. 1376 of 2020

text: The instant appeal, preferred by the original defendant, arises out of the judgment & order dated 17.08.2011 passed by the High Court of Bombay, whereby it confirmed the decree dated 04.03.2009 passed by the Principal District Judge, Pune in Regular Civil Suit No.214/2004, in favour of the original plaintiff (Respondent herein). CIVIL APPEAL NO.7382 OF 2012. The dispute concerns the validity & enforceability of an agreement relating to immovable property. The following questions arise for consideration:- (a) Whether the agreement creates an enforceable interest in the suit property? (b) Whether the transaction was vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation & suppression of material facts, and whether Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies? Raghunathrao, owner of the property, possessed agricultural land bearing Gat No.145/2, admeasuring 2 Hectares 17 Ares, situated at Village-Khadki, Taluka-Haveli, District-Pune. He executed an agreement dated 12.06.1998 in favour of defendant No.1, containing specific terms & conditions concerning the proposed transfer. According to the plaintiff, Rs.2,75,000/- was paid towards consideration; however, despite repeated demands, the defendant failed to execute the sale deed. A legal notice dated 19.09.2002 demanded completion within 15 days. By reply dated 02.10.2002, the defendant denied the transaction and alleged that the document was invalid & obtained through misrepresentation. The plaintiff instituted Special Civil Suit No.89/2003, seeking specific performance, declaration & permanent injunction. The defendant contended that the agreement created no lawful right, title or interest and disputed the signatures appearing thereon. Reliance was placed upon Document Exhibit (“P-17”), Mutation Entry No.5632 dated 28.11.1999, and registered notice dated 06.01.2003. The plaintiff submitted that mutation entries are fiscal in character and cannot, by themselves, confer or extinguish title. The Trial Court framed issues under Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. By judgment dated 04.03.2009, the suit was decreed. The First Appellate Court, vide judgment dated 22.07.2010, affirmed the findings. The defendant thereafter preferred the present appeal under Section 100, raising questions concerning limitation, jurisdiction, evidentiary value & enforceability of the disputed document. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, examined the record and considered the statutory provisions, this Court finds no perversity, procedural irregularity or jurisdictional error. The evidence on record sufficiently establishes the circumstances, and no substantial question of law arises for determination. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed; the impugned judgment & decree are affirmed, and the parties shall bear their respective costs. The decree shall be drawn accordingly. In a suit for specific performance, the plaintiff must establish readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract continuously from the date of the agreement up to the date of the decree, in strict adherence to Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The record clearly establishes that the respondent had tendered substantial consideration and repeatedly called upon the appellant to perform his contractual obligations, thereby satisfying the statutory criteria. Furthermore, the defense predicated upon Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, is wholly devoid of merit. Under the second limb of Article 54, where no specific calendar date is fixed for performance, the prescribed limitation of three years commences only when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. In the case at hand, notice of refusal was conveyed by the defendant's reply dated 02.10.2002, and the suit instituted in 2003 was well within the statutory period. It is also well settled that mere revenue entries or mutation proceedings do not create or extinguish title, nor do they override a valid agreement to sell executed for valuable consideration. Therefore, the concurrent findings recorded by the courts below warrant no interference.
title: Test #18: Legal - BHC Civil Appeal No. 7382 of 2012

text: The learned Senior Civil Judge has dismissed the application reasoning that there are no admissions of the respondent/defendant and the respondent/defendant has disputed the landlord-tenant relationship and has rather claimed having been cheated. It is further reasoned that according to the respondent/defendant, he remains the owner of the property and though the respondent/defendant admits receipt of legal notice but a decree on admissions cannot be sought on the basis thereof. On 9th August, 2017 when this petition came up first before this court, it was enquired from the counsel for the petitioner plaintiff, whether there are any other proceedings filed by the respondent defendant or by any of his siblings for setting aside of the sale deed and the lease deed and whether the respondent defendant has filed any counter-claim in the suit. On the counsel for the petitioner plaintiff answering in the negative, it was further observed that the respondent defendant, without having initiated any proceedings for setting aside of the sale deed and the lease deed, the same being registered documents have to prevail and the petitioner plaintiff appeared to be entitled to a decree for possession on admissions. Hence, notice of this petition was issued. The counsel for the respondent/defendant though has not disputed that the respondent/defendant or any of his siblings have not taken any proceedings for setting aside of the sale deed or lease deed or for rescission of the same and have also not filed any counter-claim in the suit from which this petition arises but contends that filing of such a suit by the respondent defendant is still within limitation, inasmuch as the respondent/defendant learnt of the misrepresentation only in December 2014. Neither counsel is able to state the date on which the respondent defendant was served with the summons of the suit. However, the counsel for the petitioner plaintiff states that the suit was preceded by a legal notice and to which a reply was given and the respondent/defendant on receipt of legal notice also had knowledge of the claim of the petitioner plaintiff. It is further the contention of the counsel for the petitioner/plaintiff that the case of the petitioner plaintiff is squarely covered by Karan Madaan V. Nageshwar Pandey, 209 (2014) DLT 241 and that even if the counter-claim were to be filed, the same would have been rejected in terms of the said judgment. The passing of a decree for possession cannot be deferred, if the petitioner plaintiff were to be found entitled thereto, for the reason of the respondent/defendant intending to file a suit for setting aside of the sale deed and the lease deed, even if such suit is still within limitation. The fact remains that notwithstanding the written statement in the suit having been filed in February 2015, the respondent defendant till now has not filed any such suit. Thus, as of now there is no step taken by the respondent defendant for rescission of the registered documents aforesaid which establish the title of the petitioner plaintiff to the property (though in a suit between landlord and tenant, such title is not necessary) and the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties. The said registered documents have to prevail, particularly when the execution and registration thereof is admitted. The plea of the documents having been got executed by misrepresentation, cannot be a defence to a suit on the basis of the said documents unless the said documents are so declared by a competent court of law. Supreme Court in Gorakh Nath Dube v. Hari Narain Singh, 1973 (SLT Soft) 620, though in the context of jurisdiction of the Consolidation Officer under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, held that a distinction has to be made between cases where a document is wholly or partially invalid so that it can be disregarded by any court or authority and a document which has to be actually set aside before it can cease to have legal effect.
title: Test #18: DHC PA Typing - 09/03/2019

text: This civil suit, instituted under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, seeks a decree of permanent injunction alongside damages of Rs. 5,00,00,000/- for alleged defamation and commercial disparagement, wherein the plaintiff news conglomerate seeks an ex-parte ad-interim injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC commanding the defendants, an investigative digital media foundation and individual editors, to forthwith take down, remove, and retract an investigative news broadcast published on 14th January, 2025 accusing the plaintiff corporation of editorial bias and state influence. The plaintiff asserted that it is an internationally accredited multimedia news agency operating television channels and digital news feeds. On 14th January, 2025, the defendants published an investigative documentary video and companion articles alleging that the plaintiff systematically disseminated sponsored political narratives and acted as a corporate mouthpiece. The plaintiff contended that these publications were malicious, sensationalist, and calculated to destroy its global professional reputation, resulting in loss of institutional sponsorship. In the interim application, the plaintiff sought an immediate gag order restraining the defendants from circulating the impugned broadcast or publishing any further commentary pending trial, asserting that damages would be an inadequate remedy to compensate for ongoing reputational loss. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the plaintiff submitted that an ex-parte injunction is imperative to arrest ongoing defamation. It was argued that the right to reputation is an inseparable component of the right to life and personal dignity guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the defendants opposed the application, submitting that the documentary was the product of four months of rigorous journalistic research based on publicly accessible telecast archives, commercial balance sheets, and regulatory filings. The defendants asserted their defense of truth, justification, and fair comment on matters of public interest under Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Dismissing the application for interim injunction, this Court holds that free speech cannot be silenced through preemptive judicial restraint. In the locus classicus ruling in Bonnard v. Perryman, reported in [1891] 2 Ch 269, affirmed in Fraser v. Evans, reported in [1969] 1 QB 349, and Tata Sons Limited v. Greenpeace International, reported in (2011) 178 DLT 705, the courts established that an interim injunction should not be granted in defamation actions where the defendant raises a defense of justification and indicates an intention to prove truth at trial. In the landmark authority in Bloomberg Television Production Services India Private Limited v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Limited, reported in 2024 SCC OnLine SC 426, the Hon'ble Supreme Court cautioned that pre-trial gag orders stifle the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). An injunction can be granted only in the rarest of rare cases where the publication is indisputably false and demonstrably malicious. The defendants having raised a credible defense of truth based on source documents, the public interest in journalistic scrutiny overrides the claim for interim censorship. The application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC is accordingly dismissed. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that where an executive authority withholds statutory compensation in direct contravention of declared constitutional law, alternative remedies do not bar writ jurisdiction. In Tarsem Singh (supra), the Supreme Court categorically held that treating landowners under the National Highways Act differently from those acquired under the general land acquisition statute results in artificial classification devoid of intelligible differentia. Applying Section 30(1) and Section 80 of the 2013 Act, the petitioners are statutorily entitled to one hundred percent solatium on the market value.
title: Test #19: Legal - DHC I.A. NO. 4812 of 2025

text: The new proviso to Section-19 mandating that the competent authority shall endeavour to convey the decision on the proposal for sanction within a period of three months can only be read and understood as a compelling statutory obligation. In the first place, the consistent effort made by all branches of the State, the Judiciary, the Legislative, and the Executive, to ensure early decision-making by the competent authority cannot be watered down by lexical interpretation of the expression endeavour in the proviso. Public confidence in the maintenance of the Rule of Law, which is fundamental in the administration of justice, is at stake here. By causing delay in considering the request for sanction, the sanctioning authority stultifies judicial scrutiny, thereby vitiating the process of determination of the allegations against the corrupt official. Delays in prosecuting the corrupt breeds a culture of impunity and leads to systemic resignation to the existence of corruption in public life. Such inaction is fraught with the risk of making future generations getting accustomed to corruption as a way of life. Viewed in this context, the duty to take an early decision inheres in the power vested in the appointing authority to grant or not to grant sanction. The intention of the Parliament is evident from a combined reading of the first proviso to Section-19, which uses the expression endeavour with the subsequent provisions. The third proviso mandates that the extended period can be granted only for one month after reasons are recorded in writing. There is no further extension. The fourth proviso, which empowers the Central Government to prescribe necessary guidelines for ensuring the mandate, may also be noted in this regard. It can thus be concluded that the Parliament intended that the process of grant of sanction must be completed within four months, which includes the extended period of one month also. If it is mandatory for the sanctioning authority to decide in a time-bound manner, the consequence of non-compliance with the mandatory period must be examined. The criminal proceedings must be quashed if the decision is not taken within the prescribed period. The new proviso to Section 19 also has to be read against the backdrop of the larger purpose of the Prevention of Corruption Act, which is to ensure that those who hold public office are held answerable for the abuse of that office. The requirement of prior sanction was introduced as a protective filter, so that honest public servants are shielded from frivolous and vexatious prosecution. It was never meant to operate as a shield for the dishonest. When the sanctioning authority sits over a request for months or years without any explanation, the safeguard is turned into an instrument of obstruction, and the very object of the statute stands defeated. A protection designed for the innocent cannot be allowed to become a refuge for the guilty. The statutory timeline must therefore be treated as an integral part of the sanctioning power itself. Delay is not a neutral act. Witnesses grow old or pass away, documents are misplaced or destroyed, memories fade, and the evidentiary foundation of the prosecution steadily erodes. The accused, on the other hand, continues to hold office or to enjoy the benefits of the position, sometimes even influencing the very evidence on which the case depends. A prolonged silence on the part of the competent authority thus prejudices both the prosecution and the fairness of the trial, and it is the public interest that ultimately suffers. It is true that the legislature has employed the word endeavour, and ordinarily that expression would indicate an effort rather than an absolute command. But the meaning of a word cannot be divorced from its setting. Where the first proviso is followed by a limit on extension, a bar on further extension, and an enabling power to frame guidelines, the scheme as a whole point unmistakably towards a firm outer limit.
title: Test #19: MPHC JJA 2023 - 21/09/2023 - S1

text: This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is directed against the final judgment and order dated 18th May, 2001 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in Criminal Appeal No. 248-DB of 1999, affirming the judgment of conviction and sentence of life imprisonment recorded by the learned Sessions Judge, Sangrur under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the appellant caused the death of the deceased in legitimate exercise of his right of private defense of body. The prosecution case stemmed from a violent confrontation that took place on 15th July, 1991 in Village Chatha, District Sangrur, regarding irrigation water distribution rights between adjoining agricultural fields. While the appellant and his aged father were repairing an irrigation boundary channel, the deceased Gurcharan Singh, accompanied by four adult sons armed with lethal gandasas and heavy wooden lathis, launched a sudden aggressive assault, shouting threats to kill. The assailants inflicted five blunt-force injuries on the appellant's father, causing compound skull fractures and loss of consciousness. When the deceased lunged toward the appellant with an upraised sharp gandasa, the appellant picked up a single-barrel licensed agricultural gun and fired a solitary gunshot, striking the deceased in the chest, which resulted in fatal injuries. The trial court and the High Court convicted the appellant under Section 302 IPC, holding that the appellant exceeded the right of private defense by utilizing a firearm against non-firearm weapons. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the courts below failed to apply the statutory provisions of Section 100 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. It was argued that when an accused is confronted with an aggressive mob inflicting grievous skull fractures on his father and facing an imminent lethal assault with a sharp weapon, a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt arises. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab, reported in (2010) 2 SCC 333, authoritatively restated the governing legal principles under Sections 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The Court held that the right of private defense is a defensive right designed to serve a vital social purpose, intended to arouse and encourage self-reliance in law-abiding citizens faced with unlawful aggression. The law does not expect a citizen to act like a coward or flee when his life or the life of his family is in mortal peril. Under Section 100 clauses First and Secondly of the IPC, the right of private defense of the body extends to causing death if the assault occasions a reasonable apprehension that death or grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence. In Salim Zia v. State of U.P., reported in AIR 1979 SC 391, this Court settled that under Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the accused is not required to prove the right of self-defense beyond reasonable doubt; discharging the onus by a mere preponderance of probabilities is sufficient. A person facing imminent death cannot be expected to weigh his blows in golden scales or modulate his defensive force with clinical precision. Finding that the appellant acted under justified terror of mortal injury, the conviction under Section 302 IPC is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted of all charges. The Court observed that while the traditional nineteenth-century legal presumption held that time is not of the essence in immovable property contracts, that rule arose when real estate values were stable and inflation was negligible. In the modern economic era characterized by galloping land prices and rapid urban commercialization, the presumption cannot be applied blindly to defeat clear contractual intent. An agreement that explicitly specifies installment deadlines and incorporates an unambiguous stipulation that payments on due dates are the essence of the contract cannot be rewritten by the court.
title: Test #20: Legal- SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1057 of 2022

text: The prosecution case rested exclusively on circumstantial evidence, alleging that the appellant, an unmarried rural woman, delivered an infant out of wedlock on 14th November, 2004, murdered the newborn to conceal her pregnancy, and threw the corpse into a village pond. The trial court and the High Court convicted the appellant, relying primarily upon the post-mortem report and the testimony of lady medical officer (PW-11), who deposed that clinical examination revealed physical symptoms consistent with recent parturition. However, scrutiny of the trial record disclosed that during the recording of the appellant's statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the trial judge framed only four vague, composite questions regarding village rumours, completely omitting to confront her with the medical opinion of PW-11 or the findings of the post-mortem examination. Furthermore, the trial court treated her denial of pregnancy as a false defense, utilizing it as a missing link to complete the circumstantial chain.
