Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the omission to put material incriminating circumstances to the accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. vitiates the conviction. The Court held that Section 313 is not an empty judicial ritual, but an essential manifestation of natural justice rooted in the maxim audi alteram partem. Its primary object is to establish a direct dialogue between the court and the accused, ensuring that every incriminating circumstance appearing in prosecution evidence is specifically, clearly, and separately put to the accused to afford him a fair opportunity of explanation. In Premchand v. State of Maharashtra, reported in (2023) 5 SCC 522, and Kalicharan v. State of U.P., reported in (2023) 2 SCC 583, this Court reaffirmed that an incriminating circumstance not put to the accused in Section 313 examination must be completely excluded from judicial consideration. Furthermore, the answers given under Section 313 or a false denial cannot be utilized by the prosecution to fill up gaps or supply missing links in a defective circumstantial chain. The accused has a constitutional right to silence under Article 20(3) and a fundamental right to dignity and privacy under Article 21. Since the foundational medical circumstances were never put to the appellant, they could not be used to convict her. The circumstantial evidence being incomplete, the conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC are set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is directed against the judgment and order dated 20th April, 2010 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Baikunthpur in Criminal Appeal No. 605 of 2005, affirming the judgment of conviction and sentence of life imprisonment recorded by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Baikunthpur under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the trial court failed to put essential incriminating circumstances to the appellant during her examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Indrakunwar v. State of Chhattisgarh, reported in (2024) 14 SCC 595, authoritatively restated the constitutional and statutory significance of Section 313 Cr.P.C. (now Section 351 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023). The Court held that an accomplice is a person who participates in the commission of the crime with criminal mens rea. A trap witness or decoy who acts under official instructions to detect public corruption is not an accomplice in the strict sense of Section 133 of the Evidence Act, as he lacks criminal intent. However, a trap witness is an interested and partisan witness who is keenly interested in the success of the trap operation he participated in. Therefore, as a rule of prudence and caution, the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness cannot form the sole basis for convicting a public servant.
title: Test #20: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1730 of 2012

text: The present Revision Application, preferred by the original accused, challenges the judgment & order dated 11.03.2025 passed by the Sessions Court, whereby the conviction recorded by the learned Magistrate under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, was affirmed. The following questions arise for consideration:- (i) Whether the cheque was issued towards a legally enforceable liability? (ii) Whether the statutory presumption under Sections 118(a) & 139 stands rebutted? (iii) Whether the complaint was instituted within the prescribed period of limitation? According to the complainant, the accused obtained a loan of Rs.3,60,000/- on 18.07.2022 and, towards repayment, issued Cheque No. 482716 dated 10.01.2023, drawn upon "National Cooperative Bank". The cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned unpaid with the endorsement "FUNDS INSUFFICIENT" dated 13.01.2023. A statutory notice dated 27.01.2023 was thereafter issued by Registered Post A.D., calling upon the accused to pay the cheque amount within 15 days. The notice was served on 02.02.2023; however, the accused made no payment. The complainant instituted Summary Criminal Complaint No. 56/2023. The accused entered appearance and denied the transaction. It was contended that the cheque had been obtained as a security instrument and that no independent liability existed on the date of presentation. Reliance was placed upon Exhibit-"C-11", bank statement dated 16.09.2022, Exhibit-"C-14", acknowledgment receipt, and Document No. "R-7/2023". The defence alleged material alteration, misuse of the cheque & absence of proof regarding the source of funds. The Trial Court, after framing the necessary points, recorded the evidence of PW-1 and examined the record. By judgment dated 22.08.2024, the accused was convicted and directed to pay compensation of Rs.4,20,000/- within 30 days. The Appellate Court, vide order dated 11.03.2025, confirmed the conviction, holding that the statutory presumption remained unrebutted and the defence was not supported by reliable evidence. The accused thereafter preferred the present Revision Application before this Court for final determination, raising grounds concerning limitation, admissibility, burden of proof, procedural compliance & appreciation of evidence. Having heard the learned counsel and examined the record, this Court finds that the concurrent findings are neither perverse nor contrary to settled principles of law. The accused failed to establish any probable defence capable of displacing the statutory presumption. No jurisdictional error or manifest illegality is demonstrated. Accordingly, the Revision Application is dismissed. The judgment & order of conviction are affirmed. The record & proceedings shall be returned forthwith in accordance with law and statutory mandate. Under the statutory scheme of Chapter XVII of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, once the signature on the cheque is admitted or satisfactorily established, the presumption under Section 139 mandates the Court to presume that the instrument was issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or liability. As reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan and Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, while this presumption is rebuttable, the standard of proof required from the accused is that of a preponderance of probabilities. A bare denial of liability or a casual assertion that the cheque was delivered merely as a security document does not suffice to rebut the statutory presumption, unless substantiated by cogent documentary or circumstantial evidence. In the present proceedings, the petitioner failed to step into the witness box or adduce any independent proof to establish that the underlying financial debt had been settled. The mandatory requirements regarding dishonor, notice, and institutional limitation under Section 142 stand fully complied with. Consequently, the concurrent judgments of conviction and compensation do not suffer from any illegality.
title: Test #21: Legal- BHC Criminal Case No. 287 of 2024

text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 227 of the Constitution of India read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, calls in question the legality and validity of the order dated 14th June, 2023 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Greater Mumbai in Criminal Revision Application No. 214 of 2022, rejecting the petitioner’s application seeking stay of criminal proceedings in C.C. No. 892/SS/2021 instituted under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 on the ground of statutory interim-moratorium operational under Section 96 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The petitioner executed a personal guarantee in favour of the respondent financial creditor on 14th March, 2018 to secure corporate credit facilities advanced to a textile manufacturing company. Towards discharge of his co-extensive liability, the petitioner issued four post-dated commercial cheques aggregating to Rs. 3,50,00,000/- drawn on Union Bank of India. Upon presentation, the cheques were dishonoured with the endorsement ‘funds insufficient’. Following statutory demand notice, the respondent filed a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Subsequently, on 12th January, 2022, the respondent bank filed an insolvency application against the petitioner personal guarantor before the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench under Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). The petitioner moved the Metropolitan Magistrate, contending that under Section 96(1)(b) of the IBC, an interim-moratorium takes effect immediately upon filing the application, operating to stay all pending legal actions or proceedings in respect of any debt. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that Section 96 is wider in scope than Section 14. Placing heavy reliance upon the seminal three-judge Bench ruling of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in P. Mohanraj v. Shah Brothers Ispat Private Limited, reported in (2021) 6 SCC 258, it was argued that proceedings under Section 138 NI Act are quasi-criminal in nature, aimed at recovery of debt, and therefore fall within the protective umbrella of the moratorium. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that criminal culpability cannot be extinguished through insolvency filings. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court holds that Section 96 of the IBC does not shield individuals from criminal prosecution. In Ajay Kumar Radheyshyam Goenka v. Tourism Finance Corporation of India Limited, reported in (2023) 10 SCC 545, and Saranga Anilkumar Aggarwal v. Bhavesh Dhirajlal Sheth, rendered on 4th March, 2025, the Supreme Court clarified that the ruling in P. Mohanraj was confined strictly to corporate debtors protected under Section 14. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 creates a penal offence enacted to preserve commercial credibility in negotiable transactions. The primary objective of criminal proceedings is penal deterrence, not debt recovery. While Section 96 of the IBC stays civil execution and attachment of assets during individual resolution, it does not immunize a personal guarantor from facing trial for committing a statutory criminal offence. The legislative intent behind Part III of the IBC was never to turn insolvency into a safe haven for cheque-bounce offenders. The learned Magistrate was fully justified in declining to stay the trial. The criminal writ petition is accordingly dismissed. The Tree Authority considered public representations, imposed binding compensatory plantation conditions under Section 8(5), and secured corporate undertakings for five years of post-plantation maintenance. The scope of judicial review under Article 226 is confined to the decision-making process, not the merits of planning policy. Finding no procedural perversity, the writ petition is dismissed, subject to strict monitoring of compensatory afforestation.
title: Test #21: Legal - BHC Cr. Writ P. No. 4182 of 2023

text: This statutory appeal under Section 23 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now corresponding to Section 67 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019) is directed against the final judgment and order dated 23rd October, 2018 passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC), New Delhi in Consumer Complaint No. 706 of 2017, whereby the learned Commission allowed the consumer complaint filed by the respondent homebuyer, directing the appellant developer to refund the entire deposited sum of Rs. 4,48,43,023/- along with interest at the rate of 10.7% per annum on account of gross contractual delay in handing over physical possession of residential apartment No. 1402 in Tower-C. The relevant factual matrix discloses that the respondent entered into an Apartment Buyer's Agreement with the appellant promoter on 8th May, 2012 for the purchase of a four-bedroom luxury condominium in the project designated as 'Araya' situated at Sector 62, Golf Course Extension Road, Gurugram. Under Clause 11.2 of the agreement, the developer promised to hand over possession within thirty-nine months from the date of sanction of building plans, with a grace period of one hundred and eighty days, which expired on 8th August, 2015. The respondent deposited ninety-five percent of the total sale consideration amounting to Rs. 4,48,43,023/- as per the construction-linked payment schedule. However, the appellant failed to secure the statutory occupancy certificate from the Director General of Town and Country Planning until 28th August, 2018, nearly three years beyond the agreed completion deadline. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant builder contended that the delay was occasioned by force majeure events, including administrative embargoes imposed by the National Green Tribunal on groundwater utilization and transport strikes. It was argued that under Clause 11.5 of the agreement, the purchaser was only entitled to delay compensation quantified at Rs. 10/- per square foot per month. Relying upon the contractual terms, it was urged that once an occupancy certificate was obtained during the pendency of the consumer complaint, the purchaser was legally obligated to take physical possession and could not demand a full refund. Refuting these contentions, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the builder-buyer agreement was ex-facie one-sided, harsh, and oppressive. While Clause 6.4 penalized the buyer with eighteen percent interest for any default in installment payments, Clause 11.5 offered a negligible delay compensation to the allottee, constituting an unfair trade practice under Section 2(1)(r) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. Affirming the decree of the National Commission, this Court holds that a homebuyer cannot be compelled to wait indefinitely or accept possession offered almost three years after the contractual deadline. In Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan, reported in (2019) 5 SCC 725, this Court ruled that one-sided terms incorporated in standard-form real estate contracts amount to unfair trade practices, and the purchaser has an unassailable right to rescind the contract and claim refund with reasonable interest. Furthermore, in Wg. Cdr. Arifur Rahman Khan v. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd., reported in (2020) 16 SCC 512, this Court reaffirmed that developers cannot retain homebuyers' savings without performing mutual contractual obligations. Accordingly, the civil appeal is dismissed, with modified directions to disburse the refund along with nine percent interest per annum within eight weeks.
title: Test #22: Legal - SCI Civil Appeal No. 12238 of 2018

text: Learned counsel appearing for the claimant respondents raised preliminary objections, submitting that the appeal is fundamentally defective and not maintainable in the eyes of law. It was argued that the statutory pre-deposit is an absolute condition precedent for the entertainment of an appeal, and presentation of a memorandum of appeal without the requisite deposit is invalid. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant corporation submitted that depositing funds is a directory procedural requirement, and subsequent compliance cures the initial defect retrospectively. The claim petition arose out of a fatal motor vehicular collision that occurred on 12th January, 2015 on the Aligarh-Bulandshahr highway, involving a state roadways passenger bus and an agricultural tractor-trolley. The Tribunal held the bus driver entirely negligent, awarding compensation under Section 166 of the Act. The appellant corporation filed this statutory appeal before this Court on 18th July, 2018 within the prescribed ninety-day limitation period under Section 173(1). However, the memorandum of appeal was presented without annexing the mandatory treasury receipt or bank draft certifying the pre-deposit of statutory funds. Under the second proviso to Section 173(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, no appeal by a person who is required to pay any amount under an award shall be entertained by the High Court unless he has deposited with it twenty-five thousand rupees or fifty percent of the amount so awarded, whichever is less. The Stamp Reporter endorsed a formal objection on 20th July, 2018. The appellant tendered the deposit only on 14th December, 2018, nearly five months beyond limitation, filing an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963. This first appeal from order, preferred under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, is directed against the judgment and award dated 14th March, 2018 passed by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal Additional District Judge, Court No. 4, Bulandshahr in Motor Accident Claim Petition No. 184 of 2015, whereby compensation of Rs. 14,82,500/- with seven percent interest was awarded in favour of the claimant respondents, holding the appellant transport corporation solely liable to pay compensation without proof of statutory pre-deposit under the mandatory proviso. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that compliance with the second proviso to Section 173(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is mandatory and jurisdictional. The right of appeal is not an inherent or common law right, but a statutory privilege conditioned upon fulfilling the legislative stipulations enacted by Parliament. In State of Haryana v. Maruti Udyog Ltd., reported in (2000) 7 SCC 348, and Rambir Singh v. Smt. Gayatri Devi, reported in (2018) SCC OnLine All 1420, it was established that the phrase 'no appeal shall be entertained' operates as an express prohibition against judicial cognizance.  An appeal presented without the statutory pre-deposit cannot be treated as an appeal in the eye of law; it matures into a valid appeal only on the date the deposit is actually tendered in the Registry. If the deposit is made beyond the statutory ninety days, the appellant must explain each day's delay by showing sufficient cause. The appellant offered no explanation for withholding the statutory deposit for five months while holding the award amount. Finding no grounds to condone the inordinate delay, the delay condonation application is rejected, and the first appeal from order is dismissed as barred by limitation. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that symbolic possession on official files cannot defeat the beneficial provisions of the Repeal Act. In Hari Ram (supra), affirmed in Gajanan Kamlya Patil v. Additional Collector, reported in (2014) 12 SCC 523, the Supreme Court authoritatively established that requirement of taking physical possession under Section 10(5) and Section 10(6) of the 1976 Act is mandatory. Mere paper transfer or mutation in revenue records does not constitute actual physical dispossession.
title: Test #22: Legal - AHC FAFO No. 2145 of 2018

text: This intra-court appeal, preferred under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent against the judgment and order dated 14th November, 2024 rendered by the learned Single Judge in Writ Petition No. 14210 of 2024, calls in question the quashing of charge memo Rc. No. 42/T1/2012 dated 18th July, 2012 issued by the Superintendent of Police, Krishna District under Rule 20 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991, whereby disciplinary proceedings initiated against the respondent police officer were quashed solely on the ground of an inordinate, unexplained administrative delay of twelve years in concluding the formal departmental inquiry. The respondent entered service as a Sub-Inspector of Police in 1994. Disciplinary proceedings were initiated in July 2012 alleging improper handling of case files during the investigation of Crime No. 97 of 2003 registered at Alamuru Police Station. The respondent submitted a detailed written statement of defense on 3rd December, 2014, denying all imputations. Successive inquiry officers were appointed through administrative memorandums dated 25th November, 2013 and 16th September, 2014, yet oral inquiry proceedings were repeatedly adjourned without examining material prosecution witnesses. A parallel criminal prosecution arising out of the same transaction terminated in the respondent's complete acquittal on 12th August, 2019. Despite the respondent attaining the age of superannuation on 30th June, 2021, the disciplinary authority failed to conclude the proceedings, withholding terminal benefits and full pensionary emoluments under Rule 9 of the Andhra Pradesh Revised Pension Rules, 1980. Learned Government Pleader appearing for the State contended that departmental proceedings operate on the principle of preponderance of probabilities and are not automatically vitiated by acquittal in criminal trials. It was argued that G.O. Ms. No. 679, General Administration (Services-C) Department, dated 1st November, 2008, prescribing a six-month time limit for completing departmental inquiries, is directory in nature and does not operate as an absolute jurisdictional bar. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent employee submitted that keeping disciplinary proceedings pending for more than a decade without any justification constitutes a flagrant violation of Article 14, Article 16, and Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Reliance was placed on the landmark decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of A.P. v. N. Radhakishan, reported in (1998) 4 SCC 154, and P.V. Mahadevan v. MD, T.N. Housing Board, reported in (2005) 6 SCC 636, wherein it was authoritatively established that inordinate delay in concluding disciplinary proceedings causes serious prejudice, continuous mental agony, and loss of promotional avenues, disentitling the employer from proceeding further. Having reviewed the counter-affidavit and administrative records, this Court finds that the department offered no plausible explanation for the protracted delay between 2014 and 2024. The delinquent employee cannot be subjected to perpetual harassment throughout his post-retirement life. In Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Prabhash Chandra Mirdha, reported in (2012) 11 SCC 565, the Apex Court observed that where proceedings remain stalled due to administrative lethargy without any fault on the part of the employee, the charge memo must be quashed. Concurring with the learned Single Judge, this Court dismisses the writ appeal, quashes the charge memo, and directs the State to release all withheld pensionary benefits and gratuity along with interest at six percent per annum within sixty days.
title: Test #23: Legal - APHC Writ Appeal No. 1069 of 2025

text: The Petitioners, Ramesh Dattatray Jadhav & Meena Ashok Patil, have approached this Court against the State of Maharashtra & Competent Authority, seeking enforcement of 4% RESERVATION in public employment. The Petitioners challenge the ORDER dated 14.09.2018 alleging failure to implement reservation. The Petitioners relied upon disability certificates, recruitment records, roster statements & Government Resolutions. Ramesh Dattatray Jadhav submitted an application dated 21.03.2018, followed by NOTICE dated 17.07.2018. Meena Ashok Patil produced Exhibit-("P-11") and relied upon Roster Register No. "RR/46/2018". It was contended that 4% reservation must be calculated against sanctioned cadre strength and cannot be denied because the authority claims no suitable vacancy existed. The respondents filed an affidavit-in-reply and raised preliminary objections regarding maintainability, roster position and eligibility. The respondents submitted that recruitment had concluded and the Petitioners lacked requisite merit. Reliance was placed upon Office Memorandum No. "PWD/72/2018" dated 08.08.2018, Selection Statement Exhibit-"R-7" and Document No. "ADM/184/2018". According to the respondents, the roster disclosed no available post during that recruitment year. The Petitioners disputed this and submitted that the authority must identify, maintain, carry forward & fill reserved posts. During the hearing, learned counsel for the Petitioners submitted that non-maintenance of a proper roster would defeat the object of reservation. It was argued that EQUAL OPPORTUNITY under Articles 14 & 16 cannot be a mere FORMALITY. The Court examined certificates, recruitment papers, roster entries, Resolutions & correspondence. Having heard counsel for Ramesh Dattatray Jadhav, Meena Ashok Patil & respondents, and examined the RECORD, this Court finds that compliance with 4% reservation has not been established. The impugned ORDER dated 14.09.2018 gives insufficient reasons for rejecting the claim. Administrative inconvenience cannot override statutory obligation. Accordingly, the Petition is ALLOWED. The impugned ORDER dated 14.09.2018 is QUASHED & SET ASIDE. The Competent Authority shall verify the roster, determine reserved vacancies, consider eligibility and pass a reasoned order within 8 weeks. The Petitioners shall receive an opportunity of HEARING. No order as to costs in law. The decision shall be communicated to all concerned parties, and the entire exercise shall remain subject to applicable statutory provisions, relevant Government Resolutions, roster rules, principles of natural justice & constitutional guarantees governing disability reservation in public service. The mandate of Section 34 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, imposes a positive, affirmative obligation on every appropriate Government establishment to appoint in every government establishment not less than four per cent of the total number of vacancies in the cadre strength in each group of posts. As ruled by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in landmark pronouncements including Union of India v. National Federation of the Blind and Rajeev Kumar Gupta v. Union of India, the computation of reservation for persons with disabilities has to be computed on the total number of vacancies in the strength of a cadre, and not merely on the identified posts. The state cannot escape its constitutional and statutory commitments by pleading that the recruitment process has concluded or that administrative inconveniences preclude retrospective roster realignment. Reservation for disabled citizens is an integral facet of distributive equality guaranteed under Articles 14, 16, and 21 of the Constitution of India. Therefore, the respondents must scrupulously calculate backlog vacancies, maintain reservation registers, and provide equal opportunities without bureaucratic impediments.
title: Test #23: Legal - BHC PIL No. 46 of 2018

text: This criminal revision petition, instituted under Section 19(4) of the Family Courts Act, 1984 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is directed against the judgment and order dated 21st September, 2020 passed by the learned Principal Judge, Family Court, Gurugram, in Maintenance Petition No. 184 of 2018, whereby the petition filed by the respondent-wife under Section 125 Cr.P.C. was allowed in part, directing the revision petitioner-husband to pay a monthly maintenance allowance of Rs. 28,000/- to the respondent and their minor school-going child from the date of application. The matrimonial union between the petitioner and the respondent was solemnized on 18th November, 2014 in accordance with Hindu rites and ceremonies at Ambala. A male child was born out of the wedlock on 14th August, 2016. Matrimonial discord surfaced between the spouses, culminating in the respondent leaving the matrimonial home on 12th February, 2018, citing persistent demands for dowry under Section 498-A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and mental cruelty. The respondent thereafter instituted proceedings under Section 125 Cr.P.C. on 10th May, 2018, asserting that she is an unemployed homemaker without independent financial resources, whereas the petitioner is employed as a Senior Technical Lead in an information technology multinational corporation, earning a gross monthly salary of Rs. 1,45,000/- alongside substantial ancestral agricultural rentals in District Karnal. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the learned Family Court awarded an exorbitant maintenance quantum without considering the financial encumbrances of the petitioner. It was submitted that the petitioner is servicing an equated monthly installment (EMI) of Rs. 42,500/- towards a home mortgage loan borrowed from the State Bank of India, alongside medical insurance liabilities of aged dependent parents. Relying on Kalyan Dey Chowdhury v. Rita Dey Chowdhury Nee Nandy, reported in (2017) 14 SCC 200, it was argued that maintenance should not ordinarily exceed twenty-five percent of the net take-home salary of the husband. Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the petitioner voluntarily suppressed actual income tax returns and salary bonus slips to evade legitimate familial obligations. Reliance was placed on the landmark judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajnesh v. Neha, reported in (2021) 2 SCC 324, wherein comprehensive guidelines were formulated mandating the disclosure of comprehensive Affidavits of Assets and Liabilities by both spouses to ensure that maintenance awards are realistic, just, and commensurate with the socio-economic status of the parties. Having considered the rival contentions and scrutinized the income affidavits filed in terms of Rajnesh v. Neha, this Court observes that the primary object of Section 125 Cr.P.C. is benevolent and social in nature, designed to prevent destitution, penury, and vagrancy. The maintenance allowance must be determined using the yardstick of equistatus, ensuring that the dependent spouse and growing minor child are entitled to live with the same dignity and comfort as they would have enjoyed in the matrimonial home. Voluntary debt repayments and non-essential financial deductions cannot take precedence over the statutory duty to maintain wife and children. Considering the living expenses, inflation indices, and school tuition fees, the monthly sum of Rs. 28,000/- is neither oppressive nor unreasonable. Finding no jurisdictional error, perversity, or patent illegality in the impugned order, this revision petition is dismissed, affirming the maintenance award.
title: Test #24: Legal - PHHC CRR(F) No. 279 of 2021

text: The petitioners were absolute owners of agricultural lands comprised in Survey Nos. 114 and 115 situated at Narakodur village, acquired for the public purpose of excavating irrigation canals under the Krishna Western Delta Modernization Project. The Land Acquisition Officer passed an ex-parte award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on 24th October, 2016, evaluating compensation at an arbitrary rate of Rs. 3,50,000/- per acre. Crucially, the Collector omitted to pronounce the award in the presence of the landholders, nor was any mandatory notice of the award served upon the petitioners in terms of Section 12(2) of the Act. The petitioners first acquired knowledge of the award when compensation cheques were deposited into their joint bank accounts on 14th August, 2017. Thereupon, on 20th September, 2017, within five weeks of acquiring knowledge, the petitioners filed an application before the Land Acquisition Officer under Section 18(1), seeking reference to the Civil Court for enhancement of compensation to Rs. 25,00,000/- per acre. The Reference Court dismissed the application as time-barred, calculating the six-month period from the date of the Collector's signature on 24th October, 2016. Learned counsel appearing for the revision petitioners contended that the Reference Court committed a grave jurisdictional error. It was submitted that under Section 18(2)(b), the phrase 'date of the award' means the date on which the award is communicated or the date when the party acquires actual or constructive knowledge of its essential contents. Learned Government Pleader for Land Acquisition supported the dismissal, arguing that Section 18(2) enacts an outer limitation of six months from the date of the award, which admits of no extension under the Limitation Act. Setting aside the order, this Court holds that an uncommunicated administrative decision cannot operate to bar constitutional rights to compensation. This civil revision petition, preferred under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, challenges the order dated 18th March, 2021 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge, Guntur in Land Acquisition Original Petition L.A.O.P. No. 42 of 2018, rejecting the reference application filed under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 on the preliminary ground of limitation, holding that the application preferred by the landholder-claimants was barred by time as it was presented beyond six months from the date of the award passed by the Land Acquisition Officer. In the celebrated Constitution Bench authority in Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, reported in AIR 1961 SC 1500, and State of Punjab v. Qaisar Jehan Begum, reported in (1964) 1 SCR 971, the Hon'ble Supreme Court authoritatively settled that the date of the award under Section 18(2)(b) must mean the date when the award is either made known to the party or the date when the party acquired knowledge of the award. The award of the Collector is merely an administrative offer of compensation. If the landholder was not present when the award was made and no notice was issued under Section 12(2), limitation begins to run only from the date when the landowner acquired knowledge of the contents of the award. A citizen cannot be deprived of statutory remedies by keeping an award concealed in government files. Since the application was filed within six weeks of receiving compensation in their bank accounts, the reference was within time. The revision petition is allowed, and the Reference Court is directed to adjudicate the compensation on merits. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the right to be considered for promotion is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 16 of the Constitution of India. It was argued that placing recommendations in a sealed cover on the basis of a preliminary vigilance inquiry without a formal charge sheet violates binding constitutional precedents. Learned Government Pleader for Services opposed the petition.
title: Test #24: Legal - APHC Cr. P. No. 1420 of 2021

text: Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the High Court completely overlooked the mandatory requirements of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. It was argued that the plaintiff merely pleaded formal readiness in the plaint without adducing credible documentary evidence, such as bank account balances, fixed deposit receipts, or loan sanction letters, to prove financial capacity to pay the substantial balance sum of Rs. 15,00,000/- during the crucial contractual period. Reliance was placed on the landmark decision of this Court in His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, reported in (1996) 4 SCC 526, and N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, reported in (1995) 5 SCC 115, wherein it was established that readiness refers to capacity to pay the purchase money, whereas willingness refers to the conduct and mental disposition of the purchaser. In response, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the vendor committed breach by failing to secure revenue conversion permissions, thereby disabling the respondent from completing the transaction. It was urged that where the vendor is in default, the purchaser cannot be faulted for not tendering the balance sum. Having meticulously scrutinized the evidence on record, this Court finds that the compliance of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act is an indispensable condition precedent that must be proved from the date of agreement up to the date of the final decree. In Janardan Das v. Durga Prasad Agrawalla, reported in 2024 INSC 748, this Court reiterated that a plaintiff cannot succeed merely by showing default on the part of the defendant; the plaintiff must stand on the strength of their own continuous readiness and willingness. In the present case, the respondent produced no bank statements or witnesses to substantiate financial capacity between 1993 and 1995. Furthermore, specific performance is an equitable relief governed by judicial discretion under Section 20 of the Act. Consequently, the judgment of the High Court is set aside, the decree for specific performance is revoked, and the appellants are directed to refund the earnest deposit of Rs. 3,50,000/- along with interest at nine percent per annum. This civil appeal arises from the impugned judgment and decree dated 14th November, 2008 passed by the High Court of Karnataka in Regular First Appeal No. 418 of 2002, whereby the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court dated 28th January, 2002 in Original Suit No. 1045 of 1995, and decreed the suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable agricultural land in favour of the respondent-plaintiff under Section 16(c) and Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The essential facts disclose that on 15th April, 1993, the predecessor-in-interest of the appellants entered into a written agreement to sell a parcel of fertile agricultural land admeasuring four acres situated at Survey No. 82/1, Devanahalli Taluk, Bangalore Rural District, for a total agreed sale consideration of Rs. 18,50,000/-. The respondent paid an earnest money deposit of Rs. 3,50,000/- on the date of execution, with the balance consideration payable within six months upon the vendor obtaining non-agricultural conversion approvals from the competent revenue authorities. Disputes erupted when the vendor issued a termination notice dated 20th October, 1993, asserting that the respondent failed to tender the remaining balance consideration despite reminders. Conversely, the respondent instituted the civil suit on 12th December, 1995, claiming continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract and seeking a registered conveyance deed.
title: Test #25: Legal - SCI Civil Apeeal No. 2187 of 2011

text: This criminal appeal, preferred by the accused facing trial for offences punishable under Section 302 and Section 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, challenges the interlocutory order dated 26th July, 2024 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Agra, rejecting the application filed under Section 207 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 seeking supply of the comprehensive list and inspection of un-relied documents seized by the police during investigation in terms of Rule 11 of the Draft Criminal Rules on Practice, 2021. The defense moved an application before the trial court under Section 207 Cr.P.C. read with Rule 11 of the Draft Criminal Rules on Practice, 2021, seeking a verified list and inspection of all seized material objects and un-relied documents. The learned Sessions Judge dismissed the application, holding that under Section 207, the prosecution is obligated to supply only those documents that it proposes to rely upon, and that the accused could seek un-relied documents only at the stage of leading defense evidence under Section 91 Cr.P.C. The High Court declined to interfere under Section 482 Cr.P.C. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that withholding material exculpatory evidence collected during investigation violates the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial under Article 21 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Ashok Kumar Tomar v. State of U.P., rendered on 28th February, 2025, and Manoj v. State of Madhya Pradesh, reported in (2023) 2 SCC 353, authoritatively restated the statutory mandate governing criminal discovery. The Court held that a criminal trial is not an adversarial game of hide-and-seek, but a solemn search for truth. In the landmark suo motu proceedings in In Re: Inadequacies & Deficiencies in Criminal Trials, reported in (2021) 10 SCC 598, this Court mandated the incorporation of Rule 11 in criminal court manuals across all High Courts. Under Rule 11, the investigating agency is under an inflexible legal duty to prepare and furnish along with the police report three distinct lists: (i) a list of statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C., (ii) a list of documents and materials relied upon, and (iii) a comprehensive list of statements, documents, and seized material objects that the prosecution does not propose to rely upon. In Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi), reported in (2010) 6 SCC 1, this Court affirmed that the Public Prosecutor owes an overarching duty of fairness to the court and to the accused. If the police seize exculpatory material that demonstrates innocence, withholding it from the accused violates natural justice and vitiates the trial. Trial courts cannot postpone disclosure of un-relied documents to the defense stage. The impugned orders are set aside, and the prosecution is directed to supply the complete list and permit inspection of all un-relied records before framing charges under Section 228 Cr.P.C. Furthermore, the answers given under Section 313 or a false denial cannot be utilized by the prosecution to fill up gaps or supply missing links in a defective circumstantial chain. The accused has a constitutional right to silence under Article 20(3) and a fundamental right to dignity and privacy under Article 21. Since the foundational medical circumstances were never put to the appellant, they could not be used to convict her. The circumstantial evidence being incomplete, the conviction and life sentence under Section 302 IPC are set aside, and the appellant is acquitted. During the investigation of a sensational murder case, the police seized twelve mobile telephone handsets, forensic call detail records (CDRs), tower dump analytics, and closed-circuit television (CCTV) hard drives. However, while submitting the charge sheet under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., the investigating officer selected only two call records supporting the prosecution narrative, suppressing eight forensic CDRs and tower location logs that established the plea of alibi set up by the accused.
title: Test #25: Legal - SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1817 of 2024

text: This Writ Petition in the nature of Habeas Corpus is filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a direction to the respondent authorities to produce the person of a young man, aged approximately twenty-two years, who has been missing since 10th February 2026. The petitioner, who is the mother of the missing individual, alleges that her son was taken into informal custody by the local police for questioning regarding a neighborhood dispute and has not returned home since then. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the state has fulfilled its constitutional obligation to protect the life and liberty of a citizen and whether the police have conducted a diligent search to locate the person in question. The petitioner argues that the failure of the police to register a First Information Report (FIR) promptly and their lackadaisical approach to the investigation points toward a potential case of illegal detention or custodial disappearance. The facts of the case reveal that despite several visits to the police station and representations to the Commissioner of Police, no concrete information has been shared with the family. The learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri Rahul Mehra, argues that the right to life and liberty is the most sacred of all fundamental rights and cannot be suspended even for a moment without the due process of law. He submits that the burden of proof in a Habeas Corpus petition lies on the state to show that the individual is not in their custody and that every effort is being made to trace him. He contends that the closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage of the area where the individual was last seen has not been preserved by the investigating officer, which raises serious doubts about the transparency of the police action. In response, the learned Standing Counsel for the Government of NCT of Delhi argues that the individual was never taken into custody by the police. He submits that the police are treating this as a case of a missing person and have already flashed a wireless message to all police stations in the neighboring states. He contends that there is no evidence to suggest that the police were involved in the disappearance and that the individual might have left his home voluntarily due to domestic pressure. The State maintains that a Special Investigation Team (SIT) has been constituted to look into the matter and that all leads are being followed. The respondent further argues that a Writ of Habeas Corpus is not maintainable when there is no prima facie evidence of illegal detention by the state machinery. Having heard both sides and perused the status reports filed by the police, this Court observes that the investigation has been sluggish and lacks the urgency required in cases of personal liberty. The Delhi High Court emphasizes that a Writ of Habeas Corpus is a high prerogative writ and is the greatest safeguard against arbitrary power. The law is well-settled that the High Court, in the exercise of its jurisdiction, has the power to oversee the investigation and ensure that the state does not shirk its responsibility. In the present case, the initial delay in registering the FIR has resulted in the loss of crucial evidence, including the CCTV footage mentioned by the petitioner. The "Rule of Law" requires that the police must act as the protectors of the people, and any allegation of "unrecorded detention" must be met with a rigorous inquiry. The Court finds that the current status report is vague and fails to inspire confidence. The right of a mother to know the whereabouts of her son is an integral part of her dignity under Article 21. The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that if the state fails to produce the person, the court can direct a probe by an independent agency like the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). The sanctity of human life and the freedom from illegal restraint are the cornerstones of our democracy. The administrative convenience or the "heavy workload" of the police cannot be used as an excuse for failing to trace a missing citizen.
title: Test #26: Legal - DHC W.P. (CRL) No. 3120 of 2026

text: The present Writ Petition, filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, challenges the ORDER dated 18.04.2025 passed by the Competent Authority, whereby the petitioner’s application for restoration of service benefits was rejected. The dispute concerns the legality, validity & procedural fairness of the impugned decision. The following questions arise for consideration: - (i) Whether the authority acted within its statutory jurisdiction? (ii) Whether the petitioner was denied a reasonable opportunity of HEARING? (iii) Whether the impugned order suffers from arbitrariness, non-application of mind & violation of natural justice? The petitioner was appointed as a Clerk on 07.06.2018 and served at the District Treasury Office. On 16.09.2023, a departmental NOTICE was issued alleging unauthorized absence during the period from 03.08.2023 to 21.08.2023. The petitioner submitted an explanation dated 28.09.2023, denying the allegations and producing attendance records, medical documents & correspondence marked Exhibit- "P-11". However, the authority, without considering the documents, passed the disputed order dated 18.04.2025. The petitioner submitted a representation dated 02.05.2025, requesting reconsideration of the findings. The representation was rejected by communication No. "ADM/472/2025" dated 19.06.2025. It was contended that the authority had relied upon an incomplete attendance register and had ignored the written explanation. Reliance was placed upon Document-"P-17", Office Memorandum dated 11.01.2024, and Dispatch Register No. 54/2025. The petitioner submitted that procedural safeguards are not empty formalities and that every affected person is entitled to a fair opportunity before an adverse order is passed. The respondent-authority opposed the Petition and contended that the impugned ORDER was based upon records and that no prejudice had been caused to the petitioner. It was further submitted that the Court, exercising jurisdiction under Article 226, should not ordinarily re-appreciate disputed facts unless the decision is perverse, arbitrary or legally unsustainable. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, examined the RECORD and considered the statutory provisions, this Court finds that the authority failed to consider documents produced by the petitioner. The impugned order does not disclose proper reasons for rejecting the explanation. Such non-consideration amounts to violation of PRINCIPLES OF NATURAL JUSTICE and renders the decision unsustainable. Accordingly, the Writ Petition is ALLOWED. The impugned ORDER dated 18.04.2025 is hereby QUASHED & SET ASIDE. The matter is remitted to the competent authority for consideration after granting opportunity of HEARING to the petitioner. The exercise shall be completed within 8 weeks from receipt of this order. No order as to costs. It is an elemental canon of administrative law that justice must not only be done, but must manifestly and undoubtedly be seen to be done. When a disciplinary or administrative authority proceeds against an employee on charges of willful absenteeism, the burden lies squarely upon the administration to establish by cogent material that the absence was deliberate and devoid of legitimate justification. The constitutional guarantee enshrined in Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India mandates non-arbitrariness in state action. An administrative order inflicting adverse civil consequences upon an employee without addressing the defense explanations, medical proof, or official dispatch records violates the sacred doctrine of audi alteram partem. Reasons are the indispensable heartbeat of any quasi-judicial adjudication, linking the raw facts to the ultimate administrative conclusion. In the absence of reasoned articulation, the supervisory court exercising extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is duty-bound to intervene and restore procedural equilibrium. Consequently, the competent authority must reconsider the entire defense repository afresh and render a speaking order within the prescribed time limit.
title: Test #26: Legal - BHC Writ Petition No. 3847 of 2025

text: This appeal, filed under Section 173 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, is directed against the judgment and award dated 28th February, 2019 passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Pune in Motor Accident Claim Petition No. 412 of 2015, whereby the Tribunal awarded a total compensation of Rs. 38,45,000/- along with interest at the rate of 7.5% per annum from the date of the claim petition until realisation, holding the appellant insurance company jointly and severally liable with the owner of the offending motor truck bearing registration No. MH-12-FC-8821. The claim arose out of a fatal vehicular accident that occurred on 16th October, 2014 near Shirwal on the Pune-Bengaluru National Highway. The deceased, Ravindra Deshmukh, aged thirty-six years, was driving his motorcycle when the offending truck, driven in a rash, reckless, and negligent manner at high speed, collided with the two-wheeler from behind, inflicting catastrophic head injuries that resulted in instantaneous death. The deceased was employed as a permanent Senior Quality Supervisor in an engineering enterprise, drawing a gross monthly salary of Rs. 32,500/- as evidenced by salary slips Exhibit-34 and bank statements Exhibit-36. The surviving legal heirs, comprising his widow, two minor daughters, and aged dependent parents, instituted proceedings under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 claiming compensation of Rs. 60,00,000/-. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant insurance company contended that the Tribunal erred in computing future prospects and committed serious arithmetical errors by failing to deduct professional tax and income tax liabilities under the Income Tax Act, 1961. It was further argued that excessive amounts were granted under non-pecuniary heads, violating established principles. On the other hand, learned counsel for the claimants submitted that the assessment of loss of dependency strictly adhered to binding constitutional precedents. Heavy reliance was placed on the Constitution Bench judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi, reported in (2017) 16 SCC 680, wherein it was established that where the deceased had permanent employment and was between thirty to forty years of age, an addition of 50% must be made toward future prospects. Reliance was also placed on Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation, reported in (2009) 6 SCC 121, governing the application of the appropriate multiplier of 15 and deduction of one-fourth toward personal living expenses where the number of dependent family members is five. This Court, upon re-evaluating the evidence, finds that the Tribunal correctly adopted the multiplier of 15 and added 50% for future prospects after deducting income tax. However, regarding conventional heads, in Magma General Insurance Company Limited v. Nanu Ram, reported in (2018) 18 SCC 130, and Pranay Sethi, the Supreme Court ruled that each dependent is entitled to consortium of Rs. 40,000/- comprising spousal, parental, and filial consortium, alongside Rs. 15,000/- each for loss of estate and funeral expenses, without any separate entitlement under love and affection. Accordingly, the award is modified to Rs. 41,20,000/- with 7.5% interest per annum, and the appeal is disposed of with directions to release the deposited amount.
title: Test #27: Legal - BHC First Appeal No. 3039 of 2019

text: All judicial systems, world-over, have barred the admission of hearsay evidence, because to act upon hearsay evidence is risky as it does not provide any medium or instrument like cross-examination to test the truthfulness, falsity or reliability of this type of evidence. Evidence in the nature of the statement of the deceased i.e. dying declaration made about the circumstances in which his death resulted also falls in the category of hearsay evidence. Hence, any such statement of the deceased as such remains irrelevant and inadmissible in evidence, but out of necessity a compulsion arises to meet a peculiar situation which has made this type of evidence, namely dying declaration, relevant and therefore admissible by creating an exception to the general rule against admissibility of hearsay evidence. Hence, if his statement about the circumstances in which his death occurred is not admitted in evidence during criminal trial, then the only evidence of crime would be lost and as a consequence, the offender would go scotfree and thus cause miscarriage of justice. It is derived from a belief or enunciation in its favour on the basis that the dying man's deep faith in his religion would not allow lies on his lips, while he is dying and when he knows that he is soon to meet his Maker, i.e., God. The earliest judicial pronouncement making dying declaration admissible in evidence inspite of its being in the nature of hearsay evidence is found in the case of King Versus William Woodcock, (J789) 1 Leach, 500. Judge Eyre, Chief Baron laid down as under: -"The general principles on which this species of evidence is admitted, is that they are declarations made in extremity when the party is at the point of death and when every hope in this world is gone. When every motive to falsehood is silent and the mind is induced by the most powerful consideration to speak the truth, a situation so solemn, and so awful is considered by the law as creating obligation equal to that which is imposed by a positive oath administered in a Court of justice. The Indian law of evidence has incorporated this principle in clause (1) of Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, which provides that statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead are themselves relevant facts when the statement is made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question. Such statements are relevant whether the person who made them was or was not, at the time when they were made, under expectation of death, and whatever may be the nature of the proceeding in which the cause of his death comes into question. Thus, the English rule that the declarant must have been under a settled and hopeless expectation of death has not been adopted in India. However, the courts have consistently held that a dying declaration, being a weak piece of evidence by its very nature, must be scrutinised with great care and caution. It is now well settled that a dying declaration can form the sole basis of conviction, if the court is satisfied that it is true, voluntary and free from tutoring, prompting or imagination. Where the court finds that the declaration is wholly reliable, no corroboration is required. But where it is suspicious, inconsistent or doubtful, the court should look for independent corroboration before placing reliance upon it. The court must also be satisfied that the deceased was in a fit state of mind to make the statement. A certificate of the doctor to that effect is desirable, though it is not an indispensable requirement of law. The statement is ordinarily recorded by a Magistrate, who is expected to ascertain that the declarant is conscious and coherent. In the absence of a Magistrate, however, a statement recorded by a police officer, a doctor or even a private person may be accepted, if it inspires confidence.
title: Test #27: MPHC JJA 2024 - 20/01/2025 - S1

text: This petition has been preferred under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) seeking the quashing of First Information Report No. 112 dated 18th May, 2023 registered under Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 at Police Station Civil Lines, District Ludhiana, along with all consequential proceedings arising therefrom, including the final investigation report filed under Section 173(2) of Cr.P.C. and the summoning order dated 24th January, 2024 passed by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class. The genesis of the prosecution case stems from a commercial complaint lodged by Respondent No. 2, managing partner of an agro-industrial firm, alleging that the petitioners, as directors of an exporting corporate entity, dishonestly induced the complainant into executing a supply agreement dated 10th February, 2021. It was alleged that despite receiving agro-commodities valued at Rs. 1,84,50,000/-, the petitioners issued forged purchase orders, altered consignment notes, and cancelled delivery receipts, thereby misappropriating the consignment and causing wrongful financial loss. However, during the pendency of trial proceedings, with the active intervention of respectable members of society and mutual trade mediators, the parties executed a comprehensive deed of compromise dated 12th December, 2024, resolving all monetary and business differences amicably. Pursuant to the compromise, the entire agreed settlement sum of Rs. 1,84,50,000/- was duly transferred via Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) transactions on 15th January, 2025 into the commercial bank account of Respondent No. 2. Learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the dispute is pre-eminently of a private and civil nature arising out of commercial dealings, without any element of public interest, mental depravity, or moral turpitude. He submitted that when the dispute stands amicably settled and all dues have been liquidated, continuation of criminal prosecution would amount to a sheer abuse of the process of the court. Heavy reliance was placed upon the landmark three-judge Bench ruling of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Gian Singh v. State of Punjab, reported in (2012) 10 SCC 303, wherein it was authoritatively held that the inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is distinct from the statutory power of compounding under Section 320 Cr.P.C. The High Court, to secure the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of any court, is fully empowered to quash criminal proceedings even in non-compoundable offences having commercial, mercantile, civil, or partnership overtones. Reliance was further placed upon the five-judge Full Bench decision of this Court in Kulwinder Singh v. State of Punjab, reported in 2007 (3) RCR (Criminal) 1052, and the Supreme Court decision in Parbatbhai Aahir v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2017) 9 SCC 641, which delineated the broad governing principles for quashment based on compromise. The learned State counsel, along with the counsel for Respondent No. 2, conceded that the compromise is genuine, voluntary, and executed without undue influence, and the complainant has filed a formal supporting affidavit dated 15th March, 2025 affirming complete restitution. It was further acknowledged that the dispute has not generated any social disharmony or affected the public peace at large. Having examined the record, this Court holds that no useful purpose would be served by keeping the prosecution alive when the chances of ultimate conviction are bleak and remote. In State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, reported in 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, the Supreme Court held that where criminal proceedings are manifestly attended with mala fides or where allegations do not disclose the commission of any offence, the Court must exercise its extraordinary powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. Continuance of the trial would cause undue harassment, burden the judicial docket, and waste precious judicial time.
title: Test #28: Legal - PHHC CRM-M 34005 of 2025

text: It must be noted that the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 did not contain any provision regarding the pre-arrest bail, also known as anticipatory bail. It is only in 1973 that the Anticipatory Bail became part of the Cr.P.C, on the recommendation of the Forty First Law Commission Report. The Commission underlined the necessity of introducing a new section concerning pre-arrest bail and recommended for the inclusion of such provision. It was observed that many cases are instigated against a person just because of political motivation or personal vendetta. They lack enough evidence and are meant to harass a person by getting him arrested. As arbitrary arrests (often leading to harassment and humiliation of citizens) continue to be a pervasive phenomenon in the country, therefore, protection should be given to the people. This was the underlying reason for the enactment of Section 438 in the CrPC. Thus, the provision of anticipatory bail was included to protect the arbitrary violation of the right to personal liberty of an individual so that no person can be confined or detained in any manner unless he has been held guilty. Further, it was observed that when there are reasonable grounds for believing that a person accused of an offence is not likely to abscond or misuse his liberty while on Bail, then there is no need to first submit him to custody, make him/her remain in prison and then apply for Bail. In such cases, Bail could be granted earlier. The confusion relating to the provision of anticipatory bail started and increased when different courts expressed different and contradictory views regarding its scope as to whether the same could be time bound or not. The grant of anticipatory bail should not be limited by time. Also, the court has wide discretion to impose appropriate conditions on a case to case basis. The Supreme Court in the case of Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre Versus State Of Maharashtra rejected the notion that anticipatory bail could be for a limited time and opined that there can be no time limit as to the life of an anticipatory bail. The scope and rationale of Section 438 were authoritatively settled by a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia Versus State Of Punjab, (1980) 2 SCC 565. The Court observed that the provision, being a procedural safeguard for the protection of personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution, must receive a liberal interpretation and should not be hedged in by rigid or inflexible conditions which the Legislature itself did not intend to impose. It was held that the High Court and the Court of Session must exercise their discretion judicially, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, instead of laying down a uniform formula for all situations. The Court further clarified that a person who apprehends arrest need not wait until a First Information Report is registered, but there must exist a reasonable belief, founded upon concrete facts and not on mere fear, that he may be arrested for a non-bailable offence. Sub-section (1) of Section 438 enumerates certain factors which the court must keep in view while considering such an application. These include the nature and gravity of the accusation, the antecedents of the applicant, including whether he has previously undergone imprisonment on conviction by a court in respect of any cognizable offence, the possibility of his fleeing from justice, and whether the accusation has been made with the object of injuring or humiliating the applicant by having him so arrested. Sub-section (2) empowers the court to impose conditions as it may deem fit, such as a direction that the person shall make himself available for interrogation by a police officer as and when required, that he shall not directly or indirectly make any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case, and that he shall not leave India without the previous permission of the court.
title: Test #28: MPHC JJA 2024 - 20/01.2925 - S2

text: This criminal appeal is directed against the final judgment and order dated 8th January, 2018 passed by the High Court of Gujarat in Criminal Appeal No. 1120 of 2016, whereby the High Court set aside the judgment of acquittal dated 14th July, 2015 rendered by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ahmedabad in Criminal Case No. 892 of 2012, and convicted the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The factual matrix involves a transaction wherein Respondent No. 2 advanced an alleged commercial loan of Rs. 22,50,000/- to the appellant between 1st April, 2011 and 15th December, 2011. In discharge of the purported legally enforceable liability, the appellant issued three CTS cheques bearing Nos. 402115, 402116, and 402117 dated 25th January, 2012 drawn on the Bank of Baroda, Ellisbridge Branch, Ahmedabad. Upon presentation, the said cheques were returned unpaid by the drawee bank with the memo endorsed 'funds insufficient' on 28th January, 2012. Following statutory demand notice dated 14th February, 2012 under Section 138 clause (b) of the Act and failure to pay within fifteen days, criminal complaint was registered on 15th March, 2012. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the complainant failed to prove financial capacity to lend such cash amounts. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellant argued that the High Court erred in reversing the well-reasoned judgment of acquittal. He submitted that the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is rebuttable, and the accused is only required to raise a probable defence by preponderance of probabilities. Relying on Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, reported in (2008) 4 SCC 54, it was urged that the burden of proving debt remains primarily upon the complainant. He also cited Vijay v. Laxman, reported in (2013) 3 SCC 86, contending that the absence of formal loan agreements or income tax disclosures was sufficient to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 118(a) of the Act. In counter-argument, learned counsel for Respondent No. 2 submitted that the appellant had admitted his signature on the dishonoured cheques and the execution of a written acknowledgement deed dated 10th January, 2012. Heavy reliance was placed on the three-judge Bench decision of this Court in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan, reported in (2010) 11 SCC 441, which overruled Krishna Janardhan Bhat and held that the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act indeed includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Scrutinizing the evidence, this Court observes that once the execution of the negotiable instrument and signatures thereon are admitted, Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 erect a statutory reverse onus clause against the drawer. The accused cannot merely raise speculative doubts or vague assertions regarding the complainant's income sources. In Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, reported in (2019) 4 SCC 197, this Court reaffirmed that even a blank signed cheque leaf voluntarily handed over to a payee attracts the statutory presumption until disproved by cogent evidentiary rebuttal. Furthermore, in Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian, reported in (2021) 5 SCC 283, it was held that once signature is established, the court is duty-bound to presume consideration unless the drawer discharges the burden by leading positive evidence. Since the appellant failed to lead defense evidence under Section 315 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or prove non-existence of debt, the statutory presumption remained intact. Consequently, the conviction recorded by the High Court under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is affirmed, with modified sentence directing payment of compensation of Rs. 30,00,000/- within two months.
title: Test #29: Legal - SCI Cr. A. No. 508 0f 2019

text: The instant appeal, preferred by the original defendant, arises out of the judgment & order dated 17.08.2011 passed by the High Court of Bombay, whereby it confirmed the decree dated 04.03.2009 passed by the Principal District Judge, Pune in Regular Civil Suit No.214/2004, in favour of the original plaintiff (Respondent herein). CIVIL APPEAL NO.7382 OF 2012. The dispute concerns the validity & enforceability of an agreement relating to immovable property. The following questions arise for consideration:- (a) Whether the agreement creates an enforceable interest in the suit property? (b) Whether the transaction was vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation & suppression of material facts, and whether Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies? Raghunathrao, owner of the property, possessed agricultural land bearing Gat No.145/2, admeasuring 2 Hectares 17 Ares, situated at Village-Khadki, Taluka-Haveli, District-Pune. He executed an agreement dated 12.06.1998 in favour of defendant No.1, containing specific terms & conditions concerning the proposed transfer. According to the plaintiff, Rs.2,75,000/- was paid towards consideration; however, despite repeated demands, the defendant failed to execute the sale deed. A legal notice dated 19.09.2002 demanded completion within 15 days. By reply dated 02.10.2002, the defendant denied the transaction and alleged that the document was invalid & obtained through misrepresentation. The plaintiff instituted Special Civil Suit No.89/2003, seeking specific performance, declaration & permanent injunction. The defendant contended that the agreement created no lawful right, title or interest and disputed the signatures appearing thereon. Reliance was placed upon Document Exhibit (“P-17”), Mutation Entry No.5632 dated 28.11.1999, and registered notice dated 06.01.2003. The plaintiff submitted that mutation entries are fiscal in character and cannot, by themselves, confer or extinguish title. The Trial Court framed issues under Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. By judgment dated 04.03.2009, the suit was decreed. The First Appellate Court, vide judgment dated 22.07.2010, affirmed the findings. The defendant thereafter preferred the present appeal under Section 100, raising questions concerning limitation, jurisdiction, evidentiary value & enforceability of the disputed document. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties, examined the record and considered the statutory provisions, this Court finds no perversity, procedural irregularity or jurisdictional error. The evidence on record sufficiently establishes the circumstances, and no substantial question of law arises for determination. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed; the impugned judgment & decree are affirmed, and the parties shall bear their respective costs. The decree shall be drawn accordingly. In a suit for specific performance, the plaintiff must establish readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract continuously from the date of the agreement up to the date of the decree, in strict adherence to Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The record clearly establishes that the respondent had tendered substantial consideration and repeatedly called upon the appellant to perform his contractual obligations, thereby satisfying the statutory criteria. Furthermore, the defense predicated upon Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, is wholly devoid of merit. Under the second limb of Article 54, where no specific calendar date is fixed for performance, the prescribed limitation of three years commences only when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. In the case at hand, notice of refusal was conveyed by the defendant's reply dated 02.10.2002, and the suit instituted in 2003 was well within the statutory period. It is also well settled that mere revenue entries or mutation proceedings do not create or extinguish title, nor do they override a valid agreement to sell executed for valuable consideration. Therefore, the concurrent findings recorded by the courts below warrant no interference.
title: Test #29: Legal - BHC Civil Appeal No. 7382 of 2012

text: The petitioner entered into government service as a Junior Assistant on 12th July, 1988 and served with an unblemished record for over three decades until reaching the age of superannuation on 31st May, 2024. In the year 2010, the Government of Andhra Pradesh issued G.O.Ms. No. 52, Finance (PC-I) Department, dated 25th February, 2010, revising the pay scales of non-gazetted employees and providing automatic advancement scales upon completion of sixteen and twenty-four years of incremental service. The petitioner was granted step-up increments vide official proceedings dated 18th August, 2012 passed by Respondent No. 3. However, nearly twelve years after the fixation of said pay scale, on the eve of processing the final pension papers under the Andhra Pradesh Revised Pension Rules, 1980, the audit authorities raised an objection alleging erroneous excess computation of basic pay. Consequently, without issuing any show cause notice or affording any reasonable opportunity of hearing, the impugned recovery order dated 14th November, 2024 came to be passed. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner strenuously contended that the action of the respondents in effecting recovery post-superannuation is patently illegal, arbitrary, and impermissible in law. It was submitted that there was neither any misrepresentation nor fraud attributable to the petitioner in the fixation of pay scales. Reliance was placed on the celebrated decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Rafiq Masih (White Washer), reported in (2015) 4 SCC 334, wherein the Apex Court crystallized five specific situations where recoveries by employers from employees are strictly impermissible in law, specifically including recovery from retired employees or employees who are due to retire within one year of the order of recovery, and recovery from employees belonging to Class-III and Class-IV service. Learned counsel further cited Syed Abdul Qadir v. State of Bihar, reported in (2009) 3 SCC 475, wherein the Supreme Court held that excess payment made due to wrong interpretation of rules without employee fraud cannot be recovered. Learned Government Pleader appearing for the State opposed the writ petition, contending that the State exchequer cannot be burdened with erroneous payments made contrary to statutory service rules. It was argued that under Rule 9 of the Andhra Pradesh Revised Pension Rules, 1980, the Government reserves the right to withhold or withdraw pension if the pensioner is found guilty of causing pecuniary loss. Reliance was placed on High Court of Punjab & Haryana v. Jagdev Singh, reported in (2016) 14 SCC 267, contending that an undertaking was executed by the employee at the time of receiving annual increments. Having heard both learned counsel, this Court finds that the ratio in Jagdev Singh applies strictly where an explicit undertaking is furnished at the time of revision of pay scales. In the instant case, the petitioner is a retired non-gazetted Group-C employee, and no undertaking was ever executed during pay revision. The alleged excess payment was made due to the unilateral calculation error of the department without any misrepresentation by the petitioner. Pension and gratuity are not bounties distributed by the State, but valuable constitutional property rights earned through continuous dedicated service. Withholding retiral dues without due process deprives the retired employee of property under Article 300-A of the Constitution. Consequently, the writ petition is allowed, the recovery order is quashed, and the respondents are directed to refund the withheld amount with interest at six percent per annum within sixty days. This petition, filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, challenges the impugned recovery proceedings dated 14th November, 2024 issued by Respondent No. 2, the Director of Treasuries and Accounts, whereby an amount of Rs. 4,82,650/- was ordered to be recovered and withheld from the retiral gratuity and pensionary benefits of the petitioner.
title: Test #30: Legal - APHC Writ P. No. 36482 of 2025

text: Insurable interest exists when an insured person derives a financial or other kind of benefit from the continuous existence, without repairment or damage, of the insured object (or in the case of a person, their continued survival). A person has an insurable interest in something when loss of or damage to that thing would cause the person to suffer a financial or other kind of loss. Normally, insurable interest is established by ownership, possession or direct relationship. For example, people have insurable interests in their own homes and vehicles, but not in their neighbours' homes and vehicles and almost certainly not those of strangers. Insurable interest refers to the right of property to be insured. It may also mean the interest of a beneficiary of a life insurance policy to prove need for the proceeds. Insurable interest is no longer strictly an element of life insurance contracts under modern law. Exceptions include agreements and charitable donations. The principle of insurable interest on life insurance is that a person or organization can obtain an insurance policy on the life of another person if the person or organization obtaining the insurance values the life of the insured more than the amount of the policy.
