In this way, insurance can compensate for loss. A company may have an insurable interest in a President/CEO or other employee with special knowledge and skills. A creditor has an insurable interest in the life of a debtor, up to the amount of the loan. A person who is financially dependent on a second person has an insurable interest in the life of that second person. Legal guidelines have been established in many jurisdictions which establish the kinds of family relationships for which an insurable interest exists. The insurable interest of family members is assumed to be emotional as well as financial. The law allows insurable interest on the presumption that a personal connection makes the family member more valuable alive than dead, Thus, close relatives are assumed to have an insurable interest in the lives of those relatives, but more distant relatives, such as cousins and in-laws cannot buy insurance of the lives of others related by these connections. A married person has an insurable interest in the life of his spouse and minor children have an insurable interest in their parents. A person is also presumed to have an insurable interest in his or her own life. Broadly speaking, without an immediate family or a relationship that is recognized by law, there is no insurable interest. No insurable interest is recognized for cohabiting couples. Although many insurers will accept such policies, they could potentially be invalidated because they have not been tested in court. In recent years, there have been moves to pass clear statutory provisions in this regard, which have not yet borne fruit. Under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, the Government of India, an autonomous corporation was set up by the Employee State Insurance Act 1948, which is known as Employees' State Insurance Corporation and launched a scheme under the said ESI Act. The Employees' State Insurance is one type of an integrated social safeguard system having multi-dimensional and customized to offer security and protection to the employees of India and respective States. This Act basically focuses on the safety of employees by providing help in case of sickness, death in the work-field, injury, maternity etc. According to the rules and regulations, all factories are mandatorily liable to register their employees under the said ESI Act. All Government establishments as well as shops or offices employing twenty persons or more will register themselves under the said Act. But, as everything has exemptions, this law also has certain exemptions. They are seasonal factory activities like cotton ginning, jute pressing, decoration of grounds or factories engaging workers not more than seven months in a year, are exempted from registering under the said ESI Act.
title: Test #30: DHC JJA Typing - March 2022 - P15

text: Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the Petitioner challenges the show cause notice dated 29th June, 2022 and the final assessment order dated 21st December, 2023 passed by Respondent No. 3, along with the consequential third-party recovery notice dated 21st November, 2025 issued by Respondent No. 4, as arbitrary, illegal, and violative of Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India. The Petitioner company, incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, is engaged in infrastructure development and civil engineering projects across the State of Maharashtra. In the regular course of commercial operations, the Petitioner received statutory permissions and mining leases from the State Government and remitted requisite royalty charges between 1st July, 2017 and 31st August, 2021. The Additional Commissioner of CGST and Central Excise issued a consolidated notice dated 29th June, 2022 under Section 74(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (CGST Act) and the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (MGST Act), proposing an aggregate tax demand of Rs. 2,54,40,532/- alongside applicable interest under Section 50 and penalty under Section 122(2)(b). Despite written representations dated 13th September, 2022 and personal hearings conducted on 14th September, 2023 and 19th December, 2023, the impugned adjudication order dated 21st December, 2023 confirmed the consolidated liability and directed immediate attachment of bank accounts maintained at Punjab National Bank under Section 79(1)(c) of the Act. The learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the Petitioner strenuously contends that the impugned show cause notice is manifestly devoid of jurisdiction, being barred by limitation and fundamentally flawed by the impermissible clubbing of multiple distinct financial years into a solitary proceeding. Heavy reliance is placed upon the authoritative ruling of this Court in Writ Petition No. 2203 of 2025 (M/s Milroc Good Earth Developers v. Union of India & Ors.), wherein the Division Bench categorically held that Section 73(10) and Section 74(10) of the CGST Act mandate separate annual assessments. The statutory framework strictly contemplates a definite tax period linked to the furnishing of annual returns, thereby precluding the Revenue from issuing a consolidated show cause notice amalgamating divergent financial years. Reliance is further placed on Paras Stone Industries v. Union of India (Writ Petition No. 7718 of 2025) and Asawa Brothers Corporate Avenue v. Union of India (Writ Petition No. 11644 of 2025), which affirmed this principle without reservation. In counter-argument, the learned counsel appearing for the Revenue vehemently resisted the maintainability of the writ petition, citing Civil Appeal No. 6719 of 2012 (Rikhab Chand Jain v. Union of India & Ors.) and Writ Petition No. 12116 of 2025. The Respondents contend that the Petitioner has an efficacious statutory alternate remedy of appeal under Section 107 of the CGST Act, 2017 upon making the mandatory pre-deposit. It was further submitted that having sought installments during personal hearings, the Petitioner is now equitably estopped from questioning jurisdiction. Having meticulously scrutinized the record, this Court finds that when an authority acts wholly without jurisdiction, the existence of an alternative remedy does not operate as an absolute bar to invoking the extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. In Chief Justice of Andhra Pradesh v. L.V.A. Dikshitulu, reported in (1979) 2 SCC 34, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that an order passed by a forum lacking inherent jurisdiction is coram non judice and a complete nullity in law. Furthermore, as reaffirmed in Lalita Panjabrao Phalke v. Jeevan Tulshiram Phalke, reported in 2023 (6) Mh.L.J. 619, an order suffering from patent lack of jurisdiction is non est, and neither estoppel, acquiescence, nor admission can confer competence upon a defective proceeding.
title: Test #31: Legal - BHC Writ P. No. 4061 of 2026

text: This civil suit, instituted under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, seeks a decree of permanent injunction alongside damages of Rs. 5,00,00,000/- for alleged defamation and commercial disparagement, wherein the plaintiff news conglomerate seeks an ex-parte ad-interim injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC commanding the defendants, an investigative digital media foundation and individual editors, to forthwith take down, remove, and retract an investigative news broadcast published on 14th January, 2025 accusing the plaintiff corporation of editorial bias and state influence. The plaintiff asserted that it is an internationally accredited multimedia news agency operating television channels and digital news feeds. On 14th January, 2025, the defendants published an investigative documentary video and companion articles alleging that the plaintiff systematically disseminated sponsored political narratives and acted as a corporate mouthpiece. The plaintiff contended that these publications were malicious, sensationalist, and calculated to destroy its global professional reputation, resulting in loss of institutional sponsorship. In the interim application, the plaintiff sought an immediate gag order restraining the defendants from circulating the impugned broadcast or publishing any further commentary pending trial, asserting that damages would be an inadequate remedy to compensate for ongoing reputational loss. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the plaintiff submitted that an ex-parte injunction is imperative to arrest ongoing defamation. It was argued that the right to reputation is an inseparable component of the right to life and personal dignity guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the defendants opposed the application, submitting that the documentary was the product of four months of rigorous journalistic research based on publicly accessible telecast archives, commercial balance sheets, and regulatory filings. The defendants asserted their defense of truth, justification, and fair comment on matters of public interest under Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Dismissing the application for interim injunction, this Court holds that free speech cannot be silenced through preemptive judicial restraint. In the locus classicus ruling in Bonnard v. Perryman, reported in [1891] 2 Ch 269, affirmed in Fraser v. Evans, reported in [1969] 1 QB 349, and Tata Sons Limited v. Greenpeace International, reported in (2011) 178 DLT 705, the courts established that an interim injunction should not be granted in defamation actions where the defendant raises a defense of justification and indicates an intention to prove truth at trial. In the landmark authority in Bloomberg Television Production Services India Private Limited v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Limited, reported in 2024 SCC OnLine SC 426, the Hon'ble Supreme Court cautioned that pre-trial gag orders stifle the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). An injunction can be granted only in the rarest of rare cases where the publication is indisputably false and demonstrably malicious. The defendants having raised a credible defense of truth based on source documents, the public interest in journalistic scrutiny overrides the claim for interim censorship. The application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC is accordingly dismissed. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that where an executive authority withholds statutory compensation in direct contravention of declared constitutional law, alternative remedies do not bar writ jurisdiction. In Tarsem Singh (supra), the Supreme Court categorically held that treating landowners under the National Highways Act differently from those acquired under the general land acquisition statute results in artificial classification devoid of intelligible differentia. Applying Section 30(1) and Section 80 of the 2013 Act, the petitioners are statutorily entitled to one hundred percent solatium on the market value.
title: Test #31: Legal - DHC I.A. NO. 4812 of 2025

text: The present civil writ petition has been instituted under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India seeking the issuance of a writ in the nature of Mandamus directing the respondent authorities to consider and regularize the services of the petitioners w.e.f. the date of completion of ten years of continuous service on the posts of Assistant Lineman (ALM) and Lower Division Clerk (LDC) in the Haryana State Electricity Utility Department, with all consequential monetary benefits and seniority. The petitioners were initially appointed on contractual and temporary basis against sanctioned vacant posts during the years 2012 to 2014 after undergoing a competitive selection process. The petitioners have been discharging their official duties continuously for over twelve years without any break in service, and their tenure has been extended periodically by official notifications. The nature of duties, working hours, and operational responsibilities assigned to the petitioners are identical to those performed by regular employees holding corresponding posts in the department. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioners submitted that the petitioners submitted a formal legal notice dated 23.03.2026 to Respondent No. 2 requesting regularization of their services under the prevailing government regularization policies. It was forcefully argued that the action of the respondent department in continuing the petitioners on contractual wages for over a decade while regular vacancies exist constitutes unfair labor practice and violates Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. Reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in CWP No. 31304 of 2025 titled Joginder v. State of Haryana and CWP No. 24673 of 2025 titled Bhupesh Kumar v. Punjab Health System Corporation, decided on 12.02.2026. On the other hand, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent State submitted that contractual appointments do not confer a vested legal right to seek automatic absorption or regularization into regular cadre posts. It was further submitted that regular appointments must adhere strictly to statutory recruitment rules framed under Article 309 of the Constitution, and contractual workers engaged through external agencies cannot bypass competitive recruitment procedures. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record, this Court notes that the Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Umadevi [(2006) 4 SCC 1] and subsequent rulings in Nihal Singh v. State of Punjab [(2013) 14 SCC 65] laid down that continuous engagement of qualified personnel against sanctioned posts for prolonged periods obligates the State to consider their cases under fair regularization schemes. Where temporary workers are engaged against sanctioned vacancies and perform duties identical to regular staff, prolonged contractual exploitation without considering regularization attracts judicial scrutiny under Article 14. Furthermore, in identically situated proceedings involving contractual technicians, this Court directed the respondent authorities to examine individual service credentials and grant regularization benefits where candidates satisfy eligibility parameters. The learned counsel for the petitioners limited his prayer to seeking a direction to Respondent No. 2 to decide the pending legal notice dated 23.03.2026 by passing a reasoned speaking order within a specified timeframe. In view of the limited relief sought and without expressing any definitive opinion on the merits of the claims, Respondent No. 2 is directed to consider and decide the legal notice dated 23.03.2026 in light of the binding precedents in Bhupesh Kumar (supra) and Joginder (supra). The decision shall be taken by passing a reasoned speaking order after affording an opportunity of hearing to the petitioners within a period of three months from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this order. The writ petition stands disposed of accordingly.

text: An assessee may, in respect of a case relating to him, make an application, before adjudication, to the Settlement Commission to have the case settled, in such form and in such manner as may be prescribed and containing a full and true disclosure of his duty liability which has not been disclosed before the Central Excise Officer having jurisdiction, the manner in which such liability has been derived, the additional amount of excise duty accepted to be payable by him and such other particulars as may be prescribed including the particulars of such excisable goods in respect of which he admits short levy on account of misclassification, undervaluation, inapplicability of exemption notification or Cenvat credit or otherwise and any such application shall be disposed of in the manner hereinafter provided: Provided that no such application shall be made unless (a) the applicant has filed returns showing production, clearance and Central excise duty paid in the prescribed manner; (b) a show cause notice for recovery of duty issued by the Central Excise Officer has been received by the applicant; (c) the additional amount of duty accepted by the applicant in his application exceeds three lakh rupees; and (d) the applicant has paid the additional amount of excise duty accepted by him along with interest due under section 11AA. Provided further that the Settlement Commission, if it is satisfied that the circumstances exist for not filing the returns referred to in clause (a) of the 1st proviso to sub-section (1), may after recording the reasons thereof, allow the applicant to make such application: Provided also that no application shall be entertained by the Settlement Commission under this subsection in cases which are pending with the Appellate Tribunal or any court: Provided also that no application under this subsection shall be made for the interpretation of the classification of excisable goods under the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. Every application made under sub-section (1) shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. An application made under sub-section (1) shall not be allowed to be withdrawn by the applicant. On receipt of. an application under.sub-section (1) of section 32E, the Settlement. Commission shall, within seven days from the date of receipt of the application, issue a notice to the applicant to explain in writing as to why the application made by him should be allowed to be proceeded with, and after taking into consideration the explanation provided by the applicant, the Settlement Commission, shall, within a period of fourteen days from the date of the notice, by an order, allow the application to be proceeded with, or reject the application as the case may be, and the proceedings before the Settlement Commission shall abate on the date of rejection: Provided that where no notice has been issued or no order has been passed within the aforesaid period by the Settlement Commission, the application shall be deemed to have been allowed to be proceeded with. A copy of every order under sub-section (1), shall be sent to the applicant and to the Commissioner of Central Excise having jurisdiction. Where an application is allowed or deemed to have been allowed to be proceeded with under sub-section (1), the Settlement Commission shall, within seven days from the date of order under sub-section (1), call for a report along with the relevant records from the Principal Commissioner of Central Excise or Commissioner of Central Excise having jurisdiction and the Commissioner shall furnish the report within a period of thirty days of the receipt of communication from the Settlement Commission: Provided that where the Commissioner does not furnish the report within the aforesaid period of thirty days, the Settlement Commission shall proceed further in the matter without the report of the Commissioner. Where a report of the Commissioner has been furnished within the period specified in that sub-section, the Settlement Commission may, after examination of such report.

text: The petitioner has approached this Court by filing the present writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a Writ of Mandamus declaring the action of the 2nd respondent in issuing the impugned reversion proceedings vide Proc. Rc. No. G/2772/2019 dated 25.03.2026 as illegal, arbitrary, unjust, violative of principles of natural justice, and contrary to the executive instructions contained in G.O. Ms. No. 257, General Administration Department, dated 10.06.1999. The petitioner further prays for a consequential direction to the respondent authorities to allow her to continue as District Backward Classes Welfare Officer, Srikakulam, with all attendant service benefits. The essential facts underlying the case are that the petitioner was initially appointed as Assistant B.C. Welfare Officer and was subsequently placed in the zone of consideration for promotion to the post of District B.C. Welfare Officer in the year 2020. However, her promotion was initially deferred due to the pendency of departmental disciplinary proceedings under Rule 20 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991. Aggrieved by the deferment, the petitioner filed W.P. No. 7604 of 2020, wherein this Court directed the respondents to consider her case for ad-hoc promotion in terms of G.O. Ms. No. 257 dated 10.06.1999 pending finalization of the disciplinary inquiry. In compliance with the judicial directions, the 2nd respondent issued proceedings promoting the petitioner on an ad-hoc basis as District B.C. Welfare Officer. The petitioner joined the promoted post and has been discharging her official duties satisfactorily. Subsequently, the disciplinary authority concluded the departmental proceedings vide final order dated 27.02.2026, imposing the minor penalty of 'censure'. Following the conclusion of the inquiry, the 2nd respondent issued the impugned order dated 25.03.2026 reverting the petitioner to her substantive lower post of Assistant B.C. Welfare Officer on the ground that the minor penalty disqualified her from continuing in the promoted post. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that under G.O. Ms. No. 257 dated 10.06.1999, the imposition of a minor penalty like 'censure' does not automatically warrant reversion of an officer who has already been promoted on an ad-hoc basis and served for several years. It was submitted that a minor penalty only postpones consideration for regular promotion during the penalty currency period, but cannot be invoked retrospectively to issue a reversion order without issuing a show cause notice. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Services submitted that ad-hoc promotions granted during the pendency of disciplinary proceedings are strictly conditional. It was argued that upon finalization of disciplinary proceedings resulting in a penalty, the employee's promotion must be reviewed, and reversion to the substantive post is legally permissible under state service regulations. Having considered the rival submissions and perused the statutory provisions, this Court finds that the 2nd respondent failed to follow due process prior to issuing the reversion order. Under established service jurisprudence, even an ad-hoc appointee who has served continuously for years cannot be reverted based on a minor penalty without being afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit an explanation. Imposing reversion without issuing a prior show-cause notice violates the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem). Consequently, the operation of the impugned reversion proceedings dated 25.03.2026 is hereby stayed pending final disposal of the writ petition. The respondents are directed to allow the petitioner to continue as District B.C. Welfare Officer, Srikakulam. The respondents shall file their counter affidavits within four weeks.
title: Test #33: Legal - APHC - Writ P. No. 8624 of 2026

text: This writ petition, instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and constitutionality of the rejection order dated 24th August, 2020 passed by Respondent No. 3, the District Basic Education Officer, Prayagraj, whereby the application submitted by the petitioner seeking compassionate appointment under Rule 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Recruitment of Dependants of Government Servants Dying-in-Harness Rules, 1974 was rejected solely on the ground that the petitioner is a married daughter of the deceased primary school teacher and hence excluded from the statutory definition of family. The petitioner's father was employed as a permanent Headmaster in a primary school administered by the Uttar Pradesh Basic Shiksha Parishad, who died in harness on 14th November, 2018, leaving behind his widow, an infirm minor son, and the petitioner daughter. The family was plunged into severe financial penury, with no other earning member. The petitioner, despite being married, resided in the parental home providing primary financial, medical, and emotional subsistence to her parents, as her spouse was unemployed and medically incapacitated. The petitioner submitted an application on 12th February, 2019 along with a dependency certificate issued by the competent Tehsildar. However, the respondent department rejected her claim under Rule 2(c)(iii) of the 1974 Rules, which recognized sons and unmarried daughters as family members, but omitted married daughters. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the exclusion of married daughters while including married sons in employment regulations constitutes hostile gender discrimination violating Articles 14, 15, and 16 of the Constitution of India. Placing heavy reliance upon the seminal Full Bench judgment of this Court in Smt. Vimla Srivastava v. State of U.P., reported in 2015 SCC OnLine All 4325, it was submitted that marital status cannot be used as a gendered disqualification to deprive a daughter of compassionate consideration. Learned Standing Counsel for the State submitted that compassionate appointment is an exception to the general constitutional rule of open competitive recruitment under Article 16, and eligibility must strictly adhere to the express provisions of statutory rules. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that marriage does not sever the filial relationship between a daughter and her deceased parents. In Vimla Srivastava (supra), affirmed by the Division Bench in State of U.P. v. Noopur Srivastava (Special Appeal Defective No. 418 of 2021), this Court ruled that excluding married daughters from the purview of Rule 2(c)(iii) while extending benefits to married sons is founded on archaic patriarchal stereotypes and is manifestly arbitrary. A daughter continues to remain a daughter after marriage, and the decisive test for compassionate appointment is actual financial dependency at the time of the breadwinner's death, not marital status. Recognizing this constitutional principle, the State Government subsequently notified the U.P. Recruitment of Dependants of Government Servants Dying in Harness (Twelfth Amendment) Rules, 2021, formally incorporating married daughters into Rule 2(c). The impugned rejection order dated 24th August, 2020 is quashed, and the respondents are commanded to consider the petitioner's application for compassionate appointment on merits within eight weeks. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that copyright law does not protect abstract ideas, historical themes, or general plots. In the locus classicus ruling in R.G. Anand v. Delux Films, reported in (1978) 4 SCC 118, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that copyright subsists not in ideas, but solely in the original expression of ideas. Where the same broad idea is developed in different ways, similarities are bound to occur. Under the doctrine of scenes-a-faire, thematic tropes, stock characters, and plot devices that are customary or indispensable to a dramatic genre cannot be monopolized by any author.
title: Test #33: Legal- AHC Writ A. No. 24139 of 2021

text: The need of our country is more production, larger development at a faster rate and larger savings for productive investment, in order to meet the needs of employment and higher living standards, there should be progressive acceleration in the rate of development of our economy. The tempo of development has to be kept high. Obviously, the ensuing plan has to be larger. With the need for a big plan, the pressure on resources, domestic and foreign, should obviously prove larger. During the last two years, so far as foreign resources were concerned, we were able to pull through only the core of the plan with finance from abroad substantially through governmental agencies. Our capacity to borrow has been strained. Our requirements are bound to grow higher at a faster rate of economic development. Having regard to this, our ideas and policies would need some alteration. Some adjustment in the quantum of foreign exchange demand is possible through a discerning policy on imports. Imports are already greatly pruned, but further scrutiny is possible in certain directions. Essential developmental needs should be able to get precedence over production of less essential goods. There may be selective imports giving higher priority to developmental imports to meet the more basic needs of the economy. Even with these changes, the demand for foreign exchange would remain considerable and beyond our capacity with our present technique of borrowing. The Government and the Planning Commission should study the industrial policy from the point of view of an appropriate re-shaping. Apart from Government to Government borrowings from abroad, foreign capital both in the shape of private loans and equity participation should be induced to come into the country, work with the people shoulder to shoulder in the development of the country's economy and share the prosperity. Such private projects will be automatically moving forward. So far as internal resources are concerned, many concerned, many economists and experts have engaged themselves in analysing and working out the effects of increased national income and the channels of utilisation. They have also been assessing the percentage of national income to be saved for development and what and how it could be attracted, to the exchequer. The invariable conclusion of the experts appears to have been that adequate resources are not saved by the society on account of increased consumption arising from higher national income. This has led the government to the policy. To encourage savings and channel them into nation-building efforts, the government must formulate policies that offer attractive incentives for long-term investments. When citizens save a higher portion of their income, it provides the necessary capital for developing infrastructure, expanding agriculture, and boosting industrial growth. Public savings can be mobilized through bank deposits, government bonds, and small savings schemes, which help finance major development projects without relying excessively on external debt. Furthermore, increasing national productivity requires a well-planned balance between consumer demand and capital formation. If consumption consumes the bulk of national income, very little remains for reinvestment in key sectors of the economy. Therefore, economic policy must focus on curbing unnecessary expenditure while rewarding thrift and investment. Industrial growth should also be supported by simplifying regulations and creating a favorable environment for local entrepreneurs as well as foreign investors. By ensuring that domestic industries receive adequate financial support and modern technology, the country can reduce its dependence on foreign goods and achieve self-reliance. At the same time, rural development must receive equal attention, as a large section of the population depends on agriculture for their livelihood. Improving rural credit facilities, irrigation, and storage facilities will increase farm output and raise the purchasing power of rural households.
title: Test #34: BHC - Economic Development - Passage 12

text: It is settled by catena of decisions that mental cruelty can cause even more serious injury than the physical harm and create in the mind of the injured appellant such apprehension as is contemplated in the Section. It is to be determined on whole facts of the case and the matrimonial relations between the spouses. To amount to cruelty, there must be such wilful treatment of the party which caused suffering in body or mind either as an actual fact or by way of apprehension in such a manner as to render the continued living together of spouses harmful or injurious having regard to the circumstances of the case. The word 'cruelty' has not been, defined and it has been used in relation to human conduct or human behaviour. It is the conduct in relation to or in respect of matrimonial duties and obligations. It is a course of conduct and one which is adversely affecting the other. The cruelty may be mental or physical, intentional or unintentional. There may be cases where the conduct complained of itself is bad enough and per se unlawful or illegal. Then the impact or the injurious effect on the other spouse, need not be enquired into or considered. In such cases, the cruelty will be established if the conduct itself is proved or admitted. The cruelty alleged may largely depend upon the type of life the parties are accustomed to or their economic and social conditions, their culture and human values to which they attach importance. Judged by standard of modern civilization in the background of the cultural heritage and traditions of our society, a young and well educated woman like the appellant herein is not expected to endure the harassment in domestic life whether mental, physical, intentional or unintentional. Her sentiments have to be respected, her ambition and aspiration taken into account in making adjustment and her basic needs provided, though grievances arising from temperamental disharmony. Each case depends on its own facts and must be judged.on. these facts, The concept of cruelty has varied from time to time, from place to place and from individual to individual in its application according to social status of the persons involved and their economic conditions and other matters. The question whether the act complained of was a cruel act is to be determined from the whole facts and the matrimonial relations. between the parties. In this connection, the culture, temperament and status in life and many other things are the factors which have to be considered. The legal concept of cruelty which is not defined by statute is generally described as conduct of such character as to have caused danger to life, limb or health (bodily and mental) or to give rise to reasonable apprehension of such danger. The general rule in all question of cruelty is that the whole matrimonial relations must be considered, that rule is of a special value when the cruelty consists not of violent act but of injurious reproaches, complains accusations or taunts. It may be mental such as indifference and frigidity towards wife, denial of a company to her, hatred and abhorrence for wife or physical, like acts of violence and abstinence from sexual intercourse without reasonable cause. It must be proved that one partner in the marriage however mindless of the consequences has behaved in a way which the other spouse could not in the circumstances be called upon to endure, and that misconduct has caused injury to health or a reasonable apprehension of such injury. There are two sides to be considered in case of cruelty. From the appellant's side, ought this appellant to be called on to endure the conduct? From the respondent's side, was this conduct excusable? The court has then to decide whether the sum total of the reprehensible conduct was cruel. That depends on whether the cumulative conduct was sufficiently serious to say that from a reasonable person's point of view after a consideration of any excuse which the respondent might have in the circumstances, the conduct is such that the petitioner ought not be called upon to endure.
title: Test #34: DHC JJA Typing - March 2022 - P14

text: The petitioners have approached this Court by invoking the Extraordinary Special Original Jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking the issuance of a Writ of Mandamus or any other appropriate writ, order, or direction declaring the action of the respondent authorities in withholding the administrative benefits and declining to extend the age of superannuation from 60 years to 62 years as illegal, arbitrary, unconstitutional, and violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution of India. The petitioners further pray for a consequential direction to the respondent authorities to permit them to continue in active service until attaining the revised age of superannuation of 62 years, with all attendant monetary benefits, service seniority, and arrears of salary as per G.O. Ms. No. 15, Finance (HR-IV-FR and LR) Department, dated 21.01.2022. The factual matrix giving rise to the present writ petition is that the petitioners were originally recruited as executive staff under the Andhra Pradesh Beverages Corporation Limited (APBCL) and subsequently served under the Department of Prohibition and Excise, Government of Andhra Pradesh. Upon completing 60 years of age on 31.08.2024, the petitioners were relieved from service by the 3rd respondent vide impugned proceedings dated 25.08.2024. The petitioners submitted detailed administrative representations dated 10.09.2024 and 15.10.2024 to the 1st and 2nd respondents, requesting the implementation of the policy decisions embodied in G.O. Ms. No. 15 dated 21.01.2022, which enhanced the superannuation age for state public sector undertakings and government employees across Andhra Pradesh. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners contended that the refusal of the respondent corporation to extend the enhanced age of superannuation to employees of public sector corporations while extending the same to regular state government servants constitutes class legislation without any intelligible differentia, directly violating Article 14 of the Constitution. Reliance was placed on the decision of the Division Bench of this Court in Thupakula Venkateswara Rao and others v. State of Andhra Pradesh, wherein the principles governing service extension and non-discriminatory service conditions were elaborately considered. On the other hand, the learned Additional Advocate General appearing for the respondent State submitted that public sector corporations governed by independent statutory rules and board resolutions cannot automatically claim parity with regular civil servants unless the board of directors specifically adopts the government orders under relevant corporate bye-laws. It was further pointed out that the financial implications and cadre management rules of APBCL require prior approval from the Finance Department under Section 102 of the Andhra Pradesh State Enterprises Act. Having heard the learned counsel for both parties and having perused the material documents placed on record, this Court finds that the primary issue raised for consideration is whether the benefit of enhanced retirement age under G.O. Ms. No. 15 applies to employees of statutory corporations without explicit board adoption. It is a well-settled principle of administrative law that executive policy decisions modifying service conditions do not operate automatically across autonomous statutory entities in the absence of enabling board resolutions or statutory amendments. Furthermore, as held by the Supreme Court in Radhey Shyam v. Chhabi Nath and reaffirmed by this Court in W.A. No. 484 of 2025, judicial review under Article 226 cannot override corporate service regulations unless patent arbitrariness or mala fides are established. Since the Board of Directors of APBCL has not passed any formal resolution adopting G.O. Ms. No. 15 dated 21.01.2022, no mandamus can be issued directing automatic service extension. Consequently, the Writ Petition is dismissed as devoid of merits.
title: Test #35: Legal - APHC Writ P. No. 13746 of 2024

text: This criminal appeal, preferred by the convict appellant under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is directed against the final judgment and order dated 18th May, 2001 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in Criminal Appeal No. 248-DB of 1999, affirming the judgment of conviction and sentence of life imprisonment recorded by the learned Sessions Judge, Sangrur under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, on the ground that the appellant caused the death of the deceased in legitimate exercise of his right of private defense of body. The prosecution case stemmed from a violent confrontation that took place on 15th July, 1991 in Village Chatha, District Sangrur, regarding irrigation water distribution rights between adjoining agricultural fields. While the appellant and his aged father were repairing an irrigation boundary channel, the deceased Gurcharan Singh, accompanied by four adult sons armed with lethal gandasas and heavy wooden lathis, launched a sudden aggressive assault, shouting threats to kill. The assailants inflicted five blunt-force injuries on the appellant's father, causing compound skull fractures and loss of consciousness. When the deceased lunged toward the appellant with an upraised sharp gandasa, the appellant picked up a single-barrel licensed agricultural gun and fired a solitary gunshot, striking the deceased in the chest, which resulted in fatal injuries. The trial court and the High Court convicted the appellant under Section 302 IPC, holding that the appellant exceeded the right of private defense by utilizing a firearm against non-firearm weapons. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant contended that the courts below failed to apply the statutory provisions of Section 100 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. It was argued that when an accused is confronted with an aggressive mob inflicting grievous skull fractures on his father and facing an imminent lethal assault with a sharp weapon, a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt arises. Allowing the appeal, this Court in Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab, reported in (2010) 2 SCC 333, authoritatively restated the governing legal principles under Sections 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The Court held that the right of private defense is a defensive right designed to serve a vital social purpose, intended to arouse and encourage self-reliance in law-abiding citizens faced with unlawful aggression. The law does not expect a citizen to act like a coward or flee when his life or the life of his family is in mortal peril. Under Section 100 clauses First and Secondly of the IPC, the right of private defense of the body extends to causing death if the assault occasions a reasonable apprehension that death or grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence. In Salim Zia v. State of U.P., reported in AIR 1979 SC 391, this Court settled that under Section 105 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the accused is not required to prove the right of self-defense beyond reasonable doubt; discharging the onus by a mere preponderance of probabilities is sufficient. A person facing imminent death cannot be expected to weigh his blows in golden scales or modulate his defensive force with clinical precision. Finding that the appellant acted under justified terror of mortal injury, the conviction under Section 302 IPC is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted of all charges. The Court observed that while the traditional nineteenth-century legal presumption held that time is not of the essence in immovable property contracts, that rule arose when real estate values were stable and inflation was negligible. In the modern economic era characterized by galloping land prices and rapid urban commercialization, the presumption cannot be applied blindly to defeat clear contractual intent. An agreement that explicitly specifies installment deadlines and incorporates an unambiguous stipulation that payments on due dates are the essence of the contract cannot be rewritten by the court.
title: Test #35: Legal- SCI Cr. Appeal No. 1057 of 2022

text: It is, thus, clear that the power conferred on the Divisional Board under Regulation 102 to amend the result of the examination in respect of any candidate or candidates on its being found that it has been affected by error, malpractice, fraud, improper conduct, etc.is a suo motu power of the Board. The Regulation in any case does not confer any right on an examinee to demand revaluation, disclosure, inspection or verification of his answer-books or other related documents. The right of verification conferred by clause 1 is subject to limitation contained in the same clause that no revaluation of the answer books or supplements shall be done and further restrictions imposed by clause 3 prohibiting disclosure or inspection of all the answer books. From the judgment of the Supreme Court, it is thus clear that all the questions issues raised concerning Regulations 104 and 102 of the Regulations were settled unequivocally and no grey area was left out for further interpretation. In the face of settled position of law, in our opinion, it is not open for the Court to direct revaluation of the answer books in any case whatsoever. Against the backdrop of the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the aforementioned judgment we now proceed to see as to what was the question raised in the writ petitions. The petitioners therein were also students of the English medium school and had appeared for S.S.C examination conducted by the State Board in 2005. The case set up by all the petitioners was that all throughout they had scored good marks in all the subjects including English. The grade of marks earned by them, in the final examination conducted by the Board, in the subject of English were, however, not upto their satisfaction and expectations. Therefore, they had applied for revaluation though there is no provision in the Act or Regulations to make such request. The Board, by its reply to the said application, informed them that the only remedy available to them was to apply for verification and not for revaluation. Since all the petitioners apprehended that the verification may not serve the purpose they had filed the writ petitions in the High Court for redressal of their grievance praying for relief of revaluation of answer books. Validity of Regulation 57, which is pari materia with Regulation 104, was also challenged on the ground that it is unreasonable, arbitrary and unconstitutional. The learned Division Bench, while considering the challenge, did make reference to the judgment of the Supreme Court in Paritosh Bhupesh Kurmarsheth’s case to hold that challenge to the constitutionality of Regulation 104 is not open. The judgment of Orissa High Court in Rajkishore Mohanty’s case, however, seems to have influenced the learned Judges for giving directions to the Board to re-evaluate the answer books of all the petitioners. While so doing, they observed that when the court comes across cases where brilliant students securing more than 80% marks in other subjects fail only because of failure in English, though from an English medium school, it can be said that something is wrong somewhere. It was further observed that where students from a particular school are victimised, such cases constitute an exception to the rules. With due respect to the learned Judges, in our opinion, the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Paritosh Bhupesh Kurmarsheth’s case was not appreciated in its proper perspective. In Rajkishore Mohanty’s case, the learned Division Bench of Orissa High Court was considering the challenge to the correctness of marks awarded in various papers on the ground of improper valuation. Although a committee was appointed to deal with applications for re-addition of marks, it was categorically observed in paragraph 7 of the report that since revaluation is not permissible, the court did not consider it fair to direct revaluation. Consequently, creating an exception to the statutory prohibition against revaluation is legally unsustainable and contrary to settled law.
title: Test #36: Legal - BHC Writ P.etition 6395 of 2006 Passage 4

text: Having considered the views of some other High Courts, the Calcutta High Court came to the conclusion that "the fact that the complainant acted as the Presenting Officer by itself will not vitiate a domestic enquiry if no other question of prejudice is there. There is no principle of natural justice which requires that a person who had lodged a complaint cannot be a Presenting Officer and a prosecutor in a domestic enquiry". It further went on to observe that "In a domestic enquiry the management has the right to present its case against the delinquent employee. This is done through the Presenting Officer. His job is to adduce evidence in support of the charges. Generally, he is not a witness. But if he also appears as a witness on behalf of the management, he has to be offered for cross-examination by the delinquent employee. The enquiry will stand vitiated if the delinquent is not allowed to cross-examine him. A plain reading of the above findings, clearly and unequivocally indicate that, in the opinion of the Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court, there is no bar in law for a Presenting officer to appear as a witness on behalf of the management in the domestic enquiry. However, the said dictum of the Calcutta High Court does not come to the aid of the management, inasmuch as, in the present case the Presenting Officer was produced as a solitary witness before the Industrial Adjudicator, in order to prove the enquiry including report. Upon a further reading of paragraph 17 of the decision in SVS Marwari Hospital (supra) itself it is clearly reflected that the relevant finding of the Full Bench in relation to the factual matrix of the present case was that "While the Enquiry Officer himself must necessarily be completely impartial and unbiased, the same cannot be expected of a Presenting Officer. He is after all, the management's representative and his job is to advance the Management's case." In view of the foregoing, reliance placed on behalf of the management, on the above decisions, does not advance its case and if we may say so, on the contrary, it can be inferred that the production of a Presenting Officer before an Industrial Adjudicator to prove the Enquiry Report is impermissible, in view of the circumstance that the Enquiry Officer's job is to advance the Management's case which would make him an interested witness in the outcome. In this behalf, we must further observe that it is not the bias attached to the Presenting Officer, as much as, the likelihood of the bias on account of his being a representative of the Management which is a determining factor. A plain reading of the above-extracted paragraphs clearly and unequivocally indicates that; it was held by the learned Single Judge that the Enquiry Officer was not examined as a witness nor were other employees; the Presenting Officer was not an independent witness to appear in Court to prove the enquiry proceedings against the workman. It was further held that the Presenting Officer is not expected to become a prosecutor and that he is a biased witness. In the facts and circumstances elaborated hereinabove, we do not find any error with the conclusion arrive at by the learned Single Judge in the impugned order dated 17.01.2018. The issue is accordingly decided against the management in the facts and circumstances of the case. In this behalf, it is also observed that in the present case, the Enquiry Officer was not cited as a witness on behalf of the Management before the Industrial Adjudicator. Furthermore, there was no attempt made to produce the Enquiry Officer in order to prove the enquiry proceedings against the workman. What was done was to present the Presenting Officer as the sole witness to prove the said report. It is in this view of the matter that, the Industrial Adjudicator as well as the learned Single Judge of this Court arrived at a conclusion that the management had failed to prove that a fair and proper enquiry was conducted against the workman. We see no reason to interfere with the findings arrived at in the impugned order.
title: Test #36: DHC JJA Typing - March 2022 - P12

text: The petitioner, a convict undergoing life imprisonment under Prisoner No. C-4851 at Nashik Road Central Prison, has preferred the present writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950, challenging the rejection order dated 28.02.2025 passed by Respondent No.1 Additional Chief Secretary (Home), State of Maharashtra, rejecting the petitioner’s application for premature release under Category 6(a) of the Guidelines for Premature Release dated 15.03.2010 framed under Rule 3 of the Maharashtra Prisons (Review of Sentences) Rules, 1972. The procedural narrative of the present case reveals that the petitioner, along with three co-accused persons, was prosecuted in Sessions Trial No. 35 of 2002 before the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Dhule, for offences punishable under Section 302, Section 364-A, Section 394, Section 397, Section 201 read with Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) and Section 3(1)(25) of the Arms Act, 1959. By judgment and order dated 11.10.2002, the Sessions Court convicted all four accused under Section 302/120-B IPC and sentenced them to death, subject to confirmation by this Court under Section 366 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) in Confirmation Case No. 4 of 2002 along with Criminal Appeal No. 371 of 2002. Upon reference, a Division Bench of this Court by judgment dated 16.12.2003 acquitted the petitioner and co-accused of all charges. Aggrieved by the acquittal, the State of Maharashtra preferred Criminal Appeal No. 654 of 2024 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 1240 of 2005) before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India. By judgment dated 21.01.2009, reported in (2009) 4 SCC 712, the Apex Court allowed the appeal in part, set aside the judgment of acquittal, convicted the petitioner under Section 302 IPC, and commuted the capital sentence to imprisonment for life with a fine of Rs. 25,000/- i/d simple imprisonment for two years. The petitioner contends that as on 31.12.2025, he has completed an actual incarceration period of 18 years, 4 months, and 12 days, and with earned remissions under Section 432 Cr.P.C., total period of sentence served exceeds 23 years, 8 months. The learned Additional Public Prosecutor Mr. S. V. Gavand relied upon the advisory board report dated 14.01.2026 prepared under Section 59 of the Prisons Act, 1894, wherein the convicting Court (Sessions Judge, Dhule) gave a negative opinion under Section 432(2) Cr.P.C., citing the severity of the crime involving Section 364-A IPC. Learned counsel for the petitioner, appointed through Legal Aid Scheme under Article 39A of the Constitution, relied upon the decisions in Raosaheb Ramchandra Thombare v. State of Maharashtra [2017 ALL MR (Cri) 3412], Kamlakar Tanaji Shinde v. State of Maharashtra [2025:BHC-AUG:10670-DB], and Union of India v. V. Sriharan [(2016) 7 SCC 1]. It was forcefully argued that under Section 433A Cr.P.C., the statutory mandate requires an inmate convicted of a capital offence to undergo a minimum of 14 years of actual imprisonment before executive clemency or remission under Article 161 of the Constitution can be considered. The rejection of premature release based solely on an unreasoned judicial opinion under Section 432(2) Cr.P.C. without independent application of mind by the Home Department violates Article 14 and Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, the provisions of Sections 432, 433, and 433A Cr.P.C., corresponding to Sections 473, 474, and 475 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), obligate the Appropriate Government to consider the conduct report issued by the Prison Superintendent under Form No. IV of the Jail Manual. The petitioner’s conduct in Nashik Central Prison has been certified as exemplary, with zero jail punishments recorded under Section 45 of the Prisons Act, 1894 during the past fifteen years. Having evaluated the rival submissions and perused the original record in Criminal Writ Petition No. 447 of 2026, this Court finds that the impugned order dated 28.02.2025 suffers from non-application of mind.
title: Test #37: Legal - BHC Cr. Writ Petition No. 447 of 2026

text: The present Revision Application, preferred by the original accused, challenges the judgment & order dated 11.03.2025 passed by the Sessions Court, whereby the conviction recorded by the learned Magistrate under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, was affirmed. The following questions arise for consideration:- (i) Whether the cheque was issued towards a legally enforceable liability? (ii) Whether the statutory presumption under Sections 118(a) & 139 stands rebutted? (iii) Whether the complaint was instituted within the prescribed period of limitation? According to the complainant, the accused obtained a loan of Rs.3,60,000/- on 18.07.2022 and, towards repayment, issued Cheque No. 482716 dated 10.01.2023, drawn upon "National Cooperative Bank". The cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned unpaid with the endorsement "FUNDS INSUFFICIENT" dated 13.01.2023. A statutory notice dated 27.01.2023 was thereafter issued by Registered Post A.D., calling upon the accused to pay the cheque amount within 15 days. The notice was served on 02.02.2023; however, the accused made no payment. The complainant instituted Summary Criminal Complaint No. 56/2023. The accused entered appearance and denied the transaction. It was contended that the cheque had been obtained as a security instrument and that no independent liability existed on the date of presentation. Reliance was placed upon Exhibit-"C-11", bank statement dated 16.09.2022, Exhibit-"C-14", acknowledgment receipt, and Document No. "R-7/2023". The defence alleged material alteration, misuse of the cheque & absence of proof regarding the source of funds. The Trial Court, after framing the necessary points, recorded the evidence of PW-1 and examined the record. By judgment dated 22.08.2024, the accused was convicted and directed to pay compensation of Rs.4,20,000/- within 30 days. The Appellate Court, vide order dated 11.03.2025, confirmed the conviction, holding that the statutory presumption remained unrebutted and the defence was not supported by reliable evidence. The accused thereafter preferred the present Revision Application before this Court for final determination, raising grounds concerning limitation, admissibility, burden of proof, procedural compliance & appreciation of evidence. Having heard the learned counsel and examined the record, this Court finds that the concurrent findings are neither perverse nor contrary to settled principles of law. The accused failed to establish any probable defence capable of displacing the statutory presumption. No jurisdictional error or manifest illegality is demonstrated. Accordingly, the Revision Application is dismissed. The judgment & order of conviction are affirmed. The record & proceedings shall be returned forthwith in accordance with law and statutory mandate. Under the statutory scheme of Chapter XVII of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, once the signature on the cheque is admitted or satisfactorily established, the presumption under Section 139 mandates the Court to presume that the instrument was issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or liability. As reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa v. Sri Mohan and Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, while this presumption is rebuttable, the standard of proof required from the accused is that of a preponderance of probabilities. A bare denial of liability or a casual assertion that the cheque was delivered merely as a security document does not suffice to rebut the statutory presumption, unless substantiated by cogent documentary or circumstantial evidence. In the present proceedings, the petitioner failed to step into the witness box or adduce any independent proof to establish that the underlying financial debt had been settled. The mandatory requirements regarding dishonor, notice, and institutional limitation under Section 142 stand fully complied with. Consequently, the concurrent judgments of conviction and compensation do not suffer from any illegality.
title: Test #37: Legal- BHC Criminal Case No. 287 of 2024

text: The concept of Vicarious Liability serves as a cornerstone of the Law of Torts and is increasingly integrated into statutory frameworks governing commercial relations. In its most fundamental essence, this doctrine holds one person liable for the harmful actions or omissions of another, even though the former did not personally commit the act. This legal attribution of guilt is primarily rooted in the master-servant relationship, operating on the traditional maxim Qui facit per alium facit per se, which implies that he who acts through another is deemed in law to do it himself. The objective of this legal terminology is not to absolve the actual wrongdoer but to provide a broader avenue for the victim to seek compensation from a party with the financial capacity to provide redress. While vicarious liability is largely a product of judicial precedents, it finds specific resonance in several Indian statutes. For instance, under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, if a company commits an offense such as a cheque bounce, every person who was in charge of the business at that time is deemed guilty. Similarly, in the realm of motor accidents, the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, frequently invokes this principle to hold the owner of a vehicle liable for the negligence of the driver. To establish a successful claim, two essential facts must be proven: first, that there existed a specific relationship of master and servant, and second, that the tortious act was committed during the Course of Employment. The determination of whether an act falls within the course of employment is a delicate judicial exercise. The law distinguishes between a Servant and an Independent Contractor. While an employer is vicariously liable for the servant, they are generally not liable for the contractor, because the employer lacks the power to control the manner in which the contractor performs the task. However, the modern Organization Test suggests that if a person is integrated into the employer’s business, the liability remains with the master. The facts of various cases show that even if a servant performs a lawful act in an unauthorized manner, the master remains liable. Conversely, if the servant goes on a frolic of his own, performing an act entirely unrelated to his duties, the master is protected from liability. The overarching philosophy of this terminology is encapsulated in the doctrine of Respondeat Superior, meaning let the superior answer. This principle is based on public policy, ensuring that a business that creates a risk by employing others must also bear the burden of the losses caused by that risk. The "Rule of Law" dictates that between two innocent parties the victim and the employer—the employer is better suited to bear the loss as they could have prevented the accident through better supervision or training. This creates a high standard of Administrative Accountability in both private and public sectors. Under Article 300 of the Constitution, even the State can be held vicariously liable for the tortious acts of its officials if the act was not performed in the exercise of sovereign functions. Accordingly, this exposition clarifies that vicarious liability is an indispensable tool for maintaining the Sanctity of Obligations in a complex society. It bridges the gap between individual error and corporate responsibility, ensuring that the "Executive Power" of an employer is tempered by the legal duty to protect third parties from harm.
title: Test #38: Legal - The Doctrine of Vicarious Liability

text: It is well known that the company cannot act by itself but that does not necessarily mean that in the absence of any finding that someone is liable for the company; the fine imposed in a proceeding is to be realized from him. There may be cases where a company is represented by its chairman or the managing directors as they are the persons who normally represent the company but in actuality, the offence has been committed by someone else who is in charge of the affairs of the company and is directly involved in the alleged offence. It is relevant to state here that earlier under Section 9 of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, the offence was relatable to one who avoided the payment of duty or removed any excisable goods in contravention of the provisions of the Act. This provision has made it clear that the person in charge as well as the company is liable. The person in charge suffers the punishment if found guilty. The company also suffers. There may be cases when the prosecuting agency may not choose to proceed against the company and may proceed against the person in charge. It is imperative that a finding is necessary that the offence has been committed by the company but it is not a prerequisite that the company should be made an accused. A prosecution against a person who is in charge or responsible at the time of commission of offence is maintainable without the company being made a party to the proceeding. Once it is concluded that the company has its own liability, the realization of fine to be made from the company. The mode for realization is provided under Section 421 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, wherein it has been stipulated that the court has the authority to issue a warrant for the levy of the amount by attachment and sale of any movable property belonging to the offender and further can issue a warrant to the Collector of District authorizing him to realize the amount as arrears of land revenue or movable or immovable property or both the defaulter. The legal dues of a company can be realized only by attaching the assets of the company and not by putting the managing director or any of the directors in prison. It is to be kept in mind that the company is the offender or the defaulter. It is the company as a person from whom the fine is realizable. There may be cases where under the company law a managing director or director may be liable for the company. But in the absence of any fixation of liability on any particular person on behalf of the company, it is the liability of the company and company alone, and the company having a separate legal personality, having independent corporate existence, the issuance of a non-bailable warrant or distress warrant against the managing director or director to realize the same is not permissible. The other submission that after the company has already been wound up and an official liquidator has been appointed, the petitioner as the managing director should not be proceeded against, has substantial force. It is the admitted position that the company in question has already been wound up. The finding of the court below that the official liquidator has only taken over the assets of the company but not the liability is an absolute legal misconception. It is settled in law that the official liquidator not only takes over the assets of the company but has obligations, if determined in accordance with law, to meet the liabilities from the assets of the company. Once it is held that the payment of fine by the company is its exclusive liability, steps are to be taken for realization of the same in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, keeping in view that the company is now in liquidation. Under this changed circumstance, a non-bailable warrant or distress warrant cannot be issued against the managing director in his individual capacity. In view of the above analysis, I conclude and hold that the petitioner is not to be proceeded against and there was no justification on the part of the court below to issue a non-bailable.
title: Test #38: DHC JJA Typing - March 2022 - P11

text: This Appeal by Special Leave is filed under the Constitution of India, challenging the judgment of the High Court which refused to direct a search engine and several legal news portals to remove a judgment from their platforms. The appellant was acquitted of all charges in a criminal case involving a matrimonial dispute ten years ago. However, the presence of the judgment online continues to cause him social stigma and affects his employment prospects. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the "Right to be Forgotten" is an essential component of the "Right to Privacy" under Article 21, and whether a person who has been acquitted is entitled to have their past criminal records erased from the public digital domain. The facts of the case reveal that whenever the appellant’s name is searched on the internet, the first result is the judgment of the trial court where he was initially accused. The learned counsel for the appellant, Sri Kapil Sibal, argues that the "Digital Footprint" of an individual should not be a "Permanent Shack" that prevents them from moving forward in life. He submits that once the judicial proceedings have reached a finality in acquittal, the "Public Interest" in accessing that information is diminished. He contends that the "Right to Erasure" is recognized globally and must be balanced against the "Freedom of Speech" and the "Right to Information." He relies on the landmark "Puttaswamy Judgment" to assert that informational privacy includes the right to control one's personal data over time. In response, the learned Additional Solicitor General argues that the "Supreme Court" and "High Courts" are courts of record. He submits that judgments are "Public Documents" and their removal would interfere with the "Historical Integrity" of the judicial system. He contends that search engines are mere "Intermediaries" and cannot be tasked with the "Adjudication" of what content should stay online. The State maintains that the "Transparency of the Judiciary" is a cornerstone of democracy and that the "Right to be Forgotten" cannot be used to rewrite history or to create a "Sanitized Version" of one's past. The respondents argue that such a right would lead to a "Censorship" of legal reporting and would hinder legal research and the development of precedents. Having heard both sides and perused the international protocols on data protection, this Court observes that the "Right to be Forgotten" is indeed a facet of the "Right to Privacy." The Supreme Court emphasizes that "Identity" is dynamic, and a person should not be forever haunted by a "Past Error" or a "False Accusation" that has been legally cleared. However, this right is not "Absolute." It must be balanced against the "Right to Know" and the "Freedom of the Press." The law must distinguish between a "Hardened Criminal" and a person involved in a "Private Dispute." In cases of "Matrimonial Discord" or "Minor Offences" where an acquittal has been recorded, the "Privacy Interests" of the individual outweigh the "Public Interest" in the archival of the judgment. The Court finds that the "Intermediaries" have a duty to ensure that the "Search Algorithms" do not unfairly penalize an individual. The "Right to be Forgotten" does not necessarily mean the "Physical Destruction" of the court records, but it certainly includes "De-indexing" the judgment from search results using the name of the individual as a keyword. The High Court erred in holding that such a direction would violate the "Autonomy of the Press." The "Rule of Law" requires that the "Dignity of the Individual" be protected from the "Tyranny of the Internet." The Court refers to the "Data Protection Act" and the "Principles of Fairness" to hold that the "Storage Limitation" of personal data should apply to the digital publication of legal proceedings. Consequently, this Court finds that the appellant is entitled to a "Limited Relief." The Civil Appeal is allowed. The respondent search engines are directed to "De-index" the judgment in question so that it does not appear in results when the appellant’s name is searched.
title: Test #39: Legal Matter - SCI Civil A. No. 1024 of 2025

text: Aadhaar is a serious invasion into the right his/her life profile and movement as well on his/her use of Aadhaar. There has been no other subject matter in recent past which has evoked the kind of intensive and heated debate wherein both sides, for and against, argue so passionately in support of their respective conviction. The petitioners in these petitions belong to the latter category and are demanding scrapping and demolition, which is the bedrock of the Indian Constitution. The petitioners have challenged the Aadhaar project which took off by way of administrative action in the year 2009. Even after Aadhaar got a shield of statutory cover, challenge persists as the very enactment known as Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016 is challenged as constitutionally impermissible. The wide range of issues involved in this case is evident from the fact that it took almost four months for the parties to finish their arguments in these cases, and the Court witnessed highly skilled, brilliant and intellectual advocacy, with the traces of passions as well. The issue has generated heated but intelligentsia is also equally divided. There have been number of articles, interviews for discourses in favour of or against Aadhaar. Those in favour see Aadhaar project as ushering the nation into a regime of good governance, advancing socio-economic rights, economic prosperity etc. and in the process they claim that it may make the nation a world leader. Mr. K.K. Venugopal, learned Attorney General of India, referred to the commendations by certain international Aadhaar. Those opposing Aadhaar are apprehensive that it may excessively intrude into the privacy of citizenry and has the tendency to create a totalitarian state, which, would, impinge upon the democratic and constitutional values. Some such opinions of various persons were referred to during the arguments. Notwithstanding the passions, emotions, annoyance, despair, ecstasy, euphoria, coupled with rhetoric, exhibited by both sides in equal measure during the arguments, this Court while giving its judgment on the issues involved is required to have a posture of calmness coupled with objective examination of the issues on the touchstone of the constitutional provisions. Initiative in spearheading the attack on the Aadhaar structure was taken by the petitioners namely, Justice K.S. 494 of 2012. At that time, Aadhaar scheme was not under legislative umbrella. In the writ petition the scheme has primarily been challenged on the ground that it violates fundamental rights of the innumerable citizens of India, namely, right to privacy falling under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Few others joined the race by filing connected petitions. Series of orders were passed in this petition from time to time, some of which would be referred to by us at the appropriate stage. In 2016, with the passing of Aadhaar Act, these groups, NGOs, etc., some opposing the petitions and some supporting the Aadhaar scheme. Before we go into the be apposite to take note of the events in chronological order that shaped the formulation, take off and implementation of the Aadhaar scheme. The idea of a unique identity number for residents had its origins in the early years of the previous decade, when the Government of India examined ways of improving the delivery of welfare benefits and preventing leakages. In January 2009, the Unique Identification Authority of India was established through an executive notification, functioning under the Planning Commission. The first Aadhaar number was issued in September 2010. A Bill to give the project statutory backing was introduced in Parliament in 2010, but it was not enacted. Meanwhile, enrolment continued across the country, and Aadhaar was gradually linked with various welfare schemes, bank accounts and mobile connections. This expanding use alarmed many citizens, who feared that sensitive biometric and demographic information could be misused or leaked.
title: Test #39: DHC JJA Typing - March 2022 - P9

text: The facts of the case reveal that the petitioner was fully dependent on her father at the time of his death, as her husband is unemployed and has no steady source of income. Upon the death of the sole breadwinner, the family was pushed into a state of sudden financial destitution. The learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri Ashok Khare, argues that the distinction between a married son and a married daughter is a classic example of "Gender Discrimination." He submits that while a married son is considered a member of the family and is eligible for appointment, a married daughter is excluded solely based on her marital status. He contends that such a classification has no rational nexus with the objective of providing immediate financial assistance to a grieving family. He relies on the full bench judgment of this Court which previously held that the word "daughter" must include both married and unmarried daughters. In response, the learned Standing Counsel appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh argues that the rules are designed to provide relief to those who were part of the household of the deceased. He submits that once a daughter is married, she is considered part of her husband’s family and her dependency on her father legally ceases. He contends that the state has the discretion to frame rules to limit the number of claimants to ensure that the benefit reaches the most "Deserving Dependants." The State maintains that the petitioner has failed to provide sufficient evidence to show that she was residing with her father at the time of his demise. The authorities argue that the "Financial Hardship" must be assessed strictly, and since the petitioner is married, the responsibility for her maintenance lies primarily with her husband and not the state exchequer. Having heard both sides and perused the service records, this Court observes that the "Institution of Marriage" does not sever the bond between a father and a daughter. The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that "Compassionate Appointment" is an exception to the general rule of open recruitment and is intended to prevent the family of a deceased employee from "Starvation." The law is well-settled that any rule which discriminates against a woman based on her marital status is "Unconstitutional." A daughter remains a daughter for life. If a married son can look after his parents and still be eligible for a government job, there is no reason why a married daughter should be denied the same opportunity if she is otherwise qualified and in financial need. The Court finds that the respondents have acted with a "Patriarchal Mindset" that has no place in modern jurisprudence. The right to be considered for employment on compassionate grounds is a significant right for a family in crisis. The "Financial Status" of the applicant is a factual matter that must be verified through an inquiry, rather than being assumed based on marital status. The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that the "Exclusion of Married Daughters" from the category of dependants is "Ultra Vires" the Constitution. The "Rule of Law" requires the state to be a model employer that promotes "Substantive Equality." A daughter who is willing to support her widowed mother and younger siblings should be encouraged rather than disqualified by technical hurdles. Consequently, this Court finds that the rejection order suffers from a "Legal Infirmity" and is unsustainable. The Writ Petition is allowed. The order passed by the District Education Officer is hereby "Quashed and Set Aside." The respondent authorities are directed to "Reconsider the Application" of the petitioner for appointment on compassionate grounds by treating her as a member of the family, regardless of her marital status.
