The authorities shall conduct a fresh inquiry into the "Financial Condition" of the family and, if found eligible, provide her with a suitable post commensurate with her educational qualifications. This entire exercise must be completed within a period of twelve weeks from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment.
title: Test #40: Legal Matter - AHC Writ-A No. 4880 of 2025

text: We have carefully considered the records produced by the respondents as well as the submissions advanced on both sides. While evaluating performance of a Government servant, the only mirror to reflect is his confidential reports. It is not that a Government servant would not fallible in performance in a particular year. If one performs diligently to his utmost capability, he is suitably rewarded by the higher grading in the confidential report. However, if the grading consistently obtained by an officer is of a highest nomenclature, then a presumption would have to be drawn that the officer had been consistently performing well and if in a particular year he falls in his performance, nothing precludes in a judicial review with the underline principle of objectivity writing the ACR to go into the circumstance as to the recording of adverse remarks. No doubt, under the Rules of 1970 ibid, the Accepting Authority would not act as a rubber stamp by only counter signing the remarks or the grading but is at liberty on modification to record his reasoning and once it is adverse, the same has to be indicated as such. However, the objectivity in writing and the reasons recorded for such adverse remarks, which, according to the instructions contained in the confidential, roll, clearly envisages that good points as well as bad points are also to be incorporated and in the event the adverse remarks are given, the factual matrix in brief has to be incorporated to substantiate. In the light of above, the Accepting Authority in the present case was of the view that both Reporting Officer as well as Reviewing Authority on ignorance of the fact regarding performance of the applicant have not made an incorrect factual objective assessment. This has been substantiated on the ground that as per the records, the applicant was warned orally and in writing number of times in the past, having failed to register any improvement was graded as 'Average'. It would, thus be clear that the object of writing the confidential reports and making entries in the character rolls is to give an opportunity to a public servant to improve excellence. Article 514(j) enjoins upon every citizen the primary duty to constantly endeavour to prove excellence, individually and collectively, as a member of the group.. Given an opportunity, the individual strives to improve excellence and thereby efficiency of administration would be bel augmented. The officer entrusted with the duty to write confidential reports, has a public responsibility and trust to write the conditional/reports objectively, fairly and dispassionately while giving, as accurately as possible, the statement of facts on overall assessment of the performance of the subordinate officer. It should be founded upon the facts or circumstances. Though sometimes, it may not be part of record, but the conduct, reputation and character acquire public knowledge or notoriety and may be within his knowledge. Before forming an opinion to be adverse, the Reporting Officers, writing confidential should share the information which is not a part of the record with the officer concerned, have the information confronted by the officer and then make it part of the record. If, despite given giving such an opportunity, the officer fails to perform the duty, correct his conduct or improve himself necessarily, the same may be recorded in the confidential reports and a copy thereof supplied to the affected officer so that he will have an opportunity to know the remarks made against him. If he feels aggrieved, it would be open to him to have it corrected by appropriate representation to the higher authorities or any appropriate judicial forum for redressal. Thereby, honesty, integrity, good conduct and efficiency get improved in the performance of public duties and standards of excellence in services constantly rises to higher levels and it becomes successful tool to manage the services with officers of integrity, honesty, efficiency and devotion.
title: Test #40: DHC JJA Typing - March 2022 - P10

text: The Writ Petitions instituted before this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution arise from the political imbroglio in the State Legislature of Maharashtra. The Governor of Maharashtra issued a direction requiring Mr. Thackeray to prove his majority on the floor of the House. The Governor thereafter invited Mr. Shinde to form the government and directed him to prove his majority on the floor of the House within a period of seven days. Mr. Shinde was sworn in as the Chief Minister of Maharashtra on 30 June 2022. This Court, having regard to the constitutional questions involved, referred the matter to a Constitution Bench of five judges for authoritative determination. The Constitution Bench examined several issues of far-reaching constitutional importance. The first was whether the Governor acted in accordance with constitutional norms in directing Mr. Thackeray to face a floor test. The second was whether the appointment of Mr. Shinde as Chief Minister was barred by Article 164(1B) of the Constitution. Article 164(1B) provides that a member of a Legislative Assembly of a State who is disqualified for being a member of that House under Paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified to be appointed as a Minister under clause (1) for the duration of the period of his disqualification. The Court found that since no order of disqualification had been passed against Mr. Shinde by the Speaker, the bar under Article 164(1B) was not attracted at the time of his appointment as Chief Minister. On the question of the Governor's power to call for a floor test, this Court held that the Governor must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers and cannot act as an independent constitutional functionary in matters that are within the domain of the legislature. The Governor does not have the power to call for a floor test simply because a majority of legislators from a political party express their displeasure with their leader. The power to call for a floor test must be exercised only in exceptional circumstances, where it is evident from objective material that the incumbent government does not command the confidence of the House. The Court further held that the deletion of Paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule by the Constitution (Ninety-First Amendment) Act, 2003 is of constitutional significance. Before its deletion, Paragraph 3 provided that a split in a political party would not attract disqualification under Paragraph 2. After the deletion of Paragraph 3, the defence of a split is no longer available to members who face disqualification proceedings. The decision of the Speaker on petitions seeking disqualification must be rendered within a reasonable time, and any inordinate delay in deciding such petitions may itself be a ground for judicial intervention. The Speaker must act as a neutral arbiter and must not allow the proceedings to be delayed for political reasons. The Constitution Bench concluded as follows. The Governor's action in directing Mr. Thackeray to face a floor test was not in accordance with the constitutional norms, since it was based on communications from legislators expressing dissatisfaction with their leader, which does not constitute objective material demonstrating loss of confidence of the House. However, since Mr. Thackeray had resigned from office before the floor test was conducted, the relief of reinstating him as Chief Minister could not be granted. This Court cannot reverse the course of events that occurred after the resignation. The appointment of Mr. Shinde as Chief Minister was not barred by Article 164(1B). The Governor did not exceed the scope of his authority in inviting Mr. Shinde to form the government, given that Mr. Thackeray had already resigned. The question of disqualification of the members of the Legislative Assembly under the Tenth Schedule is to be decided by the Speaker within a reasonable time, in accordance with law and the principles laid down in this judgment. The judgment was pronounced by the Constitution Bench on 11 May 2023.
title: Test #41: Legal Matter - SCI Writ P. No. 493 of 2022

text: Although in some other writ petitions, counter affidavits have also been filed by State and Authority. The writ petitions relating to different villages are separately grouped and it shall be suffice to refer to the pleadings of the main writ petition as well as leading writ petitions of each village along with pleadings of some other writ petitions which were referred to by different learned counsel during the course of hearing for deciding this bunch of writ petitions. The facts as brought on record in the main writ petition and the reference to the pleadings in the said writ petition are sufficient to comprehend and decide the various issues which have arisen between the parties in these writ petitions. Hence, facts of the case of the main writ petition and pleadings therein shall be noted in some detail. Writ petition No. 37443 of 2011 Gajraj and others Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and others have been filed by 27 writ petitioners who claim Transferable right and owner of different plots of land situated in village of District Gautam Buddha Nagar. The notification issued by the State Government under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 notifying that the land mentioned in the schedule is needed for the public purpose namely for the planned industrial development in Gautam Buddha Nagar through Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority. The petitioners plead in the writ petition that dispensation of the inquiry under section 5A can only be an exception where the urgency cannot brook any delay. The respondents without application of mind dispensed the inquiry. The acquisition proceedings have been termed as void, unconstitutional, tainted with malafide, abuse of authority, power and non-application of mind. The provisions under section 5A is mandatory and embodied a just and wholesome principle that a  person whose property is being or intended to be acquired should have occasion to persuade the authorities that his property be not touched for acquisition. Land use of village Patwari was changed in the Master Plan 2021 after the notification under sections 4 and 6, which is colurable exercise of powers and entire exercise is arbitrary, illegal and infringes rights of the petitioners guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 300A of the Constitution of India. The petitioners have stated in the writ petition that writ petition is being filed after knowledge that the land use of village Patwari was changed in the Master Plan 2021 after the notifications under sections 4 and 6. The challenge to the acquisition further rests upon the contention that the invocation of the "urgency clause" under Section 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act was a mechanical exercise of power, devoid of any demonstrable material to justify the deprivation of the petitioners' right to object. It is a settled principle of law that the power to dispense with an inquiry under Section 5A is not a routine administrative discretion but a potent power that must be exercised with extreme caution and only in circumstances where the public interest would be irreparably prejudiced by the mere passage of time required for a hearing. The petitioners contend that the purported "planned industrial development" is a generic objective that does not, per se, constitute a situation of such unforeseen emergency as to override the principles of natural justice. Furthermore, the record suggests that a significant period elapsed between the proposal for acquisition and the actual issuance of the notification, thereby belying any claim of "extreme urgency" that the State now seeks to rely upon. The systematic exclusion of the right to be heard has rendered the entire proceedings a mere formality, stripping the landholders of their only opportunity to demonstrate that their specific parcels of land were either unsuitable for the stated purpose or that the planned development could be achieved through less intrusive means. Such an approach by the State and the Authority not only violates the statutory mandate of the Act.
title: Test #41: Legal Matter - Counter Affidavit by State & Authority

text: The present Writ Petition has been instituted under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a writ of certiorari to quash and set aside the impugned order dated January 15, 2024, passed by the Respondent No. 2. The petitioners also seek a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to reconsider the application for regularization of the subject property, in accordance with the prevailing statutory framework and the principles of natural justice. The factual matrix of the case involves a dispute over the title and possession of a parcel of land situated in the outskirts of Mumbai. The petitioners claim that the property was acquired through a registered sale deed in the year 1998. However, the respondents contend that the land in question is "Vatan" land and is subject to the restrictions imposed under the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act. The core controversy revolves around whether the transfer of the said land was in violation of Section 5 of the said Act, which prohibits the alienation of such property without the prior sanction of the Divisional Commissioner. The learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, Mr. Harish Salve, submitted that the impugned order is perverse and suffers from an error apparent on the face of the record. He argued that the authorities failed to consider the evidence of continuous possession for over thirty years. He further contended that the bar under Article 363 of the Constitution of India, which relates to disputes arising out of pre-independence covenants, is not applicable in the present case as the dispute is strictly civil in nature and involves a private agreement. It was also highlighted that the repeal of Article 362 in 1972 has significant implications on the privileges of former rulers, but it does not extinguish the fundamental rights of the citizens to hold property under Article 300A. On the contrary, the learned Government Pleader, appearing for the State, vehemently opposed the petition. It was argued that the civil suit filed by the petitioners was already dismissed by the Trial Court on the grounds of limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963. He placed reliance on Section 10 of the Companies Act, 1956, and its subsequent transition to Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013, to argue that the matter should properly reside before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) as the petitioner company is currently under liquidation proceedings. The respondents maintained that the public interest outweighs private interest in matters of state-owned land. This Court has carefully examined the rival submissions and the voluminous documents placed on record. It is a settled position of law that the extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 should be exercised with caution, especially when there are disputed questions of fact. However, the rule of law mandates that no person shall be deprived of their property save by authority of law. We must also address the issue of the "Dying in Harness" rules mentioned in the ancillary application. The petitioners had sought compassionate appointment for the legal heir of the original owner under the Service Rules. Reference is made to the Allahabad High Court ruling in Shobhit Srivastava v. State of UP, where it was held that qualifying a typing test with a speed of 25 words per minute is an essential prerequisite for such appointments. In light of the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC), particularly Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2, the petitioners had sought an interim injunction. We are of the view that the balance of convenience lies in favour of maintaining the status quo until the final adjudication of the title dispute. The authorities are directed to refrain from taking any coercive action against the petitioners for a period of eight weeks. Furthermore, we find that the Respondents failed to provide an opportunity of being heard to the petitioners before passing the adverse order, which is a clear violation of the Audi Alteram Partem principle.
title: Test #42: Legal - SCI Writ P. No. 4521 OF 2024

text: With an SC constitution bench allowing sub-categorisation within the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes reservation, a new political hot potato is now on boil. Govts also need to identify the creamy layer (children of individuals who have benefited from reservations) among SCs and STs. This exercise risks being as much political strategy, as authentic identification of those in dire need of affirmative action. Overall, sub-categorisation is a positive step. Quotas, unfortunately, have become the political class go-to arrow in its election quiver. This has had two outcomes. One, better-offs have tended to corner reservation benefits, crowding out the more marginalised. Two, SC/ST categories have expanded or become more porous. Ever-new groups get added. A community marginalised on the crowded OBC list stands a better chance at access to education, scholarship and jobs, if it is on the SC list. Such fluidity has seen communities jostling, SC/ST lists growing. Sub-categorisation, carried out efficiently and honestly, will help make the SC/ST quota more inclusive by identifying and including those worse off in terms of social capital also. Punjab, with 32% of its population SC, realised the need for subquotas back in 1975 and reserved 50% SC quota for Valmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs. Haryana, Andhra, TN tried subquotas. An SC order in 2004 cancelled such a subquota a decision the top court yesterday overturned. Thinly sliced quotas are hardly sum and substance of affirmative action. Subquotas alone can never correct endemic discrimination or counter the shrinking jobs pie. Rehabilitation of manual scavengers for instance those who managed to leave their punishing work behind has been a challenge. Addressing discrimination in school and the workplace, as policy, remains a blind spot. Special contempt is reserved for the quota-wala. Assimilation remains a huge challenge. Govt sector jobs are down and private sector jobs are elusive. So, there are caste certificate scams. The desperation for a somewhat steady livelihood finds expression in repeated returns to demands for quota as the only solution. All this speaks to policy failure. Headcounts cannot suffice for subquotas to be meaningful. There are about 1,200 SC communities and over 715 ST ones. Each of these must be parsed for their socio-economic data. That is a mammoth task, and politics will be a determinant. SC decided on the constitutionality of subquotas. How it contributes as affirmative action is now all political number games. The shift from a monolithic understanding of the Scheduled Castes to a granular, tiered approach necessitates a robust evidentiary framework that transcends mere electoral arithmetic. The Supreme Court’s mandate for "empirical data" ensures that sub-categorization does not become a tool for political gerrymandering, where dominant sub-groups are punished or favored based on their alignment with the ruling dispensation. To prevent this, the identification of the "creamy layer" must be predicated on objective socio-economic indicators—such as inter-generational educational attainment and land ownership—rather than arbitrary benchmarks. Without this precision, the risk of "inter-se" conflict between sub-castes increases, potentially fragmenting the very social solidarity required to fight systemic untouchability. Furthermore, the administrative machinery must address the bottleneck of implementation. While the legal hurdle has been cleared, the challenge of "parsing" 1,200 distinct communities requires a mission-mode census that looks beyond simple headcounts. It requires qualitative assessments of "social capital" the hidden networks of influence that often determine success in the private sector and higher academia. If sub-categorization is treated merely as a mathematical division of a shrinking pie, it will fail to address the root cause of marginalization: the lack of high-quality primary education and vocational parity. Ultimately, the efficacy of this judicial intervention hinges on whether the state views sub-quotas as a final destination or a transitional bridge.
title: Test #42: Legal Matter - Quota Quickstand

text: The Petitioner, a registered partnership firm, seeks a Writ of Mandamus against the State of Andhra Pradesh and the Transport Department. The controversy centers on the seizure of a fleet of transport vehicles and the subsequent demand for life tax and heavy penalties. The primary legal issue before this Court is the interpretation of Section 3 and Section 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1963, in conjunction with the registration requirements under Section 39 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The Petitioner argues that since the vehicles were exclusively used within a private industrial mining area and were not plying on public roads, the state lacks the jurisdiction to levy a road tax. The facts of the case reveal that the Petitioner purchased ten heavy-duty dumper trucks for internal ore movement in January 2025. These vehicles were transported to the site on trailers and were never intended for use on the public highway system. However, during a regional audit, the respondent authorities inspected the site and issued a demand notice for fifteen lakh rupees. The learned counsel for the Petitioner, Sri C. Sumon, argues that the mandate of the 1963 Act is clear: the liability to pay tax is linked to the use of the vehicle on public roads. He submits that under the Rules of 1964, the state must prove the use of public infrastructure before taxing a vehicle. He contends that the "Administrative Action" of the department in treating a private mining track as a public road is a gross misinterpretation of the law. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Transport argues that the definition of a Motor Vehicle under Section 2(28) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, is exhaustive. He submits that once a vehicle is capable of being driven on a road, it is liable for taxation, regardless of its actual place of operation. He contends that the "Private Property" argument is a loophole used by contractors to avoid contributing to the state exchequer. The State maintains that under Section 11 of the Taxation Act, the authorities have the power to seize any vehicle found without a valid tax token. The respondent further argues that the Petitioner failed to file an exemption application under Section 9 of the Act, which is a mandatory prerequisite for any vehicle claiming non-use on public roads. Having heard both sides and examined the site map and the vehicle specifications, this Court observes that the power to tax is a sovereign function that must be exercised within the four corners of the statute. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that "Taxation" cannot be based on the mere potential for use but must be grounded in the "Actual Condition" of the vehicle's operation. The law is well-settled that the tax under the 1963 Act is a compensatory tax for the use of public roads provided by the state. The "Rule of Law" requires that the "Burden of Proof" regarding the use of public roads lies initially with the department when the vehicle is found in a secluded private zone. The Court finds that the seizure of the vehicles was hit by the vice of procedural haste. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that "Mining Areas" and "Private Estates" do not fall under the definition of public roads unless they are accessible to the general public. The "Directive Principles" of state action require the government to facilitate industrial growth rather than imposing "Technical Taxes" that lack a legal basis. The "Administrative Discretion" to seize property must be balanced against the "Doctrine of Reasonableness." A dumper that cannot physically navigate narrow public streets due to its size and weight cannot be taxed for the supposed use of those very streets. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that "Justice" must prevail over "Revenue Targets" when the law is on the side of the citizen. No order as to costs. Order pronounced in the open court on this 11th day of March, 2026.
title: Test #43: Legal - APHC WRIT P. No. 28550 OF 2025

text: The case of the writ petitioners is that the Government of Assam had introduced a scheme for providing housing facilities to the families living below poverty line. According to the petitioners, in terms of the census report of 2002, all of them belong to below poverty line families and therefore, were entitled for allotment of housing under the said State Government scheme. By drawing the attention of this Court to Annexure-B to the writ petition Mr. Ahmed, learned counsel for the petitioners, submits that the petitioners have lost their fathers and therefore, the names of their respective mothers were also included in the list prepared by the Government for extending the benefit of housing scheme. However, notwithstanding the inclusion of the names, no action has been taken in the matter till date. Mr. Ahmed further submits that the petitioners had also submitted a representation dated 22.07.2010 addressed to the respondent No.4 ventilating their grievances in the matter. However, despite receipt of the same, no action has been taken by the respondents till date as a result of which the petitioners have been deprived of the benefit of the housing scheme as introduced by the Government. Mr. S. P. Choudhury, learned Government Advocate, Assam, submits that he has no instruction in the matter. In view of the above and having regard to the grievance expressed by the writ petitioners, I am of the view that instead of keeping this writ petition pending before this Court, the proper course of action would be to direct the concerned authority to look into their grievances and take appropriate steps in the matter as may be permissible under the law. In view of the above, this writ petition is disposed of with a direction upon the writ petitioners to submit a proper representation addressed to the respondent No.2 ventilating their grievances in the matter. If such a representation is filed within a period of four weeks from today, the respondent No.2 will verify the claim of the petitioners and thereafter take appropriate action in the matter as may be permissible under the law for redressal of their grievances. The said exercise shall be carried out as expeditiously as possible, preferably within a period of six months from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this order. The writ petition stands disposed of. The court further observed that the right to adequate housing is not merely a policy goal but an integral component of the right to life and dignity as enshrined under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. In the context of families living below the poverty line, the state's failure to implement its own welfare schemes in a timely manner results in a tangible deprivation of constitutional guarantees. The petitioners, having demonstrated their inclusion in the 2002 census and their subsequent identification as eligible beneficiaries, possess a legitimate expectation that the state will discharge its administrative duties without arbitrary delay. The silence of the respondents in the face of the representation dated 22.07.2010 is particularly noted; administrative apathy in welfare matters often hits the most vulnerable sections of society the hardest, leaving them in a state of perpetual uncertainty. It is imperative that the Respondent No. 2, while seized of the fresh representation, conducts a thorough verification of the list of beneficiaries to ensure that no eligible individual is excluded due to clerical errors or systemic oversight. The authority must consider the fact that many of these petitioners are fatherless households, making the expedited delivery of housing benefits a matter of urgent social justice. This court emphasizes that the "appropriate action" mandated must be meaningful and not merely a procedural formality. Should the authority find the petitioners eligible, the allotment must be processed in accordance with the seniority of the list and the available budgetary allocations under the State Government scheme.
title: Test #43: Legal Matter - Govt. of Asam Housing Scheme

text: The Petitioner, a small-scale entrepreneur, approaches this Court seeking a Writ of Mandamus to command the respondent authorities, specifically the Electricity Department and the Executive Engineer, to restore the industrial power connection of his manufacturing unit. The connection was disconnected on 22nd January 2025, following a sudden raid and the subsequent allegation of electricity theft. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the department can disconnect a high-tension supply without adhering to the mandatory notice requirements and the assessment procedure prescribed under Section 126 and Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The Petitioner argues that the action is a result of local administrative bias and that no "Provisional Assessment" was served before the physical disconnection took place. The facts of the case reveal that the Petitioner’s unit was functioning under a valid industrial load for the past five years. On the date of the incident, a vigilance team entered the premises and alleged that the "Meter Seals" were tampered with. The learned counsel for the Petitioner, Sri Rahul Agarwal, argues that the mandate of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, regarding the preparation of an inspection report in the presence of the consumer, has been completely flouted. He submits that under Section 126(2), the assessing officer is required to serve a provisional assessment order giving the consumer an opportunity to file objections. He contends that the "Executive Action" of total disconnection without a hearing has led to a financial stalemate, resulting in the non-payment of wages to twenty workers employed at the unit. In response, the learned Standing Counsel appearing for the Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited argues that the state is a victim of Line Losses and organized power theft. He submits that in cases of "Direct Theft" or "Tampering" under Section 135, the authorities have the power to disconnect the supply immediately to prevent further loss to the exchequer. He contends that during the inspection, a bypass wire was found, which is a clear violation of the Grid Code. The State maintains that the Petitioner has a history of erratic payment and that the "Vigilance Report" is a prima facie proof of dishonest abstraction of energy. The respondent further argues that the Petitioner must deposit fifty percent of the "Compounding Amount" and the assessed penalty before seeking any restoration of supply. Having heard both sides and examined the "Panchnama" prepared during the raid, this Court observes that the right to electricity is now considered an essential component of the right to livelihood under Article 21. The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that while the department has a duty to curb theft, it cannot act as a "Judge in its own cause" by bypassing the statutory safeguards. The law is well-settled that the power to disconnect is a drastic power and must be exercised with "Due Diligence." The "Rule of Law" requires that even a person accused of theft is entitled to a fair inspection and a "Reasonable Opportunity" to explain any technical discrepancy in the meter reading. The Court finds that the disconnection order is hit by the vice of procedural irregularity. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that a "Speaking Order" must be passed after considering the consumer’s explanation. The "Directive Principles" of state action require the government to ensure that small industries are not shut down based on "Vague Inspection Reports." The "Administrative Discretion" to levy penalties must be balanced against the "Doctrine of Proportionality." A mere suspicion of tampering, without a laboratory report of the meter, cannot be the sole basis for a permanent disconnection that ruins a person’s business. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that "Administrative Efficiency" cannot be achieved at the cost of "Natural Justice."
title: Test #44: Legal - AHC WRIT-C N0. 32550 OF 2025

text: This statutory appeal under Section 23 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now corresponding to Section 67 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019) is directed against the final judgment and order dated 23rd October, 2018 passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC), New Delhi in Consumer Complaint No. 706 of 2017, whereby the learned Commission allowed the consumer complaint filed by the respondent homebuyer, directing the appellant developer to refund the entire deposited sum of Rs. 4,48,43,023/- along with interest at the rate of 10.7% per annum on account of gross contractual delay in handing over physical possession of residential apartment No. 1402 in Tower-C. The relevant factual matrix discloses that the respondent entered into an Apartment Buyer's Agreement with the appellant promoter on 8th May, 2012 for the purchase of a four-bedroom luxury condominium in the project designated as 'Araya' situated at Sector 62, Golf Course Extension Road, Gurugram. Under Clause 11.2 of the agreement, the developer promised to hand over possession within thirty-nine months from the date of sanction of building plans, with a grace period of one hundred and eighty days, which expired on 8th August, 2015. The respondent deposited ninety-five percent of the total sale consideration amounting to Rs. 4,48,43,023/- as per the construction-linked payment schedule. However, the appellant failed to secure the statutory occupancy certificate from the Director General of Town and Country Planning until 28th August, 2018, nearly three years beyond the agreed completion deadline. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant builder contended that the delay was occasioned by force majeure events, including administrative embargoes imposed by the National Green Tribunal on groundwater utilization and transport strikes. It was argued that under Clause 11.5 of the agreement, the purchaser was only entitled to delay compensation quantified at Rs. 10/- per square foot per month. Relying upon the contractual terms, it was urged that once an occupancy certificate was obtained during the pendency of the consumer complaint, the purchaser was legally obligated to take physical possession and could not demand a full refund. Refuting these contentions, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the builder-buyer agreement was ex-facie one-sided, harsh, and oppressive. While Clause 6.4 penalized the buyer with eighteen percent interest for any default in installment payments, Clause 11.5 offered a negligible delay compensation to the allottee, constituting an unfair trade practice under Section 2(1)(r) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. Affirming the decree of the National Commission, this Court holds that a homebuyer cannot be compelled to wait indefinitely or accept possession offered almost three years after the contractual deadline. In Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan, reported in (2019) 5 SCC 725, this Court ruled that one-sided terms incorporated in standard-form real estate contracts amount to unfair trade practices, and the purchaser has an unassailable right to rescind the contract and claim refund with reasonable interest. Furthermore, in Wg. Cdr. Arifur Rahman Khan v. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd., reported in (2020) 16 SCC 512, this Court reaffirmed that developers cannot retain homebuyers' savings without performing mutual contractual obligations. Accordingly, the civil appeal is dismissed, with modified directions to disburse the refund along with nine percent interest per annum within eight weeks.
title: Test #44: Legal - SCI Civil Appeal No. 12238 of 2018

text: The present Appeal arises out of the impugned order dated 22.10.2024 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Crl.O.P. No. 10961 of 2023 filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court proceeded to quash the proceedings against the respondents in C.C. No. 2 of 2023 arising out of FIR No. 229 of 2021 registered for offences under Sections 417, 420, 465, 468, 471 and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The core legal issue involves determining whether criminal prosecution for forgery and cheating can be scuttled at the threshold simply because the dispute also carries a civil element or because a civil court has upheld the validity of the impugned documents. The criminal proceedings originated from a dispute rooted in the execution of three registered settlement deeds concerning valuable immovable properties situated in Chennai. The appellant, Dr. C.S. Prasad, alleged that the respondents, by abusing the advanced age and medical vulnerability of his parents, caused the execution and registration of these deeds to their unlawful advantage. Specifically, it was alleged that a Power of Attorney (PoA) granted for limited administrative purposes was misused to execute settlement deeds in favor of the respondents through fraud and impersonation. Parallel to the criminal complaint, civil proceedings were instituted in 2014 seeking a declaration that the settlement deeds were null and void. The Civil Court subsequently dismissed the suit, upholding the validity of all three deeds. Following this civil success, the respondents moved the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.PC, arguing that the continuation of criminal prosecution amounted to a misuse of the process of law as the dispute was purely civil in nature. The High Court agreed, quashing the case on the grounds of the civil decree and an unexplained delay of six years in filing the complaint. The jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Cr.PC is extraordinary and must be exercised with great caution. This Court has consistently emphasized that the High Court must avoid conducting a mini-trial or embarking upon an inquiry into the genuineness of allegations at the quashing stage. In the landmark case of State of Haryana vs. Bhajan Lal, this Court laid down specific categories where such power could be exercised, such as where allegations in the FIR, taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute any offence. Furthermore, in Neeharika Infrastructure vs. State of Maharashtra, it was clarified that the power of quashing should be an exception rather than an ordinary rule. The High Court, while exercising this power, only has to consider whether the allegations in the FIR disclose the commission of a cognizable offence. It is premature to pronounce conclusions based on hazy facts before the police are permitted to complete the investigation. The approach adopted by the High Court in treating the civil decree as determinative of criminal culpability is legally flawed. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that civil and criminal liability may arise from the same set of facts. As held in Kathyayini vs. Sidharth P.S. Reddy, the pendency or conclusion of civil proceedings on the same subject matter is no justification to quash criminal proceedings if a prima facie case exists. Adjudication in civil matters and criminal prosecution proceed on different principles. A civil decree does not necessarily record findings on criminal intent, forgery, or the dishonest use of forged documents. To permit quashing solely because of a civil suit would encourage litigants to defeat criminal prosecution by instituting parallel civil proceedings. Furthermore, delay in filing a complaint is not a ground for quashing at the threshold; rather, it is a matter of appreciation of evidence to be determined during the trial. This Court concludes that the allegations in the complaint disclose a factual foundation requiring adjudication on evidence. Issues relating to the state of mind of the executants, the role of the respondents in the execution of the deeds.
title: Test #45: Legal Matter - SCI Cr. A. 140 of 2026

text: This intra-court appeal, preferred under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent against the judgment and order dated 14th November, 2024 rendered by the learned Single Judge in Writ Petition No. 14210 of 2024, calls in question the quashing of charge memo Rc. No. 42/T1/2012 dated 18th July, 2012 issued by the Superintendent of Police, Krishna District under Rule 20 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1991, whereby disciplinary proceedings initiated against the respondent police officer were quashed solely on the ground of an inordinate, unexplained administrative delay of twelve years in concluding the formal departmental inquiry. The respondent entered service as a Sub-Inspector of Police in 1994. Disciplinary proceedings were initiated in July 2012 alleging improper handling of case files during the investigation of Crime No. 97 of 2003 registered at Alamuru Police Station. The respondent submitted a detailed written statement of defense on 3rd December, 2014, denying all imputations. Successive inquiry officers were appointed through administrative memorandums dated 25th November, 2013 and 16th September, 2014, yet oral inquiry proceedings were repeatedly adjourned without examining material prosecution witnesses. A parallel criminal prosecution arising out of the same transaction terminated in the respondent's complete acquittal on 12th August, 2019. Despite the respondent attaining the age of superannuation on 30th June, 2021, the disciplinary authority failed to conclude the proceedings, withholding terminal benefits and full pensionary emoluments under Rule 9 of the Andhra Pradesh Revised Pension Rules, 1980. Learned Government Pleader appearing for the State contended that departmental proceedings operate on the principle of preponderance of probabilities and are not automatically vitiated by acquittal in criminal trials. It was argued that G.O. Ms. No. 679, General Administration (Services-C) Department, dated 1st November, 2008, prescribing a six-month time limit for completing departmental inquiries, is directory in nature and does not operate as an absolute jurisdictional bar. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent employee submitted that keeping disciplinary proceedings pending for more than a decade without any justification constitutes a flagrant violation of Article 14, Article 16, and Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Reliance was placed on the landmark decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of A.P. v. N. Radhakishan, reported in (1998) 4 SCC 154, and P.V. Mahadevan v. MD, T.N. Housing Board, reported in (2005) 6 SCC 636, wherein it was authoritatively established that inordinate delay in concluding disciplinary proceedings causes serious prejudice, continuous mental agony, and loss of promotional avenues, disentitling the employer from proceeding further. Having reviewed the counter-affidavit and administrative records, this Court finds that the department offered no plausible explanation for the protracted delay between 2014 and 2024. The delinquent employee cannot be subjected to perpetual harassment throughout his post-retirement life. In Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Prabhash Chandra Mirdha, reported in (2012) 11 SCC 565, the Apex Court observed that where proceedings remain stalled due to administrative lethargy without any fault on the part of the employee, the charge memo must be quashed. Concurring with the learned Single Judge, this Court dismisses the writ appeal, quashes the charge memo, and directs the State to release all withheld pensionary benefits and gratuity along with interest at six percent per annum within sixty days.
title: Test #45: Legal - APHC Writ Appeal No. 1069 of 2025

text: The accused-appellant, a conductor of a UPSRTC bus, was held guilty by the learned trial Judge for offences under Sections 333 and 332 of the IPC for voluntarily causing grievous hurt to a Traffic Inspector and causing hurt to other Traffic Inspectors to deter them in the discharge of their official duties during a route inspection. The prosecution case evolved from an F.I.R. registered at Police Station Roorkee, alleging that the appellant used abusive language, instigated passengers, and physically assaulted the inspection team when asked to produce the way-bill. The prosecution case originated from an incident on August 6, 1981, involving three Traffic Inspectors of U.P. Roadways. According to the F.I.R., the inspectors boarded Bus No. UST5238 plying from Saharanpur to Haridwar. It was alleged that the conductor, Rajendra Kumar, who was not in uniform, behaved indecently and instigated passengers. At Ram Nagar Camp, Roorkee, the conductor allegedly delivered two fist blows to the face of Nathu Ram, a Traffic Inspector, resulting in two broken upper teeth and a knee injury. Another inspector, Attar Singh, intervened, only to have his official diary snatched and torn apart. Budhi Mal, the third inspector, was allegedly pulled back into the bus, threatened, and pressured to delete an unfavorable report on the way-bill. The medical evidence was established through P.W.-4, Dr. Vipin Kumar Premi, who conducted the medico-legal examinations. Nathu Ram’s report revealed two missing upper middle incisor teeth with bleeding sockets, which was classified as a grievous injury. Budhi Mal’s examination showed a contusion on the right shoulder, classified as a simple injury. Both reports noted the injuries were fresh and caused by a blunt object. The Investigating Officer, P.W.-5, subsequently submitted a charge sheet for offences under Sections 332, 333, 353, 426, and 506 of the IPC, though the trial court framed charges specifically under Sections 332 and 333. The accused denied all charges and pleaded not guilty, claiming false implication. In his statement under Section 313 of the CrPC, the appellant contended that the Traffic Inspectors had wrongly demanded a ticket for an exempted child and had beaten him, which infuriated the passengers. The defence argued that Budhi Mal recorded an apology letter of his own volition to escape the wrath of the passengers who intended to produce him before the Assistant Regional Manager (ARM). The defence further produced D.W.-3, a passenger, who testified that the inspectors started the altercation and that Budhi Mal deleted the way-bill remark and signed an apology letter after being caught by passengers. A cross-case, Sessions Trial No. 162 of 1984, was also noted, wherein an F.I.R. had been lodged against the inspectors by the conductor. To establish guilt under Sections 332 and 333 of the IPC, the prosecution must prove that the accused voluntarily caused hurt, that the victim was a public servant, and that the servant was discharging their official duty at the time. While both parties were admitted to be public servants under Section 21 of the IPC, the court closely scrutinized whether the inspectors were in the lawful discharge of their duties. The Court observed significant inconsistencies. Crucially, the prosecution failed to produce any document or authority, as required under Rule 23 of the U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Rules, 1972, proving the inspectors were authorized to conduct surprise checks on that specific route. Furthermore, Rule 21 of the 1972 Rules stipulates that only drivers and conductors are exempt from obtaining tickets, implying that inspectors themselves must be authorized to board. Regarding the injuries, the Court found the medical and ocular testimonies inconsistent. Dr. Vipin Kumar Premi testified that a fist blow resulting in broken teeth would typically cause swelling, which was absent in Nathu Ram’s report. He further suggested that the tooth loss could have resulted from a fall while running.
title: Test #46: Legal Matter - AHC Cr. A. No. 2868 of 1986

text: Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the High Court completely overlooked the mandatory requirements of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. It was argued that the plaintiff merely pleaded formal readiness in the plaint without adducing credible documentary evidence, such as bank account balances, fixed deposit receipts, or loan sanction letters, to prove financial capacity to pay the substantial balance sum of Rs. 15,00,000/- during the crucial contractual period. Reliance was placed on the landmark decision of this Court in His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, reported in (1996) 4 SCC 526, and N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, reported in (1995) 5 SCC 115, wherein it was established that readiness refers to capacity to pay the purchase money, whereas willingness refers to the conduct and mental disposition of the purchaser. In response, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the vendor committed breach by failing to secure revenue conversion permissions, thereby disabling the respondent from completing the transaction. It was urged that where the vendor is in default, the purchaser cannot be faulted for not tendering the balance sum. Having meticulously scrutinized the evidence on record, this Court finds that the compliance of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act is an indispensable condition precedent that must be proved from the date of agreement up to the date of the final decree. In Janardan Das v. Durga Prasad Agrawalla, reported in 2024 INSC 748, this Court reiterated that a plaintiff cannot succeed merely by showing default on the part of the defendant; the plaintiff must stand on the strength of their own continuous readiness and willingness. In the present case, the respondent produced no bank statements or witnesses to substantiate financial capacity between 1993 and 1995. Furthermore, specific performance is an equitable relief governed by judicial discretion under Section 20 of the Act. Consequently, the judgment of the High Court is set aside, the decree for specific performance is revoked, and the appellants are directed to refund the earnest deposit of Rs. 3,50,000/- along with interest at nine percent per annum. This civil appeal arises from the impugned judgment and decree dated 14th November, 2008 passed by the High Court of Karnataka in Regular First Appeal No. 418 of 2002, whereby the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court dated 28th January, 2002 in Original Suit No. 1045 of 1995, and decreed the suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable agricultural land in favour of the respondent-plaintiff under Section 16(c) and Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The essential facts disclose that on 15th April, 1993, the predecessor-in-interest of the appellants entered into a written agreement to sell a parcel of fertile agricultural land admeasuring four acres situated at Survey No. 82/1, Devanahalli Taluk, Bangalore Rural District, for a total agreed sale consideration of Rs. 18,50,000/-. The respondent paid an earnest money deposit of Rs. 3,50,000/- on the date of execution, with the balance consideration payable within six months upon the vendor obtaining non-agricultural conversion approvals from the competent revenue authorities. Disputes erupted when the vendor issued a termination notice dated 20th October, 1993, asserting that the respondent failed to tender the remaining balance consideration despite reminders. Conversely, the respondent instituted the civil suit on 12th December, 1995, claiming continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract and seeking a registered conveyance deed.

title: Test #47: Legal Matter - JHC C.M.P. No. 1095 of 2024

text: Under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, the appellants seek a declaration that land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 have lapsed on account of the alleged failure of the State to take physical possession and disburse statutory compensation within the prescribed five-year antecedent period prior to the commencement of the 2013 Act on 1st January, 2014. The historical backdrop demonstrates that a preliminary notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was published in the Official Gazette on 14th March, 2003 for the planned development of transport infrastructure and residential sectors by the Indore Development Authority. Following summary inquiry under Section 5-A, a declaration under Section 6 was issued on 11th June, 2004. The Land Acquisition Officer passed an award under Section 11 of the 1894 Act on 8th September, 2006, assessing the total compensation payable at Rs. 14,82,50,000/-. The State authorities drew a memorandum of possession (Panchnama) on 24th October, 2006 in the presence of independent panch witnesses and deposited the awarded amount in the government treasury under Revenue Deposit heads after the landholders declined to accept the compensation cheques tendered. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the landowners contended that mere drawing of an ex-parte Panchnama does not constitute actual physical possession. Relying upon the earlier three-judge Bench decision in Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki, reported in (2014) 3 SCC 183, it was argued that compensation cannot be regarded as paid unless it is deposited before the Reference Court under Section 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It was urged that since the money remained in the treasury and physical cultivating possession was never surrendered, both conditions of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act stood satisfied, rendering the acquisition non-est and lapsed by operation of law. Addressing the reference, the Constitution Bench of this Court in Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal, reported in (2020) 8 SCC 129, exhaustively reconsidered the statutory landscape and expressly overruled Pune Municipal Corporation. The Constitution Bench authoritatively held that the word 'or' occurring between the two negative conditions in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act must be read conjunctively as 'nor' or 'and'. Consequently, deemed lapse occurs only when both contingencies co-exist, namely, physical possession has not been taken and compensation has not been paid. The Court elucidated that taking of possession under the 1894 Act by drawing a Panchnama is the accepted, recognized mode of taking physical possession of vacant lands, which cannot be invalidated merely because landowners continue wrongful or permissive trespass. Furthermore, when the acquiring authority tenders compensation under Section 31(1) of the 1894 Act and deposits the same in the treasury, the obligation of the State stands discharged. Landowners who refuse tender or seek interim injunctions in court proceedings cannot take advantage of their own default. Section 24(2) was never intended to revive stale, concluded acquisitions where land had already vested in the State free from all encumbrances under Section 16 of the 1894 Act. Therefore, finding no infraction of statutory mandates, the civil appeal is dismissed, affirming that the acquisition remains valid, unimpeachable, and absolute.
title: Test #47: Legal - SCI Civil Appeal No. 2085 of 2020

text: The primary legal issue before this Court involves the exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent the abuse of the process of law. The Petitioner seeks the quashing of a criminal complaint alleging financial fraud, contending that the dispute is purely civil in nature and has been given a criminal color to harass the individual. This Court must determine whether the allegations in the First Information Report, even if taken at their face value, disclose the ingredients of a cognizable offense or if the litigation is a tool for malicious prosecution. The facts of the case reveal that the parties entered into a commercial agreement for the supply of industrial raw materials in January 2025. Following a dispute over the quality of the goods, the Respondent filed a criminal complaint alleging cheating under Section 420 and criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Indian Penal Code. The learned counsel for the Petitioner, Sri G.S. Chaturvedi, argues that a mere breach of contract cannot be treated as a criminal offense unless there is evidence of fraudulent intention since the inception of the transaction. He submits that the "Executive Action" of the police in registering the FIR without a preliminary inquiry is a violation of the guidelines laid down in the Lalita Kumari case. He contends that the "Rule of Law" requires the judiciary to protect citizens from being dragged into criminal trials for civil defaults. In response, the learned Additional Government Advocate appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh argues that the "Inherent Powers" of the High Court should be exercised sparingly and only in the "Rarest of Rare" cases. He submits that at the stage of quashing, the Court is not required to conduct a "Mini-Trial" or appreciate evidence. He contends that the allegations clearly suggest a dishonest misappropriation of funds, which falls within the ambit of criminal law. The State maintains that the "Statutory Mandate" of the police is to investigate whenever a cognizable offense is reported, and any interference by the Court at this premature stage would stall the "Course of Justice." The respondent further argues that the Petitioner has an alternative remedy to seek discharge before the trial court under Section 227 of the Code. Having heard both sides and perused the "Case Diary," this Court observes that the right to personal liberty is a sacred fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that "Criminal Law" should not be set into motion for the purpose of settling a "Private Score" or to exert pressure for the recovery of money. The law is well-settled that if the ingredients of the offense are not made out, the continuation of the proceedings would be an exercise in futility. The "Public Trust Doctrine" in the judiciary requires that the Court acts as a shield against "Legal Harassment." The distinction between a "Civil Wrong" and a "Criminal Offense" is thin but significant, and the "Mala Fide" intention of the complainant must be scrutinized to ensure that the process of the court is not subverted. The Court finds that the present litigation is hit by the vice of over-implication. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that a "Speaking Order" must be passed by the Magistrate before taking cognisance under Section 190. The "Directive Principles" of state policy and the "Fundamental Duties" of the citizen collectively suggest that the "Judicial Resources" should not be wasted on frivolous complaints. The "Administrative Discretion" of the police must be balanced against the "Doctrine of Proportionality." If every commercial dispute is converted into a criminal case, it would lead to a "Stalemate" in the ease of doing business and would overburden the "Criminal Justice System." Consequently, this Court finds that the Petitioner has established a clear case for judicial intervention. The Criminal Revision is allowed.
title: Test #48: Legal Matter - AHC Cr. A. No. 4520 of 2026

text: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to “pass a decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India”. It gives the Supreme Court broad inherent powers. In Prem Chand Garg v. Excise Commissioner, U.P. (1963), a Constitution Bench considered whether the Supreme Court could frame a rule or issue an order under Article 142 that was inconsistent with a fundamental right. The court held that though the power under Article 142 is wide, it cannot be exercised to make an order that is plainly inconsistent with a constitutional provision. The judgment therefore placed an important constitutional limit on the otherwise wide power. In I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the court described Article 142 as a wide and elastic power that enables it to formulate legal doctrines where necessary to meet the ends of justice. In Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India (1991), the court took a broader view of the power, holding that limitations or prohibitions contained in ordinary laws do not, by themselves, operate as limitations on the constitutional power under Article 142. The same year, in Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat (1991), the Supreme Court held that its powers under Article 142, read with Articles 32 and 136, could be exercised to quash criminal proceedings in an appropriate case to do complete justice. The court emphasised that Article 142 operates at a different level from ordinary statutory powers. It was again recognised in Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998), where the Constitution Bench described Article 142 as a plenary, supplementary and residual source of power available to the Supreme Court to ensure due process and do complete justice between the parties. But this judgment is equally important for establishing the limits of that power. In Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023), the Constitution Bench gave perhaps the clearest illustration of the breadth of Article 142. It held that the Supreme Court can, in an appropriate case, depart from procedural as well as substantive law, provided the exercise is based on fundamental considerations of general and specific public policy. The court consequently held that it could dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown and waive the statutory procedure for a second motion in a mutual-consent divorce. The first important limit came in the case of Prem Chand Garg, where the court made it clear that Article 142 cannot be used to pass an order inconsistent with the Constitution, including fundamental rights. In Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998), the court put the limit more precisely. It held that Article 142 is a curative power: it can supplement the law, but it cannot supplant substantive law. The court observed that the very nature of the power must lead the court to set limits for itself within which to exercise those powers, and ordinarily it cannot disregard a statutory provision covering a subject, except perhaps to balance the equities between the conflicting claims of the litigating parties by “ironing out the creases”. In that case, the court could not use Article 142 to suspend an advocate’s licence to practise because that power was vested by statute in the Bar Council. In the case of Shilpa Sailesh, the court subsequently clarified that this does not mean every statutory requirement is an absolute bar on Article 142. The court said that it must consider the substantive law, but may depart from it where necessary to achieve complete justice, so long as the exercise does not violate fundamental considerations of general or specific public policy. More recently, in High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (2024), the Constitution Bench reiterated that Article 142 must be used to do “complete justice” between the parties before the court and cannot be used to affect people who are not part of the case.
