text: In response, the learned Government Pleader for Services argues that compassionate appointment is not a right but a concession provided by the State to mitigate the sudden financial crisis of a family. He submits that the policy of the State is to prioritize unmarried children and spouses who are presumed to be more vulnerable. He contends that once a son is married, he is legally deemed to have started his own family unit, and the burden of supporting the parents is a moral obligation rather than a ground for seeking public employment through the back door. The State maintains that the recruitment rules must be strictly followed and that the Court cannot rewrite the policy of the government under the guise of judicial review. Having heard both sides and perused the latest administrative guidelines, this Court observes that the objective of the compassionate appointment scheme is to provide immediate succor to a family in distress. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that the definition of a dependent must be interpreted in a purposive manner. The law is well-settled that marriage per se does not disqualify a child from being a dependent if they were actually relying on the earnings of the deceased at the time of death. In a society where, joint family systems are still prevalent, excluding a married son who has no means of livelihood would frustrate the very purpose of the welfare scheme. The Court finds that the respondents have acted in a mechanical manner by relying on a restrictive interpretation of the rules. The right to be considered for compassionate appointment is a significant interest for a family that has lost its sole breadwinner. The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that if a married daughter is eligible for consideration, a married son cannot be excluded on similar grounds of marital status, as it would lead to an illogical result. The rule of law requires the administrative authorities to conduct a transparency-driven verification of the financial status of the applicant before reaching a conclusion on dependency. Consequently, this Court finds that the rejection order suffers from a legal infirmity. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to set aside the order of rejection and reconsider the application of the petitioner on its own merits. The District Collector is directed to conduct a fresh inquiry into the financial condition of the petitioner’s family and, if it is found that the family is living in penury, the petitioner shall be provided with a suitable post commensurate with his educational qualifications. This entire exercise must be completed within a period of eight weeks from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that justice should be tempered with mercy and that procedural technicalities should not stand in the way of substantive relief for a family in crisis. The Registry of this Court is directed to communicate this order to the Director of the Animal Husbandry Department for immediate compliance. No order as to costs. Order pronounced in the open court on this 7th day of March, 2026. This Writ Petition is filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a Writ of Mandamus to declare the action of the respondent authorities in rejecting the application of the petitioner for appointment on compassionate grounds as illegal, arbitrary, and contrary to the settled principles of law. The petitioner is the son of a deceased government servant who served as a Junior Assistant in the Animal Husbandry Department and died in harness on 12th May 2021. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether a married son can be excluded from the scheme of compassionate appointment solely on the ground of his marital status. The petitioner argues that the rejection of his claim is based on an outdated understanding of dependency and that his marriage does not automatically terminate his financial reliance on his father or his responsibility toward his widowed mother and younger siblings.
title: Test #49: Legal - APHC Writ (P) No. 14220 of 2022

text: India’s Supreme Court has set out an important safeguard governing citizenship disputes, ruling that no person may be declared a foreigner through a mechanical or one-sided process. The judgment held that constitutional fairness applies even when an individual ultimately fails to establish Indian citizenship. This case rests on long-standing law: the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Citizenship Act, 1955, and the Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964. The ruling held that constitutional fairness applies even when a person ultimately cannot establish Indian citizenship. The case originated in Assam, where the National Register of Citizens process and its 2019 final list, along with the ongoing special intensive revision of electoral rolls, have kept citizenship questions under continual scrutiny. The court allowed 27 separate appeals, setting aside Gauhati High Court orders that had earlier confirmed the appellants as foreigners, sending all matters back to Assam’s network of more than 300 Foreigners Tribunals for fresh hearings. The bench clarified that it was not ruling on whether the appellants were Indian citizens; instead, it examined only whether the process used to reach that conclusion met constitutional standards. Although the Foreigners Act places the burden of proof on the person to show he or she is not a foreigner, the court held that this burden operates within a lawful process rather than replacing it altogether. A reference against a person cannot be accepted merely because it has been made, nor can foreigner status be declared through a purely mechanical exercise. The tribunal, the ruling explained, must disclose the essential grounds behind any allegation so that the individual can meaningfully respond and discharge the statutory burden placed upon them. The tribunal must disclose the core grounds behind any allegation so that the person concerned can meaningfully respond and fulfil the burden placed upon them. Even when a person fails to appear despite being properly served, the tribunal remains a quasi-judicial body bound to examine the evidence placed before it and record reasons, however brief, rather than issuing an automatic finding of foreign status. An ex parte proceeding dispenses only with the presence of the absent individual, not with objective consideration of the case. These procedural safeguards, the court noted, rest on Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution, which protect the equality and liberty of any person and are not restricted to citizens alone. A person may ultimately be unable to establish citizenship, yet the process used to reach that outcome must still satisfy requirements of fairness, reasonableness, and non-arbitrariness, given that a wrongful declaration can lead to detention, deportation, separation from family, and even statelessness. Because the consequences of such rulings extend far beyond an ordinary civil dispute, the court insisted that notices must be precise rather than merely formal, giving the person a genuine opportunity to respond rather than a token one. Because the outcome of these proceedings reaches well beyond an ordinary civil matter, the court required that notices be exact rather than simply formal, offering the individual a real chance to respond rather than a nominal one. The court additionally observed that high courts should generally avoid becoming the first forum to weigh evidence in cases where tribunal proceedings had been conducted ex parte, since questions of ancestry, family linkage, and electoral history are best examined at the tribunal level in the first instance. While allowing the appeals and ordering fresh adjudication, the bench cautioned that its decision was not meant to reward earlier defaults, directing the appellants to appear before the tribunals within four weeks, cooperate fully, and avoid unnecessary delay, failing which proceedings could continue without further indulgence. The court further clarified that it had expressed no view on the genuineness or adequacy of the documents submitted by the appellants.
title: Test #49: Supreme Court on Citizenship Determination

text: This Criminal Appeal is filed under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, challenging the judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the Sessions Judge, Lucknow. The appellant was found guilty of outraging the modesty of a woman and persistent workplace harassment under Sections 354 and 354-A of the Indian Penal Code. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the internal disciplinary mechanisms of an organization can supersede the criminal liability of an offender in cases involving the safety and dignity of women at the workplace. The appellant argues that the trial court failed to appreciate that he had already been exonerated in an internal inquiry conducted by the Local Complaints Committee and that the criminal prosecution was initiated out of professional malice. In response, the learned Additional Government Advocate appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh argues that today, on International Women's Day, it is imperative to acknowledge that a woman's testimony in cases of sexual harassment carries significant weight and should not be discarded on minor technicalities. He submits that the "Internal Inquiry" mentioned by the appellant was a sham, conducted by colleagues who were biased in his favor. He contends that the fear of social stigma and professional repercussions often leads to a delay in reporting such crimes, and therefore, a three-day delay is perfectly natural. The State maintains that the "Workplace Environment" must be safe for women to realize their full potential and that the appellant exploited his position of power to intimidate a subordinate. Having heard both sides and perused the detailed evidence recorded during the trial, this Court observes that the protection of women at the workplace is not just a statutory requirement but a fundamental human right. The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that the "Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013" was enacted to ensure that the dignity of women is never compromised. The law is well-settled that an acquittal in a departmental proceeding does not act as a bar to criminal prosecution, as the "Standard of Proof" in both proceedings is entirely different. In the present case, the survivor has been consistent in her narrative, and her testimony has stood the test of rigorous cross-examination. The Court finds that the trial court was justified in placing reliance on the "Sole Testimony" of the survivor. The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that a woman who has been a victim of sexual harassment is not an accomplice but a witness of the highest order. The "Patriarchal Defense" of professional rivalry is often used to silence victims, and the judiciary must be vigilant against such tactics. The "Rule of Law" requires that the workplace be a neutral space where merit is respected and the "Physical Integrity" of every individual is protected. The appellant’s conduct was not just a breach of professional ethics but a "Criminal Offence" that warrants deterrent punishment. Consequently, this Court finds that the prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Criminal Appeal is dismissed. The judgment of conviction and the sentence of three years of rigorous imprisonment passed by the trial court are hereby upheld. The appellant, who is currently on bail, is directed to "Surrender Immediately" before the trial court to undergo the remaining period of his sentence. Furthermore, the firm where the incident occurred is directed to pay a "Compensation" of one lakh rupees to the survivor for the mental agony caused by their failure to provide a safe working environment. The District Magistrate is directed to ensure that all private establishments in the district strictly comply with the "POSH Act" mandates. Accordingly, the appeal stands dismissed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that "Zero Tolerance" toward harassment is the only way to ensure the safety and empowerment of women in our society.
title: Test #50: Legal - AHC Criminal A. No. 2150 of 2022

text: The integrity of democracy depends as much on the inclusion of eligible voters as on the exclusion of those not legally entitled to vote. The Supreme Court of India delivered this significant ruling on May 28, 2026, as it upheld the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls process under Article 324 of the Constitution. A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant noted that although the right to vote is a valuable constitutional right fundamental to democratic governance, it is not absolute. The right to vote can be subjected to reasonable regulatory conditions aimed at preserving the accuracy and purity of electoral rolls. The 124-page judgment rejected all challenges to SIR, which was initiated by the Election Commission of India under Article 324 of the Constitution and Section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. The court held that the maintenance of an accurate and credible electoral roll was of foundational importance to the democratic process, because representative governance rests entirely upon the correctness and integrity of those rolls. The court further held that any systemic distortion in the electoral roll strikes at the very root of representative governance in a democracy. The judgment carries particular significance for its detailed constitutional formulation of the right to vote, especially against the backdrop of an evolving judicial debate over whether voting rights in India are purely statutory or enjoy full constitutional protection. Referring to the Constitution Bench decision in the Section-6A Citizenship Act case delivered in 2025, the court reiterated that the right to vote under Article 326 was no longer viewed merely as a statutory right. It had acquired the status of a constitutional right through a sustained process of judicial interpretation spanning several decades. In this context, the court recalled the ruling in Rajbala versus State of Haryana, decided in 2015, where the Supreme Court had held that the right to vote under Article 326 is a constitutional right subject only to such limitations as are prescribed by law. Quoting extensively from that earlier judgment, the bench noted that through the aid of judicial construction, the right to vote had been upgraded from being a mere statutory right to a fully recognised constitutional right. At the same time, the bench clarified that the constitutional guarantee of universal adult franchise under Articles 325 and 326 necessarily contemplates mechanisms of verification, identification, and periodic revision of electoral rolls to remain meaningful in practice. The court firmly rejected the petitioners’ argument that SIR disproportionately burdened voters by compelling them to repeatedly establish their citizenship or eligibility despite already being enrolled in the electoral rolls. Procedural requirements such as proof of identity, verification of ordinary residence, and confirmation of eligibility cannot by themselves be treated as unconstitutional burdens on voting rights. Such conditions are, in fact, intrinsic to the very preservation of the right to vote, since they ensure that the electoral roll remains confined to those who are lawfully entitled to be included within it. The court held that requiring electors to furnish one among several prescribed documents, coupled with multiple opportunities to rectify omissions and to challenge proposed exclusions, did not amount to a disproportionate restriction on the exercise of voting rights. A measure aimed at refining and correcting the electoral roll, even if it entails certain compliance requirements on the part of electors, does not in itself infringe the right to vote. The court stressed repeatedly that the relevant constitutional test was not whether some hardship or exclusion might arise during implementation, but whether the overall framework incorporated adequate safeguards against arbitrary disenfranchisement. The court pointed specifically to safeguards built into the SIR process including notice before exclusion.
title: Test #50: Right to Vote Not Mean Immunity from Verification

text: Law, enacted for the benefit of the society by conferring rights on the citizens and to regulate social behaviour in many a sphere, is required to be implemented by the law enforcing agencies and the citizens are duty bound to follow the law treating it as sacred. Law has to be regarded as the foundation of a civilized society. The primary goal of law is to have an orderly society where the citizenry dreams for change and progress is realized and the individual aspiration finds space for expression of his/her potential. In such an atmosphere while every citizen is entitled to enjoy the rights and interest bestowed under the constitutional and statutory law, he is also obligated to remain obeisant to the command of law. It has been stated in Krishnamoorthy v. Sivakumar and others (2015) 3 SCC 467, “the law, the mightiest sovereign in a civilized society”. The majesty of law cannot be sullied simply because an individual or a group generate the attitude that they have been empowered by the principles set out in law to take its enforcement into their own hands and gradually become law unto themselves and punish the violator on their own assumption and in the manner in which they deem fit. They forget that the administration of law is conferred on the law enforcing agencies and no one is allowed to take law into his own hands on the fancy of his “shallow spirit of judgment”. Just as one is entitled to fight for his rights in law, the other is entitled to be treated as innocent till he is found guilty after a fair trial. No act of a citizen is to be adjudged by any kind of community under the guise of protectors of law. It is the seminal requirement of law that an accused is booked under law and is dealt with in accordance with the procedure without any obstruction so that substantive justice is done. No individual in his own capacity or as a part of a group, which within no time assumes the character of a mob, can take law into his/their hands and deal with a person treating him as guilty. That is not only contrary to the paradigm of established legal principles in our legal system but also inconceivable in a civilized society that respects the fundamental tenets of the rule of law. And, needless to say, such ideas and conceptions not only create a dent in the majesty of law but are also absolutely obnoxious. It is worthy to note that the reliefs sought in all the writ petitions have commonality, although the expression of language as well as the width of the prayer is slightly different. What really emanates as the pivotal issue requiring our contemplated consideration is the duty of this Court under the constitutional framework to deal with the primary grievance that pertains to cow vigilantism and other incidents of lynching or, if we may say so, targeted violence and commission of offences affecting the human body and against private and public property by mobs under the garb of self-assumed and self-appointed protectors of law. We shall state the facts in brief, for there are asseverations with regard to numerous incidents of lynching and mob violence which need not be specifically stated since we are going to issue certain directions covering the arena of preventive, remedial and punitive measures. We shall note the suggestions given by Mr. Sanjay R. Hegde, learned senior counsel in one of the writ petitions. We may further state that we shall refer to the facts in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 754 of 2016. The petitioner, a social activist, has preferred this writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for commanding the respondent-State Nos. 3 to 8 to take immediate and necessary action against the cow protection groups indulging in violence; and further to issue a writ or direction to remove the violent contents from the social media uploaded and hosted by the said groups. There is also a prayer to declare Section 12 of the Gujarat Animal Prevention Act, 1954, Section 13 of the Maharashtra Animal Prevention Act, 1976 and Section 15 of the Karnataka Prevention of Cow Slaughter and Cattle Preservation Act, 1964 as unconstitutional.
title: Test #51: Legal Matter - SCI Writ P. No. 754 of 2016

text: The Supreme Court of India on Wednesday, May 21, 2026, declined to pause proceedings in the high-stakes Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin gas migration dispute between the Union Government and a Reliance Industries Limited (RIL)-led consortium. The case, which has its roots in a production sharing contract signed in the year 2000, has drawn national attention due to its enormous financial and legal implications. The dispute involves allegations of gas migration across offshore blocks in the KG basin off the Andhra Pradesh coast, a region that became commercially significant after large-scale energy exploration began in the early 2000s. The Supreme Court declined to pause proceedings in this high-stakes Krishna-Godavari basin gas migration dispute between the Union Government and the RIL-led consortium. After the RIL's legal team mentioned the matter before Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, the CJI clearly stated that the hearing would continue unless both sides jointly informed the court that a resolution had been reached. The three-judge bench, comprising the Chief Justice of India and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M. Pancholi, began hearing the appeals on Tuesday, May 20, 2026. The consortium's counsel, including advocates Sameer Parekh and Mahesh Agarwal, told the court that the petitioners intended to write to the Central Government to attempt reconciliation or mediation. They pointed out that the parties were still bound under an ongoing contractual relationship and that both sides remained engaged since at least 2009-2013, the critical years during which gas was extracted from the KG-D6 block. Attorney General R. Venkataramani, appearing for the Centre, firmly opposed any halt in the proceedings and urged the bench to continue hearing the appeals without interruption. The controversy has its origin in allegations raised by the state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd (ONGC) in 2013. ONGC contended that the RIL-led consortium had drilled wells close to boundary areas and extracted natural gas that had migrated from ONGC's adjoining offshore blocks, resulting in what it described as "unjust enrichment." The Union Government subsequently sought disgorgement of gains from the consortium, claiming nearly $1.5 billion along with about $174 million in interest. At the relevant time, RIL held a 60% participating interest in the KG-D6 block, while BP Plc held a 30% stake and Niko Resources held the remaining 10%. The Attorney General submitted before the bench that the consortium had "virtually committed a theft" of gas originating in ONGC's fields. He argued that gas had migrated naturally across reservoir boundaries beneath the seabed and that the consortium was fully accountable for extracting it. The consortium, however, strongly denied the allegation, arguing that migration of hydrocarbons across underground geological formations was a natural phenomenon incapable of being prevented by any artificial means. The consortium strongly denied the allegation, contending that such migration of hydrocarbons across underground reservoirs was a natural geological phenomenon that could not possibly be prevented or controlled by human intervention. Senior Advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi, appearing for the consortium, argued that the extraction could not be characterised as deliberate or intentional siphoning. He explained that when gas is extracted under pressure from a sea block, migration from nearby formations occurs naturally and is entirely unrelated to any question of intent or voluntariness. The litigation traces back to a production sharing contract executed in 2000. Commercial production from the KG-D6 block began in April 2009. The consortium invoked arbitration, and in July 2018, an arbitral tribunal ruled in their favour. While a single judge of the Delhi High Court upheld this award in May 2024, a Division Bench reversed the ruling on February 14, 2025, setting aside the award as contrary to settled legal principles. The consortium has now challenged that judgment before the Supreme Court.
title: Test #51: KG Basin Gas Disputes and Hearing in SCI

text: Both the appeals in the above-mentioned matters have been preferred under Section 19(1) of the Family Courts Act, 1984. Since both the appeals arise out of a common judgment dated 16.02.2017 passed by the Principal Judge, Family Court, Garhwa in Original M.M. Suit No. 68 of 2016, they have been tagged together and taken up for analogous hearing and are being disposed of by this common order. F.A. No. 213 of 2019 was filed by the petitioner-appellant wife, Priyanka Sahi, against the part of the judgment dated 16.02.2017 and decree dated 06.03.2017, whereby the learned Family Court allowed the petition filed under Section 12(1)(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, and granted Rs. 30,00,000/- as permanent alimony. The said amount was challenged on the ground of miscalculation and inadequate assessment. F.A. No. 23 of 2018 was filed by the respondent-appellant husband, Siddarth Rao, challenging the same impugned judgment, contending that he was not given a proper opportunity to appear, and that the ex-parte proceedings against him were irregular and unjust. After marriage, when the petitioner went to her matrimonial home, she was introduced to one Meeruta Sharma by the family members of the respondent as his girlfriend, who had been living with him in a live-in-relationship prior to the marriage. This fact had been deliberately concealed from the petitioner and her family, and the respondent had been fraudulently presented as a man of good character and reputation. The petitioner, despite this betrayal, attempted to adjust to the situation. However, the respondent and his family soon began demanding an additional sum of Rs. 15,00,000- in cash as further dowry, which the petitioner and her parents declined to fulfill. Thereafter, the petitioner was subjected to physical and mental cruelty at the hands of the respondent and his family members. The respondent was also found to be addicted to alcohol and was unable to pass even a day without consuming wine. On 02.03.2016, the petitioner was forcibly ousted from her matrimonial home, being deprived of all her belongings and Stridhan. The petitioner thereafter filed a suit under Section 12(1)(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, seeking a decree of nullity of marriage on the ground of fraud and concealment of material facts. She also claimed permanent alimony of Rs. 1,00,00,000- under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, and further sought return of properties and cash amount of Rs. 26,40,000- with interest at 14% per annum under Section 27 of the said Act. Despite repeated summons and notices issued against the respondent, he neither appeared before the Family Court nor filed any written statement. The learned Family Court accordingly proceeded ex-parte against him vide order dated 29.07.2016. The learned Principal Judge, Family Court, Garhwa, vide judgment dated 16.02.2017 and decree dated 06.03.2017, allowed the suit, declared the marriage annulled by a decree of nullity, and directed the respondent to pay Rs. 30,00,000- as permanent alimony within six months by account-payee cheque. The Hon’ble High Court, after examining the testimonies of PW-1 (the petitioner-wife herself) and PW-2 (her mother, Chhaya Sahi), and after perusing the entire record, affirmed the decree of nullity of marriage under Section 12(1)(c) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, holding that the consent of the petitioner and her guardian was obtained by fraud and concealment of the fact of prior live-in-relationship of the respondent, which falls squarely within the ambit of Section 12(1)(c) of the Act. On the question of permanent alimony under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Hon’ble Court relied upon the leading judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Rajnesh vs. Neha and Anr., (2021) 2 SCC 324, which laid down that the objective of granting permanent alimony is to ensure that the dependent spouse is not reduced to destitution or vagrancy on account of the failure of the marriage, and is not a punishment to the other spouse.
title: Test #52: Legal Matter - JHC F.A. No. 213 of 2019

text: When a five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India delivered its landmark verdict in September 2018, in the case of Indian Young Lawyers Association vs State of Kerala, the ruling opened the doors of Kerala's Sabarimala temple to women of all ages. The original ruling was delivered through a 4:1 majority, with Justice A.M. Khanwilkar joining the Chief Justice. The decision provoked a wide range of reactions across the country. There were protests, particularly in Kerala, where many believed that the Court had overlooked, and even disrespected, deeply held religious creed. The judgment provoked a broad range of reactions throughout the nation. Especially in Kerala, where many people believed that the Court had disregarded, and even disrespected, longstanding religious belief. Others, however, saw the verdict as transformative, outlining a vision that enlivened the Constitution and upheld individual dignity. Now, close to a decade later, the Court will hear final arguments on review petitions that seek to overturn the earlier verdict and the law it laid down. The original ruling rested on three core findings. First, the Court ruled that the devotees of Lord Ayyappa did not constitute a separate religious denomination. Second, that the bar enforced on women between the ages of 1000 and 5000 years old more precisely, women between the ages of 10 and 50 from entering the temple violated their rights to freedom of religion. Third, that Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965, on which the ban was grounded, violated not only the Constitution but also Section 3 of its parent law, which promised free access to temples for all classes of Hindus. Justice Indu Malhotra's notable dissent argued that fundamental rights in a secular polity needed harmonising, and that a generic doctrine of equality cannot override the collective rights of individuals to practise their faith in line with their customs and ideals. The Constitution recognises both the freedom of religion as an individual right and the rights of religious denominations to manage their own affairs in matters of religion. Both rights are subject to public order, morality and health, and, in the case of an individual's right to freedom of religion, also to other fundamental rights. Balancing communitarian interests with individual conscience has long plagued Indian jurisprudence. Over the years, when called upon to resolve tensions of this kind, the Court has used a test that has allowed it to virtually sit in theological judgment over religious practice. That is, it examines and arrives at a factual conclusion on whether a practice in question is essential to the religion or not. This has meant that the Court has effectively determined not only those areas where it might be constitutionally justifiable for the state to intervene, but also what kinds of practices are deserving of constitutional protection in the first place. As Justice Chandrachud wrote in his judgment in Indian Young Lawyers Association, the rationale for allowing a religious community to define what constitutes an essential aspect of its religion is to protect the autonomy of religions and religious denominations. Protecting that autonomy enhances the liberal values of the Constitution. However, by entering upon doctrinal issues of what does or does not constitute an essential part of religion, the Court has, as a necessary consequence, been required to adopt a religious mantle. The test also suffers from other practical limitations. It calls upon a constitutional court to arrive at fully fleshed out factual findings without allowing parties to lead oral evidence or subject witnesses to cross-examination. What is more, the doctrine also does not offer a clear solution for what is really an obvious problem: what must a court do when a practice it finds essential to religion also undermines, or is inimical to, the dignity of individuals? It is for this reason that Justice Chandrachud proposed an "anti-exclusion test".
title: Test #52: Balancing Faith, Diginity & Constitutioal Rights

text: The primary legal issue before this Court is the rising menace of cyber-squatting and whether the "Intermediary Liability" of domain name registrars extends to the proactive blocking of "Typo squatted" domains that mirror the plaintiff’s official portal. The plaintiff argues that these fraudulent websites are being used to deceive innocent consumers into disclosing their financial credentials, thereby causing "Irreparable Injury" to the brand’s reputation and significant monetary loss to the public. The facts of the case reveal that the defendants have registered domains that vary from the plaintiff’s trademark by only a single character or a different top-level domain extension. These websites replicate the "Look and Feel" of the original site, including the color scheme and the logo, to create a "False Association" in the minds of the users. The learned counsel for the plaintiff, Sri Chander M. Lall, argues that the "Domain Name Registrars" (DNRs) are facilitating these illegal activities by providing anonymity to the registrants. He submits that under the "Information Technology Rules," the intermediaries have a "Statutory Duty" to exercise due diligence and must disable access to such infringing content once it is brought to their notice. He contends that a "Dynamic Injunction" is necessary to ensure that as soon as a new mirror website is created, it can be blocked without the plaintiff having to approach the Court repeatedly. In response, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent-registrars argues that they are merely "Technical Service Providers" and do not monitor the content or the legality of the domain names registered through their platforms. He submits that the volume of registrations is so high that "Manual Verification" of every domain against every trademark is a physical impossibility. He contends that blocking a domain without a "Specific Judicial Order" would interfere with the "Freedom of Trade" and could lead to the over-blocking of legitimate websites. The respondents maintain that they are willing to comply with the directions of the Court provided the plaintiff provides the "Specific URLs" of the infringing websites. The authorities argue that the "Safe Harbour" protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act should not be stripped away unless there is a clear "Contumacious Refusal" to comply with a legal mandate. Having heard both sides and perused the "Technical Audit Report," this Court observes that the "Digital Ecosystem" requires a higher degree of vigilance from all stakeholders. The Delhi High Court emphasizes that "Intellectual Property" is a valuable asset in the modern economy and its protection is essential for "Consumer Welfare." The law is well-settled that a domain name is not just an address but serves the function of a "Trademark" in the virtual world. When a rogue entity uses a deceptively similar name to siphon off traffic or to commit "Phishing Scams," the Court cannot remain a "Silent Spectator." The concept of a "Dynamic Injunction" has been evolved specifically to deal with such "Hydra-Headed" infringers who change their digital identity at the click of a button. The Court finds that the "Global Nature of the Internet" does not exempt entities from the "Local Laws" of the country where they conduct business. The "Doctrine of Deceptive Similarity" applies with full force to domain names. If a registrar is informed about a "Prima Facie" infringement involving a well-known mark, it cannot hide behind technicalities. The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that "Intermediaries" must act promptly to remove access to "Unlawful Content." The "Right to Property" under Article 300-A includes intangible assets like trademarks and copyrights. The "Administrative Burden" on the registrars is a small price to pay for ensuring a "Secure Digital Environment" for the citizens of India. Consequently, this Court finds that the plaintiff has made out a strong case for the grant of an "Ad-Interim Injunction."
title: Test #53: Legal Matter - DHC Writ P. Civil No. 5840 of 2025

text: Leave granted and the present appeal preferred by the claimant who suffered disability in a motor accident raises a limited yet significant issue concerning the just determination and enhancement of compensation awarded under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and calls for a careful reappraisal of the approach adopted by the Tribunal as well as the High Court while assessing the income, extent of disability and future prospects of the claimant, and the controversy essentially revolves around whether the courts below have adhered to the settled principles governing computation of compensation or have adopted a rigid and unrealistic method resulting in inadequate compensation to the injured claimant. It is required to be noticed at the outset that though the claim petition was described as one under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act the pleadings on record as well as the nature of allegations clearly indicate that the claim arose out of rash and negligent driving of the vehicle belonging to the respondent Corporation and therefore the claim is more appropriately referable to Section 166 of the Act which contemplates a fault-based liability and permits a broader and more realistic assessment of compensation based on evidence and surrounding circumstances. The appellant had asserted that he was working as a salesman earning Rs.8,000/- per month, however in the absence of documentary evidence the Tribunal adopted a notional income of Rs.3,300/- per month relying upon the schedule applicable to Section 163A and the High Court mechanically affirmed the same without considering whether such income reflected the prevailing economic conditions at the relevant time, and such an approach in our considered view cannot be sustained as it defeats the very object of awarding just and reasonable compensation. It is by now well settled that in cases where strict proof of income is not available the court must adopt a pragmatic approach and determine the income on the basis of surrounding circumstances, nature of work and minimum wage standards, and reference may be made to the decision of this Court in Ramachandrappa v. Royal Sundaram Alliance Insurance Co. Ltd. wherein even a daily wage labourer was assigned a reasonable income keeping in view economic realities. Applying the said principle and considering that the accident occurred in the year 2005 it would be appropriate to assess the income of the appellant at Rs.5,000/- per month which represents a fair and reasonable estimation rather than a strictly notional figure divorced from reality. The appellant being aged about 27 years at the time of accident the appropriate multiplier applicable would be 17 and having regard to the settled law an addition of 40% towards future prospects is also required to be made since the claimant was self-employed and would have reasonably expected an increase in income over time. As regards the disability it is evident from the medical evidence that the disability was assessed at 60% by the doctor and was reduced by the Tribunal to 50% upon consideration of functional disability and the nature of injuries sustained, and in the absence of any appeal or cross-objection by the insurer the High Court was not justified in further reducing the disability to 40% without assigning cogent reasons and such reduction appears to be arbitrary and unsustainable in law. The determination of compensation in such cases must not be approached with a hyper-technical or pedantic mindset but with a view to ensure that the injured claimant is adequately compensated for the loss of earning capacity, pain and suffering and the long-term impact of disability on his livelihood and quality of life, and therefore a balanced and rational computation is required to be undertaken. Recomputing the compensation on the revised parameters namely income of Rs.5,000/- per month multiplier of 17 addition of 40% towards future prospects and disability of 50% the loss of income is calculated at Rs.7,14,000/- and the amounts awarded under other conventional heads.
title: Test #53: Legal Matter - SCI SLP (C) No. 7347 of 2024

text: The petitioner has been serving as a dealer for several years, ensuring the supply of essential commodities to the local community. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the summary cancellation of the license, without conducting a full-fledged inquiry as mandated by the Andhra Pradesh Control Order, is sustainable in law. The petitioner argues that while a show cause notice was issued, the final order was passed in haste without providing an opportunity for a personal hearing or allowing the petitioner to cross-examine the witnesses whose statements formed the basis of the adverse report. The facts of the case reveal that an inspection was conducted on 6th February 2025, during which certain marginal variations in the stock of rice and pulses were allegedly discovered. The regional authorities served a notice on the same day, to which the petitioner submitted a detailed explanation on 13th February 2025, attributing the variations to weighment errors and moisture loss. However, without considering these technical justifications, the authorities passed the impugned order of cancellation on 18th February 2025. The learned counsel for the petitioner argues that the power of cancellation is a quasi-judicial function and cannot be exercised in a routine or mechanical manner. He contends that the right to livelihood of a dealer cannot be extinguished based on mere "subjective satisfaction" of a subordinate officer without a "speaking order" that addresses each objection raised by the licensee. In response, the learned Assistant Government Pleader appearing for the State argues that the Public Distribution System is a vital lifeline for the weaker sections of society and that any leakage or black marketing must be met with zero tolerance. He submits that the inspection report clearly established that the petitioner was not maintaining the electronic point of sale device correctly and that the physical stock did not tally with the digital ledger. He contends that in matters involving essential commodities, the "Public Interest" overrides the "Individual Right" of the dealer to continue his trade. The State maintains that the petitioner was given an opportunity to explain the discrepancies, and since the explanation was found to be unsatisfactory, the authority was well within its rights to revoke the authorization to prevent further misappropriation of government grain. Having heard both sides and perused the record, this Court observes that "Discipline" in the distribution system is essential, but it must be achieved through the "Rule of Law." The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that the power to suspend or cancel an authorization must be followed by a fair inquiry. The law is well-settled that an order of cancellation has civil consequences and must be preceded by an inquiry where the material relied upon by the department is placed before the dealer. In the present case, the authorities moved from the notice stage to the cancellation stage in just five days, which effectively denied the petitioner a "Reasonable Opportunity" to defend his case. A "Reasonable Opportunity" is not a mere formality but a substantial right. The Court finds that the respondents failed to distinguish between "Serious Financial Irregularities" and "Marginal Variations" as indicated in the Control Order. Not every mismatch in stock warrants the "Capital Punishment" of the service law, which is the cancellation of the license. For minor lapses, the authorities are empowered to impose penalties or issue warnings. The "Doctrine of Proportionality" requires that the punishment must fit the crime. By passing a summary order, the appointing authority has acted as the "Judge, Jury, and Executioner" without following the mandate of natural justice. The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that the burden of proving the charges lies on the state, and this burden cannot be shifted to the dealer through a vague show cause notice.
title: Test #54: Legal Matter - APHC Writ P. No. 5022 of 2025

text: The present criminal appeal presents a critical examination of the legality of conviction recorded under Sections 304-B and 316 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and raises substantial questions regarding the evidentiary threshold required to sustain a conviction for dowry death and consequential offences, particularly in the backdrop of alleged cruelty, harassment and presumption under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and at the very outset it becomes necessary to scrutinize whether the prosecution has discharged its burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt that soon before the death the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment in connection with demand for dowry so as to attract the statutory presumption and sustain the conviction recorded by the courts below. The factual background reveals that the marriage of the appellant’s son with the deceased took place on 02.12.2010 and it was alleged that the deceased was subjected to persistent demands of dowry including an amount of Rs.2,00,000/- and a car and that such demands were accompanied by mental and physical harassment by the members of her matrimonial home including the appellant, and on 03.08.2011 information was received by the informant that the deceased had died under suspicious circumstances leading to registration of the First Information Report against the husband, mother-in-law and other relatives. Upon completion of investigation chargesheet was filed and the accused were tried for offences under Sections 498-A, 304-B and 316 of the Penal Code along with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 and the Trial Court upon appreciation of evidence convicted the appellant along with other accused persons and imposed sentences of rigorous imprisonment, which conviction was partly modified by the High Court by acquitting the appellant of certain charges while maintaining her conviction under Sections 304-B and 316 of the Penal Code and reducing the sentence. The principal contention advanced on behalf of the appellant is that there is a complete absence of specific evidence attributing any act of cruelty or harassment to the appellant and that the prosecution has relied only upon vague and omnibus allegations without establishing any proximate nexus between the alleged harassment and the death of the deceased and therefore the essential ingredients of Section 304-B of the Penal Code have not been satisfied. On the other hand, the respondent has contended that the consistent demand of dowry coupled with the unnatural death of the deceased within seven years of marriage is sufficient to attract the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act and that the burden shifts upon the accused to rebut such presumption. Upon a careful evaluation of the evidence on record it becomes apparent that the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses including the brother and relatives of the deceased are general in nature and do not refer to any specific instance of cruelty or harassment attributable to the appellant and merely reiterate allegations of dowry demand without substantiating the same through concrete evidence or particular incidents, and such general statements in the absence of specific details cannot form the basis of conviction under Section 304-B of the Penal Code. It is also significant that the High Court itself has set aside the conviction of the appellant under Section 498-A of the Penal Code as well as under Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 which finding has attained finality and thereby weakens the prosecution case insofar as the allegation of cruelty is concerned, and once the foundational requirement of cruelty or harassment is not established the presumption under Section 113-B cannot be invoked. Furthermore, the evidence on record indicates that the death of the deceased was a case of suicide and there is no material to show that the appellant was present at the matrimonial home at the time of occurrence or that she had any direct role in causing the death of the unborn child and therefore the conviction.
title: Test #54: Legal Matter - SCI Cr. A. No. 532 of 2021

text: The case that came before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh in the year 2023 is one that touches upon an everyday commercial reality of modern India the dishonor of a cheque. In a country where millions of financial transactions are still backed by cheques, and where disputes over debts and loans fill the dockets of trial courts across every district, the question decided by this Court carries weight far beyond the parties before it. The High Court held that in the present case, the civil court’s decree was not merely a piece of evidence to be weighed alongside other evidence. It was a binding judicial determination of the parties’ rights and obligations arising from the very same transaction. A criminal court, dealing with the same parties and the same set of facts, cannot proceed on a footing that is entirely contrary to what a civil court has already decided on the same subject matter. To do so would not only create conflicting and irreconcilable judicial findings on the same set of facts, but would also be fundamentally unjust to the accused, who would face the peril of a criminal conviction for a liability that a competent court has already found did not exist to the extent claimed. This Court further noted that the principle of binding effect of civil judgments in related criminal proceedings is a well-established rule of evidence and natural justice. The civil court, in arriving at its finding that only Rs. 25,000- was due, had applied its mind to the same transaction, examined the same witnesses and documents, and applied the law to the facts. That finding cannot be lightly brushed aside or treated as irrelevant merely because the proceeding before the criminal court is governed by a different statute. The purpose of law, in its entirety, is to reach a just result. When two courts one civil and one criminal are examining the same factual question between the same parties, the later court cannot proceed as though the earlier court never spoke. Accordingly, this Court dismissed the criminal appeal and upheld the acquittal of the accused. It was held that since the civil court had determined that only Rs. 25,000- was due, the cheque amount of Rs. 75,000- could not be said to represent a legally enforceable debt to that extent, and the essential ingredient of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. The key legal principle that emerges from this judgment is clear and of lasting significance. In a prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a judgment of a competent civil court that has already determined the amount of legally enforceable debt between the same parties arising from the same transaction is binding upon the criminal court. The criminal court cannot conclude that is directly opposed to the finding of a civil court on the same question of the existence and extent of the legally enforceable debt. Where the cheque amount exceeds the judicially determined debt, the excess is not covered by a legally enforceable liability, and the offence under Section 138 cannot be said to be made out for such excess amount. This ruling is an important affirmation of the principle that judicial consistency, inter-court respect, and the binding force of civil adjudication are all essential pillars of a just legal system. A litigant cannot use the criminal process to claim what the civil court has already denied. The law, in both its civil and criminal arms, must speak in the same voice on the same facts, and this High Court, through this judgment, ensured that it did. The central issue was precise, practical, and yet profoundly important: when a civil court has already determined the exact amount of legally enforceable debt between two parties, can a criminal court under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 simply ignore that finding and proceed as though it never happened? The answer of this Court is an emphatic and well-reasoned no.
title: Test #55: Legal Matter - APHC Cheque Dishonour Law

text: The factual matrix discloses that the appellants herein had instituted a civil suit bearing T.S. No.16 of 1983 seeking declaration of right, title and interest over the suit property, which suit came to be dismissed by judgment and decree dated 17.01.1994, where after the appellants preferred a first appeal before the District Judge being T.A. No.11 of 1994 which was partly allowed by judgment dated 08.10.1999 declaring the right, title and interest of the appellants in respect of Suit Hal Plot No.53 while rejecting other reliefs relating to possession of the adjacent plot, and the said judgment having attained finality, the appellants initiated execution proceedings in E.P. No.8 of 2000 seeking delivery of possession in terms of the decree. The executing court, upon consideration of the report submitted by the Civil Court Commissioner and the bailiff indicating that possession had been duly delivered in accordance with the decree, recorded full satisfaction of the decree and disposed of the execution proceedings by order dated 26.08.2006, and it is significant to note that no objections were raised by the respondents at that stage and even a memo was filed indicating absence of objection to the delivery of possession. However, subsequent to the closure of the execution proceedings, the respondents filed an application under Section 47 CPC contending that there had been wrongful delivery of possession in respect of a different plot and seeking setting aside of such delivery, which application was entertained by the executing court and the preliminary objections raised by the decree-holder were rejected. The High Court, in exercise of its writ jurisdiction, affirmed the said order, thereby giving rise to the present appeal. Upon a careful consideration of the statutory provision contained in Section 47 CPC it is evident that all questions relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of a decree must be determined by the executing court and not by a separate suit, however such determination is necessarily required to be made during the pendency of the execution proceedings and not after the execution proceedings have culminated in full satisfaction of the decree, and any interpretation to the contrary would render the principle of finality otiose and permit endless reopening of concluded proceedings. In the present case, the execution proceedings stood concluded on 26.08.2006 upon recording of full satisfaction and it is only thereafter that the respondents sought to invoke Section 47 CPC, which in our considered view is wholly impermissible and contrary to the scheme of the Code. The respondents, having failed to raise any objection during the pendency of the execution proceedings and having acquiesced in the delivery of possession, are clearly estopped from challenging the same at a subsequent stage, and the conduct of the respondents attracts the well-settled doctrine that a party cannot be permitted to approbate and reprobate or to take inconsistent positions to the prejudice of the opposite party. It is also pertinent to note that if the respondents were aggrieved by the manner of execution or delivery of possession, the appropriate remedy would have been to challenge the order passed in the execution proceedings in accordance with law, which they failed to do, and instead they sought to reopen the matter by filing an application under Section 47 CPC after the decree had already been satisfied. Such a course of action cannot be countenanced as it would undermine the sanctity of judicial orders and encourage multiplicity of proceedings. The High Court, in affirming the order of the executing court, has failed to appreciate the limited scope of Section 47 CPC and the necessity of raising objections at the appropriate stage, and has erred in upholding an application which was ex facie not maintainable. In view of the aforesaid analysis and having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, it is evident that the application filed by the respondents under Section 47 CPC.
title: Test #55: Legal Matter - SCI Civil A. No. 1920 of 2011

text: The primary legal issue before this Court involves a challenge to the summary cancellation of a mining lease without providing a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the Petitioner. This Court must determine whether the "Executive Action" of the State in terminating the contract satisfies the mandate of Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which abhors arbitrariness in administrative decisions. The Petitioner seeks a Writ of Certiorari to quash the impugned order, contending that the principles of Natural Justice were blatantly violated as no "Show Cause Notice" was served prior to the termination. The facts of the case reveal that the Petitioner was granted a mining lease for minor minerals in the district of Dhanbad in January 2022. The lease was valid for a period of ten years, subject to the compliance of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. In February 2026, the District Mining Officer issued a summary order cancelling the lease, alleging a breach of environmental norms and illegal excavation beyond the permitted area. The learned counsel for the Petitioner, Sri Rajiv Kumar, argues that the "Termination Order" is a classic case of administrative high-handedness. He submits that under the Jharkhand Minor Mineral Concession Rules, the authority is bound to conduct a field verification and grant a personal hearing before taking any coercive steps. He contends that the "Rule of Law" requires that the State must act as a model lessor and not as an arbitrary landlord. In response, the learned Standing Counsel appearing for the State of Jharkhand argues that the mining activities were causing irreparable damage to the local ecology. He submits that the "Precautionary Principle" in environmental law allows the State to take immediate action to prevent further degradation of the "Public Trust Resources." He contends that during a surprise inspection, the Petitioner was found to be operating without a valid "Consent to Operate" from the State Pollution Control Board, which is a violation of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. The State maintains that the "Safety of the Environment" is a paramount consideration that overrides the commercial interests of an individual. The respondent further argues that the Petitioner has an alternative remedy of filing an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner and should not have invoked the "Writ Jurisdiction" of the High Court directly. Having heard both sides and perused the inspection reports, this Court observes that while environmental protection is vital, the "Procedural Safeguards" cannot be discarded. The High Court of Jharkhand emphasizes that even an administrative order which involves civil consequences must be a "Speaking Order" that reflects the application of mind. The law is well-setled that the "Right to be Heard" is not a mere formality but a substantial right intended to prevent the miscarriage of justice. The "Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation" suggests that a lessee who has invested significant capital has the right to expect that the lease will not be cancelled without "Due Process." The Court finds that the impugned order is hit by the vice of non-application of mind. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that the "Audi Alteram Partem" rule must be read into every statute unless it is specifically excluded. The "Administrative Discretion" to cancel a lease must be exercised within the bounds of "Reasonableness." If the State is allowed to terminate contracts without a notice, it would lead to a "Stalemate" in the industrial sector and discourage honest entrepreneurs. The "Public Interest" is best served when the State follows the "Sanctity of Procedure" and provides a "Level Playing Field" to all stakeholders. Consequently, this Court finds that the Petitioner has established a clear case of "Violation of Natural Justice." The Writ Petition is allowed. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that "Justice" must not only be done but must be seen to be done through "Fair Procedure."
title: Test #56: Legal - JHC Arbitrary Cancellation of Mining Lease

text: The present criminal appeal, arising from an order granting bail to an accused involved in serious offences including murder, presents a delicate interplay between the preservation of individual liberty and the imperative of ensuring a fair and unimpeded administration of criminal justice, and the core issue that arises for determination is whether the discretion exercised by the High Court in granting bail suffers from such perversity or legal infirmity so as to warrant interference by this Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction, particularly in a case where the appellant seeks cancellation of bail rather than opposing its initial grant, thereby invoking a higher threshold of scrutiny governed by well-settled principles of criminal jurisprudence. The factual matrix indicates that the incident in question occurred on 25.10.2018 when the deceased, a public figure, was fatally shot in broad daylight by unidentified assailants and was later declared dead at the hospital, and the prosecution case initially named certain accused persons while the present respondent was implicated subsequently on the basis of an alleged oral dying declaration of the deceased as well as disclosure statements made by co-accused persons during investigation. It is the contention of the appellant that the respondent is a habitual offender with a long criminal history and considerable local influence and that his release on bail poses a serious threat to witnesses and undermines the integrity of the trial process, and further that the High Court failed to consider material aspects including the gravity of the offence, the nature of evidence and the antecedents of the accused while granting bail. On the other hand, it has been argued that the present appeal does not concern the initial grant of bail but rather its cancellation and therefore must satisfy the stringent requirements laid down in judicial precedents which mandate that bail once granted should not be lightly interfered with unless there exist compelling and supervening circumstances such as misuse of liberty, interference with investigation or likelihood of absconding. It is in this context that the distinction between rejection of bail at the initial stage and cancellation of bail already granted assumes significance and the latter requires demonstration of cogent and overwhelming circumstances justifying such interference. Upon a careful analysis of the record it emerges that the respondent was not named in the First Information Report and was subsequently implicated based on statements which would require evaluation during trial, and further that the respondent had undergone incarceration for a substantial period exceeding six years prior to the grant of bail and the trial itself had progressed with several witnesses already examined. It is also noteworthy that co-accused persons similarly placed had been granted bail and the principle of parity was considered by the High Court while granting relief to the respondent. The absence of any allegation that the respondent has misused the liberty granted to him during the period subsequent to the grant of bail further weakens the case for cancellation and reinforces the principle that liberty once granted should not be curtailed in the absence of compelling reasons. The jurisprudence governing bail consistently emphasizes the need to strike a balance between individual liberty and societal interest and recognizes that pre-trial detention should not become punitive in nature, particularly where the trial is likely to take considerable time to conclude. Applying these principles to the present case it cannot be said that the order of the High Court suffers from non-application of mind or is manifestly arbitrary so as to justify interference and the considerations taken into account by the High Court appear to be consistent with the settled parameters governing grant of bail. The apprehension expressed by the appellant regarding threat to witnesses or obstruction of justice.

text: For quashing of Memo No.-918, Dated 15.07.2019, issued by the Respondent No.-6, District Superintendent of Education, Simdega, whereby and whereunder the charge sheet, Prapatra- Ka’ has been is-sued against the petitioner, since, the same kind of show cause notice issued vide letter No.- 1274, dated 08.08.2016 and assigning the same reason, the petitioner was terminated from the post of Intermediate Trained Teacher, vide Office Order issued by Respondent No.-6, vide Memo No.- 1682, Dated-04.10.2016, which was challenged by the petitioner in W.P.(S) No.-7142 of 2016, before this Hon’ble Court and the Hon’ble Court was pleased to quash the Order dated 04.10.2016, and it has been held by the Hon’ble Court that the petitioner is entitle to reinstatement in service with all consequential benefits. For staying the further proceeding in pursuance to the Memo No.-918, Dated 15.07.2019, issued by the Respondent No.-6, District Superintendent of Education, Simdega, or during the pendency of the writ petition the operation of the order contained in the Memo No.-918, Dated 15.07.2019, may kindly be stayed. For issuance of an appropriate Writ(s), Direction(s), Order(s) com-manding upon the respondents concern not to harass, torture and de-fame again and again without any valid reason." 2. The petitioner was selected in the meeting of Village Education Committee held on 13.06.2007 and was appointed as Para-Teacher vide appointment letter dated 14.06.2007. He joined on 15.06.2007 in the Upgraded Primary School, Saipur, Simdega. Thereafter, on 11.08.2007, the petitioner applied before the said Committee for grant of permission to pursue higher education i.e. graduation, and the Aam Sabha Committee vide its meeting held on 18.08.2007, has accepted the request of the petitioner for the same. The petitioner accordingly partakes in the examination of Graduation after following the proper channel. Thereafter, certificate of Graduation was issued to the petitioner by the Ranchi University. During course of scrutiny of educational qualification of the petitioner, it was found that he has acquired his degree from Simdega College, Simdega in the Academic Session 2006-09 as a regular student. Consequently, a show-cause was issued to the petitioner on 08.08.2016. The petitioner in his show cause reply vehemently and fervently conceded that he had appeared in the final examination for Bachelor of Arts with permission of the Village Education Committee, however, the District Education Establishment Committee, Simdega, observed that the petitioner was not granted permission for enhancing his educational qualification pursuant whereof his service was terminated by the District Superintendent of Education, Simdega. The petitioner being discontented with the aforesaid order of termination, moved before this Court vide W.P.(S) No.7142 of 2016, wherein this Court vide order dated 25.08.2018 allowed the writ petition directing the respondents to reinstate the petitioner and accept his joining. Subsequently, after the petitioner was reinstated and was discharging his duties to the satisfaction of all concerned, the respondents is-sued charge-sheet against the petitioner as contained in Memo No.918 Simdega, dated 15.07.2019, (Annexure-23 to the writ petition). The al-legations levelled against the petitioner in the charge-sheet are that he obtained his graduation degree in an irregular manner, and he acted in violation of the Government Servant Conduct Rules. In the said charge-sheet the petitioner was put to show cause as to why his graduation degree be not declared as illegal and a departmental proceeding be not initiated against him for violation of Government Servant Conduct Rules. Thus, the petitioner is now before this Court calling in question the impugned order as contained in Memo No.918 Simdega, dated 15.07.2019. Learned counsel representing the petitioner submits that the charge-sheet filed against the petitioner is bad in law and with an oblique motive as the allegation levelled against him with regard to enhancement.
title: Test #57: Legal Matter - JHC W.P. (S) No. 3885 of 2019

text: Habeas corpus petitions and petitions for protection filed by a partner, friend or a natal family member must be given a priority in listing and hearing before the court. A court must avoid adjourning the matter, or delays in the disposal of the case; In evaluating the locus standi of a partner or friend, the court must not make a roving enquiry into the precise nature of the relationship between the appellant and the person; The effort must be to create an environment conducive for a free and uncoerced dialogue to ascertain the wishes of the corpus; The court must ensure that the corpus is produced before the court and given the opportunity to interact with the judges in-person in chambers to ensure the privacy and safety of the detained or missing person. The court must conduct in-camera proceedings. The recording of the statement must be transcribed and the recording must be secured to ensure that it is not accessible to any other party; The court must ensure that the wishes of the detained person is not unduly influenced by the Court, or the police, or the natal family during the course of the proceedings. In particular, the court must ensure that the individuals(s) alleged to be detaining the individual against their volition are not present in the same environment as the detained or missing person. Similarly, in petitions seeking police protection from the natal family of the parties, the family must not be placed in the same environment as the petitioners; Upon securing the environment and inviting the detained or missing person in chambers, the court must make active efforts to put the detained or missing person at ease. The preferred name and pronouns of the detained or missing person may be asked. The person must be given a comfortable seating, access to drinking water and washroom. They must be allowed to take periodic breaks to collect themselves. The judge must adopt a friendly and compassionate demeanor and make all efforts to defuse any tension or discomfort. Courts must ensure that the detained or missing person faces no obstacles in being able to express their wishes to the court; A court while dealing with the detained or missing person may ascertain the age of the detained or missing person. However, the minority of the detained or missing person must not be used, at the threshold, to dismiss a habeas corpus petition against illegal detention by a natal family; The judges must showcase sincere empathy and compassion for the case of the detained or missing person. Social morality laden with homophobic or transphobic views or any personal predilection of the judge or sympathy for the natal family must be eschewed. The court must ensure that the law is followed in ascertaining the free will of the detained or missing person; If a detained or missing person expresses their wish to not go back to the alleged detainer or the natal family, then the person must be released immediately without any further delay; The court must acknowledge that some intimate partners may face social stigma and a neutral stand of the law would be detrimental to the fundamental freedoms of the appellant. Therefore, a court while dealing with a petition for police protection by intimate partners on the grounds that they are a same sex, transgender, inter-faith or inter-caste couple must grant an ad-interim measure, such as immediately granting police protection to the petitioners, before establishing the threshold requirement of being at grave risk of violence and abuse. The protection granted to intimate partners must be with a view to maintain their privacy and dignity; The Court shall not pass any directions for counselling or parental care when the corpus is produced before the Court. The role of the Court is limited to ascertaining the will of the person. The Court must not adopt counselling as a means of changing the mind of the appellant, or the detained/missing person; The Judge during the interaction with the corpus to ascertain their views must not attempt to change or influence the admission of the sexual orientation or gender identity of the appellant or the corpus.
title: Test #57: Courts Guidline in Dealing with Habeas Corpus Petitions

text: Learned counsel for the applicant submitted that however, on the basis of false allegation, applicant has been made accused in the present matter along with others but even only role of exhortation has been assigned to him and specific role of causing injury to the deceased has been assigned to co-accused Dileep. He further submitted that role of exhortation has also been assigned to co-accused Hari Chandra and he has already been released on bail by co-ordinate Bench of this Court vide order dated 23.08.2023 passed in Criminal Misc. Bail Application No. 35631 of 2023 and on facts, case of applicant is at par with him. He further submitted that applicant is not having any criminal his-tory and he is in jail in the present matter since 27.05.2024 i.e. for last more than nine months. Per contra, learned AGA however, opposed the prayer for bail but could not dispute the argument on facts advanced by learned counsel for the applicant. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record of the case. Considering the argument advanced by learned counsel for the applicant and the fact that role of causing injury to the deceased has not been assigned to the applicant and similarly placed co- accused Hari Chandra has already been released on bail by co- ordinate Bench of this Court and applicant is not having any criminal history and he is in jail in the present matter since 27.05.2024 i.e. for last more than nine months, in my view applicant is entitled to be released on bail. Accordingly, without expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, the instant bail application is allowed. Let the applicant- Banshiwala Alias Banshilal be released on bail in the aforesaid case on furnishing a personal bond and two sureties each in the like amount to the satisfaction of the court concerned with the following conditions: The applicant shall appear before the trial court on the dates fixed, unless his personal presence is exempted. The applicant shall not directly or indirectly, make inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or any po-lice officer or tamper with the evidence. The applicant shall not indulge in any criminal and anti-social activity. In case of breach of any of the above condition, the prosecution will be at liberty to move an application before this Court for cancellation of the bail of the applicant. It is clarified that the observations made herein are limited to the facts brought in by the parties pertaining to the disposal of bail application and the said observations shall have no bearing on the merits of the case during trial. FIR of the present case was lodged on 04.05.2019 against applicant and four others and according to FIR, on the exhortation of applicant, co-accused Hari Chandra, Pappu Koli and Rajo, co-accused Dileep made assault upon the niece of the informant through axe due to which, she sustained injuries and died. As per the records of the respondents, the petitioner has not been functioning as daily wager since the year 1991. The letter dated 20.04.1998 was issued by the respondent No.3 who had no legal legal authority to do so. No reliance can be placed on the same. Shri R.S.Pandey, learned counsel for the petitioner baldly dis-putes the averments in the counter affidavit. The denial on part of the petitioner of this specific averment does not hold water and is liable to be rejected. Further, even if the said submissions on part of the petitioner are taken on face value, it only raises the disputed questions of fact. The writ petition cannot be invoked to adjudicate the aforesaid disputed question of fact which entails introduction and appraisal of evidence. In aforesaid circumstances, this writ petition is disposed of with a di-rection that concerned District Basic Education Officer, will confront material in support that arrears of salary has already been paid and petitioner will be at liberty to file a reply to it, along with documents and thereafter District Basic Education Officer, will decide the issue within a short period.
title: Test #58: Legal Matter - AHC Cr. M. A.No. 29392 of 2024

text: The appellant completed the work ahead of schedule and submitted its final bill, however disputes arose between the parties regarding non-payment of certain claims including compensation for idle time of equipment, particularly a Backhoe Dredger, on account of delay in providing access to the site by the respondent. The disputes were referred to arbitration and the Arbitral Tribunal, upon consideration of the material on record and interpretation of the relevant clauses of the License Agreement, awarded compensation in favour of the appellant under Claim No.7 towards idle time charges. The respondent challenged the award under Section 34 of the Act, however the Learned Single Judge of the High Court declined to interfere, holding that the interpretation of contractual clauses by the Arbitral Tribunal was a plausible view and did not warrant interference within the limited scope of Section 34.
