Aggrieved thereby, the respondent preferred an appeal under Section 37 of the Act, and the Division Bench, by reinterpreting the contractual clauses, set aside the award in respect of Claim No.7, holding that idle time charges were payable only for major dredgers and not for a Backhoe Dredger. It is this judgment which is assailed before this Court. Upon a consideration of the rival submissions and the statutory framework governing arbitration, it is evident that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is a self-contained code intended to ensure expeditious resolution of disputes with minimal judicial interference, as reflected in Section 5 of the Act, and the grounds for setting aside an arbitral award under Section 34 are limited and do not permit a review on merits or substitution of the court’s view for that of the arbitral tribunal. The appellate jurisdiction under Section 37 is even more restricted and is confined to examining whether the court exercising jurisdiction under Section 34 has acted within the parameters prescribed therein, and it does not permit the appellate court to undertake an independent analysis of the merits of the award. It is a settled principle of law, as reiterated in decisions such as MMTC Ltd. v. Vedanta Ltd. and Konkan Railway Corporation Ltd. v. Chenab Bridge Project, that courts must exercise restraint in interfering with arbitral awards and should not disturb findings of fact or interpretation of contract unless the award is vitiated by patent illegality or is in conflict with public policy. In the present case, the Arbitral Tribunal has interpreted the relevant clauses of the License Agreement, including Clauses 38, 41 and 51, and has taken a plausible view that compensation for idle time of equipment is not restricted only to major dredgers and may extend to other equipment depending upon the circumstances, and such interpretation, being reasonable and based on the material on record, could not have been interfered with by the High Court. The Division Bench, by substituting its own interpretation of the contractual provisions, has effectively acted as a court of first appeal, which is impermissible under the scheme of the Act. The argument that the award suffers from patent illegality is also without merit, as the award contains detailed reasoning and does not violate any statutory provision or fundamental policy of law. It is well settled that where two views are possible, the view taken by the arbitral tribunal must prevail, and courts cannot interfere merely because another view appears to be more plausible. The doctrine of minimal judicial interference, which lies at the core of arbitration law, mandates that courts respect the autonomy of the arbitral process and uphold awards unless they fall within the limited grounds of interference prescribed by law. In view of the above analysis, it is clear that the Division Bench exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 37 of the Act in setting aside the arbitral award in respect of Claim No.7 and failed to adhere to the settled principles governing appellate interference in arbitral matters.
title: Test #58: Legal Matter - SCI SLP (C) No. 8803 of 2021

text: The Supreme Court of India, as the final arbiter of the Constitution, possesses the inherent power to correct its own errors to prevent a miscarriage of justice. This is primarily achieved through a Review Petition, a concept rooted in Article 137 of the Constitution of India. A Review Petition is an application made to the same bench that delivered the original judgment, requesting it to reconsider its decision. However, the scope of a review is extremely narrow. It is not a "Re-hearing" of the case or an opportunity to argue the merits again. Under the Supreme Court Rules, a review is maintainable only if there is an "Error Apparent on the Face of the Record" or if new and important evidence has been discovered which could not be produced earlier despite due diligence. Historically, the power of review was seen as the final stop in the judicial journey. However, a significant shift occurred in the year 2002 with the landmark judgment in "Rupa Ashok Hurra versus Ashok Hurra." In this case, the Supreme Court realized that even after a Review Petition is dismissed, there might be rare instances where a gross injustice persists. To address this, the Court "judicially legislated" a new remedy known as the Curative Petition. This is an extraordinary fallback mechanism intended to clear a "Pollution of the Broad Streams of Justice." Unlike a review, a curative petition is first circulated to a bench of the three most senior judges and the judges who passed the original judgment. It can only be entertained if the petitioner establishes a violation of the "Principles of Natural Justice," such as not being heard, or if there is an allegation of "Bias" against the judge. The terminology associated with these petitions is highly technical. A crucial term is "In Camera Proceedings," which refers to the fact that Review and Curative petitions are usually decided by judges in their private chambers through "Circulation" of papers, without oral arguments by advocates. Only in exceptional cases, such as those involving "Capital Punishment," does the Court allow an "Open Court Hearing" for a review. Another important term is the "Certificate of a Senior Advocate," which is a mandatory prerequisite for filing a Curative Petition. The Senior Advocate must certify that the petition meets the strict requirements laid down in the Rupa Hurra judgment. This acts as a "Gatekeeping Mechanism" to prevent the Court from being flooded with frivolous litigation that seeks to challenge the finality of judgments. The "Doctrine of Finality" is the underlying principle here. The law maintains that "Interest Reipublicae Ut Sit Finis Litium," which means it is in the interest of the State that there be an end to litigation. If every judgment could be challenged repeatedly, the legal system would collapse under its own weight. Therefore, the "Threshold" for a Curative Petition is set so high that very few succeed. In the history of Indian jurisprudence, only a handful of curative petitions have resulted in the setting aside of a previous order. This "Restraint" exercised by the Court ensures that while the door to justice is never completely closed, it is also not left "Ajar" for those who simply refuse to accept a final verdict. For a judicial typist or a stenographer, mastering words like "Coram," which refers to the composition of the bench, and "Suo Motu," where the court acts on its own motion, is vital. The use of the word "Dismissed in Limine" is also frequent in this context, meaning the petition was rejected at the very threshold without a detailed hearing. Understanding these nuances allows for greater "Contextual Accuracy" during high-speed typing sessions. The evolution of the Curative Petition remains a unique contribution of the Indian Judiciary to global "Constitutional Law," ensuring that the "Lapse of Time" or "Procedural Finality" never stands in the way of "Substantial Justice."
title: Test #59: Legal Term - The Review and Curative Petitions

text: The present appeal by special leave calls in question the correctness and legality of the judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court whereby the order of the learned Single Judge directing registration of a First Information Report was set aside and the controversy raised before this Court pertains to the interpretation and scope of Section 175(4) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 particularly with regard to the procedural safeguards available to public servants and the extent to which such protection operates at the stage of directing investigation by a Judicial Magistrate and the core issue for determination is whether the acts alleged against the accused police officers could be said to have been committed in the discharge of their official duties so as to attract the protective mechanism envisaged under the said provision and whether the Magistrate was justified in invoking such procedure instead of directing immediate registration of FIR in terms of settled law. The factual backdrop reveals that the appellant alleged commission of grave offences including sexual assault by police officials on multiple occasions and despite filing complaints before the competent authorities no effective steps were taken leading to invocation of jurisdiction under Section 210 read with Sections 173 and 175 of the BNSS seeking appropriate directions for registration of FIR and investigation into the allegations. The Judicial Magistrate upon receipt of the application invoked Section 175(4) and called for a report from the superior officer instead of directing immediate registration of FIR which led to further litigation before the High Court and subsequently before this Court. The learned Single Judge took the view that offences such as sexual assault cannot by any stretch of imagination be regarded as acts committed in discharge of official duties and therefore the protection under Section 175(4) would not apply and directed expeditious consideration of the application resulting in registration of FIR, however the Division Bench reversed the said findings holding that interference at the stage when proceedings were pending before the Magistrate was not warranted and that the statutory scheme required adherence to the procedure prescribed under the BNSS before invoking writ jurisdiction. Learned counsel for the appellant contended that the protection under Section 175(4) is not absolute and cannot be extended to criminal acts committed outside the scope of official duties and further argued that the law laid down in Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. mandates registration of FIR where a cognizable offence is disclosed without embarking upon an inquiry into the truthfulness of the allegations at the threshold stage whereas the respondents contended that the provision introduces a necessary safeguard to prevent frivolous prosecution of public servants and requires the Magistrate to follow the prescribed procedure before directing investigation. Upon a comprehensive consideration of the statutory framework and judicial precedents it is evident that sub-section (4) of Section 175 is not a standalone provision but operates as an additional procedural safeguard to be read harmoniously with sub-section (3) and the Magistrate while exercising jurisdiction must ensure compliance with both provisions and further the applicability of such safeguard is contingent upon the alleged act having a reasonable nexus with official duties which is to be determined on the facts of each case and cannot be presumed merely on the basis of the status of the accused as a public servant. In cases involving allegations of serious offences such as sexual assault the protection cannot be mechanically extended and the courts must adopt a cautious approach to ensure that the statutory safeguards are not misused to shield criminal conduct and at the same time prevent abuse of process through frivolous complaints and accordingly the legal position emerging is that while procedural safeguards under Section 175(4).
title: Test #59: Legal Matter - SCI Cr. A. No. 4629 of 2025

text: The case of Smt. Pallavi Saxena and 2 Others versus State of U.P. and 4 Others, decided by a Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad on the 21st day of November, 2023, is one of those rare judgments that goes beyond the strict boundaries of law and enters the realm of human compassion and judicial conscience. The matter was brought before this Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, and at its heart lay a deeply personal tragedy the story of a wife and her in-laws, all bound together by love and duty, struggling to keep a household alive while their husband and son lay motionless in a hospital bed, unable to speak, unable to act, and unable to recognise the faces that gathered around him each day. The husband in question, Shri Pranav Bhatnagar, was the sole breadwinner of his family. In the month of July 2017, he suffered a severe electric shock at his home in Ghaziabad, which caused a sudden cardiac arrest. He was rushed to a nearby hospital and revived through Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation. While his heartbeat was restored, the damage inflicted upon his brain by the prolonged deprivation of oxygen was severe and irreversible. Medical examinations confirmed lesions in the bilateral parieto-occipital lobes and basal ganglia. From the day of that accident onwards, Shri Pranav Bhatnagar had been lying in a state of total unconsciousness eyes sometimes open but seeing nothing, breathing but unaware, alive but entirely absent. He could not speak. He could not respond to any command or stimulus in any meaningful manner. He had, in the language of medicine, entered a Persistent Vegetative State, which he had not emerged from in over six years. Before passing any final order, this Court, through an interim direction dated 10th May, 2023, directed the constitution of a Medical Board under the authority of the District Administration, Ghaziabad, to physically examine Shri Pranav Bhatnagar and place a detailed report before the Court. The Medical Board, comprising qualified doctors including a physician, surgeon, and anaesthetist, duly examined the patient on the 22nd of May, 2023. Their findings were unambiguous and conclusive. The patient was found to be in an unconscious state, not oriented to time, place, or person. He could not speak, could not follow verbal commands, and showed no evidence of awareness or consciousness. A tracheostomy tube had been inserted in his neck to assist breathing. He was being fed through a gastrostomy tube inserted in his abdomen. His limbs showed spasticity. His reflexes, though exaggerated, were entirely involuntary. The Medical Board, in its formal opinion, concluded that the patient was suffering from severe hypoxic brain injury and was in a Persistent Vegetative State of Coma, with no realistic prospect of meaningful recovery. Upon receipt of this report, the Court turned its attention to the critical question of law: in the absence of any specific legislation governing the appointment of a guardian for a person in a comatose condition, could this Court step in and make such an appointment? Two existing statutes were examined the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Both Acts do provide for the appointment of support persons or guardians for mentally ill or disabled individuals. However, a careful reading of both enactments made it clear that they are designed for persons who retain some residual capacity to communicate, interact, or express their will, even if imperfectly. A person lying in a persistent vegetative state, with no consciousness whatsoever and no ability to interact in any form, falls entirely outside the scope of both these statutes. There was, therefore, a legislative vacuum a gap that Parliament had not addressed and that left families like that of Smt. Pallavi Saxena without any formal remedy under the existing law. It is precisely in such circumstances that the ancient doctrine of parents patriae becomes the guiding light of jurisprudence.
title: Test #60: Legal Matter - AHC Writ C No. 28192 of 2022

text: The present writ petition filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of India raises important questions regarding the legality and permissibility of certain medical practices, and in particular calls for determination of whether stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder can be offered as a routine treatment in the absence of clear statutory approval, scientific validation and regulatory control, and whether such practices are consistent with the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the New Drugs and Clinical Trial Rules, 2019, and the established principles governing medical negligence, professional conduct and standard of care, as recognised in judicial precedents of this Court. The petitioners have approached this Court in the nature of a Public Interest Litigation alleging that various clinics and medical institutions across the country are promoting and administering stem cell therapy as a cure or treatment for Autism Spectrum Disorder, despite there being no conclusive scientific evidence or statutory approval for the same, and that such practices are being carried out for commercial purposes without adherence to regulatory safeguards, thereby misleading patients and their families and exposing them to uncertain and potentially unsafe procedures. It is contended that the administration of such therapy, outside the framework of approved clinical trials, is in violation of the regulatory scheme contemplated under the New Drugs and Clinical Trial Rules, 2019, and that the absence of proper monitoring, ethical approval and compensation mechanisms further aggravates the issue. On behalf of the respondents, it has been argued that certain forms of stem cell therapy, particularly those involving minimal manipulation and use of a patient’s own cells, may not fall within the definition of a “drug” under Section 3(b) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and therefore may not attract the rigours of the statutory provisions governing drugs and clinical trials, and that such procedures are part of evolving medical practice which should not be unduly restricted. Having considered the rival submissions and the material placed on record, this Court finds that the core issue is not merely whether such therapy falls within the definition of a drug, but whether it satisfies the test of a recognised and acceptable medical practice in light of the current state of knowledge and established legal principles. It is a settled position of law that a medical practitioner is under a duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and caution while treating a patient, and such duty is measured against the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner as laid down in decisions such as Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, and any deviation from accepted medical practice may amount to negligence if it results in harm or risk to the patient. In the present case, the material on record indicates that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder has not been recognised as a standard or approved form of treatment by competent authorities, and authoritative guidelines and expert reports have consistently stated that such therapy should not be offered as a routine clinical service and should be restricted to properly regulated research or clinical trial settings. In such circumstances, offering the said therapy as a regular treatment for consideration would fall short of the standard of care expected from a medical professional and may also amount to professional misconduct. The argument based on patient consent and autonomy also does not advance the case of the respondents, as it is well established that consent must be based on adequate and reliable information, and where the efficacy and safety of a treatment are not sufficiently established, the requirement of informed consent cannot be said to be fully satisfied. Further, the right of a patient to choose a treatment does not include the right to demand or receive a treatment which is not recognised in law or supported by accepted medical practice.
title: Test #60: Legal Matter - SCI Writ (P) No. 369 of 2022

text: While the right to property ceased to be a fundamental right in 1978, it remains a robust constitutional right under Article 300-A, which mandates that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. In the contemporary Indian landscape, this power is primarily regulated by the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. This Act replaced the colonial-era law of 1894 to introduce a more humane approach to displacement. Under Section 4 of the Act, 2013, a Social Impact Assessment is mandatory for most projects to evaluate the effect on local livelihoods. Furthermore, Section 11 requires a preliminary notification to be published in the official gazette, marking the formal commencement of the acquisition process. The validity of any acquisition hinges on the definition of Public Purpose. As per Section-2 of the Act, this includes infrastructure projects, defense requirements, rural development, and housing for the poor. However, the determination of what constitutes a public purpose is often a matter of judicial scrutiny. The courts have consistently held that if the primary beneficiary of the acquisition is a private corporation without any substantial public utility, the exercise of eminent domain may be considered a colorable exercise of power. The facts of various disputes show that even the construction of a highway or a dam must be balanced against the displacement of indigenous communities. The “Rule of Law” requires that the State must act as a trustee of the land and not merely as an arbitrary landlord. One of the most litigated aspects of this terminology is the calculation of Market Value. Under Section 26, the Collector is tasked with determining the value based on recent sale deeds in the vicinity or the average sale price. To ensure fairness, the Act provides for a Solatium under Section 30, which is an additional amount of one hundred percent over the market value, paid as compensation for the involuntary nature of the acquisition. The “Doctrine of Restitution” suggests that the person whose land is taken should be placed in a financial position as close as possible to their status prior to the acquisition. Any failure to pay the determined amount within the stipulated time can lead to the “Lapse of Acquisition” under Section-24, returning the land to the original owner. Modern jurisprudence has shifted the focus from mere monetary compensation to comprehensive Rehabilitation and Resettlement. Under Section-31, the State is required to provide a package that includes housing, employment opportunities, and infrastructure at the resettlement site. This is based on the principle of Social Justice, recognizing that the loss of land often results in the loss of a way of life. The “Administrative Discretion” of the Land Acquisition Officer is subject to the oversight of the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Authority established under Section-51. This specialized body ensures that the grievances of the landowners regarding the measurement of land or the inadequacy of the award are addressed through a transparent judicial process. Accordingly, the doctrine of Eminent Domain remains a vital yet sensitive instrument of governance. It bridges the gap between the individual's “Right to Property” and the State's “Duty to Develop.” By ensuring that every acquisition is transparent and accountable, the law maintains the Sanctity of Individual Rights while paving the way for national progress and public utility infrastructure. The legal concept of Eminent Domain represents one of the most potent powers of the State, characterizing its inherent authority to take over private property for public use. This doctrine is founded upon two ancient Latin maxims: Salus Populi est Suprema Lex, meaning the welfare of the people is the supreme law, and Necessitas Publica est Major Quam Privata, which dictates that public necessity is greater than private necessity.
title: Test #61: The Legal Concept of Eminent Domain

text: The present petition raises an important question touching upon the effective implementation of the fundamental right to free and compulsory education guaranteed under Article 21A of the Constitution of India and the statutory mandate contained in Section 12 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, particularly with regard to the obligation of neighbourhood schools to admit children belonging to weaker sections and disadvantaged groups to the extent of twenty-five percent of the class strength, and the issue assumes significance in the context of ensuring substantive equality and social integration through access to elementary education in a non-discriminatory and inclusive environment. The petitioner approached the concerned authorities seeking admission of his children under the free education quota, however despite availability of vacant seats as indicated through information obtained under the Right to Information Act, the school authorities failed to act and the petitioner was constrained to approach the High Court, which dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the petitioner had not followed the prescribed online procedure, thereby effectively denying the benefit of free education to the children. It is evident from the record that the petitioner belonged to a weaker economic background and resided within the prescribed distance from the neighbourhood school, and further that the primary education officer had recommended admission of the children notwithstanding the non-compliance of online procedure, yet no effective relief was granted. Though the matter has now become infructuous due to passage of time, the issue requires examination in a broader perspective to ensure that such denial of rights does not recur in future, and therefore this Court has proceeded to examine the structural and procedural deficiencies in the implementation of Section 12 of the Act. Upon analysis of the statutory framework it is clear that the right to elementary education is a positive constitutional right imposing corresponding obligations upon multiple stakeholders including the State, local authorities, neighbourhood schools, parents and teachers, and the legislative intent underlying Section 12 is to ensure social inclusion by mandating admission of children from disadvantaged groups in common neighbourhood schools rather than segregated systems. However, practical difficulties such as digital illiteracy, lack of awareness, absence of transparency in the admission process, language barriers and absence of effective grievance redressal mechanisms have resulted in ineffective implementation of the statutory mandate, thereby defeating the constitutional objective. It is therefore necessary to streamline the procedure by ensuring availability of accessible application systems, establishment of help-desks, publication of available seats in advance, provision of a defect correction window and creation of an effective grievance redressal mechanism within prescribed timelines, and it is further essential that appropriate rules and regulations be framed under Section 38 of the Act to provide a binding and enforceable framework for implementation. In view of the above, this Court directs the appropriate authorities to formulate necessary subordinate legislation in consultation with the National and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights and to ensure strict compliance with the mandate of Section 12(1)(c) of the Act so as to make the fundamental right to education meaningful and effective, and the matter is directed to be listed for further monitoring.
title: Test #61: Legal Matter - SCI SLP C. No. 10105 of 2017

text: The petitioner was placed under suspension on 14th February 2025, following an anonymous complaint regarding alleged financial irregularities in the procurement of office equipment. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the prolonged suspension of a government servant without the issuance of a charge memo is legally sustainable under the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Classification, Control, and Appeal Rules, 1991. The petitioner argues that the power of suspension is being used as a punitive measure rather than an interim administrative step, thereby violating the fundamental right to life and livelihood under Article 21. The facts of the case reveal that despite the lapse of ninety days from the date of the initial order, the authorities have neither initiated a regular departmental inquiry nor reviewed the necessity of continuing the suspension. The learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri P. V. Krishnaiah, argues that the mandate of Section 20 of the CCA Rules has been completely ignored. He submits that as per the latest administrative guidelines, a preliminary investigation must be completed within a reasonable timeframe. He contends that the respondent authorities have acted in a mechanical manner, failing to record any subjective satisfaction that the presence of the petitioner in the office would interfere with the investigation or tamper with the evidence. The petitioner emphasizes that being kept away from duties based on a vague allegation causes irreparable loss to his reputation and career progression. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Services argues that the suspension is not a punishment but a necessary step to ensure an impartial inquiry into the serious charges of embezzlement. He submits that under Section 8 of the CCA Rules, 1991, the appointing authority is vested with the power to place a member of the service under suspension where an investigation into a criminal offence or disciplinary case is contemplated. He contends that the delay in issuing the charge sheet was due to the voluminous nature of the records and the complexity of the audit trails. The State maintains that the petitioner is being paid the mandatory subsistence allowance and therefore cannot claim a violation of his financial rights. The respondent further argues that the court should not interfere with the internal administrative decisions of the department at such a premature stage. Having heard both sides and perused the service file produced by the department, this Court observes that the sword of suspension cannot be kept hanging over an employee indefinitely. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that the right to a speedy inquiry is an integral part of fair play. The law is well-settled that if the charge sheet is not served within ninety days, the suspension order must be reviewed by the competent authority to decide whether it should be extended with recorded reasons. In the present case, the "Rule of Law" requires that the state must justify the deprivation of the petitioner's right to work. The "Administrative Apathy" in failing to draft a simple charge memo for three months suggests that the authorities are using suspension as a tool for harassment. The Court finds that the continued suspension of the petitioner is hit by the vice of arbitrariness. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that if the investigation is not progressing and the employee is not in a position to influence the witnesses, he should be reinstated to a non-sensitive post. The "Directive Principles" of state action require that the power of the employer should be exercised for the welfare of the service and not for the victimisation of the staff. The "Administrative Discretion" to suspend is not unfettered and must stand the test of proportionality. A government servant, even under a cloud of suspicion, is entitled to a "Reasonable Opportunity" to defend himself through a time-bound process.
title: Test #62: Legal Matter - APHC Writ P. No. 19442 of 2025

text: The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act delegates vast rule-making powers to the executive. The IT Rules themselves have been amended at least annually since 2021. Govt’s Fact Check Unit was struck down by the Bombay high court in 2024, barely a year after its notification. Courts can’t keep pace: by the time one provision is struck down, two replace it. The current IT Rules consultations have a 15-days deadline. The implementation timeline for the last one was 10 days. When the IT secretary reportedly says that platforms should have started preparing to implement based on consultation drafts, it appears that outcomes are predetermined. Over the past month, several internet users have received notifications from X or Instagram that some of their posts, or even complete accounts, have been censored and blocked. Facebook pages with millions of followers have been banned. It’s not just users. Supabase, a service developer use for building apps, found itself blocked in India, without notice. It was reinstalled only after developers complained, and Supabase tagged the IT minister on X. But why is this happening? In March 2015, the Supreme Court delivered what remains the foundational verdict on online speech in this country. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the court struck down the breathtakingly overbroad section 66A of the IT Act, which had been used to jail people for Facebook posts. But the case did something equally important that gets less attention. The court strengthened the safe harbour provision under section 79, which protects platforms from liability for what users say online. Until then, the provision’s ambiguity was being exploited to pressure platforms into pulling down even perfectly legal speech by sending informal requests. The SC also upheld the blocking powers under section 69A, reasoning that it came with structural safeguards: reasons recorded in writing, orders issued at least by a joint secretary-level officer, examined by a review committee. Crucially, the court said that the affected user, if identifiable, needed to be informed and given a hearing. In the eleven years since the judgment, these protections have been dismantled, and a digital censorship infrastructure has emerged. First, amendments to the IT Rules in 2021 expanded the scope of section 79, bringing digital news outlets under a provision that doesn’t regulate them. Despite two High Court orders staying these provisions, the govt circumvented them via notifications and administrative practices. Two, the home ministry’s Sahyog portal functions, without parliamentary sanction, as a hotline from govt to platforms for takedown orders under Section 79. Thirty-three states, seven central agencies, and 72 companies are onboarded. Users neither receive notice nor are orders provided on request. X Corp told the Karnataka high court it received 29,118 such requests in the first half of 2025, roughly 160 a day. At this volume, no platform can assess legality, and platforms end up censoring by default to preserve safe harbour, precisely what the SC had prevented in the Shreya Singhal case. Three, the amendments to IT Rules in Feb 2026 compressed the compliance window for blocking orders from 36 to three hours, the shortest in the world. News reports suggest a further reduction to one hour. This applies to all speech without exemptions for satire, journalism, or political criticism, and erasing any distinction between emergency and contestable orders. Meanwhile, blocking orders and review committee proceedings remain secret. At this scale and speed, platforms almost always act first, think never, censor always. Four, the architecture has widened laterally: more govt agencies now have the power to block speech under section 69A. The proposed amendments to rule 8(1) would extend oversight of the ministry of information and broadcasting from registered publishers to all users posting news content or commenting on them, including ordinary Indians sharing videos of potholed roads.
title: Test #62: New Digital Rules Diluting SCI Safeguards

text: The Petitioner, a small-scale manufacturing unit, seeks the issuance of a Writ of Certiorari to quash the order of the Assistant Commissioner of State Tax. The impugned order, dated 20th January 2025, involves the cancellation of the Petitioner's GST registration and the imposition of a heavy penalty. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the summary cancellation of a GST license, without providing a clear and specific show cause notice, satisfies the mandate of Section 29 of the Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The Petitioner argues that the department failed to adhere to the principles of natural justice and that the electronic portal was used as a tool for administrative convenience rather than for ensuring fair play. In response, the learned Standing Counsel appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh argues that the state is a trustee of public revenue and must act swiftly to curb the menace of bogus firms and input tax credit (ITC) fraud. He submits that under Section 16 of the Act, 2017, the entitlement to credit is subject to the condition that the taxpayer maintains a verifiable place of business. He contends that during a surprise field inspection conducted under Section 67, the premises were found locked, and no signboards were visible. The State maintains that the portal records show a pattern of suspicious transactions that warranted the immediate suspension of registration to prevent further loss to the exchequer. The respondent further argues that the Petitioner has an alternative remedy of filing an appeal under Section 107 and should not have approached the High Court directly. Having heard both sides and perused the screenshots of the portal notifications, this Court observes that the right to carry on trade and business is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that “Taxation” is not a penalty but a contribution to the state, and the process of collection must be dignified and lawful. The law is well-settled that a show because notice is the foundation of any quasi-judicial proceeding. If the foundation is shaky, the entire edifice of the final order must fall. In the present case, the “Rule of Law” requires that the department should have granted a physical hearing. The “Administrative Apathy” in using a pre-drafted, “one-line” reason for cancellation in the digital notice is a gross violation of the Statutory Framework. The Court finds that the cancellation order is hit by the vice of non-application of mind. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that the “GST Portal” is a facilitator and not a substitute for the statutory procedure. The “Directive Principles” of state action require the government to promote small-scale industries rather than strangulating them through technical hurdles. The “Administrative Discretion” to cancel registration must be balanced against the “Doctrine of Proportionality.” A taxpayer who has been paying taxes for years should not be treated as a criminal based on a single inspection report that was prepared without his presence. Consequently, this Court finds that the Petitioner has established a clear case of procedural high-handedness. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to restore the GST registration of the Petitioner within forty-eight hours of receiving this order. However, the department is at liberty to issue a “Fresh Show Cause Notice” with specific allegations and provide the Petitioner with a “Reasonable Opportunity” for a personal hearing. Furthermore, the Commissioner of State Tax is directed to issue a “General Circular” to all field officers to ensure that notices are not issued in a vague or cryptic manner. The Petitioner shall be allowed to file his pending returns without any late fees for the period during which the registration remained suspended. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions.
title: Test #63: Legal Matter - AHC Writ Tax No. 30550 of 2025

text: These appeals raise a substantial question of law concerning the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and the determination of proprietary rights over the trademark “Gloster” in the context of a corporate insolvency resolution process, wherein the correctness of the judgment of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dated 25.01.2024 is assailed and the controversy centres around whether the Adjudicating Authority could have declared the trademark “Gloster” as an asset of the Corporate Debtor and consequently of the Successful Resolution Applicant in the absence of a properly instituted proceeding for adjudication of title. The factual matrix reveals that the Corporate Debtor, Fort Gloster Industries Limited, was subjected to insolvency proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC and a resolution plan submitted by the appellant-SRA was approved by the Committee of Creditors with a majority vote share, however during the pendency of approval, Respondent No.1 filed an application under Section 60(5) seeking exclusion of the trademark “Gloster” from the assets of the Corporate Debtor on the ground that the said trademark was not its property but belonged to the respondent by virtue of various agreements including Technical Collaboration Agreement dated 02.05.1995, Trademark Agreement dated 29.07.2004, Supplemental Agreement dated 15.07.2008 and Deed of Assignment dated 20.09.2017, and it was contended that the assignment of trademark was absolute and effective and that the Corporate Debtor had no subsisting right, title or interest therein. The Adjudicating Authority while considering the said application held that the assignment was invalid being in violation of the restraint order passed by the BIFR and further held that the transaction was hit by Sections 43 and 45 of the IBC as a preferential and undervalued transaction, and accordingly concluded that the trademark “Gloster” formed part of the assets of the Corporate Debtor, however the NCLAT reversed the said finding holding that the Adjudicating Authority had exceeded its jurisdiction and that in the absence of any application by the Resolution Professional under the avoidance provisions, such a declaration could not have been made. Learned counsel for the appellant contended that the Adjudicating Authority was empowered to examine such transactions and that the assignment was a sham and void transaction, whereas learned counsel for the respondent contended that the issue of title to a trademark is beyond the scope of Section 60(5) and cannot be adjudicated in summary insolvency proceedings, and that the assignment operated independently of registration and vested proprietary rights in the respondent. Upon consideration of the rival submissions and the statutory scheme it becomes evident that the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority under Section 60(5) though wide is not unlimited and is confined to matters arising out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution process, and disputes which are independent of insolvency and pertain to determination of civil rights such as title to intellectual property cannot be conclusively adjudicated in such proceedings, particularly when the resolution plan itself acknowledges the existence of rival claims and does not conclusively settle the issue of ownership. It is also significant that no application was filed by the Resolution Professional under Sections 43, 45 or 66 of the IBC to avoid the transaction and the respondent was not put to notice regarding any such challenge, and therefore the Adjudicating Authority could not have, on the mere filing of an application by the respondent, proceeded to declare title in favour of the appellant, as such an exercise would amount to enlarging the scope of Section 60(5) beyond its intended limits and would encroach upon the jurisdiction of competent civil fora. In view of the settled principles that the residuary jurisdiction under the IBC cannot be invoked for adjudication of matters.
title: Test #63: Legal Matter - SCI Trademark Insolvency Case

text: In response, the learned Standing Counsel for the Government of NCT of Delhi argues that the petitioner accepted the terms of the contract, which explicitly stated that she would not be entitled to any benefits beyond the consolidated monthly remuneration. He submits that the school operates on a limited budget and that providing paid leave for six months to guest teachers would cause an "Administrative Stalemate" and financial burden. He contends that the petitioner’s services are required on a day-to-day basis to ensure the continuity of education for the students. The State maintains that the "Contractual Autonomy" of the employer must be respected and that the petitioner is at liberty to rejoin the services after her period of absence, subject to the availability of a vacancy, but without any claim for back wages. Having heard both sides and perused the statutory provisions, this Court observes that today, being International Women's Day, it is essential to reiterate that the "Reproductive Rights" of a woman are part of her personal liberty. The Delhi High Court emphasizes that the purpose of the Maternity Benefit Act is to ensure that a woman is able to balance her professional responsibilities with her role as a mother without facing economic hardship. The law is well-settled that the benefits under this Act are "Status-Neutral." Whether a woman is a daily wager, a contractual worker, or a permanent officer, she is entitled to the protection of the law. The "Biological Reality" of womanhood cannot be used as a tool to push women out of the workforce. The Court finds that the stand taken by the respondent is not only legally untenable but also morally regressive. The "Right to Motherhood" is an inalienable right, and any hurdle placed by the employer in the exercise of this right is a violation of the "Rule of Law." The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that the "Maternity Benefit Act" overrides any private contract or service rule to the contrary. The "Social Security" of women in the unorganized or contractual sector is a matter of national priority. A woman should not have to choose between her job and her child. The "Welfare State" has a proactive duty to ensure that the workplace is inclusive and supportive of the needs of women employees. Consequently, this Court finds that the petitioner is entitled to the full range of benefits. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to "Sanction Maternity Leave" of twenty-six weeks to the petitioner and pay her the full salary for the said period as if she were on duty. The "Arrears of Wages" shall be calculated and paid to the petitioner within six weeks from today. Furthermore, the respondent is directed to ensure that the petitioner is allowed to "Resume her Duties" in the same capacity without any break in service. The Directorate of Education is directed to issue a "General Circular" to all schools in the national capital territory, affirming that maternity benefits are mandatory for all female employees, including guest teachers. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that "Justice" for women in the workplace is the cornerstone of a civilized society. The "Registry" of this Court is directed to communicate this order to the Chief Secretary of Delhi for immediate compliance and policy oversight to prevent future litigation on this settled issue. No order as to costs. Order pronounced in the open court on this 8th day of March, 2026. This Writ Petition is filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a Writ of Mandamus to direct the respondent authorities to grant maternity leave and consequential financial benefits to the petitioner, who is working as a guest teacher in a government-aided school. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the benefits under the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, can be denied to an employee solely on the ground that her employment is purely contractual or temporary in nature.
title: Test #64: Legal - DHC Writ P. (C) No. 3820 of 2022

text: The present criminal appeal by the State under Article 136 of the Constitution of India calls in question the legality and correctness of the judgment dated 26.08.2014 passed by the High Court whereby the High Court set aside the well-reasoned judgment of conviction rendered by the trial Court under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and acquitted the respondent by extending benefit of doubt, and the central issue that arises for consideration in these proceedings pertains to the evidentiary value, reliability and admissibility of the dying declaration recorded in accordance with law and whether the High Court was justified in discarding the same on hyper-technical and conjectural grounds. The prosecution case in brief is that on 07.12.2009 the respondent poured kerosene oil upon his wife Saro Devi at their residence and set her ablaze by lighting a matchstick, as a result of which she sustained extensive burn injuries and was shifted to hospital where despite treatment she ultimately succumbed to her injuries on 15.01.2010, and during the course of investigation the statement of the deceased was recorded on 08.12.2009 by the Tehsildar-cum-Executive Magistrate after obtaining medical opinion regarding her fitness, which statement was treated as a dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Upon completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed and the trial Court after appreciation of evidence convicted the respondent and sentenced him to life imprisonment, however the High Court in appeal reversed the conviction and acquitted the respondent primarily on the ground of alleged inconsistencies regarding the time and manner of recording of the dying declaration and by placing reliance on hostile witnesses and defence evidence suggesting self-immolation. Learned counsel for the appellant-State contended that the dying declaration recorded by a competent Magistrate in the presence of independent witnesses clearly established the guilt of the respondent and that the High Court committed grave error in discarding such crucial evidence, whereas learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the dying declaration was suspicious and unreliable and that the prosecution failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Upon consideration of the rival submissions and the material on record it is evident that the dying declaration in the present case was recorded by an independent public officer after obtaining medical opinion and in the presence of responsible officers and there is no material to suggest tutoring, coercion or manipulation, and it is well settled that a truthful and voluntary dying declaration can form the sole basis of conviction without corroboration, and minor discrepancies regarding time or manner of recording do not affect its evidentiary value. The High Court erred in rejecting the dying declaration on speculative grounds and in placing undue reliance on the testimony of hostile witnesses whose statements were inconsistent and unsupported by independent evidence, and further the defence theory of self-immolation does not inspire confidence in view of the consistent prosecution evidence and surrounding circumstances. It is also well settled that in an appeal against acquittal interference is warranted where the judgment of the High Court is perverse or based on misappreciation of evidence resulting in miscarriage of justice, and in the present case the High Court failed to properly appreciate the cogent and reliable evidence on record and adopted an erroneous approach in reversing the conviction. Consequently, this Court is of the considered view that the prosecution has proved the guilt of the respondent beyond reasonable doubt and the impugned judgment of acquittal passed by the High Court is liable to be set aside, and accordingly the appeal is allowed and the judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by the trial Court are restored and the respondent is directed to surrender forthwith to undergo the remaining sentence in accordance with law.
title: Test #64: Legal Matter - SCI Cr. A. No. 430 of 2018

text: The petitioner is the eldest daughter of a deceased agriculturist who passed away intestate in January 2021. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether a daughter, by virtue of her birth, has an equal right as a coparcener in the ancestral property of her father, regardless of her marital status or the date of her marriage. The petitioner argues that the local Tahsildar rejected her application for a succession certificate based on a stereotypical notion that a married daughter ceases to be a member of her parental family, thereby violating the fundamental principles of gender justice enshrined under Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Revenue argues that the petitioner was married in the year 1998, well before the central amendment came into force. He submits that the family had already entered into an oral partition prior to the death of the father, and the revenue records were updated based on the possession of the sons. He contends that the petitioner did not raise any objection for over two decades and therefore her claim is barred by the doctrine of laches. The State maintains that the revenue officials act based on the "Record of Rights" and cannot adjudicate complex questions of title which are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the civil courts. The respondent further argues that the mutation of names is a fiscal entry and does not create or extinguish any substantive right over the property. Having heard both sides and perused the genealogical tree of the family, this Court observes that today, being International Women's Day, it is fitting to reaffirm the constitutional mandate of gender equality. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that the right to property is a significant tool for the empowerment of women. The law is well-settled that a daughter's right to a share in ancestral property is absolute and is not dependent on whether her father was alive at the time of the 2005 amendment. The "Patriarchal Mindset" that views daughters as liabilities or as outsiders after marriage is a hurdle to the social and economic progress of the nation. In the present case, the oral partition claimed by the brothers has no legal sanctity unless it is supported by a registered deed or a decree of a competent court. The Court finds that the revenue authorities failed in their duty to recognize the "Succession Rights" of the petitioner. Mutation is not just a formality; it is often the basis for obtaining crop loans and government subsidies, which are essential for an agriculturist. Denying a woman her name in the revenue records is equivalent to denying her identity as a farmer. The High Court refers to the principles of "Distributive Justice," holding that the state must ensure that women have equal access to land resources. The "Administrative Inaction" in this case has forced a woman to litigate for her rightful share, which is a matter of serious concern. Consequently, this Court finds that the petitioner has established a prima facie case of discrimination. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to "Set Aside the Rejection Order" and process the mutation application of the petitioner by including her name as a joint owner of the subject land along with her brothers. The Tahsildar is directed to issue a "Joint Pattadar Passbook" to the petitioner within six weeks. Furthermore, the District Collector is directed to issue a "General Circular" to all revenue officers in the district, sensitizing them about the equal rights of daughters in ancestral property to prevent such unnecessary litigation in the future. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment serves as a tribute to the spirit of womanhood and reinforces the principle that "Justice" is not a privilege but a right that must be accessible to every daughter of this land. The "Registry" of this Court is directed to communicate this order to the Principal Secretary of the Revenue Department for immediate compliance and policy oversight.
title: Test #65: Legal - APHC Gender Inequality & Right to Inheritence

text: The present civil appeals arising out of the judgment dated 25.01.2024 passed by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal raise substantial questions of law regarding the scope and ambit of jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and the determination of title to intellectual property assets during the corporate insolvency resolution process, and the controversy essentially revolves around whether the Adjudicating Authority while dealing with an application under the Code could declare the trademark “Gloster” as an asset of the Corporate Debtor and consequently vest the same in the Successful Resolution Applicant despite the existence of rival claims and prior agreements governing the said trademark. The factual matrix discloses that the Corporate Debtor Fort Gloster Industries Limited was subjected to insolvency proceedings under Section 9 of the Code and a resolution plan submitted by the Successful Resolution Applicant was approved by the Committee of Creditors and attained finality, however during the pendency of approval proceedings the respondent Gloster Cables Limited filed an application asserting exclusive ownership rights over the trademark “Gloster” and sought exclusion of the said trademark from the assets of the Corporate Debtor on the basis of prior agreements including Technical Collaboration Agreement dated 02.05.1995 Trademark Agreement dated 29.07.2004 Supplemental Trademark Agreement dated 15.07.2008 and Deed of Assignment dated 20.09.2017. The Adjudicating Authority upon consideration of the material on record held that the assignment of the trademark was invalid being in violation of the restraint order passed by the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction and further held that the transaction was hit by provisions relating to preferential and undervalued transactions under Sections 43 and 45 of the Code and accordingly declared the trademark as an asset of the Corporate Debtor, however the Appellate Tribunal reversed the findings holding that the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction and that in absence of a proper application by the Resolution Professional such findings could not have been recorded. Learned counsel for the appellant contended that the assignment was void ab initio and that the trademark formed part of the assets of the Corporate Debtor whereas learned counsel for the respondent contended that the assignment was valid and that title had already passed prior to commencement of the insolvency proceedings and that the issue of title could not be adjudicated in summary proceedings under the Code. Upon a careful consideration of the rival submissions and the statutory framework it is evident that the resolution plan itself recognized the existence of rival claims over the trademark and did not confer an absolute and undisputed title in favour of the appellant and the jurisdiction under Section 60(5) though wide is not unlimited and cannot be invoked to adjudicate complex questions of title which do not arise directly out of or in relation to the insolvency resolution process and the Adjudicating Authority cannot under the guise of exercising residuary jurisdiction enlarge the scope of proceedings and grant declaratory reliefs affecting substantive rights of parties dehors the insolvency proceedings. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority must have a direct nexus with the insolvency resolution process and cannot extend to matters which require detailed examination of evidence and independent adjudication under appropriate forums and in the present case the determination of ownership of the trademark involves intricate questions of fact and law arising from contractual arrangements statutory rights and prior transactions which cannot be conclusively decided within the limited framework of insolvency proceedings. Consequently the finding of the Adjudicating Authority declaring the trademark as an asset of the Corporate Debtor is unsustainable in law and the Appellate Tribunal was justified in setting aside the said finding.
title: Test #65: Legal Matter - SCI Civil. A. No. 2996 of 2024

text: The facts of the case reveal that the petitioner emerged successful in the written examination and was called for the verification of certificates. However, during the interview stage, her candidature was rejected on the ground that her degree, obtained through the distance mode, is not equivalent to a regular degree for the purpose of teaching posts. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Higher Education argues that the state has the “Prerogative” to set higher standards for the recruitment of teachers to ensure the quality of education in government institutions. He submits that the Equivalence Committee, consisting of academic experts, has specifically recommended that for the specialized post of a Lecturer, a regular degree involving face-to-face institutional interaction is essential. He contends that the “Judicial Review” of academic policy is limited and that the Court should not interfere with the wisdom of the experts unless the decision is patently irrational or biased. The State maintains that “Equivalency” is not a matter of right and that the burden of proving that a distance degree is at par with a regular degree lies heavily on the candidate. Having heard both sides and perused the expert committee reports alongside the UGC circulars, this Court observes that the “Policy of Equivalency” must be consistent and transparent. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that while the state can prescribe qualifications, it cannot act in defiance of the national standards set by the UGC. The law is well-settled that the degrees awarded through distance mode by recognized universities are to be treated as equivalent to corresponding degrees of traditional universities for the purpose of employment under the Central and State Governments. In the present case, the state has failed to provide any “Empirical Data” or “Reasoned Analysis” to show how the petitioner's degree is inferior to a regular degree in terms of subject knowledge or pedagogical skills. The Court finds that the “Rejection of Candidature” at the final stage of the selection process has caused immense mental agony to the petitioner. The “Rule of Law” requires that the eligibility criteria must be clearly defined in the recruitment notification itself. Changing the rules of the game after the process has started is a violation of the “Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation.” The High Court refers to several precedents where it was held that if a degree is recognized for the purpose of higher studies, it cannot be ignored for the purpose of employment. The “Administrative Discretion” to determine equivalency should be exercised to promote inclusivity rather than to exclude qualified candidates on the basis of the mode of learning. Consequently, this Court finds that the petitioner is entitled to the relief sought. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to “Set Aside the Disqualification” of the petitioner and treat her degree as equivalent to the regular degree for all intents and purposes related to the present recruitment. The State is directed to complete the “Interview and Selection Process” for the petitioner within six weeks and, if she is found otherwise meritorious, appoint her to the post of Lecturer with all consequential benefits, including seniority from the date her peers were appointed. Furthermore, the State Council of Higher Education is directed to issue a “Comprehensive Guideline” on equivalency to prevent future litigation on the status of distance education degrees. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that “Education” in any form is a tool for empowerment and that the state must be a model employer that values merit over the technicalities of the delivery system. The “Registry” of this Court is directed to communicate this order to the Secretary of the Higher Education Department for immediate compliance. No order as to costs. Order pronounced in the open court on this 9th day of March, 2026.
title: Test #66: Legal Matter - APHC Writ (P) No. 20440 of 2025

text: The present appeals arise out of the common judgment dated 17.01.2025 passed by the High Court whereby the High Court allowed the writ petitions filed by the respondents and directed the State to consider their candidature for appointment as Ayurvedic Staff Nurse, and since the appeals involve common questions of law and facts they are being disposed of by this common judgment. The State has impugned the orders passed by the High Court contending that the respondents were admitted to the Ayurvedic Nursing Training Course pursuant to advertisement issued for admission and not for appointment and that mere admission in the course does not confer any right of appointment. It has been submitted that as per Government Order dated 12.11.1986 the procedure was prescribed only for selection of candidates for training and not for appointment and that Clause 9 of the advertisement clearly provided that in case a candidate is selected for government service after completion of training, such candidate shall be required to serve the State for a minimum period of five years and execute a bond, however such condition did not guarantee appointment. It has further been contended that subsequent to the notification dated 21.10.2011 private institutions were also permitted to impart training in Ayurvedic Nursing Course resulting in a substantial increase in the number of candidates and therefore the earlier practice of granting automatic appointment could not be continued and a proper selection process was required to be followed through the Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Services Selection Commission in terms of notification dated 15.12.2014. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondents submitted that from 1986 till 2015 the consistent practice of the State was to grant appointment to candidates who successfully completed the training course and therefore the respondents had a legitimate expectation of appointment particularly when they were admitted in a government institution and the advertisement issued at the time of their admission did not expressly deny such appointment. It was further contended that the respondents had completed the training and had made representations seeking appointment which were rejected by the State on the ground of absence of service rules and change in selection process, which according to the respondents was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. Upon consideration of rival submissions and the material placed on record it is evident that the earlier practice of granting appointment to candidates who completed training was based on the limited number of seats and availability of vacancies at that point of time when only government institutions were imparting training and the number of candidates was small, however after the policy change permitting private institutions to impart training the number of candidates increased manifold and the available vacancies became insufficient to accommodate all candidates and therefore the State was justified in introducing a structured selection process to ensure that the most meritorious candidates are selected. It is well settled that the doctrine of legitimate expectation cannot be invoked to claim a right which is not founded on any statutory provision or express promise and that such expectation must be reasonable and based on consistent past practice which has not undergone any substantial change, and in the present case the change in policy and circumstances clearly indicates that the earlier practice cannot be continued and the respondents cannot claim automatic appointment merely on the basis of admission to the training course. It is also evident that no candidate admitted after the session 2010-11 was granted appointment under the old system except a few appointments made pursuant to court orders and therefore there is no discrimination or violation of Article 14 as similarly situated candidates have not been treated differently.
title: Test #66: Legal Matter - SCI Civil A. No. 14250 of 2025

text: In response, the learned Standing Counsel appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh argues that “Pay Scales” are a matter of policy and are determined by the executive based on the mode of recruitment and the financial capacity of the exchequer. He submits that the petitioner’s appointment was a “Stop-gap Arrangement” and does not confer any right to claim parity with those who have cleared the competitive examination conducted by the Selection Board. He contends that the “Doctrine of Equal Pay for Equal Work” is not a fundamental right but a directive principle that must be balanced against the “Administrative Efficiency” of the department. The State maintains that the petitioner is a “Contractual Appointee” who accepted the terms of his engagement voluntarily and is therefore estopped from challenging the salary structure at this late stage. Having heard both sides and perused the service records, this Court observes that the “Dignity of Labor” requires that every person be paid a fair wage for the work performed. The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that the state must be a “Model Employer” and should not resort to “Litigious Resistance” when the facts clearly demonstrate a case of discrimination. The law is well-settled that if the qualifications, duties, and responsibilities are the same, the mode of recruitment cannot be used as a shield to deny equal pay. In the present case, the petitioner has been discharging his duties with “Unblemished Record” for ten years, proving that he is as competent as any regular teacher. The “Financial Hardship” of the state is not a valid ground to bypass the constitutional mandate of fairness. The Court finds that the “Artificial Distinction” created by the respondents is hit by the vice of irrationality. The right to equal pay is an integral part of the right to life under Article 21, as a meager salary affects the “Quality of Life” and the ability to maintain a family. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that the state cannot continue to employ persons on a “pittance” for years on end. The “Rule of Law” requires that the state should provide a “Level Playing Field” for all its employees. The “Administrative Discretion” to fix wages must be exercised within the bounds of “Social Justice.” A teacher who is worried about his basic survival cannot be expected to provide the best education to the students. Consequently, this Court finds that the petitioner has made out a strong case for the grant of minimum of the pay scale. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to “Fix the Pay” of the petitioner at the minimum of the regular pay scale applicable to the post of Lecturer, without any allowances, from the date of filing of this petition. The “Arrears of Salary” shall be calculated and paid to the petitioner within a period of twelve weeks. Furthermore, the State is directed to consider the “Regularization” of the petitioner’s services in accordance with the existing rules and seniority. The “Director of Education” is directed to ensure that this order is implemented in “Letter and Spirit” to avoid further harassment of the teaching community. Accordingly, the petition stands allowed with these mandatory directions. This judgment reinforces the principle that “Equal Work” must be met with “Equal Pay” to uphold the moral and legal fabric of our democracy. The “Registry” of this Court is directed to communicate this order to the Chief Secretary of Uttar Pradesh for policy review and compliance. No order as to costs. Order pronounced in the open court on this 9th day of March, 2026. He submits that the state cannot act as an exploitative employer by taking full-time work from an individual while denying him a "Living Wage" that is commensurate with his professional status. He contends that the "Classification" between regular and ad-hoc employees for the purpose of remuneration is arbitrary when their duties are indistinguishable.
title: Test #67: Legal Matter - AHC Writ-A No. 15420 of 2025

text: These appeals by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution of India call in question the legality and correctness of the common judgment dated 19th December, 2023 passed by the High Court whereby the High Court allowed the writ petitions and set aside the appointment of the appellant as the Vice-Chancellor of the Puducherry Technological University while permitting him to continue temporarily to avoid administrative vacuum, and the core issue arising for consideration pertains to the validity of the constitution of the Search-cum-Selection Committee under Section 14(5) of the Puducherry Technological University Act, 2019 vis-a-vis Regulation 7.3 of the UGC Regulations, 2018 and the applicability of the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 of the Constitution. The facts reveal that the University was established under the PTU Act, 2019 and the appointment of the Vice-Chancellor was required to be made from a panel recommended by a duly constituted Search-cum-Selection Committee consisting of persons of eminence, and pursuant to notification dated 20th January, 2021 such Committee was constituted and an advertisement dated 22nd February, 2021 was issued inviting applications from distinguished academicians, and after evaluation a panel was prepared and the appellant was appointed as the first Vice-Chancellor vide order dated 17th December, 2021 for a tenure of five years. The said appointment was challenged before the High Court on the ground that the constitution of the Committee was not in conformity with Regulation 7.3 of the UGC Regulations, 2018 as it did not include a nominee of the Chairman, UGC and further included a member connected with the University, thereby giving rise to conflict of interest, and the High Court after examining the constitutional scheme under Article 246 read with Seventh Schedule and relying upon precedents including Kaiser-I-Hind Pvt. Ltd. v. National Textile Corporation, Dr. Preeti Srivastava v. State of M.P. and Gambhirdhan K. Gadhvi v. State of Gujarat held that the UGC Regulations being framed under Entry 66 of List I have overriding effect and any inconsistency with State legislation renders such provision ultra vires, and consequently Section 14(5) of the PTU Act was declared invalid to the extent of inconsistency and the appointment of the appellant was set aside. Assailing the said judgment learned counsel for the appellant contended that the Presidential assent granted to the PTU Act was general in nature and therefore validated the legislation in its entirety and that the composition of the Search-cum-Selection Committee falls within the domain of Entry 25 of List III relating to education and not within Entry 66 of List I dealing with standards in higher education, and it was further argued that the appellant possessed all requisite qualifications and there was no allegation regarding his competence or integrity and therefore he should be permitted to continue in office. Per contra learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the UGC Regulations are mandatory and binding and that any deviation from the prescribed standards renders the appointment invalid and further contended that the field relating to coordination and determination of standards in higher education is exclusively occupied by Parliament under Entry 66 of List I and therefore the State legislation cannot override such standards. Upon consideration of rival submissions and examination of the constitutional scheme it is evident that the UGC Regulations, 2018 framed under the UGC Act are traceable to Entry 66 of List I and therefore have overriding effect in matters relating to standards in higher education, and the requirement of inclusion of a nominee of the Chairman, UGC in the Search-cum-Selection Committee is a mandatory condition which has not been complied with in the present case, and further the inclusion of a person connected with the University violates the requirement of independence of the Committee.
title: Test #67: Legal Matter - SCI C. A. No. 54-55 of 2025

text: This Writ Petition is filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a Writ of Certiorari to quash the order passed by the District Magistrate, Lucknow, which directed the cancellation and surrender of the arms license of the petitioner. The petitioner is a businessman who has held the license for over fifteen years for self-protection without any history of misuse or involvement in criminal activities. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the administrative authority can cancel a firearms license solely on the basis of a pending First Information Report (FIR) without an independent assessment of the actual threat to public peace or public safety. The petitioner argues that the right to possess a licensed weapon for self-defense is a significant aspect of personal security and that the cancellation order was passed in a mechanical manner, violating the principles of natural justice and the statutory provisions of the Arms Act, 1959. The facts of the case reveal that the police department recommended the cancellation of the license after a minor scuffle occurred in the petitioner’s neighborhood, leading to a cross-FIR under Sections 323 and 504 of the Indian Penal Code. Although the petitioner was not the main accused and the firearm was not used in the incident, the licensing authority concluded that the petitioner is of a volatile nature and his possession of a weapon is detrimental to the public tranquility. The learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri Manish Tiwary, argues that the mere pendency of a criminal case is not a sufficient ground for the revocation of a license under Section 17 of the Arms Act. He submits that the licensing authority must record a specific finding that the possession of the arm by the licensee is dangerous to the public peace. He contends that the "subjective satisfaction" of the District Magistrate must be based on objective material and not on the "whims and fancies" of the local police station. In response, the learned Standing Counsel appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh argues that the possession of a firearm is a "privilege" and not a "fundamental right." He submits that the District Magistrate, as the custodian of law and order, has the discretion to revoke a license if there is a reasonable apprehension of its misuse. He contends that the involvement of the petitioner in a criminal case, regardless of the gravity of the charges, creates a doubt regarding his suitability to carry a weapon in public spaces. The State maintains that the "preventive action" taken by the authorities is necessary to maintain the "majesty of law" and to prevent any potential escalation of violence in the locality. The authorities argue that the safety of the community at large must take precedence over the individual preference of the licensee. Having heard both sides and perused the police report and the impugned order, this Court observes that the "right to bear arms" in India is strictly regulated by statute, but the exercise of power by the licensing authority must be "fair" and "non-arbitrary."
