The High Court of Allahabad emphasizes that a license cannot be cancelled on "vague or flimsy grounds." The law is well-settled that the "licensing authority" cannot act as a "rubber stamp" for the police department. There must be a clear nexus between the conduct of the licensee and the perceived threat to public safety. In the present case, the FIR relates to a "simple hurt" case which has no connection to the use or display of the licensed firearm. Cancelling a long-standing license on such a trivial basis amount to "administrative overkill." The Court finds that the District Magistrate failed to conduct an independent inquiry into the background of the petitioner. The "right to life" under Article 21 includes the "right to protect oneself" within the bounds of the law. If a citizen is under a genuine threat and has followed all the legal requirements to obtain a license, the State should not withdraw that protection without "compelling reasons."
title: Test #68: Legal Matter - AHC Writ (P) No. 12240 of 2024

text: At the outset, this Court takes note of a matter of significant public concern that has come to light in the course of hearing this appeal the widespread delay and inefficiency in the disposal of motor accident compensation claims across the country. Leave is granted. The instant appeal has been filed by the appellant, who is the owner of the offending vehicle, assailing the final order passed by the High Court of Allahabad in First Appeal No. 3303 of 2018, whereby the appeal preferred by the appellant against the award passed by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal was dismissed. The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, hereinafter referred to as MACT, had allowed the claim petition and awarded a total compensation of Rs. 31,90,000 (Rupees Thirty-One Lacs and Ninety Thousand only) along with interest at 7 per cent per annum. The said compensation was directed to be paid by the insurance company, which was saddled with liability, with a further direction to recover the same from the appellant. Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to this appeal are that on the date of accident, i.e., 29.07.2012, the deceased was 24 years old and was working as Managing Director of DRV Drinks Pvt. Ltd. While the deceased was returning from his factory to his residence, his motor vehicle was hit from behind by a bus owned by the appellant on the bypass road near Sanhwali village, Uttar Pradesh. The deceased sustained severe injuries and died on the way to hospital. A claim petition was filed by the legal representatives of the deceased before the Claims Tribunal in MACP No. 1107 of 2012 seeking compensation of Rs. 4,19,00,000. The MACT computed the compensation by applying a multiplier of 18 on the annual income of the deceased after making deductions towards personal expenses, and assessed the loss of dependency accordingly. The principal issue of liability in this appeal centred on whether the appellant had a valid and effective permit to ply the offending vehicle on the route where the accident occurred. On perusal of the material on record, it clearly emerged that on the date of the accident, the appellant did not have a valid permit. The appellant neither produced the original permit before the Claims Tribunal nor was he able to prove the information received under the Right to Information Act (RTI). The alleged permit was issued on a Sunday, and no explanation was furnished as to why the deposit fee was asked on the next working day. Having regard to these concurrent findings of fact by the Courts below, this Court did not find it necessary to interfere. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed, thereby confirming the liability of the appellant as the owner of the offending vehicle. However, the Court observed that during the course of hearing, learned counsel representing the parties expressed deep concern regarding the inordinate delay in disposal of motor accident claims cases at the trial court as well as appellate stage. The Court noted that the Motor Vehicles Amendment Act, 2019, hereinafter referred to as the M.V. Amendment Act, is a benevolent legislation enacted with the intent to ensure that compensation is paid to the family of the deceased and to persons suffering from injuries including permanent disability, in as expeditious a manner as possible. The Court further noted that the mandate of Sections 146, 149, 159, 160, 161, 164, and 166 of the M.V. Amendment Act has not been followed by stakeholders including Claims Tribunals working under the subordination of different High Courts, insurance companies, investigating officers, and State authorities. The Court examined the evolution of the Motor Vehicles Act vis-a-vis its 2019 amendment in considerable detail. Section 159 of the M.V. Amendment Act casts a duty on the Station House Officer of every police station to prepare an Accident Information Report in the prescribed form and submit the same to the Claims Tribunal as an application for compensation. Section 164 empowers a claimant to file an application directly before the Claims Tribunal without the necessity of a lawyer, and entitles the claimant to compensation. Section 149(2) of the Act.
title: Test #68: Legal- SCI Suo Motu Writ Petition (C) 07/2024

text: The Appellant challenges the final judgment of the High Court regarding the validity of a “Land Acquisition” notification. The central controversy involves the invocation of the “Urgency Clause” under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the State can dispense with the “Right to Object” under Section 15 by invoking the urgency powers under Section 40 of the Act, 2013, for the construction of a commercial tourism complex. The Appellant argues that the “Right to be Heard” is a fundamental component of the rule of law and cannot be brushed aside for projects that do not fall under the category of “Emergency” as defined by the legislature. The facts of the case reveal that the State Government issued a preliminary notification in November 2024 for the acquisition of fifty hectares of fertile agricultural land. By invoking the urgency provisions, the State bypassed the social impact assessment required under Section 4 and the public hearing mandate. The learned counsel for the Appellant, Sri Kapil Sibal, argues that the mandate of Section 40(2) is restricted to minimum land required for the defense of India, national security, or for any “unforeseen natural calamity.” He submits that a luxury resort or a tourism hub, while economically beneficial, does not constitute an “Urgency” that justifies the total exclusion of the landowners’ right to file objections. He contends that the “Executive” has acted with “Colorable Exercise of Power” to avoid the rigorous compensation and rehabilitation standards prescribed by the Act. In response, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the State argues that the project is part of a “National Infrastructure Corridor” and is essential for the economic revival of the region. He submits that under Section 40(1), the appropriate Government has the “Prerogative” to take possession of the land within thirty days of the notification in cases of urgency. He contends that the “Judicial Review” of what constitutes an urgency should be limited, as the State is the best judge of its development priorities. The State maintains that the “Compensation” has already been calculated at four times the market value and deposited with the Collector. The respondent further argues that any delay in the project would result in an “Escalation of Cost” and would be detrimental to the public exchequer. Having heard both sides and examined the “Cabinet Minutes” of the acquisition proposal, this Court observes that the “Right to Property,” though no longer a fundamental right, remains a valuable constitutional right under Article 300-A. The Supreme Court emphasizes that no person shall be deprived of his property save by “Authority of Law.” The law is well-settled that the “Urgency Clause” is an exceptional power and not a routine shortcut. The “Rule of Law” requires that the “Due Process” must be followed unless the emergency is of such a nature that even a delay of a few weeks would be catastrophic. In the present case, the “Administrative Convenience” of a tourism department cannot override the “Livelihood Rights” of small-scale farmers. The Court finds that the invocation of Section 40 was “Ultra Vires” the Act. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that the “Right to Object” is a safeguard against the “Arbitrary Exercise” of the power of eminent domain. The “Directive Principles” of state policy require the government to protect the interests of the weaker sections. The “Administrative Discretion” must be exercised within the bounds of “Reasonableness.” If the State is allowed to bypass the “Social Impact Assessment” for commercial projects, it would render the protective umbrella of the 2013 Act completely illusory. The “Sanctity of Procedure” is the only protection the common citizen has against the might of the State.
title: Test #69: Legal Matter - SCI Civil Appeal No. 4550 of 2026

text: The present civil appeal arising out of a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 of the Constitution of India assails the legality, correctness and sustainability of the impugned judgment rendered by the Division Bench of the High Court of Kerala whereby the arbitral award was set aside under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the scope of appellate interference under Section 37 thereof was invoked, and the controversy essentially revolves around the interpretation of the dispute resolution mechanism contained in Clauses 24, 25 and 25.3 of the General Conditions of Contract read with Sections 16, 21 and 23 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, particularly concerning the jurisdictional competence of the Arbitral Tribunal, the necessity or otherwise of issuance of notice under Section 21, and the extent to which arbitral proceedings can encompass disputes not expressly specified at the stage of invocation, thereby raising substantial questions of law relating to waiver, procedural compliance, and the doctrine that a party cannot be permitted to take advantage of its own wrong in arbitral jurisprudence. The factual backdrop, though appearing confined to contractual disputes arising out of road maintenance contracts awarded under the Kerala State Transport Project, discloses a sequence of events wherein multiple disputes relating to price adjustment, escalation, interest and valuation of work were initially referred to the Adjudicator under Clause 25.1 of the contract and were partly allowed in favour of the appellant, however the respondent-State, being dissatisfied with the findings, sought to invoke arbitration albeit belatedly and only in respect of one of the disputes, thereby giving rise to a jurisdictional objection regarding the scope of reference before the Arbitral Tribunal. It is the case of the respondent that the arbitral tribunal could adjudicate only the dispute specifically referred and that absence of notice under Section 21 of the Act in respect of other disputes rendered the award vulnerable to challenge, whereas the appellant contends that the arbitration clause is widely worded and encompasses all disputes arising out of or in connection with the contract and that the conduct of the respondent in seeking to reopen the entire adjudicator’s decision clearly manifests an intention to submit all disputes to arbitration. Upon a careful evaluation of the contractual scheme and statutory framework it becomes evident that the dispute resolution mechanism envisages a multi-tier process commencing with decision of the Engineer, followed by reference to the Adjudicator and culminating in arbitration, however such procedural stipulations, though contractual in nature, are capable of being waived either expressly or by conduct of the parties, and where a party itself disregards such stipulations or acts in a manner inconsistent with strict adherence thereto, it cannot subsequently rely upon such procedural deviations to defeat the claim of the other party. The material on record reveals that the respondent itself failed to adhere to the stipulated timelines for reference to arbitration and further sought to challenge the entire decision of the Adjudicator before the Arbitral Tribunal, thereby enlarging the scope of disputes beyond the limited reference initially made, and such conduct disentitles the respondent from contending that the Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the additional disputes. The object of Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is primarily to determine the commencement of arbitral proceedings for the purpose of limitation and does not operate as a jurisdictional bar precluding a party from raising additional claims which fall within the ambit of the arbitration agreement, and it is well settled that once an arbitral tribunal is constituted, the claimant is entitled to file a statement of claim containing all disputes arising out of the contract subject to the terms of the arbitration agreement.
title: Test #69: Legal Matter - SCI Civil A. No. 39 of 2026

text: The petitioner, a retired Veterinary Assistant, attained superannuation on 31st December 2024, after thirty years of unblemished service. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the state can recover alleged excess payments made due to a wrong fixation of pay after the employee has retired, especially when there is no allegation of fraud or misrepresentation on the part of the employee. The petitioner argues that such a recovery is a violation of the fundamental right to property and the settled principles of the Andhra Pradesh Revised Pension Rules, 1980. The facts of the case reveal that the authorities discovered a technical error in the pay fixation that occurred in the year 2012. Instead of rectifying the error at that time, the department waited until the petitioner's retirement to slap a recovery notice. The learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri K. G. Krishna Murthy, argues that the mandate of Section 9 of the Pension Rules and the guidelines issued by the Finance Department have been completely ignored. He submits that as per the leading judgment of the Supreme Court in the State of Punjab versus Rafiq Masih, recovery from retired employees or those due to retire within a year is prohibited. He contends that the respondent authorities have acted in a mechanical manner, ignoring the fact that the petitioner is now dependent on a fixed pension and any substantial deduction would cause immense financial hardship. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Services argues that the state is a trustee of public funds and is duty-bound to recover any amount paid in excess of the entitlement. He submits that under Section 52 of the Andhra Pradesh Financial Code, the government has the inherent power to rectify clerical errors and recover overpayments made from the exchequer. He contends that the "Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment" applies to the petitioner, as he has received a benefit to which he was not legally entitled. The State maintains that the recovery is being done in easy installments and that the petitioner’s basic pension remains untouched. The respondent further argues that the "Mistake of Fact" in the 2012 pay fixation was a bona fide error by the accounting staff and does not create any vested right in favor of the petitioner to retain the excess money. Having heard both sides and perused the service register of the petitioner, this Court observes that the "Pensionary Benefits" are not a bounty to be distributed at the sweet will of the employer. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that pension is "deferred wages" for the long years of service rendered to the state. The law is well-settled that if the excess payment was not a result of any trickery by the employee, the state cannot punish the individual for its own administrative negligence after a decade. In the present case, the "Rule of Law" requires that the state should be a model employer and show compassion toward its senior citizens. The "Administrative Apathy" in failing to audit the pay fixation for twelve years cannot be shifted onto the shoulders of a retired subordinate employee. The Court finds that the recovery order is hit by the vice of inequity. The High Court refers to several landmark judgments where it was held that recovery from Class III and Class IV employees after their retirement is harsh and arbitrary. The "Directive Principles" of state action require the government to ensure social security for the elderly. The "Administrative Discretion" to recover funds must be balanced against the "Doctrine of Proportionality." A retired employee, living on a limited income, should not be subjected to a sudden financial shock due to a mistake committed by the department years ago. The state must bear the loss of its own errors rather than recovering it from the most vulnerable section of the service. Consequently, this Court finds that the petitioner has established a clear case of hardship and legal protection. The Writ Petition is allowed. The respondent authorities are directed to set aside the recovery order dated 15th January 2025 and refund any amount already deducted from the petitioner's gratuity within a period of eight weeks.
title: Test #70: Legal Matter - APHC Writ P. No. 24880 of 2025

text: The present appeals arise from the common judgment and order dated 28.11.2023 passed by the High Court of Karnataka whereby the High Court quashed and set aside the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court and convicted the appellants for offences punishable under Sections 302, 120-B, 201, 506 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and sentenced them to undergo life imprisonment along with fine and other sentences, and since both the appeals arise out of the same judgment and pertain to the same incident, they are being disposed of by this common judgment. The prosecution case originates from a missing complaint lodged on 16.12.2011 stating that one Martandgouda had been missing since 11.12.2011 and upon further investigation suspicion was raised against the accused persons on account of prior civil disputes relating to land and property, and it was alleged that due to such disputes and animosity the accused entered into a criminal conspiracy, abducted the deceased, murdered him and disposed of the dead body in order to screen themselves from punishment, and upon completion of investigation charge-sheet came to be filed for offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 120-B, 364, 302, 201 and 506 of IPC read with Section 149. During trial the prosecution examined several witnesses and relied upon circumstantial evidence including motive, last seen theory, recovery and conduct of the accused, however the Trial Court upon appreciation of evidence acquitted all the accused holding that the prosecution failed to establish a complete chain of circumstances and that mere suspicion cannot substitute proof particularly in a case based on circumstantial evidence. Aggrieved thereby, the State and complainant preferred appeals before the High Court and the High Court by impugned judgment reversed the acquittal and convicted accused nos. 1 to 4 while confirming acquittal of accused nos. 5 and 6, and therefore the present appeals have been filed before this Court. Learned counsel for the appellants contended that there is no reliable evidence connecting the accused with the alleged offence, that the prosecution has failed to establish motive, conspiracy or last seen circumstance and that the sole eye-witness PW-5 is unreliable as his statement was recorded after 21 days and contains material contradictions, and it is further submitted that medical evidence does not support the prosecution case and that recovery and discovery are not duly proved and crucial witnesses were not examined. It is also contended that the Trial Court had taken a plausible view based on evidence and therefore the High Court ought not to have interfered with the acquittal merely because another view was possible. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the prosecution has established the case beyond reasonable doubt, that disclosure statements of the accused led to recovery of dead body and are admissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and that evidence of PW-5 along with medical evidence sufficiently proves the guilt of the accused. Having considered the rival submissions and the material on record it emerges that the case is based primarily on circumstantial evidence and the prosecution was required to establish a complete and unbroken chain of circumstances pointing only towards the guilt of the accused, however from the evidence it is evident that the testimony of PW-5 is not reliable as there is unexplained delay in recording his statement, contradictions in his versions and absence of any independent corroboration, and further the medical evidence does not fully support the prosecution case regarding time of death, and the alleged recovery and confessional statements cannot by themselves form the basis of conviction when other links in the chain are missing. It is well settled that in an appeal against acquittal the appellate court should not interfere unless the findings of the Trial Court are perverse or based on misreading of evidence and if two views are possible the view favourable to the accused must be adopted.
title: Test #70: Legal Matter - SCI Cr. A. No. 2120 of 2024

text: This Writ Petition is filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, seeking a Writ of Mandamus to declare the action of the respondent authorities in rejecting the medical reimbursement claim of the petitioner as illegal, arbitrary, and in violation of the Andhra Pradesh Integrated Medical Attendance Rules. The petitioner is a retired school teacher who underwent an emergency "Cardiac Bypass Surgery" at a private multi-specialty hospital in Hyderabad. The primary legal issue before this Court is whether the State can deny the reimbursement of life-saving medical expenses solely on the ground that the surgery was performed in a "Non-Empanelled Hospital" without obtaining prior permission from the department. The petitioner argues that in a situation of a medical emergency, the life of a citizen takes precedence over procedural technicalities and that the "Right to Health" is an integral part of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. The facts of the case reveal that the petitioner suffered a massive heart attack on the night of 15th August 2023. Given the critical nature of the blockage, the local doctors advised immediate surgical intervention to save his life. The nearest empanelled hospital was located over two hundred kilometers away, and the family, acting in "Bona Fide" interest, shifted him to a nearby recognized private hospital. The learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri K. V. Raghu Veer, argues that the "Emergency Scenarios" are exempted from the requirement of prior referral under the prevailing government memos. He submits that the petitioner has spent his hard-earned savings of six lakh rupees on the treatment and that the "Technical Objections" raised by the treasury department are heartless and lack legal merit. He contends that the State, as a "Welfare Employer," has a moral and legal obligation to provide medical security to its retired employees. In response, the learned Government Pleader for Services-III argues that the medical reimbursement scheme is governed by strict "Financial Guidelines" to prevent the misuse of public funds. He submits that the petitioner chose a high-cost private hospital despite the availability of government-run super-specialty facilities. He contends that the "Package Rates" for various surgeries are fixed by the government, and the petitioner is only entitled to reimbursement at the "CGHS Rates" applicable to empanelled hospitals. The State maintains that the "Scrutiny Committee" rejected the claim because the petitioner failed to produce an "Emergency Certificate" in the prescribed format from the treating surgeon. The authorities argue that allowing such claims would open the floodgates for "Unregulated Billing" and put an immense burden on the state exchequer. Having heard both sides and perused the "Discharge Summary" and the "Medical Bills," this Court observes that a "Citizen in Distress" cannot be expected to search for a list of empanelled hospitals while gasping for breath. The High Court of Andhra Pradesh emphasizes that the "Medical Attendance Rules" are social welfare legislations and should be interpreted in a "Liberal Manner." The law is well-settled that the State cannot shirk its responsibility of providing medical assistance by citing "Procedural Lapses." If the ailment is genuine and the treatment was necessary, the "Reimbursement" cannot be denied simply because the hospital was not on the official list. The "Right to Survival" is the most fundamental of all rights, and "Administrative Red-Tapism" should not be allowed to stifle it. The Court finds that the respondents have acted in a "Mechanical Manner" without applying their mind to the medical records. The discharge summary clearly indicates that the petitioner was admitted in a "Gaspy Condition" with unstable angina. In such a state, every minute is crucial. The High Court refers to the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of "Shiva Kant Jha versus Union of India," where it was held that the "Actual Expenses" incurred in an emergency must be reimbursed even if the treatment is taken in a non-empanelled hospital.
title: Test #71: Legal Matter - APHC Writ P. No. 34480 of 2023

text: This appeal arises from the judgment and order dated 16.12.2016 passed by the High Court at Calcutta whereby the High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant herein and thereby affirmed the order passed by the Company Law Board, Kolkata Bench condoning the delay of 249 days in filing the appeal under Section 58(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 by the respondent herein. The appellant company is a private limited company having a total of 631 fully paid-up equity shares and Ms. Mehroo Mazda, the mother of the respondent, was a shareholder holding 20 shares of the appellant company which are the subject shares. The said shareholder passed away on 22.07.1989 and prior to her demise she had bequeathed the subject shares to the respondent through her last will and testament dated 19.06.1987 and the respondent obtained probate of the will on 30.11.1990, however, after a considerable delay of about 23 years, vide letter dated 01.03.2013 the respondent’s advocate issued a notice to the appellant company seeking registration of transmission of the subject shares, which request came to be refused by the appellant company vide communication dated 30.04.2013. At the relevant time Section 111 of the Companies Act, 1956 was in force which provided that an appeal against refusal must be filed within a period of two months, and the said period expired on 30.06.2013 but the respondent failed to take any action within the prescribed time period. It is the case of the respondent that being a resident of London and a practising barrister he visited Kolkata in July, 2013 and upon legal advice issued another communication dated 18.07.2013 requesting registration of transmission and indicating that appropriate legal action would be initiated, however no reply was received from the appellant company and in the meantime the Companies Act, 2013 came into force in phases and Section 58 replaced Section 111 with effect from 12.09.2013, thereby rendering the earlier provisions inoperative. The respondent thereafter attempted to file a petition under the erstwhile provisions which contained defects and subsequently filed a fresh appeal under Section 58 of the Act, 2013 on 07.02.2014 before the Company Law Board seeking directions for registration of the shares, rectification of the register of members and consequential benefits, and along with the said appeal an application under Regulation 44 of the CLB Regulations, 1991 was filed seeking condonation of delay of 249 days in preferring the appeal. The Company Law Board vide order dated 27.05.2016 allowed the application and condoned the delay observing inter alia that the delay had occurred due to the respondent’s residence abroad, procedural complications and the earlier filing under incorrect provisions and that the technical ground of delay should not come in the way of substantive justice particularly when probate had already been granted and reasonable steps had been taken from 2013 onwards. Being aggrieved by the said order the appellant company preferred an appeal before the High Court which came to be dismissed and the High Court upheld the order of the Company Law Board holding that although the CLB is a quasi-judicial body the principles underlying the Limitation Act, 1963 could be applied and that Section 58(3) of the Act, 2013 prescribes a limitation period but does not expressly bar filing beyond such period, and reliance was placed on judicial precedents including Canara Bank v. Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. and Smt. Nupur Mitra v. Basubani Ltd. wherein it was held that the principles of limitation could be applied to such proceedings, and it was further observed that an appeal is a continuation of proceedings and therefore the change in law brought by Section 433 of the Act, 2013 could also be taken into consideration and no vested right had accrued in favour of the appellant company so as to prevent such application, and accordingly the High Court found no reason to interfere with the order passed by the Company Law Board and dismissed the appeal.
title: Test #71: Legal Matter - SCI C.A,No. 92 of 2026

text: The doctrine of Lis Pendens is a significant legal principle that governs the transfer of property while a lawsuit regarding that property is pending in a court of competent jurisdiction. Derived from the Latin term meaning a pending suit, this doctrine is founded on the necessity of maintaining the status quo during the course of litigation. The primary objective of this rule is to prevent the parties to a suit from alienating or transferring the subject matter of the litigation in a manner that would prejudice the opposite party or render the final decree of the court impossible to execute. It ensures that the court’s authority is not bypassed by the strategic disposal of assets before a final judgment is pronounced. In the Indian legal framework, the doctrine of Lis Pendens is enshrined under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. It stipulates that during the pendency in any court having authority within the limits of India of any suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the court and on such terms as it may impose. This statutory provision acts as a constructive notice to the entire world that the property is currently under judicial scrutiny. A crucial aspect of this terminology is the concept of a Pendente Lite purchaser. This refers to a person who acquires an interest in the property after the institution of the suit but before its final disposal. Under the rule of Lis Pendens, such a purchaser is bound by the outcome of the litigation, regardless of whether they had actual notice of the pending suit or acted in good faith. The law presumes that a person who buys property that is the subject of a legal dispute does so at their own peril. The purchaser steps into the shoes of the seller and takes the property subject to the eventual decree of the court. This prevents a "Multiplicity of Proceedings" where a successful plaintiff would otherwise have to file fresh suits against every subsequent purchaser to recover their rightful property. For the doctrine of Lis Pendens to apply, several essential conditions must be satisfied. First, there must be a suit or a proceeding pending in a court of competent jurisdiction. Second, the suit must not be collusive, meaning it should not be a fraudulent arrangement between the parties to defeat the rights of a third party. Third, the right to immovable property must be directly and specifically in question in the suit. Fourth, the transfer must be made by a party to the litigation. If these conditions are met, any transfer made during the pendency of the suit is not void, but it is voidable at the instance of the affected party, or more accurately, it is subservient to the rights eventually established by the court. However, the doctrine is not an absolute bar on the transfer of property. A party may transfer the property with the explicit permission of the court. Furthermore, the rule does not apply to involuntary transfers, such as a sale conducted by a court in the execution of a decree or a sale for the recovery of government dues, unless specifically prohibited. It is also important to note that the doctrine remains in force from the time the plaint is presented until the final decree or order has been completely executed or has become barred by limitation. This extended period ensures that the successful litigant can actually enjoy the fruits of the decree without facing obstacles created by the judgment debtor through mid-litigation transfers. The philosophy behind Lis Pendens is rooted in public policy and the administration of justice. It is based on the maxim Ut Lite Pendente Nihil Innovetur, which implies that nothing new should be introduced during the pendency of a suit.

text: Assailing the final judgment and order dated 06.08.2019 passed in Writ Petition No. 18947 of 2016 (S-CAT) connected with Writ Petition No. 54254 of 2016 (S-CAT) by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru (hereinafter referred to as ‘High Court’), the appellants have filed these appeals. For the sake of brevity, we will refer to the parties as per their status in Civil Appeal arising out of Special Leave Petition (C) No. 4743 of 2020. The dispute in the present appeals is regarding the claim of a reserved category candidate i.e., Respondent No. 1, who availed relaxation in the Preliminary Examination but was placed higher in merit than the unreserved candidate i.e., Respondent No. 3 in the final merit list based on total marks awarded in Main Examination (Written) and Personality Test, to be treated as a General merit candidate for the purpose of cadre allocation against a General Insider vacancy for State of Karnataka in the Indian Forest Service (hereinafter referred to as ‘IFS’). Being aggrieved by the notification dated 13.03.2015 issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change (hereinafter referred to as ‘MoEFCC’), allocating Tamil Nadu Cadre to Respondent No. 1 instead of Karnataka, Respondent No. 1 preferred an Original Application No. 170/239 of 2015 (hereinafter referred to as ‘OA’) before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Bangalore Bench (hereinafter referred to as ‘Tribunal’) and vide order dated 15.03.2016, the Tribunal allowed the Original Application holding that a meritorious Scheduled Caste (hereinafter referred to as ‘SC’) candidate cannot be denied allocation against a General vacancy solely on the ground of availing relaxation in the SC cut-off marks at the stage of Preliminary Examination. The Tribunal directed to allocate the General Insider vacancy in the State of Karnataka to Respondent No. 1. Being aggrieved by the said order, WP No. 18947 of 2016 (S-CAT) was filed by Respondent No. 3 (who was allocated the General insider vacancy) and WP No. 54254 of 2016 (S-CAT) was filed by the Union of India (hereinafter referred to as ‘UOI’), which came to be dismissed by the common impugned order of the High Court, affirming the view of the Tribunal. Hence, the present appeals. Challenging the impugned notification, Respondent No. 1 filed the OA before the Tribunal on 26.03.2015 asking to quash the notification in so far as it relates to him and Respondent No. 3 and also sought a consequent direction to UOI and UPSC to allot him the General Insider vacancy in the State of Karnataka with all consequential benefits. The Tribunal, by order dated 15.03.2016 allowed the OA, which was affirmed by the High Court vide impugned order dated 06.08.2019. The High Court was of the view that since Respondent No. 1 had secured a higher rank in Main Examination (Written) compared to Respondent No. 3, and the Preliminary Examination was merely a screening test and marks obtained therein were not to be considered to draw the final merit, therefore, for cadre allocation, the former should be treated as General category candidate and would be entitled to get allocation of Karnataka cadre in General Insider vacancy. Assailing these findings, present appeals have been preferred by UOI and Respondent No. 3. Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned Senior Counsel and Additional Solicitor General of India, with vehemence submitted that the allocation of cadre is governed by the Exam Rules, 2013 and the Policy. Rule 14 of the Exam Rules, 2013 specifically bars the adjustment of reserved category candidates against unreserved vacancies if they have availed relaxation at any stage in eligibility or selection criteria. He put forth emphasis to phrase ‘any stage of the examination’ and argued that Respondent No. 1 could not secure marks above cut-off for General category in the Preliminary Examination. He had appeared in Main Examination after getting benefit of relaxed standard in SC category, therefore, having availed a relaxation in Preliminary Examination.
