text: In an age when machines are becoming capable of almost everything predictable, the irreplaceable act remains the human one: a teacher who sees potential in a student that the student cannot yet see in themselves. OECD’s 2026 Teacher Knowledge Survey distinguishes between knowing a subject and the ability to teach it. Its findings posit that subject knowledge does not always translate into effective pedagogy. The point is simple but important: knowing something deeply and knowing how to help another person learn it are not the same skill. Teaching is an art, requiring an understanding of human connections, pedagogy and some theatrics for the classroom. The UNESCO Global Report on Teachers, 2024, places a hard number on what neglecting this profession costs. The world needs 44 million additional primary and secondary teachers by 2030, and over half are needed simply to replace those already leaving. Meanwhile, the McKinsey Global Institute estimates that between 75 million and 375 million workers globally will need to switch occupational categories by 2030 due to automation. In such a scenario, the value of competent teachers is more than ever. No one remembers the exact day they learned to read. But almost everyone remembers the teacher who taught them. That asymmetry, between the forgettable moment and the unforgettable person, tells us something essential about teaching. A teacher leaves behind something that cannot be easily measured: the confidence to try, the discipline to persist, the curiosity to ask, or sometimes simply the belief that one is capable of more. Thus, teaching cannot be classified as anything less than an art. The Latin phrase: Non scholae sed vitae discimus. We learn not for school, but for life.  And the teacher, the true artist of human possibility, is the person who makes that possible. The National Awards to Teachers, conferred each year by the Hon’ble President of India, honour a chosen few whose contribution has risen above the rest. Nonetheless, in every corner of the country, in classrooms, skill labs, polytechnics, sports grounds, and music rooms, students find their own way to say thank you. A handwritten note. A moment of recognition in a morning assembly. A quiet acknowledgement that stays with a teacher long after the day is over. These are not lesser celebrations but, in many ways, the truest ones. The data, however, tells us a parallel concerning story. India has acknowledged this challenge and is responding with intent. The four-year Integrated Teacher Education Program, launched in consonance with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, integrates subject mastery and pedagogy into a single undergraduate degree, attracting the best minds into teaching by design. To ensure congruent standards amongst the in-service teachers, the National Professional Standards for Teachers (NPST) tie career advancement to demonstrated teaching quality rather than mere seniority. To benefit from cross-sectoral learning, the National Mission for Mentoring (NMM) provides structured support to teachers to learn from mentors from various fields. I, too, have registered as a mentor for this mission. India is also expanding who counts as a teacher, and that is perhaps the most novel idea of all. Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society (ULLAS), the New India Literacy Program, is built on the principle that anyone who is literate can teach someone who is not. As we celebrate International Literacy Day this year, nine states and union territories have been declared fully literate under this program. This spirit is further embodied in the Vidyanjali portal of the Ministry of Education. It connects over 8.75 lakh government schools to volunteers who bring their expertise, whether in dance, mathematics, public speaking, or craft, into classrooms as a gift. Every one of them acts as a teacher. Every subject they bring is valued equally. Because at its core, teaching is not a technical function but a craft. Every lesson plan is a composition. Every explanation is a performance.
title: Test #02: Teacher - The Artists of Education

text: Jute is one of the most significant natural fibres in India, valued for its wide range of applications and environmental sustainability. The history of jute in India can be traced back to the 3rd century BC. However, it emerged as a significant commercial commodity during the British Colonial period owing to its strategic military applications. The East India Company established numerous jute mills in Bengal, positioning the region as a Centre for jute cultivation and processing. India’s independence in 1947 and the subsequent partition significantly disrupted the integrated jute economy of Bengal. Nearly 80 percent of the jute-growing areas became part of East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). But most jute mills remained in India, resulting in an acute shortage of raw material for processing in these mills. To address this imbalance, the government launched the "Grow More Jute" campaign in September 1949. The farmers were encouraged to shift from paddy cultivation to jute. Consequently, India’s raw jute production more than doubled from 6.7 lakh tonnes (1951-52) to 14.56 lakh tonnes (1961-62). The Jute Packaging Act, 1987, further strengthened the sector by mandating the use of jute sacks for packaging essential commodities. In the trade and industrial context, Jute and Mesta are collectively classified as raw jute due to their comparable end uses. Mesta is a bast fibre crop cultivated as a cost-effective alternative to jute, particularly in drier Agro-Climatic regions. Owing to its characteristic golden colour and silky lustre, jute is commonly referred to as the “Golden Fibre”. This move ensured a stable market for Indian jute farmers. Over time, jute emerged as a strategic green fibre, contributing to rural livelihoods and environmentally sustainable industrial development. Presently, West Bengal contributes the largest share of raw jute cultivation in the country, followed by Bihar, Assam, Odisha, and Jharkhand. Jute is generally sown during March-April and harvested within 100-110 days. It thrives under hot and humid conditions with rainfall between 700-1,500 mm during the crop-growing period. Given these agro-climatic requirements, its cultivation is concentrated mainly in eastern and northeastern India and is predominantly rainfed. The crop is primarily grown by small and marginal farmers. Jute is a biodegradable and recyclable natural fibre characterised by its rapid growth, cost-effectiveness, and wide availability. It is strong, durable, breathable, and highly versatile, with applications spanning packaging, construction, agriculture, and industrial textiles. Jute also possesses favourable functional attributes, including thermal and acoustic insulation, high moisture absorption, and low static generation. It blends well with both natural and synthetic fibres, facilitating a wide range of value-added and textile applications. Jute Geotextile (JGT) is a versatile, diversified jute product belonging to a class of technical textiles. It can be applied in many fields like civil engineering, soil erosion control, road pavement construction and protection of river banks. JGT can be made from jute fibers through special treatment and weaving processes. It is increasingly gaining acceptance due to its functional effectiveness, environmental compatibility, favourable techno-physical properties, and price competitiveness. From an ecological standpoint, JGT is fully biodegradable, thereby improving soil structure and fertility. Moreover, JGT is globally recognized as an effective natural solution for soil stabilization, erosion control, and ecological restoration in degraded landscapes. This is because it helps in regulating the micro-environment by maintaining lower soil temperatures and reducing surface disturbance. Hence, it supports seed germination and early plant establishment. India’s jute sector has evolved into a key driver of sustainable and inclusive development. It supports millions of farmers, workers, artisans, and entrepreneurs across the value chain. Policy support, innovation, and improved production have strengthened the sector’s competitiveness.
title: Test #03: Jute - India's Golden Fibre

text: Quantum physics has made numerous strange predictions, and scientists have checked and confirmed many of them. But one of the strangest ones persists unresolved. In the 1930s, the German physicists Werner Heisenberg and Hans Heinrich Euler proposed that empty space is not really empty. Instead, they predicted that in the presence of a magnetic field, the vacuum of space would behave like a crystal, changing the properties of light passing through it. Sometimes the core of a dead star can collapse to form a neutron star. Neutron stars with powerful magnetic fields are called magnetars. The international team focused its attention on one magnetar named 1E 1547.0-5408, located 14,700 lightyears away. The trouble with testing this prediction called vacuum birefringence is that the magnetic field has to be extraordinarily strong. In a study published in Nature on August 5, astronomers from Australia, Canada, Japan, South Africa, Taiwan, and the U.S. reported it had observed such birefringence using two satellites and a telescope in Australia, almost confirming the prediction at long last. The work could prove ‘nothingness’ is actually a complex and active medium and also potentially help scientists refine their maps of the universe. In classical physics, a vacuum is absolute nothingness. But in quantum electrodynamics (QED) which is a theory in quantum physics a vacuum is a soup of virtual particles: pairs of electrons and anti-electrons that constantly pop in and out of existence, and so quickly that they cannot be observed. Normally, these virtual particles have a negligible effect on light. But when a magnetic field nearby becomes strong enough, it changes how the short-lived charged particles can move, so they respond differently to light depending on the direction in which its electric field is vibrating. This part of space will then behave like a calcite crystal when light passes through it, splitting it into different paths depending on its electric field. (As an electromagnetic wave, light consists of electric and magnetic fields travelling through space.) For vacuum birefringence to become noticeable, the magnetic field has to be around 88 trillion times stronger than the earth’s magnetic field, and more than 500 million times as strong as the ultra-powerful magnets in the world’s largest science experiment, the CERN supercollider. These are staggering numbers far beyond the abilities of current technologies, so physicists have been looking for proof of vacuum birefringence in outer space, where objects called magnetars generate the universe’s most extreme magnetic fields. By combining X-ray and radio frequency measurements, then, the team could piece together the geometry of the magnetar’s magnetic field. As X-rays leave the magnetar and move through the surrounding space, QED predicts that their electric field will have to lock itself into one of two directions a condition that unmagnetised space does not impose thus polarising the light. Since these directions are defined by the direction of the magnetic field, the X-rays’ polarisation is effectively railroaded along the magnetic field lines. And as the X-rays travel away from the magnetar, their polarisation will stay fixed even as the magnetic field becomes less and less able to ‘hold on’. According to the team, the amount of polarisation dropped as the energy of the X-rays increased, which QED predicts as well. The team was also able to elucidate that the magnetar rotated along an axis that aligned almost perfectly with its magnetic poles, like a top spinning upright a detail that informed the team’s models of how the X-rays from the magnetar would look with and without vacuum birefringence. The models that did not account for the phenomenon fit substantially worse with the telescope data than those that included it. Other than IXPE, the team had also used the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer instrument onboard the International Space Station and the Murriyang radio telescope in Australia.
title: Test #04: Magnetic Field Could Prove Space is Not Empty

text: India’s tourism sector stands at an inflexion point. In FY23, it created 7.6 crore jobs and contributed 5% to GDP. The sector accounts for over 5% of GDP and supports over 13% of total employment. In the Union Budget 2026-27, the government allocated 2,438 crore to tourism, announced plans to transform 15 iconic archaeological sites into experiential heritage destinations, launched thematic tourism trails across mountains, coasts, and biodiversity zones, and proposed a National Institute of Hospitality to professionalise the sector (source). The ambition is clear. Walk through Hampi at dawn, when the granite boulders still hold the night’s coolness and the Tungabhadra catches the first light. This UNESCO World Heritage Site spans 4,187 hectares and contains over 1,600 surviving remains of what was once, in 1500 CE, the world’s second-largest city. Medieval European travellers crossed oceans to document its splendour. The capital of the Vijayanagara Empire continues to speak through every carved pillar and every temple gopuram rising against the boulder-strewn landscape. And yet, Hampi receives approximately 4.5 lakh visitors annually (2024 data records 4,66,279 visitors). India is home to 44 UNESCO World Heritage Sites and over 3,600 centrally-protected monuments. Across these, there are approximately 50 site museums roughly one for every 70 protected sites. Italy, with a long history of investing in cultural institutions, offers a useful contrast: over 4,500 museums and a dense network of local cultural infrastructure that invite engagement over time. In Hampi’s villages, artisans continue to practise black pottery, stone carving, basketry, and metalwork traditions carried through generations. At the Konark Sun Temple, at Thanjavur, and dozens of other remarkable sites, the pattern is the same: visitors encounter the monument alone, with little assistance in understanding the engineering, symbolism, or worldview that shaped it. Consider what these sites could become if each had a visitor centre to situate what is being experienced, a craft village, maybe something modelled on the Delhi Haat, where artisans demonstrate and sell their work, food courts rooted in regional cuisine, and the kind of collaborations between designers, artisans, local chefs, and brands entering regional markets that can anchor livelihoods around heritage. Spaces curated to this level of cultural relevance would also generate social media storytelling organically, extending the allure and reach of a site well beyond the visit itself. When heritage sites lack this infrastructure, visitors spend less time, participate less deeply, and are less likely to return. The impact is felt most directly by local communities. When traditions are not made visible through storytelling, artisans lose opportunities for exchange. Without an understanding of the skill, time, and knowledge embedded in a stone carving or woven textile, visitors are unlikely to recognise its worth. This is how local food traditions and handmade practices are gradually replaced at heritage sites because they are less understood. What follows is quieter but more enduring. When cultural practices no longer sustain livelihoods, communities disengage from their care and younger generations move elsewhere. The diversity that gives India its cultural depth risks becoming uniform through the absence of connection. The loss we are facing is economic, yes, but more than that, it is one of cultural inheritance and memory. On this regulatory foundation, the city has built a dense ecosystem of craft and visitor experience. Kyoto is home to 74 designated categories of traditional industries, 17 holding national status, spanning nishijin textiles, kiyomizu ceramics, lacquerware, bamboo craft, and dozens more. The city government supports these through artisan subsidies, training programmes for young practitioners, and initiatives connecting traditional skills with contemporary markets. India already holds comparable depth. Its diversity of traditions, continuity of practice, and community-held knowledge remain remarkable.
title: Test #05: Heritage Tourism Sites Need Better Storytelling

text: Generally, a glacial collapse refers to the sudden detachment of a large mass of ice, rock and water from a glacier on a steep mountain slope. Geological factors like earthquakes, temperature changes, or other physical changes unfolding within a glacier can influence such events. A glacier forms when snow accumulates and survives over several melting seasons. These deposits are compressed into a layer called firn the midpoint between fresh and glacial snow before recrystallising into solid ice as part of a glacier. Once this glacial mass achieves sufficient weight, it can flow outward. Mountain gradients on which ice moves in a steep flow are the cause of glacial collapse. Warming temperatures cause lots of melted water to get collected in subglacial channels. These channels open up after the glacier's lower portion collapses, leading to water gushing through in large volumes. As this mass flows through uneven terrain, the accompanying acceleration creates stress that exceeds the strength of the glacial structure holding the ice together. Sustained movement can ultimately fracture the ice. Structural weakness also comes from surface melting on a glacier. Water can pool inside cracks over cycles of melting and freezing. Eventually, this water pushes hard, splitting the ice all the way through. In cases of glacial collapse like the recent one, what sits under the glacier also plays a role. When glaciers rest on soft mud or clay, trapped water moves through the networks of cracks within the glacier to travel downwards. In these wet base glaciers in the Himalayas, water is collected at the base of the glacier in large quantities and is also occasionally connected by tunnels. When such glaciers collapse, it causes a sudden rush of water that mixes with loose dirt, rocks and riverbed materials. This volatile mixture can race down narrow mountain valleys at great speeds. Another complication is posed by the piles of rock and ice that get left behind, which can block narrow river channels and form temporary natural dams. When such a temporary dam breaks under continuous pressure, a second round of flooding can be unleashed something also witnessed in Nepal this week. The flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal and Tibet this week have been attributed to a glacial collapse in the Himalayas. It sent ice and rock debris hurtling into the Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi river system, eventually reaching inhabited valleys. In recent years, the incidence of glacier breakages has increased, owing to the faster warming of the Himalayas due to climate change. As physical conditions become more challenging, this can affect how future search-and-rescue missions are conducted. Advanced preparation via remote seismic monitoring and high-altitude early warning systems then takes on greater importance. Experts also note the need for correctly zoning critical infrastructure like hydropower plants so they are not erected in high-risk areas. Events like the Nepal floods also point to the need for international cooperation so that upstream glacial instability is communicated downstream before disaster strikes. Scientists distinguish this event from a related phenomenon called a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, in which a lake dammed by loose rock and ice debris bursts open, releasing its contents in a single catastrophic surge. The two processes often occur together, since collapsing ice frequently feeds the very lakes that later breach. The Himalayas are considered especially vulnerable because thousands of glacial lakes have formed as retreating ice leaves depressions behind, many growing rapidly each decade. Past disasters, such as the 2021 Chamoli disaster in Uttarakhand, where a chunk of a hanging glacier broke away and destroyed hydropower infrastructure downstream, show how quickly such events can turn deadly. Researchers increasingly rely on satellite imagery to track lake growth and glacier movement, flagging unstable formations before they fail.
title: Test #06: What is Glacier Collapse?

text: The Western Ghats, running 1,600 kilometres along the edge of the peninsula, are nothing less than the living ecological spine of India. Recognised as one of the world’s eight hottest biodiversity hotspots, these mountains harbour extraordinary life nearly half of India’s flowering plant species, a third of its vertebrate fauna, and over 300 globally threatened species find refuge here. Several species, like the Katlekan Marsh Nut and the Gund Day Gecko, are exclusive to the very forests I visited. Yet the significance of the Ghats runs deeper than species counts. They gather the first impact of the southwest monsoon and release it as the lifeblood of the Deccan: The Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, and Tungabhadra rivers originate here, sustaining hundreds of millions across six states. Their dense forests temper regional climate, draw down carbon, hold the soil in place, and soften the runoff and flooding that would otherwise devastate downstream plains. It is no exaggeration, then, to call these rainforests “India’s Amazon”. Like their South American counterpart, they behave as a vast living organism breathing in carbon dioxide, exhaling oxygen, and cycling moisture back into the atmosphere to sustain the monsoon itself. Their layered canopies, dripping with epiphytes and echoed by the calls of hornbills and lion-tailed macaques, weave a self-renewing tapestry of life that sustains the climate and waters of the entire peninsula. Just as the Amazon Basin constitutes the lungs of South America, the Western Ghats are the lungs and wellspring of India. The canopy closes overhead as the monsoon sky lowers, and the Katlekan dark forest of North Kanara slips into an almost absolute blackness. It is the middle of the day. A few hundred yards in, the light dies so completely that you reach for a torch just to discern the brook gurgling a few yards away. Hornbills call through the dripping understory, mountain imperial pigeons murmur in the vaulted gloom, and eagle owls send their low hoots echoing between ancient trunks. Here, in this living darkness, the dry, fragmented woodlots that pass for forests in “the New India” reveal themselves as paltry shadows of the aranya that inspired poets like Rabindranath Tagore a primordial realm that still breathes and governs itself, reminding the visitor that true wilderness does not merely survive in India; it thrives in the damp air and the dark. If we let it. Having done my doctoral dissertation on forest management and seen jungles across four continents, I thought I knew what a forest was. I was wrong. The Katlekan darkness is merely the most intimate face of a mountain chain whose influence extends far beyond its forested slopes. Experts warn of extreme landslide risks in this geologically fragile zone, where blasting for underground structures like tunnels and powerhouses with heavy industrial explosives threatens catastrophe. With an installed renewable energy capacity of 20.23 GW, Karnataka needs diversified solutions such as Battery Energy Storage Systems, pumped storage, compressed air energy storage and gravity energy storage to manage the intermittency of renewable energy. Critics acknowledge this need. However, meeting this need by destroying forever, a carbon-storing ecological backbone such as the Sharavathi Lion-Tailed Macaque Wildlife Sanctuary in the Western Ghats, which justly enjoys the highest levels of legal protection is indefensible. To defend the ecology of the irreplaceable Western Ghats entails renewing our ties to the natural world. No trite nostrum along the lines of “sustainable development” will suffice. Sustainability is about what we can go on taking from nature without finding the courage to face our organised, well-disguised greed. Ecological renewal and reciprocity imply that we honour what our ancestors have bequeathed to us a stable, healthy ecology. It means we creatively renew a culture long integrated with nature, until the winds of accelerating industrial modernity begin to sunder them.
title: Test #07: The Dark Forest of Katlekan - Amazon of India

text: India has followed Indian Standard Time (IST) for decades. The new Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026, make it the legally enforceable reference for official and commercial use, requiring systems across sectors to synchronise to time traceable to IST. The larger objective is a common national time reference. “‘One Nation, One Time’ means having one time reference. At present, different organisations may refer to different sources. It is like each person establishing their own starting point; you then cannot properly compare events or measurements,” she said. Indian Standard Time has been in place for decades. Under an Act of Parliament, CSIR-NPL is the National Metrology Institute mandated to maintain the country’s scientific standards. Maintaining and disseminating IST has been part of our mandate. In fact, IST (Indian Standard Time) is a registered trademark of CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (CSIR-NPL). It has been a team effort over the years, involving scientists and technical staff at NPL, with the guidance and support of successive Directors. But until now, time itself did not have legal status in the country. You could not enforce a requirement that someone’s time be traceable to IST. NPL is the standards body, while enforcement comes under the Department of Legal Metrology. They already enforce measurements such as mass and volume: inspectors can check measurements at a petrol pump or verify the weights used by an establishment. They did not have an equivalent capability for time. Five Regional Reference Standards Laboratories now maintain secondary time scales that are traceable to Indian Standard Time (IST) through CSIR-NPL. ISRO also maintains IST traceability links from NPL. This enables IST to be disseminated and realised at multiple locations while maintaining traceability to the national reference maintained by CSIR-NPL. The broader purpose is to make IST the country’s common legal time reference for commercial and other purposes, including the display of time. This can also improve cybersecurity, reduce crime and make critical infrastructure more resilient. Take the time on your computer. It has to come from somewhere. In the date and time settings, you can select an NTP, or Network Time Protocol, server. The default server may be abroad, so it is not directly providing IST. At present, people obtain time from many sources, often indirectly from GPS. A telecom provider may give you the time maintained in its data centre, but there can be a lag of seconds or even minutes. While travelling, one FM station may say it is seven according to its studio clock, while another says it is 7.01. That is the issue: different people are referring to different sources. IST would become the common national time reference. Traceability can be established through different technologies. NPL has an NTP service with a domain name. If you synchronise your computer with it, your computer becomes traceable to Indian Standard Time. NTP is the most common and accessible method and operates over the internet. Other options include PTP, or Precision Time Protocol, satellite and optical links, and NavIC. The method depends on the accuracy required. The required accuracy depends entirely on the application. ISRO has to be traceable to IST within nanoseconds, while we maintain the country’s time within a few nanoseconds of the international reference, UTC. For many ordinary applications, NTP can provide millisecond-level accuracy. PTP can provide microsecond-level accuracy and works particularly well within a local area network. Any clock or oscillator begins to drift after synchronisation. NTP therefore checks the reference at polling intervals, which can be adjusted depending on how closely a system must remain aligned with IST. For more demanding applications, satellite links are used for highly precise time transfer. NPL provides ISRO with time through satellite links; techniques include Common-View GNSS and two-way satellite time and frequency transfer.
title: Test #08: India is Making IST Legally Enforceable

text: Dark energy is a mysterious force whose effect is pushing galaxies and other cosmic bodies farther apart from one another. It is a hypothetical force with negative pressure that fills the universe, and under the theory of relativity its effect resembles the opposite of gravity. Albert Einstein, whose general theory of relativity appeared in 1915, added a similar term, the cosmological constant, to his equations in 1917 to represent an effect opposing gravity. Until 1990, most physicists treated this constant as a mathematical convenience rather than physical reality. Dark energy itself came to scientific attention in 1998, when two teams of astronomers surveyed distant supernovae, bright stellar explosions marking the death of certain stars, a discovery honoured with the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. These surveys found that the supernovae appeared fainter, and therefore farther away, than earlier models had predicted, indicating that the expansion of the universe had been accelerating rather than slowing down. Before this discovery, it was generally believed that the expansion of the universe was gradually slowing down because of the pull of gravity. Scientists initially doubted the reliability of these results, since clouds of gas or dust might have dimmed the supernovae, or existing estimates of their true brightness might simply have been wrong. After careful re-examination of the available data, researchers concluded that some unknown force, now called dark energy, really does exist and is driving the accelerating expansion. According to current estimates, the universe is composed of about 74% dark energy, 22% dark matter and only around 4% ordinary matter, the kind of matter that telescopes and laboratory instruments can directly detect. Ordinary matter is the only component that scientists understand reasonably well, even though it makes up a small fraction of the universe’s total mass and energy. Dark matter, unlike dark energy, pulls objects together through gravity, but it has never been directly detected in a laboratory despite considerable indirect evidence for its existence. The density of dark energy is extremely low, estimated at about 10-29 grams per cubic centimetre, which makes it almost impossible to detect directly in a laboratory. The most widely accepted explanation for dark energy is the cosmological constant theory, which treats it as an intrinsic energy contained within empty space itself. This constant, often called vacuum energy, is thought to carry a negative pressure equal to its own energy density, and this negative pressure is what drives the accelerating expansion of the universe. Observations of supernovae indicate that this accelerating expansion began roughly 5 billion years ago, once galaxies had drifted far enough apart for dark energy’s effect to outweigh the pull of gravity. As the universe continues to expand, the density of dark matter decreases much faster than that of dark energy, which appears to remain constant regardless of the universe’s size. As the universe keeps expanding, the density of dark matter falls far more quickly than that of dark energy, which seems to stay constant no matter how large the universe becomes. If this trend continues, distant galaxies will eventually cross the cosmic horizon and disappear from view, since the space between them would be expanding faster than the speed of light, without violating the theory of relativity. Nearby galaxies bound together by gravity, including our own would remain largely unaffected, even as the rest of the universe recedes from view. Two broad scenarios have been proposed for the distant future of the universe under the influence of dark energy. In one scenario, known as the Big Rip, the effect of dark energy keeps increasing until it eventually overwhelms every fundamental force, tearing apart galaxies, stars, planets and even atoms. In the other, known as the Big Crunch, the effect of dark energy eventually weakens, allowing gravity to dominate and pull the universe back into a single point.
title: Test #09: Dark Energy: Expanding Universe

text: The Great Living Chola Temples are a group of three magnificent Hindu temples in Tamil Nadu that showcase the extraordinary architectural and artistic achievements of the Chola dynasty. Built primarily between the 11th and 12th centuries CE, these temples remain active places of worship even today, unlike many ancient monuments that survive only as ruins. The Chola dynasty, which had established a powerful kingdom by the 9th century CE, ruled the region for several centuries and reached the peak of its influence under Rajaraja Chola-I, who reigned from 985-1014. His son and successor, Rajendra Chola-I, extended the empire further and reigned from 1012-1044, during which the second of the three great temples was completed around 1035. The first temple, the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, was completed around 1010 and remains the tallest of the three structures, with its vimana rising to nearly 60 metres. The third temple, the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram, was built later by Rajaraja Chola-II, roughly around 1166, and is smaller in scale but is celebrated for its intricate stone carvings. Each of the three temples is dedicated to Lord Shiva and was built mainly using granite, showing the technical skill of Chola architects and stonemasons. The Thanjavur temple, also known as Rajarajesvaram, contains a massive Shiva lingam in its sanctum, while its outer walls carry sculptures of various Hindu deities. The temple has a graceful, curved vimana rising to about 53 metres, softer than the straighter tower at Thanjavur. The temple at features a graceful, curved tower reaching about 53 metres in height, softer than the straight tower at Thanjavur. This temple is known for its stone sculptures of Dakshinamurti, Nataraja, Ardhanari, Durga, Sarasvati and Vishnu, and bronze images of Bhogasakti and Subrahmanya. The Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram is smaller than the other two but is admired for its ornate carvings and for the Rajagambhiran Tirumandapam, a hall shaped like a stone chariot. Its walls contain miniature friezes of the 63 Nayanmars, the Shaivite saints of Tamil tradition, linking temple art with Shaivism. All three temples contain Tamil inscriptions on royal donations, land grants and administration, valuable for Chola-era history. These inscriptions, found across all three temples, record royal grants, land donations and administration, offering evidence about Chola-era society. The temples also display mural paintings from the Chola period, some depicting religious scenes, though later paintings were added during the Nayaka period. Collectively, these inscriptions, sculptures, bronzes and paintings record Chola administration, religion, art and society across the 11th and 12th centuries. The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage Site list in 1987, while the temples at Darasuram were added to the same listing in 2004. Since the temples continue to host daily worship, festivals and traditional rituals, they are regarded as living heritage rather than abandoned archaeological remains. This continued religious use, combined with their architectural grandeur and artistic richness, makes the Great Living Chola Temples an important part of Tamil cultural heritage and South Indian temple tradition. Together, the three temples illustrate the evolution of Dravidian architecture and remain significant for understanding the religious, artistic and administrative history of the Chola dynasty. Scholars and archaeologists continue to study their inscriptions, sculptures and paintings to learn more about medieval Tamil society, administration and religious practice. Today, the three sites also draw large numbers of visitors and researchers, sustaining a link between their eleventh and twelfth century origins and present-day Tamil Nadu.
title: Test #10: Chola Temples and Magnificient Chola Arctitecture

text: The hush that greets visitors at Sarnath today belies the revolution that began here more than 2,500 years ago. Just a few kilometres from the bustling lanes of Varanasi, this serene landscape witnessed one of history’s defining moments when Gautam Buddha delivered his first sermon after attaining enlightenment in Bodh Gaya, setting in motion the ‘Dharmachakra’, or the Wheel of Law. Over centuries, emperors, monks, pilgrims and archaeologists have all left their imprint on Sarnath, transforming it into a living chronicle of faith, art and civilisation. On July 25, 2026, this ancient Buddhist site was officially inscribed as a Unesco World Heritage Site on July 25, 2026, during the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, South Korea. With this inscription, India now has 45 World Heritage sites. Tim Curtis, director and representative, Unesco Regional Office for South Asia, said in his note: "For more than 2,500 years, Sarnath has been a place of pilgrimage and inspiration for Buddhists around the world. It is here that the Buddha delivered his first sermon, sharing teachings of compassion, wisdom and peace that continue to resonate today. Its temples, stupas, and monasteries bear witness to centuries of faith, devotion, and shared human heritage. Safeguarding this exceptional site is our collective responsibility for present and future generations." The Unesco inscription covers the Chaukhandi Stupa and the archaeological remains of Sarnath, located about 626 metres apart. Chaukhandi commemorates Buddha’s meeting with his five disciples after enlightenment, while the archaeological complex includes the Dhamek Stupa, Dharmarajika Stupa, the Ashokan Pillar and extensive monastic remains. Together, they preserve the site where Buddha delivered the Dhamma-Chakra-Pravartana (First Sermon), setting the Wheel of Dhamma (or dharma) in motion and laying the foundation of the Buddhist Sangha. The entire area is known as the Deer Park. For Buddhists across the world, Sarnath marks one of the defining moments in the faith’s history. The sacred landscape has sustained a pilgrimage tradition for nearly 2,500 years and preserves some of the earliest surviving examples of Buddhist monastic architecture, art and learning. Conservation architect Abha Narain Lambah, who prepared Sarnath’s Unesco nomination dossier, said the site’s exceptional value lay in the combination of its history and living traditions. "Sarnath uniquely brings together the place of Buddha’s First Sermon, the beginnings of the Buddhist Sangha and an unbroken pilgrimage tradition spanning nearly 2,500 years. That is what gives it an exceptional place in world heritage," she said. "According to him, not birth but character was to be honoured." The observation, recorded in B. Majumdar’s ‘A Guide to Sarnath’, first published in 1937, captures the essence of the Buddha’s teachings at Isipatana, the ancient name of Sarnath. The book explains how the Buddha challenged ritualism and social hierarchy by placing moral conduct above birth, an idea that resonated deeply across ancient India. It also identifies Sarnath as the place where the Buddhist Sangha was first established after the Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths to his five former companions, making it the birthplace of organised Buddhism. Few places in India have yielded such an extraordinary archaeological harvest. Majumdar’s guide remarks that nowhere else have excavations rewarded historians so richly. Sarnath preserves masterpieces spanning nearly a millennium from the mirror-like polish of Mauryan craftsmanship to the sublime sculptures of the Gupta age. Every mound, broken pillar and sculpted fragment tells the story of a civilisation that blended spirituality with artistic brilliance. The story of Sarnath begins in the sixth century BCE when the Buddha, having attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, walked to the Deer Park in search of the five ascetics who had once abandoned him. Here he expounded the Middle Path, rejecting both luxury and extreme asceticism.
title: Test #11: Sarnath Eternal Dialogue With History

text: You must familiarize yourself with the different available types of perfumes. Then only you will be able to choose the one best suited for you. You may be attracted to one particular scent. But to fully enjoy it your knowledge of different perfume types is important to help you choose the right variant. Different perfume types do not necessarily affect the scent or the overall quality of the product. They merely point out the concentration of the fragrance oils in the perfume. There are five common types of perfumes that exists. The main difference between these five perfume types is their fragrance oil concentration. Parfum is the perfume type with the highest fragrance oil concentration. It is for this reason that it remains to be the most expensive of the perfume types. A parfum contains about fifteen to forty percent fragrance oil concentration. This hight concentration makes it heavier and stronger and oily as well. Only a few dabs of parfum on the pulse points will last you the whole day. Its stronger scent makes it easier to identify compared to other perfume types. Eau de parfum is sometimes simply referred to as parfum and holds a fragrance oil concentration of ten to fifteen percent. They hold a lighter oil concentration and more alcohol and water concentration compared to parfum. Eau de parfum is still quite a strong perfume type and will last on your body for six to eight hours. Eau de parfum is not very easy to identify as it housed in a spray bottle or stopper bottle. Eau de toilette contains four to fifteen percent fragrance oil concentration. This lighter fragrance perfume is normally housed in a spray bottle due to its relatively lower fragrance oil concentration and high alcohol content. It lasts anywhere from two to four hours. This means that you will have to refresh it at some point during the day. Or replace it with stronger eau de parfum at night. Its relatively light body makes it a suitable option for office wear or any occasion where you do not want your perfume to be offensive. Eau de toilette is suitable for the warmer weather during the summer and spring seasons. Eau de cologne perfume type is originally formulated for people who want a lighter variation of a certain fragrance scent. Eau de cologne primarily holds a two to five percent fragrance oil concentration. Eau de cologne also lasts for two to four hours. This diluted perfume type is not only light but also offers the option of the fragrance scent you love at a cheaper price. Many expensive fragrances for men that come in an eau de cologne characteristic are normally marketed as a splash on or aftershave fragrance. Eau de fraiche is also known as fragrance water. It is the least expensive and least concentrated of the perfume types. It contains between one to three percent fragrance oil concentrations. Because of this ultra light fragrance oil concentration and high alcohol concentration this will usually dissipate within an hour or two and are housed in a spray bottle. Eau de fraiche loosely translates to freshwater. It is a great summer product for occasions at the beach or gym. You can use it to refresh after a workout or while chilling at the beach. Choosing the right perfume type also depends on your skin type since perfumes tend to react differently depending on the natural oils present on the skin. People with oily skin often find that fragrances last longer on them compared to those with dry skin. This is because oily skin holds onto the fragrance molecules for a longer duration. It is also worth considering the occasion before applying a particular perfume type. A stronger parfum may be more suitable for an evening event while a lighter eau de toilette works better for daytime or office settings. Storage of perfumes also plays an important role in maintaining their quality over time. Perfumes should always be kept away from direct sunlight and extreme heat since these conditions can alter the chemical composition of the fragrance oils. Keeping the bottle tightly closed also helps in preventing the alcohol from evaporating too quickly.
title: Test #12: Perfumes - MP CPCT - 11/01/2025 - S2

text: John Sherbrooke Banks, popularly known as ‘Major Banks’ in the annals of Lucknow’s history, was born on October 7, 1811, in Kildare, Ireland. He was the offspring of Samuel Banks, a physician in the army, and his spouse, Lucinda. His early life and formative years unfolded in relative mediocrity, with a career in medicine, akin to his father’s profession being a remote possibility. Consequently, in 1828, he chose to enlist as a cadet in the Bengal Native Infantry of the British East India Company, arriving on Indian soil in December 1829. His military ascent began in earnest, achieving the rank of Lieutenant in October 1835, followed by a promotion to Captain in January 1846. His service took him to the battlegrounds of Kabul and Burma, and by July 1855, he was deployed to Lucknow, where he served under Outram, the Resident at the time. During his tenure in India, Banks had become proficient in Hindustani and Persian, skills that rendered him an invaluable asset at the Military Secretary’s office in Calcutta. Though initially reluctant to assume a civilian role in Lucknow, destiny intervened. Major Banks took residence in Kothi Hayat Baksh, constructed during the reign of Sa’adat Ali Khan, the sixth Nawab of Awadh. This residence would then be known as ‘Bank’s House.’ Over the decades, the structure would undergo numerous transformations, ultimately becoming the Governor’s House, and it remains today as the official residence of the Governor of Uttar Pradesh, recently re-christened as Jan Bhawan. During the events of 1857, after the British soldiers had abandoned their makeshift barracks at the Chaupar stables, Banks had moved to Martin Gubbins’ house in the Residency. Gubbins was the controversial Financial Commissioner, then stationed at Lucknow, whose approach to the rebellion was quite different and often at variance with Lawrence’s views. This was understandable, since Lawrence was a military man and Gubbins was a civil servant. Earlier, Banks had married Elizabeth Hutchinson, the daughter of a Major General, in 1855, in Ooty. The couple had one daughter, Frederica, who was born in Lucknow in June, 1857. By this time, Lucknow was already engulfed in the First War of Independence, after the annexation of Awadh by the British in 1856. It was Major Banks, who had accompanied Outram, during his meetings with Wajid Ali Shah, before the annexation. On February 7, 1856, Wajid Ali Shah conveyed to the Resident his firm resolution not to sign the proposed Treaty. This prompted Outram to act immediately, taking over the government under his direct control as Chief Commissioner. For the purposes of administration, the city was made over to Major Banks, who assumed the charge of his new office as Commissioner, with the help of the city Kotwal. By mid-day, all the departments of the erstwhile nawabi government were brought under the control of Banks the ministers and nobility of the kingdom being divested of their authority and responsibilities. Henry M Lawrence assumed charge of Chief Commissioner in Lucknow in March 1857. He resided within the Residency complex here, which became the focal point of the freedom struggle. Under the directions of Lawrence, Banks, accompanied by a military force, raided the Qaiserbagh palaces and recovered ‘a large amount of most valuable jewellery, comprising a richly-ornamented throne, crowns richly studded with gems, gold pieces from Venice and Spain, a variety of necklaces, armlets, rings and native ornaments.’ He also came across a large brass 21-pounder gun, complete with carriage and wagon. The confiscated treasure was moved to the Residency, some of the valuables being looted during the movement by the British soldiers themselves. Henry Lawrence died of a shell wound on July 4, 1857, but not before he had ‘nominated’ Major Banks, his close confidant and advisor as successor, i.e. Chief Commissioner. Banks proved his mettle in both civilian and military roles and took to visiting the various outposts in the beleaguered Residency.
title: Test #13: Legacy of Major Banks in Lucknow History

text: A quiet transformation is unfolding inside the factories of Sandila, an industrial belt situated in the Hardoi district of Uttar Pradesh. As fresh investment worth thousands of crores flows into this manufacturing hub, growing numbers of women are stepping into assembly lines, quality-control units and automated production sections. For countless families, this marks the first instance of a woman entering formal factory employment, signalling a gradual change in household economics and long-standing gender roles. Close to 5,000 workers are currently employed across the Sandila industrial estate, and nearly 1,000 of them, about one-fifth of the total workforce, are women, based on figures collected between 2019 and 2025. This period, especially the years 2023-2024, has seen a sharp rise in female participation within the local industrial workforce. Among the most significant contributors to this change is a paint manufacturing unit built at a cost of nearly Rs 1,000 crore, where the entire colourant and stainer sections are operated exclusively by women. This unit commenced commercial production in 2023 and currently employs around 200 women. Overall investment proposals recorded for the Sandila belt have crossed Rs 6,000 crore, reflecting the scale of industrial expansion taking place in the region. Hardoi, once known chiefly for agriculture, is gradually emerging as a notable manufacturing hub within Uttar Pradesh. State officials tracking industrial growth note that women entering factory jobs for the first time are likely to influence employment patterns within their communities for years to come. Skill-development programmes linked to these factories have expanded steadily since 2021, supporting a more structured entry of women into technical and production roles. Officials monitoring industrial growth in the state note that women taking up factory jobs for the first time may shape employment patterns in their communities for years ahead. With investment proposals continuing to rise and new manufacturing units under construction, the number of women joining the industrial workforce in Sandila and the wider Hardoi belt is expected to grow further in the coming years. Uttar Pradesh’s One District One Product initiative, launched in 2018, has strengthened several such industrial clusters across the state, including those situated in Hardoi district. Invest UP, the state’s nodal investment agency, has recorded thousands of proposals from various sectors since the initiative began, with manufacturing and food processing among the leading contributors. Industrial parks similar to Sandila have emerged in other districts as well, following a broader pattern of decentralised industrial growth away from traditional urban centres. Employment trends suggest that such clusters, spread across smaller towns, could add lakhs of jobs over the next decade, with women expected to form a growing share of this new workforce. Between 2018 and 2025, the state has witnessed a steady rise in factory-based employment for women, moving away from decades when such roles remained rare in smaller industrial towns. The steady rise of women workers in this belt, first-generation entrants in most cases, is being viewed as an early sign of wider social and economic change spreading across the district. Other companies functioning within the same industrial belt, including Varun Beverages, Haldiram, ITC, Balaji Wafers and Hindustan Foods, have also widened employment opportunities for women over the past few years. At Paras Dairy, another major unit within the industrial estate, more than half of the workforce today comprises women, many of whom lead individual sections and verticals. A quick note on what I built in: the first confusion trap is the third sentence, landing right at word 80. The second trap is the sentence beginning "Among the leading contributors to this shift", echoing the earlier paint-unit sentence. The third trap is "Officials monitoring industrial growth in the state note that", echoing the earlier officials sentence.
title: Test #14: Industrial Boom in Sandila More Women to Work

text: Children marriage refers to the formal or informal union in which one or both individuals have not attained the age of eighteen years. International law recognises it as a violation of the rights of the child because it deprives young people of the freedom to make informed decisions about one of the most significant commitments of life. Although many societies have enacted laws prohibiting the practice, child marriage continues to affect millions of children, particularly girls, across Asia, Africa, and parts of Latin America. It is not merely a legal concern or a social custom inherited from the past. It is a question of human dignity, personal autonomy, equal opportunity, and justice. Child marriage affects education because many children, especially girls, are forced to leave school before completing their studies. Without education, they lose opportunities for employment, financial independence, and informed participation in society. This cycle often continues across generations, as children born into such families may also face poverty and limited educational opportunities. Health consequences are equally serious. Early pregnancy exposes young mothers to greater risks during childbirth and increases the likelihood of health complications for both mother and child. Emotional stress, anxiety, and depression may also arise because young individuals are required to shoulder responsibilities for which they are not mentally prepared. Governments, educational institutions, civil society organisations, and community leaders all have important roles in ending child marriage. Strong enforcement of laws, accessible education, awareness campaigns, and financial support for vulnerable families can reduce the pressure that leads to early marriages. Communities should encourage girls and boys to complete their education, develop life skills, and make informed decisions about their futures. Parents also have a crucial responsibility. Instead of viewing marriage as an immediate solution to financial or social problems, they should invest in the education, health, and personal growth of their children. Religious and community leaders can influence public opinion by promoting the importance of equality, respect, and children's rights. Ending child marriage is not only about enforcing legislation but also about changing attitudes. Every child deserves the freedom to dream, learn, and choose the course of life without coercion. A society that protects children from early marriage builds healthier families, stronger communities, and a more prosperous future. By working together, governments, families, schools, and citizens can ensure that every child grows up with dignity, opportunity, and hope. To fully comprehend the persistence of child marriage, one must examine the deep-rooted socio-economic drivers that sustain it across diverse cultures. Poverty remains one of the most powerful catalysts. In economically disadvantaged households, marrying off a young daughter is often erroneously perceived as a mechanism to alleviate financial strain by reducing the number of dependents to feed and clothe. In some contexts, traditional practices such as dowry or bride price further incentivize families to marry off daughters at an early age. However, rather than curing financial distress, this practice typically locks families deeper into a persistent cycle of generational poverty, as young brides lose the chance to acquire marketable job skills and income-generating capabilities. Gender inequality acts as another formidable pillar supporting child marriage. In patriarchal societies, girls are frequently assigned a subordinate status where their worth is measured primarily through domestic labor and reproductive capacity rather than intellectual or professional potential. When families face scarce resources, investments in sons' education are often prioritized over daughters', under the archaic assumption that girls will eventually move into their husbands' households. This systemic discrimination denies young females the fundamental right to self-determination, trapping them in predefined roles that stifle personal growth and restrict their contributions to the broader community.
title: Test #15: Child Marriage Below 18 Years - JKSSB

text: A conventional data centre, running websites or cloud storage, relies largely on CPUs, and an average rack in such a centre draws about 8kW. In an AI data centre, GPUs do the heavy lifting. A high-density AI rack can draw over 2,000 units of electricity a day at 80% utilisation. A large AI data centre can therefore consume millions of units daily. Nearly all that electricity ends up as heat. Rack for rack, a cutting-edge AI system can emit about 14 times as much heat as the average conventional rack. An AI rack is, in effect, a 120-kW electric heater that happens to answer questions. High electricity use and heat generation are a feature of AI, not a bug. According to the International Energy Agency, data centres consumed 415 TWh in 2024, enough to meet the average annual needs of 353 million Indian households. Many leading hyperscalers advertise their vast purchases of renewable power as proof of corporate virtue. But renewable energy did not spring fully formed from capitalism’s generous heart. It was helped along by subsidies, regulation and decades of political pressure over climate change. That is precisely how markets are supposed to work: governments set a direction and draw a line around what is no longer acceptable, and capitalism gets to work, finding progressively cheaper ways to meet the constraint. Hyperscalers in India has bought a lot of renewable energy (and offsets) to power their centres. But to someone familiar with the innards of electricity adjustment, the relative opacity in how they match seasonal and diurnal generation with constant use invites further scrutiny. If we as a country are subsidising that cost (through generous policy support), what precisely are we getting in return? Moving electrons generate heat. Seen this way, a transistor is like a tiny heater powered by electricity. Engineers pack these transistors onto chips thin pieces of silicon that resemble miniature cities, with transistors as buildings, wires as roads, electrons as traffic, and clocks as traffic lights that work to keep everything in step. The Intel chip in my laptop contains more than a billion transistors: an entire miniature city of tiny heaters. The CPU (central processing unit) is a generalist: it can open a browser, check email or play music, handling tasks as directed, in careful sequence. The GPU (graphics processing unit) is a specialist. In its early days, it drew the millions of pixels needed for videogames by performing many similar calculations simultaneously. It turns out this works brilliantly for the math behind AI, which involves multiplying vast grids of numbers to train and run models. Nvidia, the company most closely associated with GPUs, has unsurprisingly become the rockstar of the AI world. Chips, along with memory, storage, networking, power and cooling hardware, are packed into servers. Servers are stacked in racks. Racks together make a data centre. On a visit to one such centre, Joanna Stern, reporting for The Wall Street Journal, said it was hot enough around the servers to “blow-dry my hair”. Cooling involves two separate tasks: lifting heat away from the chips and servers, and ejecting it from the building. The first can be done in several ways: by blowing cold air through servers; through direct-to-chip cooling, in which cold plates sit on GPUs and a sealed liquid loop carries heat away. The latest is immersion cooling, in which servers are submerged in a non-conducting liquid that absorbs their heat. Once the heat reaches the edge of the building, it can be ejected through dry coolers that use little or no water; through evaporative cooling towers, which can consume about 1.5 to 2 litres per kW-hour of computing electricity; or via a hybrid of the two. Thus, depending on the combination of technologies and the local climate, a 100 MW AI data centre can consume almost no onsite water for cooling or over 2 million litres a day. Water usage effectiveness, or WUE, measures litres of onsite water consumed per unit of computing electricity.
title: Test #16: AI Data Centres Run Hot and Drink Deep

text: There is something extraordinary about radio that no other medium has managed to replicate. A voice can inform, comfort, warn, persuade and accompany us in ways that television, newspapers and even social media rarely can. Radio does something different. It accompanies. It sits quietly in kitchens before dawn, in taxis caught up in traffic, in fishing boats at high sea and in tractors crossing fields. It asks for nothing except attention, and in return it creates something increasingly rare: Trust. A battery-powered radio or a basic mobile phone is often all that is needed. In a country as vast and unequal as India, that matters. For millions of people, especially those on the margins, radio remains the most affordable and accessible source of information. Radio also possesses something increasingly rare: A sense of intimacy. Unlike television, which demands our eyes, or social media, which constantly competes for our attention, radio speaks directly to the listener. There is no screen to distract, no endless scrolling and no barrage of competing images. There is simply a voice telling a story. That is why radio has often been called the theatre of the mind. It leaves space for imagination while creating a relationship of trust between the broadcaster and the listener. At its best, radio is much more than entertainment. It is a public service. It warns communities before floods arrive, explains new government policies, tells farmers about weather patterns and market prices, alerts parents to vaccination drives, carries election results, and preserves local languages and cultures. It informs people not just about the world, but about the lives they are living. Few media have served democracy so quietly or so consistently. Which makes India’s relationship with radio all the more puzzling. Despite being the world’s largest democracy, India still does not allow private FM radio stations to produce and broadcast independent news. They can play music, host celebrity interviews and entertain audiences, but they cannot report on a local election, investigate corruption in a municipal office or tell listeners that a bridge has collapsed nearby. Radio asks very little of its audience. It does not require literacy, expensive technology or high-speed internet. It asks only that someone listens. That simple quality has made radio one of the most democratic forms of communication ever created. It reaches people where other media often cannot: In remote villages, on fishing boats, in the hills, on highways, in fields and factories. Every medium has its strengths. Newspapers offer depth and context. Television captures the immediacy of events. The internet delivers information at remarkable speed. If they broadcast news at all, it must come unedited from All India Radio, the state broadcaster. Community radio stations, despite their deep roots in villages and small towns, face the same restriction. The policy has remained largely unchanged for more than two decades. In 2013, the public interest organisation Common Cause challenged the restrictions in the Supreme Court, arguing that they violate the constitutional guarantee of free speech and preserve an unnecessary state monopoly over the airwaves. More than a decade later, the issue remains unresolved. Meanwhile, every other major news platform in India has been liberalised. Radio alone remains fenced off from independent journalism. The government’s concerns are understandable. Monitoring thousands of local broadcasts is difficult. False information can spread quickly, and irresponsible reporting can inflame communal tensions or threaten public order. But these are challenges faced by every news medium. Television, newspapers and digital platforms are regulated through law and professional standards, not prevented from reporting. It is difficult to see why radio alone should be treated differently. Around the world, governments have reached a different conclusion. Britain has commercial radio broadcasting news alongside the BBC.
title: Test #17: Who is Afraid of Radio?

text: Power has always fascinated the human imagination. It promises the ability to shape events, influence lives, and leave a lasting mark upon history. Yet no possession tests human character more severely than authority itself. Lord Acton expressed this truth in words that have become timeless: "Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely." His observation is not merely a criticism of rulers. It is a profound insight into the nature of human character. William Pitt voiced the same concern when he remarked, "Unlimited power is apt to corrupt the minds of those who possess it." These reflections remind us that the real danger lies not in the existence of power, but in the disappearance of the restraints that keep it answerable to law, morality, and public reason. Power is indispensable to every organised society. No government can function without authority. No legal system can survive without the capacity to enforce justice. Every institution depends upon some form of leadership if it is to fulfil its purpose. The issue, therefore, is not whether power should exist. The question is how power should be exercised. Authority serves society only when it remains accountable to principles greater than the individual who holds it. The corrupting influence of power seldom appears in dramatic form. It begins with small changes in attitude. A leader becomes accustomed to obedience. Criticism gradually disappears from the surrounding environment. Agreement is mistaken for wisdom, and authority begins to appear indistinguishable from truth. The individual who once regarded power as a responsibility slowly begins to experience it as a privilege. This transformation is often invisible to the person exercising authority. Yet it is clearly visible to those who live under it. History demonstrates that unchecked authority inevitably breeds tyranny. When institutions fail to maintain robust checks and balances, power consolidates into the hands of a few, eroding the foundational pillars of justice and equality. Democratic societies are specifically designed to disperse authority, recognizing that human nature is inherently fallible. Separation of powers, independent judiciaries, free press, and active civic participation serve as vital bulwarks against authoritarian drift. Without these vigilant safeguards, even the most noble political systems can degenerate into autocratic rule where dissent is criminalized and institutional transparency is replaced by secrecy. Furthermore, the psychology of authority reveals that power alters perception. Leaders surrounded by deferential subordinates often lose touch with ground realities. They mistake sycophancy for competence and loyalty to a person over loyalty to constitutional principles. This cognitive distortion fosters an echo chamber wherein warning signs are ignored until systemic failure becomes inevitable. To counteract this vulnerability, effective governance requires institutional mechanisms that welcome constructive criticism, protect whistleblowers, and mandate regular peaceful transfers of authority. Ethics and morality must remain inextricably linked to the exercise of public office. Power devoid of ethical grounding becomes mere domination, sustained purely by coercion rather than legitimacy. True leadership recognizes that authority is a temporary stewardship entrusted by the public, not a personal entitlement. Public servants are custodians of the collective trust, and their decisions must be measured against the greater good rather than narrow partisan interests. When governance prioritizes integrity, transparency, and public welfare, it fosters social trust and strengthens the democratic fabric. In the contemporary era, the diffusion of information and the rise of digital platforms have introduced new dimensions to the dynamics of power. While technology empowers citizens by democratizing information, it also provides authoritarian regimes with sophisticated tools for surveillance, manipulation, and censorship. The struggle between state control and individual liberty continues to evolve, making digital literacy and cybersecurity fundamental components of modern citizenship. Preserving freedom requires constant vigilance, ethical technological innovation, and an unwavering commitment to human rights across all domains of society.
title: Test #18: Unlimited Power & Human Character - JKSSB

text: India grows enough food to feed its people, yet millions remain vulnerable to food insecurity while tonnes of perfectly edible produce are lost every day. Moreover, our finance minister, Nirmala Sitharaman, has laid down the roadmap to achieve Viksit Bharat in her Union Budget 2026, making agriculture, technology, logistics and rural growth the soul of the country’s development plan. However, one obstacle continues to stand in the way as it is witnessed that a significant share of the food India produces never reaches consumers. Nearly 78.2 million tonnes of food is wasted annually, eroding farmer incomes, straining natural resources, and limiting access to food for those who need it most. Public debate around food waste often focuses on consumer behaviour, overly elaborate celebrations, or surplus food discarded by households and restaurants. While these factors contribute to the problem, they overlook a more fundamental issue which implies that a significant portion of the food is gone long before it reaches consumers. The missing link in India's struggle against food loss lies in what happens between the farm and the fork. The ripple effects are far-reaching. Every kg of food that never reaches the consumer represents wasted water, energy, land, labour, and other resources invested in its production. When discarded food decomposes in landfills, it releases methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide. India's food loss problem is, therefore, not merely a waste management concern; it is a food security, climate, and farmer income challenge that requires greater attention. The country has invested significantly in agricultural infrastructure through initiatives such as the ‘Agriculture Infrastructure Fund,’ cold storage projects, and food processing schemes. Yet, gaps in storage, transportation, and market access continue to hamper the movement of perishable produce. Small farmers often lack access to scientific storage, temperature-controlled logistics, and reliable market linkages, causing perfectly consumable food to lose quality and value before it reaches buyers. For farmers, this often means watching a part of their hard-earned produce lose value before it can generate the income they depend on. Think about a crate of mangoes leaving an orchard, a litre of milk collected from a village dairy, or the day's catch arriving at a coastal harbour. Their value depends not only on production, but also on how quickly and efficiently they reach the market. Without proper temperature management, handling systems, and distribution networks, food loss becomes inevitable. The problem is not a lack of food production. It is the inability to preserve and move food efficiently. Cold chains are often seen as a logistics requirement. In reality, they are a critical link between agricultural production and consumer access. They extend shelf life, reduce spoilage, improve quality retention, and allow producers to access distant markets while improving value realisation. More importantly, they create the conditions necessary for reducing avoidable food loss at scale. When supported by integrated logistics networks, temperature-controlled transportation, and seamless coordination across the supply chain, cold chains can help ensure that perishable products move faster, travel farther, and retain their value for longer. The benefits are shared across stakeholders. Farmers realise better prices, businesses reduce wastage-related costs, consumers gain access to fresher products, and the environment benefits from lower emissions. Technology is helping improve efficiency and transparency through real-time visibility, predictive planning, and data-driven decision-making. Addressing food waste requires action across multiple fronts, including consumer awareness, redistribution initiatives, food processing, and circular economy solutions. However, preventing food from being lost in the first place remains the most effective intervention. Behind every tonne of food lost is a farmer's effort, precious natural resources, and a missed opportunity to feed someone.
title: Test #19: The Missing Link in India's Food Security

text: French mathematician, astronomer, historian and geodesist Jean Baptiste Joseph Delambre and fellow mathematician, astronomer and surveyor Pierre Francois Andre Mechain embarked on an expedition from Paris. Their objective was to establish the definitive length of the metre by taking geodetic measurements between Dunkirk and Barcelona as it formed an arc section of the meridian that passed through Paris. This arc measurement, which took them the better part of six years from 1792-98, thereby served as the basis for the very first definition of the metre. Once the revolution was underway in 1789, the French public demanded uniform weights and measures everywhere in the nation in order to facilitate trade and avoid confusion. By 1790, this project was green flagged by the National Assembly and a basic unit of length measurement, the metre, was proposed. We live in a hyperconnected modern world where the accurate measurement be it of length, weight, or anything else and precise definition are non-negotiables. From the smallest of electronic gadgets to the largest of buildings or transportation systems, global economies today function in a way such that items that make up the whole are sourced from around the world. For this earthly jigsaw puzzle to function at scale, the interchangeability and reproducibility have to be a given as the pieces have to fit perfectly every time, right from the first time. History-buffs out there will surely know the French Revolution as one of the biggest political, societal and historical events in history. What many might not know is the fact that it also served as the origin of the metric system. There was a clamour to replace the diverse regional systems of Europe with a new universal decimal system that was founded upon some “natural and invariable base”. The origin of the metric system was thus intertwined with the birth of the metre. We take this for granted now as we live in a time when the standards have been established beyond doubt and accuracy of measurement is probably at its best through history. Things, however, were rather different earlier, even if we were to dial back a little over 230 years and head to a time late in the 18th Century. Even as Delambre and Mechain were triangulating their way towards an accurate measure, the French National Assembly, on August 1, 1793, “affirmed the decimal system and the meridianal definition of the meter, ordered the continuation of the work, and decreed that the Academy provide for the manufacture, distribution, and explanation of provisional meters for general use while it prosecuted its measurements.” Following the survey of the arc, three platinum standards and several iron copies of the metre were made. Additionally, in order to help the populace familiarise with the new measure, it was decided to place the standard in the busiest places. More than 10 were installed in Paris alone and a couple of them have even survived to this day. In case you were under the impression that that was it, it wasn’t. For decades later, it was revealed through subsequent examinations that Delambre and Mechain had erred in their measurement. Given that many years had since passed, the metre was redefined rather than alter its length. Therefore, instead of a metre being one ten-millionth of the distance between the terrestrial pole and the equator, it was redefined as the distance between the two marks on a bar. The 1875 Treaty of the Meter, or the Meter Convention, was signed on May 20 to “assure the international unification and improvement of the metric system”, helping create the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (French: Bureau international des poids et mesures, BIPM). The BIPM, a diplomatic organisation tasked with the responsibility of maintaining an international system of units, continues to facilitate the standardisation of measurements world-wide to this day. In its 151 years of existence, the definition of the metre has been altered a number of times to the current version that we now learn at schools. One ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole, measured along a meridian passing through Paris.
title: Test #20: The First Definition of the Metre

text: The Union Cabinet on Friday (July 31, 2026) approved an outlay of 84,084 crore for the Oil Ministry’s National Offshore Exploration Scheme. ‘Samudra Manthan’ seeks to provide a fillip to India’s ambitions in deepwater and ultra-deepwater explorations. The scheme, which, among other things, seeks to de-risk offshore exploration and catalyse private investments, calls for the corpus to be utilised through fiscal year 2030-31. Hydrocarbon exploration by its very nature is a complex, capital-intensive activity which holds long gestation periods typically five to ten years spanning from when an exploration block is awarded to the commencement of commercial production. Deepwater and ultra-deepwater which entail extracting oil and gas from beneath the ocean’s floor require further advanced technology and enhanced investment. The Oil Ministry sees future hydrocarbon potential in India’s deepwater and ultra-deepwater basins, such as Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Mahanadi and the Andaman region. According to government estimates, a single deepwater exploratory well in these frontier areas could cost approximately $125 million to $150 million.
