Ideally, the life cover you need is an amount that covers any outstanding liability, needs of all dependents and the value of any visible and important goals (until retirement). An assessment of the current lifestyle is done to ascertain a ballpark figure for future goals. Plus, the medical history of the individual being covered is also taken into account as a risk factor. If you already have life cover through another insurer, your employer or a credit card, reduce the required cover by that amount. The insurance market is flooded with investment-linked plans, savings-cum-protection plans and return-of-premium policies. None of these is necessary if your objective is simply to protect your family’s finances in the event of your death. What you need is a plain term insurance policy. For a INR1 crore cover, a savings-cum-protection guaranteed-return endowment plan may cost a 40-year-old around INR10 lakh a year in premiums. A pure term insurance policy offering the same cover would cost around INR15,000 a year. While the claim settlement ratio is important, experts recommend looking beyond the overall average and examining individual death claim settlement ratios, both by number of claims settled and by the value of claims paid.
title: Test #42: How Much Life Insurance is Enough?

text: THE MIGHTY Yangtze, running 6,300km from the Tibetan plateau to Shanghai, is sometimes known as China’s “mother river”. Yet it was not always treated with much respect. Sewage and industrial waste were poured into its waters. In the 1950s over 400,000 tonnes of fish were taken from the river every year; by the time the ban came into force in 2021 the catch had fallen to less than 100,000 tonnes. River patrols, drones, surveillance cameras and tough fines help enforce the ban. Xi Jinping, China’s supreme leader, personally champions it, and in recent years local officials’ promotion prospects have been tied to environmental metrics. Though some illegal fishing still occurs, it appears to be relatively small-scale and diminishing; last year the number of related criminal cases fell by 40% from 2024. But not all the damage is permanent. Asia’s longest river is now making a remarkable comeback. Sweeping protection measures in place since 2021 seem to be aiding a recovery. Fish biomass (the estimated total weight of all the fish in the river) has risen by over 200% since then, after seven decades of decline, according to a study released in February. The latest government figures, meanwhile, 1,400 finless porpoises a chubby, snub-nosed relative of the baiji that locals call a “river pig” now live in the river’s basin, up from low of 1,000 in 2017. Millions of tonnes of fish were dragged out. Mega-dams clogged up its channels. It was all too much for some of the Yangtze’s most wondrous inhabitants. The baiji, a white-bellied, nearly sightless dolphin, is probably extinct; so is the gigantic, sword-nosed paddlefish. The Chinese Communist Party, once famous for pillaging from the natural world, has set to protecting parts of it. State-run media claim China is now a “global biodiversity champion”. In April other scientists witnessed a rare type of sturgeon breeding in the wild for the first time in two decades. Another study published in July found that a significantly greater proportion of fish in the river were reaching sexual maturity, good news for the prospects of the next generation. At least in the case of the Yangtze, the results have been impressive. The river’s rapid turnaround might offer lessons for other ravaged watercourses, such as the Mekong in South-East Asia. But China’s “eco-authoritarian” approach top-down and intolerant of resistance deserves scrutiny before being imitated. The government does not listen to the people that its environmental policies harm. And sometimes it does not listen to environmentalists, either. At the same time the Yangtze’s waters have become cleaner. Officials closed or relocated thousands of chemical factories near its banks. They planted forests on its upper reaches to bind the soil together, so less slipped into the water. And they “spongified” many cities in the river’s basin by adding artificial wetlands, permeable surfaces and greenery to absorb more rainfall. That reduced flooding and helped clean stormwater before it entered the river. All this has made the waterway more hospitable to wildlife. The Yangtze’s initial recovery is testament to China’s “immense” ability to concentrate state resources on environmental problems, says Wang Limin, a veteran Chinese conservationist. He is encouraged most by the rise in the finless porpoise population because, as an “indicator species” and top predator, the porpoise is a sensitive barometer of the health of the overall ecosystem. It is also cute enough to attract lots of public attention. Mr Wang hopes the tale of the Yangtze’s decline and rebound will make the Chinese people more environmentally aware. Even so, the human cost of the Yangtze’s recovery has been substantial. Some 230,000 fishermen lost their jobs and their boats, which were destroyed or confiscated. According to China’s state-run media, they were given compensation, were retrained and in some cases found new jobs that were better paid than their old ones. But a visit to former fishing communities paints a different picture.
title: Test #43: China's Mightiest River Coming Back From Brink

text: Girish Bharadwaj, known as the Bridge Man of India, died in Sullia at the age of 76, after decades of building suspension footbridges across rural India. He built over 140 footbridges (1989-2019), linking villages long separated by rivers and forests. He was born on 12 May 1950 in Aletty village, Sullia taluk. The nearest school stood almost 5 kilometres away, reachable only through dense forest, so he began his formal education directly in Class-5. After finishing school, Bharadwaj pursued Mechanical Engineering and completed his degree in 1973. A turning point arrived in 1989, when residents of his own village approached him with an unusual request: to construct a hanging bridge over the Payaswini River. Bharadwaj hesitated at first, since he had no background in bridge engineering, but the villagers insisted that his general engineering knowledge would suffice. Accepting the challenge, he devised a simple suspension footbridge built from indigenous materials and local skills. Villagers pooled resources, supplied labour and raised the towers and anchorages, while Bharadwaj contributed his technical expertise without charge, and the structure was finished by August of that same year. Word of this low-cost bridge travelled quickly, and within a few years, government departments began asking him to repeat the design in other locations. The original bridge in Sullia has since remained a symbol of what community effort can achieve. Over the following three decades, Bharadwaj built suspension footbridges across Karnataka, Kerala, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and several other states. He drew inspiration from well-known suspension structures such as the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco and the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan, adapting the underlying technology to suit rural conditions through inexpensive, locally sourced materials. His work sometimes took him into difficult and unsettled terrain. While building bridges in Odisha, he came across Naxal activity in certain areas but continued his projects rather than withdrawing. In parts of Odisha, his projects proceeded despite encounters with Naxal groups, and he chose not to halt construction in those difficult zones. In one such location, he built a bridge after observing villagers struggling to carry bicycles across a water body, a sight that convinced him of the project’s urgency. Bharadwaj received the Padma Shri in 2017, along with several other honours over the years, though he consistently treated bridge-building as a form of service rather than a commercial pursuit. He held the view that rural connectivity formed the foundation of national development, and alongside his bridge work, he also took part in water conservation efforts within his region. Once his course ended, he worked briefly as a farmer before setting up a small engineering workshop in Sullia on his parents’ advice. In its early years the workshop survived mainly on seasonal repair of farm machinery, fabrication jobs and automobile repairs, and business remained slow. During those initial years the workshop depended largely on occasional farm machinery repairs, small fabrication tasks and vehicle servicing, and growth stayed limited. Matters improved only after a government-run rubber factory opened in the vicinity, bringing steadier work to the struggling unit. By the time of his death, his contribution amounted to more than 140 structures built over roughly three decades, connecting communities that had once depended on unsafe river crossings. His story remains tied closely to the villages he served, from the first footbridge raised near his home in 1989 to the many suspension bridges that followed across southern and eastern India, each one built to bring people closer together. Bharadwaj passed away on a Tuesday, leaving behind a legacy of grassroots engineering spanning more than three decades of quiet, dedicated service. Doubts over the genuineness of such a will, allegedly penned by an illiterate agriculturist 18 years before his death, gave a widow from Himachal Pradesh.
title: Test #44: Bridge Man Connected Villages

text: Premature menopause means periods stop before age 40, which raises the risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, memory problems, and mood disorders because of early loss of oestrogen. Globally, about 2-4% of women are affected. In Bihar, though, women aged 30 to 34 experience it at over four times the national average, and more than 12% of women aged 35 to 39 have already gone through menopause. National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) data show that a large proportion of premature menopause cases in Bihar are attributed to surgical menopause, also known as hysterectomy. Bihar is not alone in performing hysterectomies young: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana record high rates too, and research has linked this phenomenon to the availability of State insurance schemes and over-treatment at private hospitals. What sets Bihar apart is that even after surgical cases are set aside, its rate of premature menopause remains far above the national average. Something beyond the operating table is at work, and it is specific to the State. One would expect limited access to protect socio-economically disadvantaged women from surgery. It does exactly the opposite. Nationally, women with the least education reach menopause early at roughly seven times the rate of the most educated, and the same gradient runs through Bihar. But the State departs from the national pattern in one significant way: across most of India, wealthier women are less likely to reach menopause early; in Bihar, wealth offers no such protection. Whatever is driving this cuts across income, a sign that the problem is built into how care is delivered, not into who can afford it. An important factor contributing to the high numbers of hysterectomies is health insurance coverage. This counterintuitive association may be explained by the structure of reimbursement, which incentivises surgical procedures over conservative management options such as patient counselling, medication, and follow-up care for conditions like bleeding disorders. The medical literature refers to this phenomenon as supply-side moral hazard, and the data suggest that women in Bihar are experiencing its effects. Early evidence points towards the poor quality of reproductive surgical care provided to women from socio-economically disadvantaged groups. In addition to this, mass sterilisations are conducted in facilities with poor infrastructure without proper informed consent, and untreated complications that may necessitate further surgical intervention. In some cases, unsuccessful sterilisation procedures result in chronic infection or pain, ultimately leading to hysterectomy. These patterns indicate a systemic issue in the management of women’s reproductive health in the State. Understanding these results however, needs an important point to be considered: NFHS-5 survey data was used to conduct this study, and since only one cross-sectional round was used, causality cannot be established. However, the associations are consistent and robust across the indicators. Some cases may reflect women with pre-existing health conditions opting for surgery; but the disproportionate prevalence of hysterectomy among women with lower education and income levels suggests that systemic factors, rather than individual choice, are primarily responsible for the observed outcomes. These numbers have been sitting in a national survey the whole time, and no one has looked hard at what they say about Bihar. The high prevalence of premature menopause in Bihar should not be interpreted as a statistical outlier. Rather, it reflects the outcomes of a healthcare system that prioritises procedural intervention over comprehensive reproductive care for socioeconomically disadvantaged women. This is likely to have adverse long-term effects on the health and well-being of these women. Surgical removal of the uterus, often accompanied by removal of the ovaries, results in immediate menopause. Thus, the high rates of premature menopause in the State are a reflection of the prevalence of such surgical procedures.
title: Test #45: Women in Bihar Reaching Menopause in 30s

text: Simonetta Vespucci is probably one of the most painted women of the Italian Renaissance. Sandro Botticelli is widely believed to have used her as his model for Venus, and she appears, transformed and idealised, across several of his most famous works. She died in 1476, aged just 23. First, the physical changes visible across the portraits Botticelli painted her several times, from the 1470s through to the posthumous Birth of Venus (1482-1485) suggesting a tumour growing over months or years. For centuries, historians have assumed tuberculosis was to blame it was common, it was often fatal, and it fitted the pattern of a young woman fading quickly. In 2019, We examined the portraits attributed to Botticelli alongside written descriptions from the period, looking for whether the same woman’s face changed in ways that might reflect an underlying illness. Second, the symptoms described in chronicles of her final illness (letters exchanged between Piero Vespucci and Lorenzo de’ Medici, describing her collapse at a ball and the headaches, hallucinations, vomiting and fever that followed), which align closely with the clinical presentation of apoplexy. What we found was a gradual shift in her features across multiple paintings subtle changes to the jaw, the brow, the soft tissue of the face. These are the kind of changes seen in patients with a pituitary adenoma, a tumour of the small gland at the base of the brain that controls hormone production. Specifically, we suspected a tumour secreting both growth hormone and prolactin. Excess of these hormones can alter facial contours over time and, in some cases, cause unexpected lactation and one allegorical figure in Botticelli’s work appears to depict exactly that symptom. Our 2019 paper was cautious. We were not claiming proof we were offering a plausible medical reading of the visual evidence, built by combining art history with clinical endocrinology. Now, in a new paper published in Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, my team and I have gone further. We believe Simonetta’s death itself sudden, rapid, and dramatic according to contemporary accounts is consistent with a specific medical emergency: pituitary tumour apoplexy. Apoplexy occurs when a pituitary tumour bleeds or rapidly swells. It typically causes a sudden and severe headache, loss of vision, confusion, and a swift decline as the body’s hormonal regulation collapses. We argue that this would explain something that tuberculosis alone struggles to account for: how a previously healthy young woman went from apparent wellness to death within a short period. Chronic infections such as tuberculosis usually cause a slower, more visible decline. Third, two documented events in the months before her death her collapse during vigorous dancing at a ball, and an alleged violent encounter with Alfonso-II of Aragon, Duke of Calabria that could plausibly have triggered a bleed or sudden tumour expansion. None of these amounts to certainty. There is no tissue sample from 1476, no scan, no way to examine Simonetta directly only paintings, letters, and clinical reasoning applied five centuries after the fact. What we can say is that a tumour capable of slowly reshaping a person’s face is also capable, if it ruptures, of killing them quickly. Put together, the portraits and the historical record tell a more complete story than either can alone. We hope this encourages both historians and medical professionals to look again at cases like Simonetta’s. Medical knowledge can sometimes answer questions that pure historical record cannot. And, in turn, historical puzzles can push medicine to think differently about how disease unfolds in the body over time. One of the most significant debates in unravelling the geography of The Odyssey has been to pinpoint where Ithaca really was. For a long time, scholars have argued that it must be the island of Ithaki in the Ionian sea. The problem is that Ithaki is mountainous, while Homer’s Ithaca is “low-lying”.
title: Test #46: The Mystery Behind Bottocelli's Muse

text: Long before “engineering” became a formal discipline, India was practising it. Between roughly 3300 and 1300 BCE, the Indus Valley Civilization built meticulously planned cities, covered drainage systems, and refined metalwork. The Vedic period added agriculture, further metallurgy, and systematic sky-watching the base for a scholarly line running from the Rigveda to Aryabhata, Sushruta, Charaka, Varahamihira, and Bhaskaracharya. Centres of learning such as Nalanda, Vikramshila, and Takshashila brought philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, and medicine together under one roof. Aryabhata’s Aryabhatiya (499 CE) worked out trigonometric formulas, argued that the Earth itself moves, and calculated its circumference at 39,968 kilometres. Bhaskaracharya’s Lilavati laid early groundwork for algebra, and Brahmagupta set out the rules for negative numbers. The Sushruta Samhita is the earliest known text on detailed surgery, including plastic and cataract techniques, while the Charaka Samhita reads like an encyclopaedia of internal medicine. Nagarjuna’s Rasashastra covered medicinal preparation, the Surya Siddhanta calculated eclipses and planetary motion, and Varahamihira’s Panchasiddhantika merged five astronomical traditions into one. The rust-free Iron Pillar of Delhi (400 CE) still puzzles metallurgists, and Vastu Shastra drew its architectural principles from the sun’s movement, wind, and a balance of five elements. We live amid artificial intelligence, generative tools, private spaceflight, AR-VR, 5G, drones, humanoid robots, and 3D printing alongside deepening environmental crises, rising mental health difficulties, and ethics that haven’t kept pace with the technology. That gap is worth naming and worth asking what earlier Indian thought, built around balance rather than pure output, might still offer. Ayurveda, India’s traditional medical system, treats mind and body as one connected whole. Ayurvedic learning follows daily and seasonal rhythm. Dinacharya prescribes waking before dawn, exercise, bathing, and reflection. Rtucharya divides the year into six seasons Shishir, Vasant, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, and Hemant each calling for dosha adjustments; summer’s rising Pitta and Vata, for instance, call for cooling foods and plenty of water. Diet follows six tastes sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent eaten according to one’s digestive strength, since, per the Charaka Samhita, weak digestion is the root of nearly every illness. Mentally, Ayurveda describes temperament through three gunas Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. Children today carry real strain from exam pressure and constant social media exposure. Patanjali answered this centuries ago: his second yoga sutra, defines yoga as the stilling of the mind’s fluctuations peace through mastering restlessness, not eliminating its causes. The National Education Policy 2020 makes a related point, insisting self-understanding deserves as much attention as academic content. India’s older texts the Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, and Ayurveda treat mental health as one part of a wider picture spanning body and spirit. The Atharvaveda’s descriptions of mantras and healing sound anticipate what’s now marketed as sound therapy and mindfulness. Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras set out an eight-limbed path Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, and Samadhi for developing body, mind, and spirit together. Practised regularly, it builds flexibility, strength, and immunity, supports digestion and breathing, eases stress and anxiety, sharpens concentration and memory, and nurtures self-knowledge, a steadier outlook, and empathy. Global recognition is hard to overstate: when the UN marked the first International Yoga Day on June 21, 2015, 177 countries backed it. India has since made yoga compulsory in schools, and institutions as prominent as Harvard and Stanford now research its effects. A similar pattern holds for the environment. Despite real scientific progress, climate change and lifestyle disease keep worsening, partly because students rarely learn to treat environmental care as central rather than optional. Older Indian thought treated nature as alive and conscious.
title: Test #47: Science & Technology in Ancient India

text: Turns out the Z in Gen Z didn’t stand for the sleeping ZZZs. It stood for Zeal, Zest and, above all, Zero Fear. Gen-Z, the generation often dismissed as privileged, entitled, anxious, snowflake, and reels-obsessed, has taken to the streets, leaving many scratching their heads over how this happened. Sure, an Instagram meme account of a Cockroach Janta Party did go viral. But all that changed last week. And even though the CJP has agreed to withdraw the agitation, there’s no putting this genie back in the bottle. What could have remained a limited protest was handed a massive boost by the govt’s own response. For millions watching on their phones, the optics were devastating. Officers in helmets, armoured vests and riot gear on one side; unarmed students on the other. Whatever the circumstances leading up to those confrontations, the images were political dynamite. There was even a video of a ten-year-old being chased by cops. Did the Delhi Police secretly want to side with the protestors and hand them this content gold? Imagine every student across the country opening their phone first thing in the morning (yes, that’s what they do) and seeing videos of other students being chased by cops and struck with lathis. And knowing that these students were protesting because they want justice and merit, that’s all. Yet the papers leak, year after year, even though a National Testing Agency (NTA) exists specifically to prevent such failures. India has somehow managed to inject doubt into one of the few institutions young people still believed in: the promise that hard work would be rewarded fairly. The signs of this issue being a big one were always there. During the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, paper leaks emerged as a significant issue among many young voters. BJP didn’t do as well as expected, but this was attributed to other factors. However, the anger against paper leaks seems to have been simmering. There were a few token announcements made about exam reforms, a few small fry were blamed, and India hummed along. But the establishment made a basic miscalculation. It assumed Gen Z’s attention span was short because its content is short. It assumed that a generation raised on reels would eventually scroll past its anger. That assumption may turn out to be one of the biggest political misreads in recent years. Paper leaks were only the spark that ignited wider frustrations about corruption, forced ethanol blending, controversies surrounding the Ram Temple project, and a broader sense that powerful institutions increasingly operate without accountability. To many young people, these were not separate issues. They were symptoms of the same disease. However, right now, this is not only about solving a policy problem. It is also about addressing public anger. Gen Z won’t settle for tokenism, symbolism, and lollipops anymore. They want solutions. Solutions that is hard. Solutions that involve overhauling systems, making them more accountable, not more autocratic. Will the govt be able to do it? Just as support for a political candidate or party can be emotional rather than rational, so can anger. Emotions do not operate entirely on logic. The videos of police action have added fuel to the fire. Now, almost any student or even any person watching from the sidelines can understand the anger driving the protestors. It is a quagmire the govt must navigate carefully, because there is every chance that heavy-handed responses could make matters worse. In democracies, govts can afford to underestimate the moral and political power of student movements at their own risk. History offers enough examples of that. This generation is very, very upset. It does not leave its screens, abandon its feeds, and step out into the streets for nothing. If India’s most online generation has suddenly decided to become India’s most visible generation, then something has gone wrong. Take them seriously. Don’t talk down to them. Talk to them. Don’t hand them pacifiers. Hand them a say in how the country is run.
title: Test #48: Gen Z It's Gen Zeel - Reels to Resignation

text: “Geographical Indication” is what the GI tag is, a certification given to products goods corresponding to a specific geographic location origin and thereby, preventing unauthorised use of the products’ name and protecting the ‘origin’ of products . If protection was the ambition, 2004 feels recent and its visibility, even more so. The wide-scale concept of protecting goods legally, unlike the formal practice of ‘GI tagging’ we know now, dates back to the Paris Convention in 1883. It aimed to protect almost everything across countries patents, designs, trade names, you name it. Geographical Indication was among the bunch. The 1883 intellectual property treaty used “indications of source” and “appellations of origin” to showcase the importance of protecting the conditions that give rise to a distinct regional product. When WTO came into existence in 1995, Geographical Indication moved out of being known among a limited circle of countries to become part of WTO’s formal framework making it a standard all around the world. This is where India comes in. As a member of the WTO, India had to comply. Moreover, India was facing intense issues. Healing properties of neem and turmeric, and basmati rice (things that we have known and used for centuries) were patented by Western companies and researchers, making it a legal challenge. Soon, India rolled out the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act of 1999 to protect goods from misuse and biopiracy. The infrastructure and administrative setup required for proper functioning took years to complete and the Act only came into effect in September, 2003. To get a GI tag, application is required. A union of persons, organisation, or any authority who represents the interest of the producers of the goods can apply. At the end of June this year, a 220 year-old sweet from Chandannagar, West Bengal received a GI tag. The GI tag application for this sweet, called Jalbhara, made and produced by Surjya Kumar Modak and his son, was submitted in 2022. The tag took four years to materialise. The economic impact of GI tagging is gigantic and its impact on those artisans and producers who make them are direct. That’s why getting a GI tag is significant. Think of it like a unique identity that nobody can steal, puts the attention on you making you finally visible to the world, and showcases the laborious process and effort that you put into the work. It’s like Gucci or Prada branding in terms of social visibility and authenticity because we know when a Gucci bag is fake and when it isn’t. Though unlike such corporate branding, GI tags are regional, collective, and community-driven. It means that someone, say from Kerala, can’t mass-produce a product that resembles Dongria Kondh shawl and call it Dongria Kondh shawl because the shawl’s geographical location and production process is protected by GI. Thus Dongria Kondh shawl stays authentic and all its artisans continue to get work as the craft tradition does not fade. It all started when Odisha decided to celebrate Rasagola Diwas in 2015 and made a move to get a GI tag for it. The sweet, made in Pahala, was also given as offerings at the Puri Jagannath Temple in Odisha. Bengal immediately contested with claims that it was made during the British colonial era and in fact, was the work of Kolkata-based confectioner Nobin Chandra Das. After 2 years of fighting, Bengal emerged as the winner in 2017. Odisha was determined not to give up. They compiled historical evidence and claimed how the rasagola they make is different from that of Bengal Rasagulla. Eventually, efforts weren’t in vain as they too received their GI tag in 2019. There were similar sounding products with similar names outside of Hyderabad but since getting the GI tag, a market opened for the product and the makers could promote it, thus solidifying the unique identity. GI tagging brought back many significant numbers of women artisans who had to previously discontinue their work due to machines by-passing the handmade process.
title: Test #49: GI Tagging & Process All About

text: For much of its post-Independence history, beginning in 1947, India’s strategic outlook was shaped by geography. The 2,400-kilometre Himalayan arc, the 3,488-kilometre Line of Actual Control, the Indian Ocean and the immediate neighbourhood defined the nation’s security calculus. India’s 7,516-kilometre coastline reinforced the importance of territorial defence and maritime security. Pakistan and China dominated strategic discourse, while South Asia became the primary frame through which India’s external environment was viewed. That paradigm served India well during the twentieth century, when regional stability and border protection were the foremost concerns. By 2025, however, India had emerged as the world’s fourth-largest economy, a technology power, a leading maritime nation and an influential voice in global affairs. Its interests extend far beyond its contiguous borders. Strategic thinking must now evolve at the same pace as national transformation. The question before India is therefore not whether geography has ceased to matter. Geography remains immutable. The question is whether geography alone can define India’s strategic outlook. The answer is increasingly no. The twenty-first century is witnessing a fundamental shift in the way nations perceive security and influence. Traditional geopolitics was governed by Geography Mountains, rivers, borders and distance. Contemporary geopolitics is increasingly governed by what may be called the geometry of interests. Energy security begins in the Persian Gulf. Sea lanes stretching from the Strait of Hormuz to the Strait of Malacca sustain India’s economic growth. Critical minerals essential for future technologies originate in distant regions. Supply chains span continents. Cyber networks, digital infrastructure and space capabilities have compressed geography in ways unimaginable even a generation ago. Strategic proximity is therefore no longer determined solely by physical distance. It is determined by connectivity, partnerships, technology, maritime reach and the ability to shape outcomes. This is why India’s strategic horizon now extends from the Gulf and Central Asia to Southeast Asia and the Indo-Pacific. It is not an expansion born of ambition alone; it is an expansion dictated by national interests. Viewing India’s external environment through the narrow prism of South Asia no longer reflects contemporary realities. China’s rise is no longer confined to the Himalayas; it spans technology, trade, infrastructure and maritime influence across the Indo-Pacific. Pakistan will continue to demand vigilance, but India’s long-term objective should be to reduce its ability to constrain India’s wider strategic choices, rather than allowing it to dominate the national security discourse. Bangladesh today is far more than an immediate neighbour. Its stability influences connectivity to the Northeast, the security of the Bay of Bengal and India’s eastern frontier. Likewise, developments in Afghanistan shape Central Asian connectivity, counter-terrorism and regional stability. To India’s west, the Middle East has evolved from an energy source into a vital strategic partner. It underpins India’s energy security, trade, investments, diaspora interests and maritime access. To the east, the Indo-Pacific has become the arena where India’s maritime aspirations, strategic partnerships and economic future converge. None of this diminishes the importance of the immediate neighbourhood. Rather, it places it within a much broader strategic continuum, where India’s security, prosperity and global influence increasingly depend on developments extending well beyond its land borders. India possesses an advantage that is often overlooked in strategic discourse its civilisational legacy. As Governor of Bihar, I have often reflected on the enduring significance of Nalanda. More than an ancient university, it represented one of history’s earliest examples of transnational engagement. Scholars travelled from across Asia not because India exercised coercive power, but because it commanded intellectual and cultural influence. Ideas travelled where armies never did. This legacy carries contemporary relevance. Influence is rarely sustained by coercion alone.
title: Test #50: From Geography to Geometry of India

text: Caught at the crossroads of a fading Nawabi era, the lingering influences of colonial rule and the birth pangs of a newly independent India, Lucknow witnessed a cultural and linguistic shift after 1947. While Urdu and English held their ground as the dominant languages of the time, ‘Hindustani’ (modern Hindi) began its steady ascent in the daily lives of the city’s residents. This evolution was most evident in the everyday vernacular of the era, much of which has since faded into obscurity. For example, the word ‘saikda’, once the standard term for ‘one hundred’, is now rarely used. During the 1971 Indo-Pakistan War, the Hazratganj police station (demolished in 2009) sounded a loud siren daily at 9am, to keep the public alert. Next to that exists the Rajya Soochna Kendra which is a toned down version of its original form? Half a century ago, it boasted of an exceedingly rich library; it periodically screened films in the main reading room for its members. Interestingly, Soochna Kendra had an extremely powerful loudspeaker system mounted on its front façade, facing main Hazratganj. The loudspeaker blared out the evening news, with a sizeable number of bystanders listening to the announcements. This practice might have started during the 1971 war, but it continued for several years, like the police station’s siren. It was a time when humble denominations like the 10, 25 and 50 paisa coins held tangible buying power. Rooted in an older system where a single rupee was divided into 16 annas, the 25-paisa coin was universally known as a ‘chawanni’ and the 50 paisa coin as an ‘athhanni’. Even local markets possessed their own distinct vocabulary; daily provisions were available at the ‘parchuniya’ while traditional indigenous medicines were strictly the domain of the ‘pansari’. Fast forward to the present year of 2026, which was marked by a prolonged and torrid summer. Yet, interestingly, the mercury hovered around 41 to 42-DegreeC mark. This stood in stark contrast to the unforgiving summers of decades past, where soaring highs of 45 DegreeC were a regular occurrence, inevitably accompanied by ‘loo’ the fierce, scorching wind blowing from the deserts of Rajasthan that once defined a true Lucknowi summer. The city’s prominent roads would then be watered manually after sunset, by ‘bhishtis’ carrying water in their ‘mashaks’, courtesy the municipal authorities. For children, life was simple, with ‘gubbare wallahs’ selling balloons and plasticky toys. ‘Budhia ke baal’ or candy floss was very popular, due to its extreme sweetness and pink colour. It is available even today, but the peculiar name is gone and its preparation is mechanised. The origin of the pink colour remains a mystery. Another kind of confectionery, wound on top of a bamboo pole was also sold, this time white in colour. The seller would pull a strand of the elastic material, mould it into different shapes and present it to giggling children. The latter also remained busy with kites (‘patang’, ‘kankaiyya’), tops (‘lattu-latti’) and marbles (‘kancha’). The central pit in a marble game was called a ‘guchhuk’ a very interesting term indeed. All these pastimes required skills. ‘Gully cricket’ was not so popular in those days. ‘Box wallahs’ selling cosmetics, laces, crochet and embroidery material, together with a jumble of items related with ladies’ day-to-day trousseau continued to enamour the women folk; the latter bargained incessantly with the sellers, who were already burdened with their heavy wooden, glass panelled boxes balanced precariously on their heads. ‘Choodi wallahs’ exclusively sold glass bangles from their wooden display boxes. The ‘bioscope wallah’ carried a garishly coloured, multi-sided contraption, with several circular viewing ports. Women and children would gather around its sides and peep through the viewing ports, as painted slides and moving images came alive inside the box, accompanied by a squeaky soundtrack an early experience of cinema. Those were the days of gramophones and single-screen cinemas.
title: Test #51: Post-1947 Nostalgia of Lukcnow

text: India maintains one of the largest and most diverse education systems in the world, with 1420 universities, 53583 colleges, 16795 standalone institutions, and 280 research bodies functioning as of 2024-25. These institutions together generate millions of academic records each year, covering degrees, diplomas, mark sheets, and certificates for students nationwide. Each year, these same institutions produce millions of academic documents nationwide, including degrees, diplomas, certificates, and mark sheets for students. Maintaining such a vast quantity of paper-based records is expensive, slow, and difficult across thousands of institutions throughout the country. Physical documents remain vulnerable to loss, damage, and forgery, and manual verification often delays access for students, employers, and institutions alike. The National Education Policy of 2020 envisions a flexible, learner-centric, and multidisciplinary system of education for the entire nation. Programmes such as Multiple Entry-Multiple Exit, the National Credit Framework, and the Academic Bank of Credits support flexible learning pathways under this policy. As students increasingly gather learning outcomes across several institutions and stages of education, the need for a secure and easily accessible record-keeping system has grown steadily. To address these challenges, the Government established the National Academic Depository, a nationwide framework for the secure digital storage, verification, and issuance of academic awards. By keeping records in a protected digital repository, the depository allows students to access their credentials at any time without visiting issuing institutions. It also simplifies verification for employers and other organisations while lowering the risk of fraudulent documents. Since 2020, the depository has functioned through DigiLocker, a platform launched on 1 July 2015 under the Digital India programme. DigiLocker now serves as the operational platform for issuing and storing academic credentials, within which the depository functions. DigiLocker therefore acts as the operating platform for issuing and holding academic credentials, in which the depository works. A related component, the Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry, works alongside the Academic Bank of Credits to manage student credit records and support academic mobility. Together, these three components form a unified system for secure academic record management. The depository is further linked with the e-Sanad service, which enables electronic verification, attestation, and apostille of educational documents for citizens seeking opportunities abroad. The Ministry of Education acts as the parent ministry responsible for the depository, and it has designated the University Grants Commission as the nodal agency for implementation through DigiLocker. The system operates through a coordinated governance framework backed by a clear legal and regulatory structure. Educational institutions issue verified digital records, which students can access and share securely, while other organisations verify them quickly. All digital credentials carry the same legal validity as physical documents under the Information Technology Act of 2000. This framework rests on three main legal instruments. The Information Technology Act of 2000 grants legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. The Digital Locker Rules of 2016 ensure that documents are shared only with a user’s explicit consent. The National e-Authentication Framework provides secure identity verification and authentication mechanisms for all stakeholders. The system follows a structured digital workflow. Educational institutions first create academic awards such as degrees, diplomas, and mark sheets after a course or examination ends. These verified records are then uploaded into the depository through DigiLocker, where they become automatically linked to each student’s account for lifelong access.
title: Test #52: India's National Academic Depository

text: Bellagio, a small town on the shores of Lake Como in northern Italy, has drawn travellers for centuries with its narrow stone lanes and pastel houses. The lake itself was carved by glaciers roughly 12,000 years ago and now reaches a depth of more than 410 metres, making it one of the deepest lakes in Europe. Such immense natural history often makes visitors feel remarkably small against the surrounding landscape. Such immense natural history often leaves visitors feeling remarkably insignificant beside the surrounding landscape. Ancient monuments elsewhere evoke a similar feeling, built to outlast empires and individual lives alike. The Colosseum in Rome, built between 70-80 AD, has withstood earthquakes, fires, and almost 1,900 years of history. The Great Pyramid of Giza, raised near 2560 BC, remains one of the oldest surviving large structures on Earth. In India, the Taj Mahal was constructed between 1632 and 1653, employing thousands of workers over more than two decades. Much of adult life is spent trying to appear important, whether through salary, title, or professional achievement. Exhausted by that pursuit, people often spend their holidays searching for places that make them feel wonderfully small again. Differences in salary, designation, or professional standing can feel remarkably minor when viewed from 30,000 feet above sea level. Large problems, in this sense, rarely require larger solutions; they simply need a bigger backdrop against which to be measured. Anxiety tends to shrink when standing before a mountain range that has existed for millions of years. Differences in salary, rank, or professional status often feel surprisingly small when viewed from thirty thousand feet above the ground. Standing before the Himalayas, a person’s pending emails and unread messages can suddenly seem like minor irritants. A towering wave breaking on a beach can make late-night work schedules appear almost comical by comparison. When personal troubles start to feel unusually large, many people instinctively search for something vast enough to put them back into proportion. Temples and other religious structures are often built specifically to evoke this sense of scale, dwarfing the individual before them. Inside ancient sanctums, visitors often lower their voices without being told to, responding instinctively to the weight of history around them. When personal problems begin to feel overwhelming, many people instinctively seek out something vast enough to restore a sense of proportion. Such monuments do not need to say anything to make an ordinary visitor feel humbled by comparison. They simply continue standing, indifferent to the daily concerns of whoever happens to be looking at them. These places become destinations not because they are beautiful alone but because they quietly rearrange a visitor’s sense of perspective. They demonstrate, without a single word, that the world was never organised around any one person’s daily schedule. Deadlines lose their urgency beside a lake whose far shore cannot even be seen. Listening to strangers laugh about something entirely unrelated to oneself can be strangely reassuring, a reminder that life continues regardless of individual concerns. The world’s apparent indifference to personal stress is not a discouraging thought but, for many, a liberating one. Travel, in this light, may serve a purpose beyond sightseeing or collecting souvenirs of a destination. Its deeper value may lie in standing before something ancient or immense enough to offer a simple, quiet reminder: personal troubles are smaller than they appear, and life continues well beyond them.
title: Test #53: In Bellagio’s Narrow Lanes

text: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist and inventor who formulated the Periodic Law and the periodic table of elements. Mendeleev was born in the Siberian town of Tobolsk. His father died when Mendeleev was 13. His mother relocated the family to St. Petersburg, where he graduated in 1855 from Main Pedagogical Institute a teacher training institution. He took up a job as a science teacher in Simferopol, Crimea, for a short time before returning to St. Petersburg to continue his masters. He received a post graduate degree in 1856 and began to conduct research in organic chemistry. In 1861, Mendeleev published a textbook named Organic Chemistry, which won him the Demidov Prize of the Petersburg Academy of Sciences. Using the Periodic Law, Mendeleev developed a systematic table of all the 63 elements then known. He even predicted the locations of unknown elements together with their properties within the periodic table. When these predicted elements, notably gallium( 1875), scandium (1879), and germanium (1886) were discovered, Mendeleev Periodic Table began to gain wide acceptance. Incidentally, in 1870, German chemist Julius Lothar Meyer also published a paper describing the same organisation of elements as Mendeleev’s. But the latter is given credit for the table. In 1865, he became Doctor of Science for his dissertation "On the Combinations of Water with Alcohol". He was appointed professor of chemistry at the University of St. Petersburg, where he continued to teach until 1890. Unable to find a proper text for his students, Dmitri Mendeleev decided to write his own. Between 1868 and 71, he worked on a book on modern organic chemistry. It is the research for this book that led him to his most renowned work. While explaining the chemical and physical properties of elements, he discovered similarities in the progression of atomic weights. He found that the order of atomic weights could be used to arrange the elements within each group and the groups themselves. Thus, Mendeleev formulated the periodic law. His Osnovy khimii (The Principles of Chemistry) became a classic, running through many editions and many translations. In all, Mendeleev predicted 10 new elements, of which all but two turned out to exist. Element 101 is named Mendelevium in his honour. Mendeleev’s periodic table was so successful because it helped to explain why certain elements had similar properties (elements in the same column on the periodic table are called "groups’’). For example, Mendeleev noticed that lithium and sodium belonged to a group of six other elements with similar properties (now known as Group 1 on the periodic table). This suggested that there must be some underlying reason why these elements had similar properties. As it turns out, all of these Group 1 elements have one valence electron (an electron in an atom’s outermost orbital), which explains their similarities. Since Mendeleev’s time, scientists have made many improvements to his original periodic table. For example, they’ve rearranged some of the groups to better reflect similarities between elements of their electrons’ configurations (the arrangements of electrons around an atom’s nucleus). They’ve also added new groups for recently discovered elements. Today, we continue to use and refine Mendeleev’s periodic table timeline because it remains one of our best tools for understanding chemistry. From its humble beginnings as a list of elements arranged by atomic weight, to its current form as a comprehensive tool for categorising and understanding the properties of matter, the periodic table has undergone a remarkable evolution over the centuries. The earliest known version of the periodic table was devised by Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev’s table featured just 63 elements, arranged according to their increasing atomic weights. But it wasn’t long before other scientists began adding to Mendeleev’s work. By 1914, German chemist Julius Lothar Meyer had extended the periodic table and by 1930, English physicist Henry Moseley had added some more elements.
title: Test #54: Dmitri Mendeleev & Periodic Table

text: Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee, born in Kolkata in 1901, is remembered every year on 6th July, with 2026 marking his 125th birth anniversary. Raised in a family of scholars, he became the youngest Vice-Chancellor of the University of Calcutta in 1934, at just 33 years of age. Coming from a family of scholars, he took charge as the youngest Vice-Chancellor of Calcutta University in 1934, when he was only 33. His conviction, however, extended far beyond academics, shaping decisions that would influence India for decades after 1947. He entered Jawaharlal Nehru's cabinet as independent India's first Minister for Industry and Supply, but resigned within a few years over differences on national policy. In 1951, he founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, choosing the diya, or earthen lamp, as its symbol. In 1942, a devastating cyclone struck Medinipur, and Mookerjee took an active role in relief efforts that earned wide praise. The Bengal famine of 1943, one of the deadliest humanitarian crises of that era, drew his attention further, and he arranged canteens and relief centres across affected districts, later recording his anguish in a book titled Panchasher Manwantar. These experiences deepened his belief that public service could not remain separate from politics. Mookerjee held firmly to the idea of an undivided India, opposing any arrangement that would separate Jammu and Kashmir from the rest of the country. His campaign led to his arrest, and he died in detention in 1953, far from the people whose cause he had championed. His campaign led to his imprisonment, and he passed away in custody during 1953, distant from the very people whose cause he had made his own. Years later, in 1975, the imposition of Emergency curtailed civil liberties across the country, followed by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976, which many view as a blow to democratic values reminiscent of the First Amendment passed decades earlier. The abrogation of Article 370 and Article 35A in 2019 has often been described as a fitting tribute to the cause for which he gave his life. Under his stewardship as Minister for Industry and Supply, India's early industrial policy took shape through projects such as the Damodar Valley Corporation and the Sindri Fertiliser Plant, both aimed at building a self-reliant industrial base. He also worked to safeguard traditional livelihoods, extending support to handloom weavers, cottage industries, and artisans across the country. He also strove to protect traditional livelihoods, extending backing to handloom weavers, cottage enterprises, and craftsmen throughout the nation. Beyond politics and industry, Mookerjee left a lasting mark on education. As Vice-Chancellor, he expanded library facilities, encouraged scientific research, and introduced courses in agriculture at Calcutta University. He also established 24th January as the institution's foundation day, a tradition that continues to be observed. His decision to leave government office, despite holding a senior position, reflected a broader pattern in his career, one in which personal comfort was repeatedly set aside for institutional and national causes. Through the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, he sought to build a political alternative rooted in cultural continuity and national unity, at a time when few competing voices existed in Indian politics. That organisation would later evolve and influence the trajectory of Indian political life for decades afterward, extending well beyond his own lifetime and shaping debates that continue in Parliament today. His efforts in reviving industrial units, restoring cultural institutions, and defending territorial unity are still referenced in discussions on nation-building. Successive governments have periodically revisited the projects he initiated, treating them as early markers of India's pursuit of industrial self-reliance. The combination of academic achievement, administrative service, and political conviction found in his career remains uncommon among leaders of that generation, and continues to be studied by historians and policy researchers alike.
title: Test #55: 125th Birth Anniversary of Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee

text: The year is 1845. The imperial world has just abolished slavery, so there is a huge shortage of workers at the sugarcane plantations. All the tropical islands in the Commonwealth need more hands, including Trinidad & Tobago. So, the colonisers dangle a work agreement to people in British India, especially the Purvanchal region. Agreement’ gets colloquialised into girmit and the people who sign it are now girmitiyas mostly outcasts, widowers, landless, and, in general, with not much to lose. After a basic health check, they are bundled into a ship at the Calcutta port. After a 90-day journey via the Cape of Good Hope, they land at Port of Spain, Trinidad’s capital. A British clerk asks their names. A guy named Shravan answers in a Maghai accent, “Sarwan”. The clerk promptly records the phonetic spelling in English. Shravan’s descendants bear the mis-spelled last name for generations, one of them being the cricketer Ramnaresh Sarwan. That’s how a Shiv Narayan becomes Sivnarine, a Devi Prasad is a Davy Persaud, and so on. There are no last names. They left caste behind in India. The labourers tried to create a caste system in Trinidad, but due to the sheer shortage of women and a lot of inter-marriage, it died out pretty soon. Their religion, music and cuisine did not. And that’s how I could have chhole bhature outside the Brian Charles Lara Cricket stadium in Port of Spain. They call it “double” because, back in the day, they served two bhaturas with chana sandwiched in the middle. I was in Port of Spain with influencers and journalists from India to cover the India versus West Indies cricket series, staying at the same hotel as the players. Such proximity is always fun. But these are trivial pursuits one can even chance upon in a hotel in Mumbai; hence, being a purvanchali, I was fascinated more by the history of this unique place. For me, it felt like finding the Uttar Pradesh, Bihar of the 1800s preserved in the West Indies. Thankfully, the locals emigrated before the invention of gutka, hence the roads and walls are spotlessly clean. Imagine the Bihar of the 19th century, sans the caste system, paan masala, poor civic sense, but all the amazing food, the music, the sweet dialect, and devotion to their gods. Everyone’s great-grandfather was an indentured labourer, everyone started from scratch, with no systemic inequalities, no caste privilege. One can only dream of such utopia. I asked the cricketer Nicholas Pooran if he wishes to someday return to his ancestral land, to search for his roots. He didn’t seem very interested. I don’t blame him. Notably, the African-Americans celebrate the Day of Emancipation, the day when they were freed from slavery, but the Indo-Carribeans celebrate the Day of Arrival, the day they landed in the country. I asked a bunch of people in a queue at the stadium entrance, who looked of Indian-origin, with a bit of sarcasm, “So, which team do you support?” They looked at me with some distaste and revealed the maroon jersey. This is the place their grandparents were born, who spoke Creole, not Bhojpuri. For them, I was the village cousin. They were curious to know more about me, but that’s about it. They aren’t coming back to investigate their roots. That ship, as they say, has sailed.
title: Test #56: Spotting Purvanchal of 1800s in the Caribbean

text:
The world is experiencing massive disruptions across geopolitical, technological, economic, and climate fronts. In the midst of it all, there is an opportunity to future-proof India’s economy and ensure lives and livelihoods are protected while our developmental goals are met, because the climate crisis will only accelerate these uncertainties. As global demand for green products and services accelerates, India has a chance to shape an inclusive growth story that benefits every layer of India’s economy farmers, small and medium enterprises, startups, and large industries alike? Investing now in emerging clean technologies is not just a climate imperative but a strategic economic move one that could future-proof our economy and position India as a global leader in the green transition. China began investing in clean technologies more than two decades ago ranging from solar panels and batteries to electric vehicles and today dominates many of these global markets. India, too, has taken massive strides in this direction over the last decade. It must now double down on the next frontiers of clean tech areas, not only to meet our own rising demand, but also to become competitive and capture a share of the booming international green economy.
To be sure, the green economy is not about renewable energy alone. It is about seizing India’s comparative advantage in resource efficiency, circular production, bioeconomy and climate-resilience to unlock new jobs, drive technological innovation, and redefine India’s global competitiveness in emerging value chains. The numbers speak plainly. India’s bioeconomy using biological resources beyond food needs for materials, energy and beyond alone has expanded from 10 billion in 2014 to 166 billion dollars in 2024. The ministry of science and technology projects the sector will reach 300 billion by 2030! Similarly, the circular economy from wastewater reuse to recycling of battery, plastics, and construction waste could add millions of jobs to the Indian economy. Consider Odisha, for example, a resource-rich state known for its mines and coal. A recent study by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) reveals that 28 green value chains from seaweed cultivation in Chilika Lake to green hydrogen production for exports to e-waste recycling in urban centres like Bhubaneswar and Cuttack could collectively add 23% to the state’s GDP while creating one million jobs and attracting over 42 billion dollars in investments by 2030. At Invest Odisha 2025 alone, over 35% of the 13 lakh crore commitments targeted green sectors marking the first time non-mineral sectors claimed the majority share. If this is the potential of one state alone, imagine India’s green economy at scale. Our leapfrog advantage lies in unique strengths: 67 million MSMEs contributing 30% of GDP, 7,500-km of coastline for blue economy enterprises, and a thriving startup ecosystem already delivering green solutions. The early gains from this structural shift are visible on the ground as well. Take Guwahati-based Bamboostan, a startup transforming 80,000 MT of local bamboo annually into construction material while raising farmer incomes. Or Eco Recycling Limited’s Maharashtra facility, which annually recycles 25,000 tonnes of e-waste with its cutting-edge technology.
title: Test #57: Changing the Colour of India's Economy

text: In rural Patna and Nalanda, there has been a curious correlation between the liquor ban enacted almost a decade ago (April 5, 2016) and lightning deaths, with such fatalities almost quadrupling, during some years, since the ban took effect. Scientists and villagers surmise that this could be because people have been cutting down tall, water and-sap-ﬁlled palm trees, as they can no longer be used in the traditional toddy business. Back when these trees were valued for their role in manufacturing toddy, they used to act as nature’s own lightning rods, driving electrical fury away from more vulnerable targets like human life and property. People have been cutting down palm trees since they have lost interest in them. The toddy business, after the liquor ban came into effect, is ﬁnished. The then Grand Alliance govt had enforced total prohibition under pressure from women, who had mounted a sustained protest against men’s tendency to squander money on drink. Although the ban was widely hailed in almost all quarters, the draconian law came in for sharp criticism after Bihar started reporting increased lightning-strike fatalities, coupled with rampant felling of palm trees, not to mention liquor-smuggling from Jharkhand and Bengal. According to the Bihar Economic Survey and Disaster Management Department, lightning strikes have claimed 2,446 lives between 2016 and April 2025 in the state, with rural people the worst affected. Analysis of the statistics reveals how fatal lightning strikes assumed alarming proportions since 2016. The report says lightning strikes claimed 133 lives in 2015 and 114 in 2016 (although the tally compiled by central govt is higher). However, after rampant felling of palm trees began following the liquor ban, the death toll began to mount. We can’t ignore the rampant chopping of palm trees as normal, says S.K. Singh, an agriculture scientist at the Dr Rajendra Prasad Central Agriculture University, Samastipur. This was always going to prove disastrous, as we are seeing now. The trunk and roots of palm trees naturally contain moisture, allowing them to conduct electricity to the ground without obstruction. This makes it an effective natural lightning conductor. Singh feels the need of the hour is largescale palm plantation. Only then, he says, can the lightning deaths which have assumed alarming proportions be arrested. The Annual Lightning Report, 2023-24, states that lightning strikes have claimed as many as 2,937 lives in Bihar between 2014 and 2024. The govt report identiﬁes south central Bihar as more prone to lightning strikes. In 2024, 72-percent of deaths (219 out of 303) from lightning strikes were reported only from these areas. The report mentions that most lightning deaths took place between 12.30pm and 4pm, when most rural folk remain out of their homes for agriculture-related work or to tend cattle. July has claimed the highest toll with more men, expectedly, falling prey to lightning strikes. Bihar State Disaster Management Authority (BSDMA) vice-chairman said they were encouraging farmers to plant more palm trees and raising awareness about their unique ability to protect against lightning strikes. It’s well known that if there is a tall tree, lightning will strike it ﬁrst. Another ofﬁcial said lakhs of palm trees had been felled in the aftermath of total prohibition since they have lost their usefulness.
title: Test #58: Missing Palm Tress More Lightning Deaths in Bihar

text: Adi Shankaracharya, in his sublime hymns, beautifully weaves together wisdom of Vedanta and devotion of the heart, revealing the Devi as both an infinite cosmic force and an ever-nurturing mother. She is the wisdom that illumines, strength that empowers, compassion that nurtures, and fierce protector who dispels darkness. Unbound by gender or form, she manifests in countless ways, and when visualised by the seeker, her presence empowers mind and sharpens intellect. During Navratri, as these sacred hymns resound, they do more than extol her they awaken her divine presence within us, stirring dormant divinity at the very core of our being. The Supreme Being is described as Aum, Brahmn, Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss an all-pervading reality. However, when the human intellect struggled to grasp this abstract truth, sages personified it as a mother, compassionate and powerful. They proclaimed that the very origin of creation is feminine energy, primordial force from which all life emerges. As such, energy in its essence is neither male nor female, yet sages have expressed it through various forms to aid human understanding. While Navratri spans nine powerful days of intense sadhana, it also holds deep significance for holistic well-being. This sacred period coincides with natural transition of seasons, as the body adjusts from spring to summer. During this time, our metabolism and immunity may become vulnerable, making it an ideal opportunity for detoxification. Fasting during Navratri supports this process, giving the digestive system a chance to rest and rejuvenate. Alongside physical cleansing, mantra chanting and visualisation of various forms of Devi empower mind and intellect. The rhythmic recitation of mantras has a calming effect on mind; it strengthens one’s connection to the Divine. As we align with this sacred practice, we release mental clutter and negative emotions, creating space for spiritual growth, clarity, and self-awareness. Thus, Navratri offers a perfect blend of inner and outer purification, aligning the body and mind with nature’s rhythm. By embracing physical detox through fasting and the spiritual renewal through chanting, devotion and visualisation, we emerge from this period refreshed, strengthened, and more attuned to sacredness of life. This divine transformation is embodied in the Devi, hailed as a manifestation of Shiv. In this context, Shiv signifies universal consciousness boundless energy that empowers our minds to think, feel, and contemplate. Just as electricity powers a bulb, fan, or cooler, without which these devices would cease to function, conscious energy that animates our intellect, mind, and senses is what we call Shiv. The entire universe both animate and inanimate, flowers, stars, beautiful vistas is Devi. Everything in this universe is interwoven with Devi, inseparable from her essence. She is both the source and sustainer of life and its ultimate end. Devi is also hailed as the embodiment of Rudra, energy responsible for destruction, and by extension, for transformation. Destruction, creation, and sustenance are eternal cycles of existence, and the same energy that brings life into being also holds the power to dissolve it when time comes. In this, Devi embodies fullness of the universe: she is gentle and fierce, nurturing and destructive, all at once.
title: Test #59: Devi Is Not Bound by Gender & Form

text: The Kessler Syndrome describes and warns of a cascade of orbital debris that could potentially hinder the space ambitions and activities down the road. The original paper predicted that satellite collisions would become a source of space junk by the year two thousand. This will not change the humanity changed how it lofted payloads to orbit. But a timeline is not essential to the core idea. It was never intended to mean that the cascading would occur over a period of time as short as days or months. Nor was it a prediction that the current environment was above some critical threshold. The Kessler Syndrome was meant to describe the phenomenon that random collisions between objects large enough to catalogue would produce a hazard to spacecraft from small debris that is greater than the natural meteoroid environment. In addition because the random collision frequency is non linear with debris accumulation rates the phenomenon will eventually become the most important long term source of debris. Gabbard used the term when talking to a reporter shortly after the study came out. The syndrome then worked its way into the public consciousness. It became part of the storyline in some science fiction and a three word summary describing orbital debris issues. Earth orbit is getting more and more crowded as the years go by. Humanity has launched more than twelve thousand satellites since the dawn of the space age. Out of these around seven thousand remain in orbit today but only about four thousand are still operational. That means there are nearly three thousand defunct spacecraft zooming around Earth at tremendous speeds. Other big dangerous pieces of debris like upper stage rocket bodies are there to give them company. At such tremendous speeds even a tiny shard of debris can do serious damage to a spacecraft. And there are huge numbers of such fragmentary bullets zipping around our planet. According to the estimates Earth orbit harbours at least thirty six thousand debris objects that are more than four inches wide. These objects pose more than just a hypothetical threat. Many of the smaller pieces of space junk were spawned by the explosion of spent rocket bodies in orbit. But others were more actively emplaced. Spacecraft have also collided with each other on orbit. The space community is taking the orbital debris threat increasingly seriously these days. Multiple satellite mega constellations are in the works. This will make space traffic management and space junk mitigation more pressing issues than they have ever been. In addition launch and satellite construction costs continue to fall. It allows allowing more and more people to get satellites up and operate them. This includes folks with very little experience in the field. This opening of the final frontier is generally a good thing most experts say. But it further highlights the need for forethought and responsible action when it comes to satellite operation. One recommendation is that all satellites operating above two hundred and fifty miles be equipped with propulsion systems allowing them to manoeuvre away from possible collisions. Drawing the line there makes sense for multiple reasons. It is also recommended that satellite designers consider building encryption systems into the command systems of their craft. Operators who control satellites in low Earth orbit should dispose of in atmosphere within a reasonable timeframe after the end of their operational lives. The widely accepted guideline recommends that satellites in low Earth orbit be deorbited within twenty five years of mission completion. However many experts now argue that this standard is insufficient given the rapid growth of satellite populations. Some advocate for reducing that window to just five years. Beyond deorbiting guidelines there is also growing interest in active debris removal technologies. Several space agencies and private companies are developing spacecraft capable of capturing and disposing of defunct satellites and rocket bodies.
title: Test #60: Kessler Syndrome - CPCT - 31/05/2025 - S1

text: The India Cooling Action Plan (ICAP), first published by the Union Environment Ministry in 2019, projects that India’s total cooling demand will grow from roughly 121 million tonnes of refrigeration in 2017 to nearly 983 million tonnes by 2037 more than 8 times in just 2 decades. Air-conditioning in Saudi Arabia already accounts for an estimated 50% to 70% of household electricity consumption. India has adopted this model for the first time at GIFT City, or Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, in Gandhinagar, consuming 30% less energy than traditional air-conditioning systems. An estimated 8% to 10% of Indian households currently own an air-conditioner. As this figure rises sharply in the coming years, India’s share of peak electricity consumed by cooling is projected to jump dramatically from 10% to 45% by 2050. Our grid is not set up for this transformation; neither are our cities. Many still believe traditional architectural methods will come to the rescue deep verandas, courtyard homes, khus curtains, and earthen pots of water as they did in the world of R.K. Narayan’s Malgudi Days. But those days are gone. Small but vital steps are already being taken. The Union Ministry of Power’s Bureau of Energy Efficiency has, since 2020, mandated a 24-degrees Celsius default minimum temperature setting for all new air-conditioner models covered under the star-labelling programme. The India Cooling Action Plan sets sensible targets for 2037-2050: a 20% to 25% reduction in cooling demand, a 25% to 30% reduction in refrigerant demand, and a 25% to 40% reduction in overall cooling energy requirements. Cool roofs that reflect solar radiation can independently reduce indoor temperatures by 2 to 4 degrees Celsius at very low cost and with high impact. The Japanese government’s Super Cool Biz campaign encourages companies to set indoor temperatures no lower than 28 degrees Celsius in summer and to relax formal dress codes, so as to reduce overall cooling demand. Anyone who can afford air-conditioning will increasingly demand it as temperatures climb year after year. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has warned that, without strong and decisive action, indoor cooling energy demand globally could more than triple by 2050. Key drivers of this surging demand will be the massive and under-served emerging economies of India, Indonesia, and Brazil. We worry about the power demands of Artificial Intelligence, as we rightly should. But an equally significant grid story may simply be ordinary Indians trying to sleep through June. Across several countries in the Gulf region, cooling accounts for roughly half of all peak electricity demand during summer months. India will head into its own surge with a far larger population, a less stable grid, and, as of now, significantly fewer rules governing efficient adoption of cooling technology. The paradox at the heart of this crisis is genuinely troubling. Cooling is increasingly essential for productivity, learning, comfort, rest, and in extreme cases, survival itself. But if scaled through inefficient and energy-guzzling systems, one risks driving electricity demand skyward, adding dangerously to emissions, raising outdoor temperatures further, and worsening peak-load stress on a grid that already buckles visibly every summer. Equally important is the moral dimension that purely engineering discussions tend to obscure: the people making the case against rapid air-conditioner expansion are almost without exception those who already have it, while those asked to endure the heat in the name of environmental restraint are almost without exception those who do not. Japan offers an instructive example of how this challenge can be handled. With more than 90% household penetration, Japan treats air-conditioning as essential infrastructure, but its energy performance standards for air-conditioners are among the strictest in the entire world. Singapore, similarly, has strong energy-use laws and leverages district cooling a system in which chilled water from a centralised plant is distributed.
title: Test #61: The Carbon Cost of Comfort

text: In modern urban life, perhaps it takes something larger an Ecosystem. And if Ecosystems are shaping Adolescence, only Ecosystems can help heal it. In the past few years, the conversations echoing through school corridors have changed in unmistakable ways. A decade ago, anxieties felt familiar teachers worried about attendance, examination pressure, bullying, and academic performance. Parent-teacher meetings revolved around marks, homework, and classroom behaviour of adolescents. The problems were not trivial, but they belonged to the known vocabulary of growing up. Today, however, educators confront a starkly different landscape. Students arrive in classrooms after nights lost to gaming sometimes clocking 2500 minutes a week on screens scroll through social media with compulsive urgency, and display emotional volatility that teachers find difficult to interpret. These concerns cannot be resolved by stricter discipline, confiscated phones, or an occasional awareness lecture delivered over a span of 1200 seconds. They are symptoms of a deeper social transformation, one that gathered force somewhere between the years 1995 and 2010, and has only accelerated since. Children and Adolescents no longer grow up under the influence of family, school, and neighbourhood alone. They inhabit an ecosystem in which smartphones, peer networks, social media and OTT platforms, recommendation algorithms, Artificial Intelligence, and family environments interact simultaneously. The child is shaped not by one institution at a time but by friction between many worlds, some real and many virtual. The boundary between physical and digital life has blurred beyond recognition. School interactions continue on messaging groups long after the final bell rings. Friendships, identity, validation, aspiration, entertainment, and social comparison all unfold online. Adolescence itself now stretches across screens, and what appears inside the classroom is often the visible residue of what has happened outside it, or inside a phone. Excessive gaming, for instance, is rarely just entertainment. It can disturb sleep, concentration, mood, emotional regulation, and academic engagement at once. Sleep deprivation then feeds back into irritability, impulsiveness, and poor resilience a cycle that teachers across more than 3500 schools in India have begun flagging as a serious developmental concern. Social media adds its own pressures: endless comparison, curated perfection, influencer-driven aspirations, and lifestyle fantasies built for rapid consumption. The Adolescent mind, still under construction, is being asked to handle adult-scale stimulus that even fully formed adult minds struggle to process. The adolescent mind, still under development, is being required to process adult-scale stimuli that mature minds themselves find difficult to manage. This parallel is not accidental; it reflects a structural mismatch between the pace of technological change and the pace of human cognitive development. Schools increasingly act as first responders to social change. Yet educational institutions were designed to teach mathematics, language, and science not to absorb, unaided, the consequences of technological acceleration, shifting family structures, and an always-connected culture. Several countries have already recognised this reality.
