While she spoke no English herself at that time, she felt that English language teaching should be given more attention in the public education system if Brazil were to compete in a globalised world. The funds the Secretary had accessed came from the Ministry of Education (MEC) and were aimed at the improvement of high school education ensino medio in the northern States of Brazil, under a scheme known as Projeto Alvorada. So, she approached the British Council. The aim was capacity building for 374 Tocantins high school English teachers, 225 in the first year and the rest to be added in 2004. My own involvement was another surprise. I first heard about the idea of a project in Tocantins at a social encounter with Eddie Edmundson in Recife just before Christmas in 2001. Eddie was working as a consultant for the British Council between two postings and was responsible for advising the Director in Brasilia on whether a project would be viable. Although I subsequently took part, as a consultant, in the baseline testing of teachers in March 2002, I only become directly involved as project manager designate, at Eddies suggestion, in mid 2002 Framework public sector ELT in Brazil A vicious circle operates in pubic sector English teaching in Brazil, particularly in remote regions. Students generally spend four years of primary school and three or sometimes four years of high school doing English, usually with two 45-minute classes per week. This seems to be a case of too little, spread too thin. But the 10 problem is compounded by two further factors. Universities receive students with extremely low language proficiency at entry. level, and often consider that their job is to give the students an academic grounding rather than a practical knowledge of the language. It is thus perfectly possible for a teacher to graduate from university after some five years of studies with a licentiate degree in Portuguese and English or in English alone, but with an extremely poor command of the English language for practical classroom purposes. In addition, there is a flourishing private sector market for language institutes. These institutes may even have a vested interest in seeing that standards remain low in schools, since this boosts demand for their own services. At all events, there is a fairly widespread idea that communication in English cannot be taught or learnt in a public sector school.
title: Test #09: Tocantins English Project - By Satya-2

text: India just pulled off something remarkable: Eight of its universities ranked highly on PitchBook’s 2026 list of the world’s top 100 institutions for producing venture-backed entrepreneurs. Seven are public institutions, including five IITs. From those five alone, came 2,705 entrepreneurs who founded 2,256 companies and raised more than $156 billion. This is astonishing, because for decades, India’s elite public universities were known for exams, academic hierarchy, and bureaucracy. Over the past decade, however, that culture has changed, and entrepreneurship has moved into the mainstream. The schools are now competing to commercialise research, work with industry, and produce students able to start businesses. This is a national advantage for India and highlights why it should get over the inferiority complex that the West has made it suffer. One of my recurring frustrations with American academia has been the vast distance between discovery and impact. American universities spent $118 billion on research and development in fiscal 2024 alone, $64 billions of it from the federal government. A very tiny proportion creates real value; the rest produces worthless papers to help faculty secure tenure, the academic equivalent of a government job for life. For generations, Indians were conditioned to believe that Stanford, MIT, Harvard, Berkeley, and other Western institutions represented the model to emulate. Yes, India does need to invest more in scientific research, but it does not need to copy the Western model. India has real problems to solve and needs to focus on solving them. Indian students step outside their campuses into a world full of urgent problems waiting to be solved. With the entrepreneurship spirit now taking hold, they have a chance to build companies go beyond creating wealth: They can improve the lives of billions. That, then, is what India should capitalise on now. The PitchBook rankings show that this shift is already producing results. The opportunity is to turn that entrepreneurial energy into technologies, products and companies that improve lives on a massive scale. That may prove to be one of India’s great superpowers. This is what has impressed much at IIT Delhi and IIT Kharagpur in particular: At both institutions, the commitment to entrepreneurship and industry collaboration starts at the top; you don’t see anything like this in the US. Together with their Research and Innovation Park, they have already enabled more than 2,100 industry collaborations and 185 technology transfers, while incubating more than 150 startups. IIT Kharagpur is moving with equal determination. Its director, a distinguished scientist and engineer, is pushing the institute to become one of the world’s leading launchpads for deep-tech entrepreneurship, where knowledge does not end at publication and innovations do not die at the prototype stage. KGP Launchpad is part of that effort. Kharagpur has created formal mechanisms enabling faculty and students to launch startups, serve as advisers or directors, seek seed funding, and commercialise intellectual property. Its Sponsored Research and Industrial Consultancy organisation works directly with companies and has established a “Lab to Market” mechanism specifically for translational research. These two entrepreneurial launchpads enjoy a wonderful rivalry, as I have seen in working with both of them. IIT Delhi wants to demonstrate that it can work with industry faster and better, while IIT Kharagpur wants to become the country’s leading deep-tech launchpad. They are pushing each other forward, as I am sure is happening at other top universities. The entrepreneurial transformation could not be more timely. Advances in AI, robotics, sensors, synthetic biology and genomics are enabling startups to do what only governments and giant corporations could do before; as these technologies converge, they are making it possible to tackle some of humanity’s greatest challenges. This is something Indian entrepreneurs who live close to the problems humanity needs solved understand better than Americans.
title: Test #10: IITs, Emerging Technology Enabling Startups

text: India has the world’s largest school system: 14 lakh schools, 1 crore teachers and 25 crore students. Despite having roughly the same population and three times India’s land area, China has just over 2,00,000 schools (excluding pre-schools), The difference is not just the number, but their size, resources they bring together, and, ultimately, what this means for learning. India has largely achieved near-universal access to elementary schooling. Every school in India, govt and private, should have IIS. Class-5 children assessed against a common competency has standard. At roughly Rs 212 crore for all children of class-5, this would provide a school by school picture of where children actually are. Schools should then disclose these resulis alongside other infrastructure and teacher resourcing. But participation falls as they move through the system, particularly at the secondary level. The Optum challenge now is to ensure children learn well and stay on track. NIPUN Bharat (National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy), launched in 2021 following NEP 2020’s focus on foundational literacy and numeracy, has brought greater focus to this challenge. Class-3 literacy in govt schools rose from 19% in 2016 to 23% in 2024, while numeracy rose from 20% to 28% (ASER). These gains show that progress is possible, but learning is slow-moving and will require sustained effort to scale up what is working. And as China shows, larger, integrated schools are also part of the answer. For India, "developed-country level" to achieve high productivity should mean a workforce with strong foundational, cognitive and problem-solving skills, capable of sustaining upper-middle income growth and competing in a technology driven global economy. Quantified benchmarks for India reaching ‘developed’ threshold by the late 2000s would be: Enabling school readiness for 80% of six-year-olds (ASER’s 2019 Early Years found only 35% can do single-digit subtraction and 55% can complete simple early language tasks); Ensuring 80% children read with meaning by age 10 (ASER 2024 found 55% of class 5 govt-school children couldn’t read a class 2-level text); Today, children receive less than an hour of structured pre-primary education in a typical anganwadi. Telangana shifted from a shorter anganwadi day to a seven-hour day, enabling anganwadi workers to spend around 2.5 hours on pre-school education. As anganwadis are increasingly co-located with schools, extending their hours can strengthen the 3-6 age groups’ access to learning, care and childcare. Extending this model across all 14 lakh anganwadi centres, with ad-ditional incentives for anganwadi workers and helpers and an ad-ditional lunch meal for children. Would require about Rs 7,000 crore annually, of which Rs 4,000 croге would be central share. States should fully utilise existing bal-vatika (pre-primary) provisions under NIPUN 2.0 to establish dedicated balvatika teachers, learning materials and mentoring support in at least the 2.5 lakh primary schools with enrolment above 75, at an estimated cost of Rs 15 lakh per school. This should be supplemented with a national school readiness assessment at the start of class 1 to track whether children are entering school ready to learn. Extend NIPUN Bharat. Launched in 2021, the mission put foundational literacy and numeracy at the centre of primary education for the first time, and states have built real de livery muscle behind it. That mo mentum should run for five more years, extending to classes 3-5 and pre-primary, with the annual al location rising from Rs 4,737 crore to roughly Rs 5,700 crore, exclud ing pre-primary (covered through balvatika budget). Much of what is needed is already sanctioned under Samagra Shiksha but not fully drawn down; the opportunity is for more sharply defined guide lines. The new money is for the must-haves the extension makes necessary: a protected Rs 100-per-child learning recovery budget for classes 3-5.
title: Test #11: Indian Schools To Reach Standards

text: Freire argues that the banking concept of education reinforces the status quo. It treats knowledge as a gift that is bestowed “by those who consider themselves knowledgeable (the teacher) upon those whom they consider to know nothing (students).” As a result this model negates the process of inquiry. It dissuades youngsters from developing critical consciousness, and instead, makes them adapt to the existing world order rather than venture out to transform it. Ergo, Freire says, the banking education model serves the interest of oppressors, who do not want things to change. Paulo Freire is considered to be one of the foundational figures of critical pedagogy, which views education as a political act and a social tool for justice. Through his adult literacy programmes in Brazil and Chile, Freire successfully demonstrated his alternative teaching techniques, which created a buzz around the world. Freire was born in 1921 in the northeast region of Brazil, which, at that time, had extreme poverty, stark social inequality and high illiteracy. Having lived his childhood years through the Great Depression, Freire was not a stranger to hunger and financial distress. Though he studied law, he began his career as a teacher in a local school. In 1961, he was appointed as the director of the Department of Cultural Extension at the University of Recife. A year later, he was roped in to conduct an adult literacy project in Recife and, subsequently, for another such project in Angicos. His team, according to several media reports, taught about 300 rural workers basic literacy through a programme popularly known as the ‘40 Hours of Angicos’, conducted over roughly 45 days. These successes prompted the then Brazilian government to expand Freire’s idea and implement it across the country. However, a military coup in 1964, and the subsequent change of regime, ended Freire’s project. Freire himself was arrested for a period of 70 days and later exiled. He returned to Brazil only in 1980, after a gap of 16 years. To counter the banking education model, Freire proposes a problem-posing approach, which uses dialogue and mutual inquiry as learning tools. Here, the teacher does not only teach, but is also taught through her dialogue with students. Both parties are jointly responsible for the process in which all of them witness intellectual growth. Freire pitches the problem-posing approach as a humanist method of education designed to bring about liberation. “The students’ no longer docile listeners are now critical co-investigators in dialogue with the teacher. The teacher presents the material to the students for their consideration, and re-considers her earlier considerations as the students express their own,” writes Freire in Pedagogy of the Oppressed. This approach, Freire believes, will help break the vertical hierarchies within learning ecosystems, thereby encouraging teachers and students to build a new pattern of relationship. Further, when dialogue replaces narration, learning becomes a perpetual process. Students and teachers will be empowered to replace doxa (superficial knowledge) with logos (critical knowledge). The problem-posing approach also eliminates this vagueness by contextualising concepts in accordance with the social realities of a particular group of learners. This means students are introduced to academic concepts through problems connected to their lived realities. It empowers students to critically intervene in their reality to reflect and act to transform the world. Through this process, Freire argues, teachers and students overcome authoritarianism and “alienating intellectualism,” allowing them to become active subjects of their own liberation. In the 1960s, Brazilian law barred illiterate citizens from voting in elections, which meant a large section of the population lacked direct political representation. This trend was particularly stark in northeastern Brazil, where illiteracy was very high. It was here, in the small town of Angicos, that Freire experimented his ideas.
title: Test #12: Paulo Freire and Banking Model of Education

text: In an age when machines are becoming capable of almost everything predictable, the irreplaceable act remains the human one: a teacher who sees potential in a student that the student cannot yet see in themselves. OECD’s 2026 Teacher Knowledge Survey distinguishes between knowing a subject and the ability to teach it. Its findings posit that subject knowledge does not always translate into effective pedagogy. The point is simple but important: knowing something deeply and knowing how to help another person learn it are not the same skill. Teaching is an art, requiring an understanding of human connections, pedagogy and some theatrics for the classroom. The UNESCO Global Report on Teachers, 2024, places a hard number on what neglecting this profession costs. The world needs 44 million additional primary and secondary teachers by 2030, and over half are needed simply to replace those already leaving. Meanwhile, the McKinsey Global Institute estimates that between 75 million and 375 million workers globally will need to switch occupational categories by 2030 due to automation. In such a scenario, the value of competent teachers is more than ever. No one remembers the exact day they learned to read. But almost everyone remembers the teacher who taught them. That asymmetry, between the forgettable moment and the unforgettable person, tells us something essential about teaching. A teacher leaves behind something that cannot be easily measured: the confidence to try, the discipline to persist, the curiosity to ask, or sometimes simply the belief that one is capable of more. Thus, teaching cannot be classified as anything less than an art. The Latin phrase: Non scholae sed vitae discimus. We learn not for school, but for life.  And the teacher, the true artist of human possibility, is the person who makes that possible. The National Awards to Teachers, conferred each year by the Hon’ble President of India, honour a chosen few whose contribution has risen above the rest. Nonetheless, in every corner of the country, in classrooms, skill labs, polytechnics, sports grounds, and music rooms, students find their own way to say thank you. A handwritten note. A moment of recognition in a morning assembly. A quiet acknowledgement that stays with a teacher long after the day is over. These are not lesser celebrations but, in many ways, the truest ones. The data, however, tells us a parallel concerning story. India has acknowledged this challenge and is responding with intent. The four-year Integrated Teacher Education Program, launched in consonance with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, integrates subject mastery and pedagogy into a single undergraduate degree, attracting the best minds into teaching by design. To ensure congruent standards amongst the in-service teachers, the National Professional Standards for Teachers (NPST) tie career advancement to demonstrated teaching quality rather than mere seniority. To benefit from cross-sectoral learning, the National Mission for Mentoring (NMM) provides structured support to teachers to learn from mentors from various fields. I, too, have registered as a mentor for this mission. India is also expanding who counts as a teacher, and that is perhaps the most novel idea of all. Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society (ULLAS), the New India Literacy Program, is built on the principle that anyone who is literate can teach someone who is not. As we celebrate International Literacy Day this year, nine states and union territories have been declared fully literate under this program. This spirit is further embodied in the Vidyanjali portal of the Ministry of Education. It connects over 8.75 lakh government schools to volunteers who bring their expertise, whether in dance, mathematics, public speaking, or craft, into classrooms as a gift. Every one of them acts as a teacher. Every subject they bring is valued equally. Because at its core, teaching is not a technical function but a craft. Every lesson plan is a composition. Every explanation is a performance.
title: Test #13: Teacher - The Artists of Education

text: It is well known that Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, the second President of India, wished that his birthday be observed as Teachers’ Day. He was an intellectual of international repute, a renowned author and esteemed statesman, yet he regarded his role as a teacher as the most important of all. Dr A.P.J Abdul Kalam, one of India’s most beloved former presidents, was once asked whether he thought people would remember him more as a scientist or as a president. Dr Kalam replied that he would like to be remembered as a teacher. The teachers whose competence and character make them venerable, and the students devoted to such teachers, have always been our ideal. Centuries ago, in his play Malavikagnimitram, Mahakavi Kalidas wrote that a good teacher is one who possesses profound knowledge and also has the ability to transmit this knowledge effectively. To encourage independent thinking in students, to ignite their curiosity, to promote the tendency to ask questions, to sharpen their capacity for argument and judgement, and to help them grow into independent individuals these are among the most useful and rewarding dimensions of teaching. Our ancient texts prescribe that teachers should love their students as their own children, they should treat them all equally and fairly, they should not lose their temper at students, and they should remain patient, keep the well-being of their students foremost, and teach them according to their ability to learn. It is in the spirit of deep respect for such teachers that the Shikshavalli in the Taittiriya Upanishad gave the timeless message, “Acharyadevo Bhava”, nearly three millennia ago. It has been my greatest fortune to have been guided by many wise and affectionate teachers. Sometimes, our teachers would teach us in their homes even beyond school hours, and would look after us with great care. After completing Class VII, I was the first girl to venture out of the village to pursue further studies. Later, while studying in Bhubaneswar too, I was blessed to receive abundant love and encouragement from my teachers. I mention my teachers here with humility, because their story illustrates a profound truth: A loving and dedicated teacher can awaken limitless potential and inspiration within a student. Strengthened by that encouragement, students develop the courage to face life’s toughest challenges and the confidence to pursue the loftiest of goals. Teachers do far more than teach a curriculum. Through their own conduct and example, they also instruct their students in the art and skills needed to live a fruitful life. Besides being a mentor, a teacher is also a well-wisher, a friend and a fellow-traveller in the students’ quest for learning. The insight about what makes a good teacher, handed down through our culture and tradition since ancient times, remains entirely relevant even today. It is only through such inspiring education that we will rise generations of successful entrepreneurs, brilliant scientists, creative artists and citizens capable of finding innovative solutions to emerging challenges. Teaching is not merely a vocation; it is a vow. It is more than a career or a job; it is the sacred task of shaping humanity. It is the noble responsibility of illuminating the path for generations to come. My memories associated with teaching give me a special sense of fulfilment. I taught children at the Sri Aurobindo Integral School in Rairangpur, Odisha. Apart from teaching them various subjects, I used to be fully involved in helping the children prepare for their musical performances, sports activities and plays. Even today, it is exhilarating for me to reminisce about our preparations for Independence Day and Republic Day celebrations and the joyful excitement of the children during the functions. I also found great satisfaction and meaning in taking students on picnics to beautiful natural surroundings and, through play and exploration, introducing them to the world of animals, birds, trees and plants.
title: Test #14: Let's Hold Our Teachers Highest Esteem - President

text: With artificial intelligence (AI) making homework, research and even complex concepts accessible at the click of a button, teachers today face a new challenge how to ensure that technology enhances learning without replacing the process of thinking. As schools increasingly bring AI into classrooms, educators are using it as a learning aid, helping students explore ideas and brainstorm, understand difficult concepts and access information, while encouraging curiosity, reasoning and independent thought. But this new-age classroom also demands a new kind of vigilance. Teachers increasingly have to monitor the misuse of AI, from students submitting AI-generated assignments to relying on it for answers without understanding the subject. Teachers’ role, therefore, is evolving beyond simply delivering knowledge. They are also teaching students when to use AI, how to question what it produces, and when to put the technology aside and think for themselves. Teachers are also using AI to prepare presentations, look for new activities and explore different ways of explaining concepts. Teachers can also use it to find new kinds of activities and explore pedago­gical methods that could make teaching more interesting. The same technology, however, has made it difficult to determine how much of an assignment represents a student’s own effort. Sharma said teachers were finding that children were using AI to do homework, write letters and prepare projects. One response has been to bring more assessment back into the classroom. In classrooms, teachers can see whether children are able to do things on their own. Teachers are also framing more analytical questions for projects, she added. That shift is putting greater emphasis on a skill educators consider increasingly important: critical thinking. When information is instantly available and AI can produce a polished answer within seconds, students need to know how to evaluate evidence, identify bias, verify information and distinguish fact from opinion rather than accepting an answer at face value. For educators, however, there are limits to what even sophisticated technology can provide. AI can solve problems in seconds and give us the most logical answers. But a big question for students is whether it can teach judgment? Decisions involving empathy, integrity, compassion and responsibility, he said, can-not simply be reduced to data. While AI can provide information, “only humans can give wisdom”. That is why educators largely see the way forward not as keeping AI out of classrooms, but teaching children to use it with boundaries. It is a wonderful tool if it is used as a tool. “It should not be used to replace a teacher or replace the ha-rd work that needs to be do-ne, or creativity.” Teachers are also finding that AI raises new questions about fairness and equal access, since not every student has the same quality of device, internet connection or guidance at home. This gap means some children can use AI more effectively than others, and educators are being asked to design lessons that do not assume equal access outside school. At the same time, schools are working on frameworks that clearly state what kind of AI use is acceptable for homework, projects and exams, so that expectations are not left vague. Training programmes are also being introduced for teachers themselves, since many were never taught how to use such tools during their own education and must now learn alongside their students. Beyond academics, teachers say AI is changing classroom relationships too, as students increasingly turn to chatbots for reassurance or quick answers instead of asking a teacher or classmate. This has pushed some educators to build in more group work and discussion-based learning, so that collaboration and human interaction remain central to how children learn. Parents, too, are being brought into the conversation, with schools holding sessions to explain how AI can support homework without becoming a substitute for genuine effort.
title: Test #15: How AI is Reshaping Learning & Teaching?

text: India’s National Education Policy (NEP), introduced in 2020, likewise called for deeper learning over rote coverage. Memory research dates back to German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, who studied forgetting during 1880-1885 and published his findings in 1885. More than 141 years later, his key finding still holds: information grows harder to recall once it stops being revisited. A separate theory, cognitive load theory, was introduced by psychologist John Sweller in 1988 and centres on the limited capacity of working memory. Cognitive load theory holds that working memory can process only a limited amount of complex information at one time, and that learning suffers when a student is tired, distracted or overloaded with material. This has a direct bearing on the common assumption that hours spent studying equal hours of learning. Millions of Indian students prepare each year for major competitive examinations such as JEE, NEET, UPSC and CUET, following long study hours, strict timetables and repeated revision. Despite this heavy effort, many students find that on the day of the exam a familiar question does not translate into a retrievable answer. A student can spend an entire evening with a textbook, underlining passages and rewriting notes, yet retain comparatively little from that session. This has a similar bearing on the widespread belief that time spent at a desk equals material learned. A student may spend a whole evening reading a chapter, highlighting lines and copying notes, and still recall only a small part of it afterward. Visible study activity and actual learning are not necessarily the same process. Memory research also points to a separate limitation described by the forgetting curve. Newly acquired information weakens over time unless it is deliberately revisited, even though the exact rate of forgetting varies between individuals and subjects. Most study timetables, however, are built around covering a syllabus rather than around retaining it. A chapter finished on one day is simply followed by the next chapter, regardless of whether the earlier material has been consolidated in memory. As a result, a syllabus may be completed once or even twice while large sections remain only weakly retrievable. Repeated rereading can create a sense of familiarity with the material, but recognising a topic is different from being able to reproduce an answer under exam pressure. Cognitive science identifies several established techniques that address this gap. Spaced practice involves revisiting material across multiple separate sessions instead of concentrating all revision into a single block. Retrieval practice, examined in detail by researchers Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke in a widely cited 2006 study, involves recalling an answer from memory before checking notes, rather than simply rereading them. Interleaving, studied by researchers Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor in a widely cited 2007 study, involves mixing different types of problems or topics during practice instead of completing many similar questions in a row. Together, these techniques point toward measuring study progress by what a student can retrieve today that could not be retrieved the day before, rather than by the number of hours spent studying. Cognitive readiness is a further factor that most timetables do not account for. Mental energy varies through the day depending on sleep, stress, workload and emotional state, yet conventional study plans typically treat every hour as interchangeable. Adaptive learning systems that track which concepts a student is forgetting, which topics need retrieval practice, and when performance is declining represent one possible application of technology in this area, shifting timetables from a fixed plan the student must follow toward a schedule shaped by the student’s own patterns of retention. The wider evidence therefore suggests that increasing study hours does not by itself guarantee stronger exam performance.
title: Test #16: Adaptive Learning System & Cognitive Readiness

text: In many Indian Maths classrooms, a student who meets a difficult question typically pauses only for a moment before looking to the teacher for help, and within seconds a method is demonstrated, the answer is revealed, and the class simply moves on. Recent numbers explain why this habit matters: the Annual Status of Education Report for 2024 found that only 30.7 percent of Class-V students nationally could solve a division problem, up from 25.6 percent in 2022, while just 33.7 percent of Standard-III students could manage basic subtraction. The National Education Policy of 2020 and competency-based assessments introduced afterward were meant to push classrooms away from this rescue-first habit, encouraging reasoning and application over rushed procedure, yet old patterns of demonstrating solutions immediately remain widespread even years later. Learning Maths is not about avoiding difficulty but about learning to navigate it, and this is where the idea of productive struggle becomes significant. Productive struggle refers to the intellectual effort students invest in wrestling with challenging questions before receiving explicit instruction or complete solutions, and it is not about leaving learners confused or frustrated. Rather, it involves engaging them in tasks demanding enough to stretch their thinking yet achievable with persistence and carefully judged teacher support. Educators researching this idea since around 2011 have argued that an initial struggle, followed by well-timed instruction, produces a hidden efficacy that plain demonstration cannot match. Many teachers nonetheless demonstrate solutions immediately because of time pressure, crowded lesson plans, faster students requesting more problems, and a wish to spare the class visible stress, unintentionally sending the message that Maths is about receiving answers rather than constructing understanding. Students who are rescued too quickly begin to associate struggling with inability, and consequently grow reluctant to attempt unfamiliar questions on their own. Educational research consistently shows that meaningful, lasting learning occurs instead when students wrestle with ideas, try different approaches, make mistakes, and refine their reasoning under guidance. Consider a classroom where learners are encouraged to explore why the three interior angles of a triangle always add up to 180 degrees, rather than simply being told the rule. Some might draw diagrams, others fold paper triangles or reason logically, and by the time the formal rule is introduced they understand not just what it states but why it holds, since the three angles can be rearranged along a straight line. A similar exploration works for polygons, where students discover that the exterior angles of any shape, regardless of how many sides it has, always sum to 360 degrees, reasoning their way there using square tiles and the straight angles those tiles form. The teacher’s role during such exploration differs sharply from simply supplying answers. Effective teachers instead observe how students are thinking, ask probing questions, and offer prompts that push learning forward without removing the underlying challenge, inviting students to explain their reasoning, consider alternative representations, or examine what changes if one condition of the problem is altered. During this same kind of exploration, the teacher’s task is quite unlike simply handing over the correct answer, since effective teachers instead watch closely how students’ reason, pose searching questions, and offer prompts that carry learning forward while leaving the core challenge intact. Equally important is building a classroom culture in which mistakes are treated as a natural and valuable part of learning rather than something to be corrected away instantly, since every error offers a genuine window into how a student is actually reasoning. This becomes especially important as AI tools and digital solvers make it easy to generate a correct answer without any of the underlying thinking.
title: Test #17: The Struggle in Maths Learning

text: Allahabad, now known as Prayagraj and the home of the Nehru family, was a centre of the Indian independence movement for years. Strategies evolved here. It was also known as the City of Prime Ministers because several of them were either born or educated here. Concurrently, Allahabad became a Congress bastion. From the first Lok Sabha election in 1952 to 1984, seven of the eight Allahabad MPs belonged to the Congress. The only exception was socialist Janeshwar Mishra who had won the 1977 Lok Sabha polls on a Janata Party ticket. After four decades, the Congress won the prestigious Allahabad Lok Sabha seat in 2024, with Ujjwal Singh, son of Samajwadi Party leader Reoti Raman Singh, winning on a Congress ticket as part of the SP-Cong alliance. Between 1984-2019, the BJP won the seat four times, Janata Dal twice and the Jan Morcha and the Samajwadi Party once each. Alongside, the crowds at Nehru’s ancestral home Anand Bhavan and adjacent Swaraj Bhavan also started declining. Indira Gandhi shifted base to New Delhi after entering national politics and later handed over the sprawling Anand Bhavan to the government in 1970. It was converted into a museum. The Congress first exited from Prayagraj politics and thereafter from the states and national power scene as their sporadic rallies and meetings failed to give the party the desired impetus there. Now, the huge response at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s youth outreach programme, ‘Chhatron ki Goonj’, in Prayagraj on August 8 has raised hopes as many feel their days of glory are not far away. This is not the first time when a Congress rally attracted such a huge crowd despite roadblocks put up by the state government. Only the design and the theme of the rally was more appealing to Gen-Z. Prayagraj is also a centre of education with a high level of academic consciousness and is often called the Oxford of East, which draws students from across the state as well as the country. The students dominated the public space and they loved the new style of the rally - akin to a political rock show where there is dialogue instead of dull and drab speeches- with a focus on youth and their issues. It’s the vision of Gen-Z in the family and party, even though the event was organised by a Mumbai company. During his recent visit, Rahul Gandhi, along with his niece Miraya Vadra, spent some hours at their ancestral home Anand Bhavan and gave an emotional start to his speech saying, “My family had a home in Prayagraj, so coming here always feels special.” The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party saw an opportunity to embarrass the Gandhis as Rahul did not visit his grandfather Feroze Gandhi’s grave, located in a Parsi cemetery in Mumfordgang area of Prayagraj. Feroze died in 1960, and after his cremation, his ashes were interred at a Parsi cemetery. A day before, the BJP leaders paid floral tributes, insisting that they were also ensuring its upkeep. Now that the euphoria is subsiding, the party leadership is haunted by one question: Will the crowds convert into votes? The party’s concern is that even though Rahul has emerged as the viable face of the Congress and now the youth, he also represents one ideology in a vertically divided society, but where were the cadres to convert the crowds into votes. Indira, as Congress city president, knew the town like the back of her hand. Even after becoming PM, she used to interact with the common man. Once, she went to the Kamla Nehru Hospital and had a half-an-hour unscheduled meeting with nurses and midwives. People feel a shift in student-driven politics of the city but the seniors are still putting bets on Modi-Yogi. A look into history is necessary to answer Rahul Gandhi’s quest to renew the Congress bond with Prayagraj, his ancestral hometown where today the Kumbh seems to overshadow the city’s academic and political vigour.
title: Test #18: Prayagraj - City of Prime Minister & Education

text: The Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, established in May 1950 as the Eastern Higher Technical Institute, stands as the earliest of India’s premier engineering institutions, formally inaugurated on 18 August 1951 by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. The institute rose from the grounds of the Hijli Detention Camp, a site where British forces had imprisoned freedom fighters and, in 1931, shot dead two unarmed detainees during a period of colonial repression. The first academic session began with 224 students and 42 teachers spread across ten departments, a modest start that would soon expand into one of the country’s largest technical campuses. Parliament declared the institute an Institution of National Importance in 1956, granting it the authority to award its own degrees independent of any affiliating university. During the period 1958-1961, similar institutes were set up at Bombay, Madras, Kanpur and Delhi, forming the nucleus of what became the wider Indian Institutes of Technology system. Over the following decades, graduates of this system contributed greatly to India’s domestic industries and to technology firms worldwide, with several alumni going on to lead major companies abroad. Despite this record, the scientific and engineering strength within these institutes has often been undervalued next to Western research universities. For years, Indian institutes faced pressure to mirror Western universities such as MIT, Stanford and Harvard, with a familiar prescription: spend more on research, publish more papers, expand tenure tracks, and climb global rankings. American universities spend tens of billions of dollars every year on research and generate huge amounts of intellectual property, yet only a small share becomes companies, products or technologies that reach society. Each year, these universities put tens of billions of dollars into research and produce vast volumes of intellectual property, though only a limited share turns into companies, products or technologies that reach the public. Advancement in that system depends heavily on publishing papers and gathering citations, which secures long-term tenure regardless of practical impact, favouring academic recognition over turning knowledge into invention. In contrast, the IITs have moved toward closer ties with industry and applied research, pushing technologies from labs into real-world use. Institutes once wary of private industry now actively seek partnerships that turn research into commercial and social gains. Faculty across engineering, physics, biotechnology, medicine and artificial intelligence increasingly tackle complex problems instead of narrow academic exercises, and campus technologies are turned into start-ups and industry ventures faster than before. Despite this progress, red tape remains a major obstacle. Layers of approvals, committees and official rules, many inherited from the colonial era, continue to consume institutional time and resources. Wider autonomy, simpler reporting and easier industry ties are widely seen as necessary steps to speed up research across the IIT system. Rather than measuring progress solely against Western benchmarks, greater emphasis is now placed on directing scientific and engineering talent toward problems specific to India and the wider world, including clean water access, early cancer detection, affordable diagnostics, energy storage, food security and advanced manufacturing. These practical problems are not lesser forms of research, since many need real scientific breakthroughs before any workable solution can emerge. Such applied work is not treated as a secondary field of study, because genuine solutions in these areas often demand the same scientific breakthroughs as any theoretical pursuit. The strongest approach is one where industry identifies real-world problems, universities provide scientific depth and young talent, and long-term missions too broad for any single firm are backed through steady public investment. Competition among the IITs is increasingly centred not merely on placement packages, citation counts and global rankings, but on which institute builds the most affordable diagnostic tool, cleans the most polluted groundwater, or produces technologies that measurably improve millions of lives.
title: Test #19: More Autonomy for the IITs will Benefit India

text: India’s 80th Independence Day is a good time to take stock of Indian science and where it might go next. It comes at an extraordinary moment: a convergence of technologies above all, artificial intelligence (AI) is producing an acceleration that has few precedents. Modern science is downstream of prosperity. As a zeroth-order estimate, consider how many Indians have incomes above the British median at purchasing-power parity. The answer is plausibly around 20-30 million adults. Britain itself has roughly the same number of adults above its median. Thus, India already contains a prosperous population of roughly the scale that sustains British science. Over the next decade, that Indian population could approach 40-55 million. India has largely solved the first problem of scientific power: creating a sufficiently large, prosperous and educated population. Its next challenge is to turn that population, its elite institutions, and its global diaspora into a densely connected system capable of repeatedly producing work at the world frontier. I do not mean that India is ready to rival the US or, increasingly, China. A more realistic comparison is with the UK. Britain is a demanding benchmark: It still punches above its demographic weight scientifically. Yet India is already surprisingly close in broad measures of excellent science. In the Nature Index, Britain’s overall output is about twice India’s, but in physical sciences the ratio is about 1.4 to one and in applied sciences about 1.6. In chemistry, India actually exceeds Britain. The larger gap in biology and medicine suggests deficits in infrastructure rather than any general inability to do first-rate science. Farther out on the scientific tail, Britain remains dramatically ahead in Nature and Science papers and major prizes. But prizes are lagging indicators: Today’s Nobels largely reward environments of decades ago. India’s contemporary performance in highly cited research is considerably closer to Britain’s. Statistics for science done in India also understate the contribution of people produced by India. Many of India’s best scientists leave for graduate school and contribute to American, British and other systems. Britain, too, loses talent to the US. Changes in American immigration and visa policy may reduce this magnet; the long-run effects remain to be seen. Science benefits from mobility. The challenge is to turn brain drain into circulation and connectivity. The newly established Lodha Institutes, backed by substantial philanthropy, are potentially one such experiment. LIGO-India offers another model. As part of a real-time international network of gravitational-wave observatories, it will be embedded in frontier science from its first day. It bids fair to produce future Nobel-class discoveries in which important work is actually done on Indian soil. Finally, India should identify fields where it has unusual comparative advantages. Astrophysics and cosmology around LIGO are one. Genetics is another: India’s extraordinary genetic diversity means that a national resource on the scale and depth of the UK Biobank could transform global understanding of human genetics. Computer science and AI are a third, building on India’s deep software ecosystem and global technical diaspora. For much of India’s first 80 years, the binding constraint on science was scarcity. That constraint has not disappeared, but the problem has changed. India now has the people, institutions and global connections to become a major scientific power. The next level is to connect them and create a system in which great science becomes routine. First, connect India’s scientific institutions much more densely, both to one another and to the world. Britain has a geographic advantage: Oxford, Cambridge, London, Birmingham, Warwick and Bristol inhabit what is effectively one scientific labour market. India has its own accomplished scientific diaspora in the US and Britain. India’s IISc, TIFR, IITs and IISERs are scattered across continental distances.
title: Test #20: Create System to Make Science Routine

text: The Prime Minister announced that the government would provide free online coaching to students preparing for competitive examinations. Details of which examinations will be covered, eligibility and how the coaching will be delivered are yet to be announced. The announcement comes amid a growing dependence on private coaching. A government survey released last year found that 37% of Class 11 and 12 students across India took private coaching, rising to 44.6% in urban areas. Urban students spent an average Rs 9,950 a year on coaching, more than twice the Rs 4,548 spent by rural students. The Indian Express reported that this could amount to 9-12% of the annual consumption expenditure of households with children in these classes. Prime Minister outlined what he called “Saptadhara”, or seven streams of development, as a framework that will bring together several of the government’s existing policy priorities over the next five to seven years. These are manufacturing; farming and food processing; technology and innovation; infrastructure; defence; the green and blue economy; and soft power. For manufacturing, the Prime Minister stressed cost, quality and scale; under technology, he referred to areas including space, quantum, robotics and 6G; while the infrastructure stream includes high-speed rail, highways, inland waterways and port-led development. He also identified defence self-reliance, including drones, hypersonic technologies and cybersecurity, and the green and blue economy including green manufacturing, fisheries and coastal tourism among the seven areas. The Centre already runs SATHEE, launched by the Education Ministry and IIT Kanpur in 2023, which provides free preparation and mentorship for examinations. Young people were a recurring focus of the speech, with announcements spanning AI skilling, competitive-exam coaching and the identification of sporting talent. “In the coming five-seven years, we have to move ahead with the thought of Saptadhara seven streams. The government currently runs AI-skilling programmes across schools, higher education and vocational institutions. Under the IndiaAI Mission, the IndiaAI FutureSkills programme provides for AI courses, fellowships for undergraduate, postgraduate and PhD students, as well as Data and AI Labs in smaller cities. In November 2025, the government introduced YUVA AI for ALL, a free foundational course aimed at providing a basic understanding of AI. The programme itself had set a target of reaching one crore citizens, making the one-crore figure not entirely new. He added that India does not participate in nearly two-thirds of the over 300 events at the Olympics, and that the country would work towards strengthening participation in these disciplines by 2036. The Centre already runs talent identification programmes under Khelo India, where athletes identified as having potential are provided training and financial support. Details of how the talent hunt will work, and whether it will build on the existing Khelo India framework, are yet to be announced. Prime Minister Modi urged young people to help their families participate in the ongoing Census exercise, particularly through the self-enumeration facility, which allows people to fill in household details online. The 2027 Census is being conducted digitally for the first time, with self-enumeration available for 15 days before officials begin house-to-house enumeration in each state. The first phase the Houselisting and Housing Census began in April and will run till September. At present, self-enumeration is underway in Assam from August 2-16, followed by house-to-house enumeration from August 17. Manipur will begin self-enumeration on August 17. The second phase, Population Enumeration, is scheduled for February 2027 and will also include caste enumeration. The Centre has approved 12 semiconductor projects across six states, involving investments of over Rs 1.6 lakh crore. These include fabrication facilities as well as units for semiconductor assembly, testing and packaging.
title: Test #21: Saptdhara & Key Announcements in PM Speech

text: Modern astronomy research is based on three founding pillars: observations (data collection), computation (data processing and modelling), and data analysis (physical interpretation of trends in statistical datasets such as SDSS, GAIA, or India’s own AstroSat). At Australian and British universities, it is common for students to run simulations on GADGET, MESA or custom Python frameworks. Data from most large surveys such as the SDSS are publicly available to be used for such projects. Experiential learning, which strengthens intuition, requires familiarisation with the sky and the machine. A modern astronomer is as much a physicist as a programmer. Research in Astronomy relies equally on observations and computer clusters for data processing, simulations and data analysis. Tools like Python, IRAF, AstroPy, and machine learning pipelines are basic skills in global observatories and research groups. Yet Indian undergraduates arrive at postgraduate programmes having never run a script or ever heard about a FITS file. Most students at universities never get any exposure to actual research practices in Astronomy. Orbital mechanics is taught through equations on paper, and stellar evolution from textbooks. This structural handicap in Astronomy education is entirely preventable through curriculum reform. At many universities around the world, students can choose a dedicated B.Sc. Physics with Astrophysics specialisation from year one or a standalone B.Sc. Astronomy programme featuring mandatory observation projects, computational labs, and supervised research theses. The pedagogy is learn-by-doing, and theory is taught through practice. India, does not have a standalone undergraduate degree in Astronomy. The closest approximation is the BS-MS programme at IISERs and NISER, but these are broadly Physics degrees with an optional Astrophysics specialisation in the final years. The University of Delhi, Pune University, and Osmania University offer Astrophysics electives but without a structured, progression-mapped pathway. Therefore, students aiming to become astronomers must first obtain a Physics degree, qualify for a national entrance exam such as JEST or CSIR-NET and then enter an Astronomy-specific programme. The current system treats Astronomy as a postgraduate specialisation rather than a foundational discipline because of the belief that Physics is the foundation of Astronomy. While not completely false, it has become a rigid policy position, leading to astronomy enthusiasts studying subjects like solid-state physics and quantum mechanics, whether these serve their aspirations or not. A progressively designed undergraduate astronomy programme could give students an opportunity to study subjects like stellar spectroscopy, galaxy dynamics and cosmology, which are better aligned with their choices. ARIES conducts occasional workshops. IIA has a summer school for advanced undergraduates. Only around 100 students across the country get meaningful exposure to frontier astronomy research before their postgraduation. This creates a profound inequality. Students from big cities, with better faculty networks and information access, fill these slots while others are left out. The talent pool is being culled even before it is formed. A credible reform agenda has several components. The IISERs and central universities should launch B.Sc. Astronomy programmes with Maths, Physics, and Computing taught together at the foundation level. India’s existing telescopes the 2m HCT at Hanle, the 1.2m MIRO in Gujarat, Devasthal Observatory in Uttarakhand can be networked into a national telescope programme, giving students across the country remote observing access. Researchers from institutions like IIA and IUCAA can anchor open online courses in Indian languages to lower the access barrier. Public data archives of missions like AstroSat could be integrated into the undergraduate curriculum, transforming students from consumers of knowledge into producers of it. Industry partnerships with ISRO and HEIs could fund new positions, instruments, and student slots, imparting requisite skills from early days.
title: Test #22: Indian Astronomy Education Needs Makeover

text: General education beyond the high school stage was for long mostly preparing the student for college studies. However a small percentage of students because of financial constraints joined professional courses offered in the polytechnics or industrial training institutes or similar vocational institutions to be able to earn a living and thereby supplement the family income. In either case it was lopsided being all theory or all training with no attempt for the integration of theoretical education and practical training at any stage. By denying students practical training in the scheme of general education the system only encouraged them to seek white-collar jobs. University degrees became a status symbol. At the other extreme vocational training completely barred one of the benefits of general education. Unnecessary hierarchy was being created. Students with such training were not considered really educated though in economic terms they were high productive. The skilled worker was generally dubbed as a workhorse and treated as a second class citizen. Thus the traditional system of education had ushered in a class consciousness among the people those with theoretical education dubbed as the elite and these with practical training derived as the workhorse. This attitude has certainly been spoiling the growth of developing nations. The index of the level of development of any nation is the degree to which education and training facilities are offered to its people. Whatever the field be it agriculture industry health of commerce an adequately trained labour force is a must for performance of its functions efficiently. Excluding a small sector of administrators, scientists, technologists, doctors, teachers, engineers etc. all others have to be imparted education with training for gainful employment. The modern approach is that even the so called doctor and lawyer should be skilled men. Gone are the days when a doctor would like to surround himself with half a dozen persons who will perform lesser functions like taking temperature changing sheets etc. The modern concept is the doctor himself must be skilled in all these functions if he is to be really successful. A variety of skills, mental and manual have to be developed in the people and more particularly in the youth. If quality of life is to improve education and training should be oriented to meet the needs of the locality in particular and the country as a whole and afford adequate opportunities and scope for employment to the youth. To bridge the gap between classroom learning and practical work, our educational policy must combine technical skills with core subjects. When young people acquire hands-on training alongside academic knowledge, they build confidence and secure gainful work opportunities. Modern educational institutions are moving away from purely theoretical learning to adopt skill-based learning models. The Right to Education Act, 2009, along with national training guidelines, focuses on holistic growth for every student. By encouraging trade skills, computer training, and creative work, schools prepare students to face real-world challenges. Industry partnerships with vocational centers help align course content with market demand. When skilled work is respected and valued, society grows more equal and productive. Teachers must guide students to see that all honest work has dignity and value. Providing modern tools, laboratories, and workshops in rural and urban schools ensures equal opportunities for all children. Youth who master both practical skills and analytical thinking contribute directly to national economic growth. Educational planning should focus on continuous skill updates to keep pace with changing technology. In this way, combining general education with vocational training strengthens our workforce and builds a self-reliant nation.
title: Test #23: BHC - Vocational Education - Passage 15

text: One of the biggest mistakes we made when we gained Independence was not to have overhauled thoroughly our educational system and structure. We are paying for it now. It is very easy to know what one wants to do, but in a country of this size and diversity and with our Constitution, which places education on the State List, it is not very easy to change these things. Nevertheless, I am glad to say that our present Education Ministry is making a valiant effort to make certain changes. We have first of all to think of what is Education and what we want education to do for us. No doubt there is need for good institution, for good Schools and Colleges and Universities, but education is not something that is confined to the Classroom. It is something which begins from the moment is born till the last breath that the old person draws. One is learning continuously from what is happening to one or around one, from the people with whom one is mixing, from the books one is reading and even from the events of the world which may take place far away. And it is this ability to learn which is true education. Only if we know how to learn from what happens, or what we see, then can we really profit from whatever happened, good or bad, happy or sorrowful. I think this is the only education which I got. I have gone to a number of schools, some good schools, some not so good. I have been to perhaps two of the best Universities in the world. But I can honestly say that what I have learnt has not been within the walls of those classrooms but outside. I must in fairness say that these Institutions taught me how to learn outside. Education is not what a person learns but what he becomes. So, all these ideas are with us since for long, and we have to see how we can translate them into reality in our lives. There is no doubt that education has to be closely linked with the life of the community in which the child or the student lives. Each of us is one being in which everything must move in coordination. If the coordination does not work, then it is very hard for the human being. And through education we want to develop human beings who are well coordinated. True learning helps us build good values in life. It is not just about passing tests or getting top marks in school. It teaches us how to live well with others in society. Every child must get a chance to learn and grow in a safe place. When children go to school, they should learn how to think, act, and speak with care. Teachers play a key role in shaping young minds. They guide students to choose the right path in life. A good teacher brings hope and a love of learning. Schools must also focus on health, arts, and sports. These simple things help children build team work and self control. When we learn together, we see the true value of care and trust. Learning should also teach us to respect our laws and culture. It helps us know our rights and duties as good citizens. As our world changes fast, we must update how we teach our youth. We need simple books, clear lessons, and useful work. Learning should be a joyful task, not a heavy load. Children learn best when they are happy and eager to know new things. When every child gets good guidance, the whole nation grows strong. Thus, let us work to make our schools better for all. Good learning is the best gift we can give to young minds. It paves the way for a bright and peaceful future.
title: Test #24: BHC- Educational Reform - Passage 13

text: This July, the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 turns six. It is worth remembering what the world looked like when it was written: large language models were a laboratory curiosity. In India, children were not using AI to finish their homework and no teacher was worrying about whether an essay was written by a student or a machine. Students in these schools are no longer asking what AI is. They are asking what problems around them are worth solving the borewell that runs dry in March, the crops their parents grow, the neighbour who cannot read a government form, and how AI might become one of several tools to help. The district is now preparing a student challenge built around exactly those questions, and the programme is expanding to over 40 more schools. NEP 2020 was remarkably prescient. It asked for critical thinking over rote learning, competencies over content, experiential and interdisciplinary classrooms, and technology woven into teaching. It gave India the right compass. NITI Aayog’s May 2026 report on school education is a useful mirror here. It documents a decade of real gains: expanded digital infrastructure, more computers, internet connectivity and smart classrooms across states, better inclusion, and stronger foundations. It also asks the system to integrate AI for pedagogical innovation. And it is unsparing about what remains: digital access that is still deeply unequal between urban and rural schools, and children who complete years of schooling without mastering reading and arithmetic. But history offers a warning. Social media promised connection and too often delivered isolation. Every major technological revolution has increased individual capability; very few have strengthened our collective capability. AI may become the most personalised technology humanity has ever built. If AI-powered learning slowly becomes solitary learning- each child alone with an intelligent machine- we may perfect instruction while weakening one of education’s most important purposes. Because schools are not only where children learn mathematics or science. They are among the last public institutions where children from different castes, faiths and incomes learn to disagree respectfully, cooperate across differences, build trust, negotiate conflict and imagine a shared future. In an age where intelligence is becoming ever more individualised, schools become one of the few places that cultivate what AI cannot personalise: our capacity to belong to one another. This is not a soft benefit of schooling. It is democracy’s apprenticeship. But personalisation is not, by itself, transformation. A model can adapt the pace of a lesson; it cannot decide what is worth learning, or build the classroom culture in which a child is willing to be wrong in front of others. What turns AI into better learning is what has always turned resources into learning - sound curriculum, thoughtful pedagogy, and a teacher who knows when to step in and when to step back. AI amplifies good teaching. It does not substitute for it. AI is not a threat to be managed. It is the most significant invitation in a century for education to reconsider its own purpose. AI makes people more capable, but capability is not agency. It can answer questions; it cannot decide which questions are worth asking. It can produce solutions; it cannot choose which problems deserve solving. Every generation inherits some uncertainty; this one inherits it at machine speed. That places a responsibility on education beyond employability: to help young people believe they can shape the future, not merely adapt to it. But technology has not waited for our implementation timelines. The question is whether our implementation plan and pace reflects the reality that has arrived since. But statistics are only half the story. In the schools we walk through with the Shikshagraha movement, we see the other half teachers making the most of limited resources, and the gap between having technology in classrooms and using it meaningfully.
title: Test #25: NEP at 6 - Is India's Education System Ready for AI

text: In 2024, Parliament passed India’s first dedicated law against examination fraud, formally called the Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Act, meant to protect lakhs of students who appear for government exams every year. In 2024, that same Parliament approved this pioneering statute against exam fraud, formally titled the Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Act, designed to safeguard lakhs of students who sit for government exams annually. Yet despite this 2024 framework, question paper leaks and organised rackets kept surfacing across the country between 2024 and 2026, weakening public confidence in the examination process. To close these persistent gaps, the Government introduced the Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Bill 2026 in the Lok Sabha, proposing sharper punishments and a swifter trial mechanism. Under the earlier law, individual offenders faced imprisonment of three to five years along with a fine of up to 10,00,000. The amended Bill raises this substantially, prescribing five to ten years in prison and a fine reaching 50,00,000 for individual offenders. Service providers found guilty earlier paid a maximum fine of 1,00,00,000 and faced a four-year ban from conducting public examinations. Directors and senior officials held responsible previously received three to ten years imprisonment with a fine of one crore rupees, whereas the amendment sets a firmer five-to-ten-year term alongside a five-crore rupee penalty. Organised syndicates running exam-fraud networks earlier faced five to ten years imprisonment and a minimum fine of one crore rupees; the revised law extends this to seven to ten years and raises the minimum fine to ten crore rupees. Beyond punishment, the Bill reshapes how such cases are investigated. Earlier, a police officer of at least Deputy Superintendent rank handled inquiries, with an option for the Central Government to transfer matters to a Central Investigating Agency. Broadly speaking, the amendment changes the manner in which this fraud cases get examined, since earlier an officer holding at least Deputy Superintendent rank conducted inquiries, and the Central Government retained the choice to move matters to a Central Investigating Agency. The amendment adds a further avenue, allowing the Central Government to constitute a Special Task Force devoted solely to exam-fraud investigations, and once formed, this Task Force alone carries the case forward, keeping accountability concentrated in one authority. For the first time, a strict two-month deadline governs the investigation stage, counted from registration of the case, referral to the agency, or notification of the Task Force, whichever event applies first. A major structural change is the creation of Special Fast Track Courts. Every State and Union Territory must now designate a Court of Session for this purpose, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the relevant High Court. These courts must hear matters daily, without avoidable adjournments, and must conclude trials within three months of the chargesheet being filed. Cases already pending elsewhere when the amendment takes effect will be transferred to these courts and finished within three months of transfer. In essence, every State and Union Territory now has to name a Court of Session as a dedicated fast track bench, working with the concerned High Court’s Chief Justice, to handle these fraud cases swiftly. Dedicated Special Public Prosecutors will also be appointed in every State and Union Territory to argue these matters exclusively. The Bill further introduces a clear appeal pathway. Judgments, sentences, or substantive orders may be challenged before the High Court, heard by a two-judge bench that must attempt disposal within three months of admission. Even bail orders can be appealed directly to the High Court. Appeals must generally be filed within thirty days, extendable for valid reasons, though never beyond ninety days, and no other forum may entertain further appeal or revision.
title: Test #26: India Tightens the Noose on Paper Leaks

text: Once upon a time, reading challenges used to appear during summer vacations. Teachers, faced with the prospect of children spending two months attempting dangerous bicycle stunts or climbing dangerous places, encouraged them to read a few books. The objective was simple. Keep the children occupied, keep their parents sane, and prevent their brains from rusting entirely during the holidays. This ensured that when the school reopened, students could still identify a book. The reward for reading a book was generally stickers, or if you are particularly lucky, another book. Somewhere along the way, the reading challenge escaped captivity and seeped into the adult world. Books have always shaped people. The modern innovation is ensuring that everyone knows precisely which books are shaping you. On social media, bookstagrammers lurk everywhere. Make the mistake of pausing on a post about books and the algorithm immediately concludes that literature is your entire personality. Within hours, your feed is flooded with people surrounded by towering stacks of books, coffee mugs, blankets, fairy lights, candles, and decorative plants. Every January, readers emerge with ambitious declarations. Twelve books. Twenty books. Even 50 books. By March, they start calculating page counts. This is also the point at which a significant percentage of participants quietly vanish. They realise that reading 20 books requires reading 20 books. By June, the survivors strategically select novellas. Reading challenges have evolved into elaborate public declarations involving colour-coded spreadsheets, monthly targets, quarterly reviews, backup targets, stretch goals, and contingency plans in case life unexpectedly interrupts the reading schedule. The purpose of reading has moved from what is inside the book to the satisfaction of reaching the last page. Updating the journal and announcing the latest additions to the books-read-this-year tally on social media has become the main objectives. The book itself is a unit of measurement. Rereading passages, and thinking and discussing deep ideas threatens annual targets. Certain books are read to be adopted as personality traits. One does not merely read classics. One becomes “a classics reader”. The distinction is important. Likewise, one does not simply enjoy philosophy, history, or science fiction. One joins a tribe, acquires a label, and updates the list accordingly. Each one arrives bearing urgent news. “Ten books I recommend, no matter your genre.” “Five books with insane, unhinged concepts.” “Seven Indie fantasy, action, comedy books every intelligent person should read to cry, heal, grow, manifest abundance, and finally understand themselves.” Every week, someone publishes a list of books that you have probably never heard of. In fairness, this is true. New writers are emerging with alarming frequency, and fresh titles arrive on bookstore shelves so rapidly that readers can fall behind during a long lunch break. A reasonable observer might wonder how previous generations survived without access to these lists. The problem is no longer finding something to read. Readers spend so much time watching recommendations that they no longer have time to read. This is not considered a problem. Many now maintain what is known as a to-be-read pile. This is a monument consisting of books purchased with every intention of being read someday. The books remain hopeful. The modern reading challenge is about transforming yet another enjoyable human activity into a measurable achievement. At year’s end, millions proudly announce that they have read 56 books, earned 14 badges, maintained a 365-day streak, followed 43 Bookstagram accounts, and successfully met all reading objectives. As for what they learned, remembered, or loved, those metrics are not necessary. Reading was once a conversation between a writer and a reader. Somewhere along the way, a committee of apps, trackers, challenges, badges, influencers, annual goals, and recommendation algorithms joined the discussion.
title: Test #27: The Reading Race

text: No official records, meeting notes, or administrative letters from the era contain any mention of a 65% British benchmark, nor any policy to cut passing standards in half. However, the benchmark for academic honours or civil service selection is to achieve in the range between 60-65%, not a standard pass mark. The official university minutes in India show that the 33% mark was born out of pragmatic local adjustments and routine integer rounding. The institutional roots of this confusion trace back to Wood’s Despatch of 1854, the educational policy sent by the East India Company to Governor General Lord Dalhousie. The Despatch explicitly recommended that the upcoming universities in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras be modeled after the University of London a non-teaching, purely examining body. When the Calcutta University Act (Act II of 1857) was formally passed on January 24, 1857, Section IX granted the newly formed Senate absolute legal authority to frame examination statutes. However, while colonial planners successfully copied London’s administrative framework, London provided no template for pass marks suited to Indian conditions. Left without empirical precedent, the Senate had to invent marking thresholds from scratch, turning to basic fractions (1/3 for languages, 1/4 for mathematics) as tentative placeholders. In March 1857, while Bengal stood on the brink of widespread rebellion, a quieter revolution unfolded inside the Senate House in Calcutta. The newly created University of Calcutta held its very first Entrance Examination the first standardised matriculation exam on the Indian subcontinent. Recorded in the archival volume Minutes of the Senate, Provisional Committee, Syndicate & Council 1857, and these early guidelines titled Regulations for the Entrance Examination established a subject-by-subject marking framework designed to test candidates across four primary disciplines: Languages, History and Geography, Mathematics, and Natural Sciences. Rather than enforcing a single, uniform passing mark across the entire examination, the 1857 regulations established distinct thresholds for different subjects. For the Languages paper, which evaluated proficiency in English as well as selected classical or vernacular languages, the passing minimum was set at one-third or 33.3% of the total marks. Technical subjects followed a different standard altogether; Mathematics, for example, required a lower passing threshold of one-fourth, or 25%. The rules left no room for compromise: candidate success depended on clearing these specific fractions in every single subject, and failing even a single subject resulted in an overall disqualification. The severe weight of these early standards is preserved in the Calcutta University Calendar for 1858-1859. The prescribed entrance syllabus demanded that young candidates often just 14 to 16 years old demonstrate mastery over dense English texts including Addison’s Spectator, Robertson’s History of Charles V, and multi-volume Latin-translated treatises, alongside complex vernacular grammar. Out of hundreds of candidates who sat in the initial years, only a small fraction secured First Division standing. By 1860, this rigid design faced an immediate crisis. As detailed in Minutes of the Senate, Provisional Committee, Syndicate & Council 1860 under the Report of the Board of Examiners in Arts on the Entrance Examination, pass rates across the province began to collapse. The examiners reported a severe drop in successful candidates, driven primarily by widespread failures in regional and classical language papers such as Bengali, Persian, and Urdu. The report pointed to administrative supply issues, noting that required textbooks and prescribed lists had arrived late at affiliated schools. At the same time, the papers set by local examiners proved far more challenging in vernacular grammar than anticipated.
